# Matthew Newman’s Post

![View profile for Matthew Newman]()

Hello GDPR watchers! Major decision by the EU Court of Justice today in a challenge by Meta Platforms' WhatsApp against the European Data Protection Board. The EU's top court ruled that WhatsApp can directly challenge a binding decision of the EDPB before the EU courts.
The ruling opens the door to contesting EDPB binding decisions at EU level rather than through national courts, potentially shortening judicial proceedings and reshaping how companies appeal GDPR enforcement actions. The EU top court's decision, allowing a “direct action” at the General Court, unlocks six pending appeals by Meta in similar cases against the board.
The EU's top court decided to send the case back to the EU's General Court to rule on the substance.
The case arose after WhatsApp appealed a December 2022 decision of the General Court, which found its original action inadmissible on the grounds that the EDPB’s binding decision did not directly affect the company’s legal position.
WhatsApp has argued that the EDPB’s decision was binding on Ireland's Data Protection Commission, leaving it no discretion on finding data protection violations and forcing it to substantially raise a data-privacy penalty.
In a press release accompanying the judgment, the court said the EDPB's decision “was of direct concern to WhatsApp, since it brought about a distinct change in the legal position of that undertaking, without leaving any discretion to its addressees.”
In a statement, a WhatsApp spokesperson said: “The EDPB is an unelected authority whose decisions can directly impact businesses and people across the EU. We welcome the Court's final judgment on the matter which upholds our argument that those businesses and people should be able to challenge decisions the EDPB makes against them, so that it can be held fully accountable by the EU courts.”

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) GDPR Fines ---
URL: https://gdprfine.com/dpa/ireland-dpc

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a reference profile of the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC), the most-fined GDPR regulator by cumulative amount. Ireland is the EU establishment of choice for US Big Tech, making the DPC the lead supervisory authority (under Article 56 GDPR) for the largest single-issuer fines on the register. ~25 headline decisions are indexed, with the largest single fine being €1.2 billion (Meta 2023) and 5+ EDPB Article 65 cases since 2021. The DPC has been active since 1989 (GDPR: 2018).

**Mandate and constitution:** The DPC is designated under Article 51 GDPR, and as lead authority for controllers with main EU establishment in Ireland. Established under the Data Protection Act 1988, modernised under the Data Protection Act 2018. It reports to the Oireachtas through the Minister for Justice, with headquarters in Dublin (Fitzwilliam Square) and a satellite office in Portarlington. Staff grew from ~110 in 2018 to more than 230 by 2026.

**Fining philosophy:** Characterised by long inquiry timelines (3-5 years), detailed factual analysis, and rigorous Article 83(2) factor-by-factor weighting. Critics accuse the DPC of being insufficiently aggressive; the EDPB Article 65 mechanism has repeatedly recalibrated fines upward (WhatsApp: €30-50M draft to €225M final; Meta Chapter V case).

**Headline decisions:** WhatsApp €225M (Sept 2021, following EDPB BD 1/2021, first ever Article 65 decision); Instagram €405M children's data (Sept 2022, EDPB BD 2/2022); two Meta Ireland decisions totalling €390M (Jan 2023, contractual lawful basis for personalised advertising); Meta €1.2B Chapter V transfer decision (May 2023, largest GDPR fine to date, following EDPB BD 1/2023); TikTok €345M children's data (Sept 2023, EDPB BD 2/2023); TikTok €530M Chapter V China transfers (May 2025, second-largest single GDPR fine).

**Statistical record:** Cumulative DPC fines exceed €3 billion. Distribution is highly skewed; Big Tech share is ~95% of total in years with major decisions, and median annual fine count is in the tens. Complaint volumes rose steadily, exceeding 11,000 in 2024. The 2024 annual report was the most recent available, with 2025 report expected mid-2026.

**How to engage:** Data subjects can lodge complaints under Article 77 GDPR via dataprotection.ie; cross-border complaints use the one-stop-shop mechanism (lodged via local DPA, forwarded to DPC as lead, with original DPA as "concerned" authority under Articles 60/65).

**Recent enforcement trends (2024-2026):** Children's data, AI-system processing (intersecting with EU AI Act), DPIA compliance, and continued one-stop-shop relationships. The DPC moved to a three-Commissioner structure in 2024 (Des Hogan, Dale Sunderland, Niamh Sweeney), replacing the single Commissioner model (Helen Dixon, 2014-2024), to handle the workload.

**FAQ highlights:** The DPC issues many large fines because major US tech firms have EU headquarters in Ireland. The EDPB Article 65 mechanism lets concerned authorities refer draft decisions to the EDPB for binding decisions. The Spanish AEPD issues more decisions by count, but the DPC leads in cumulative amount. Fines are imposed on the EU-established subsidiary, not directly on US parents. Decisions are published on dataprotection.ie and EDPB decisions on edpb.europa.eu.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The most-fined GDPR regulator by cumulative amount. Ireland is the EU establishment of choice for US Big Tech, which makes the DPC the lead supervisory authority for the largest single-issuer fines on the register."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Ireland: DPC Issues Record 87% of EU GDPR Fines in 2023; Breach Reports Increase by 20% | Privacy Matters ---
URL: https://privacymatters.dlapiper.com/2024/06/ireland-dpc-issues-record-87-of-eu-gdpr-fines-in-2023-breach-reports-increase-by-20

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) published its 2023 Annual Report, highlighting a record year in which DPC fines accounted for 87% of all GDPR fines issued across the EU. The DPC received 6,991 valid personal data breach notifications in 2023 (a 20% increase from the prior year), with unauthorized disclosure being the leading reason for breaches (52% of the total). 146 notifications came under the ePrivacy Regulations (up 42%) and 59 under the Law Enforcement Directive. Most incidents originated from the private sector (3,766), followed by the public sector (2,968) and voluntary/charity sector (275).

In 2023, the DPC concluded 11,147 cases, held 89 statutory inquiries on-hand (including 51 cross-border inquiries), and handled over 25,130 electronic contacts, 7,085 phone calls, and 1,253 postal contacts. The most frequent GDPR topics for queries and complaints were access requests, fair-processing, disclosure, direct marketing, and right to erasure. The DPC concluded 19 inquiries in 2023 resulting in fines totaling €1.55 billion.

Notable cross-border inquiries concluded in 2023 included: two social media fines (€5.5 million for relying on contract as a lawful basis for service improvement, and €1.6 billion for transferring EU data to the US without a lawful basis) and a €345 million fine for processing children's personal data. Notable domestic inquiries included fines for Financial Services (€750,000 for ten data breaches involving unauthorized disclosure on a customer-facing app), Healthcare (€460,000 for a ransomware attack affecting over 70,000 patients), and a County Council (€50,000 for CCTV and car plate reading technology usage).

The DPC pursued 7 national judgments or final orders in 2023 (split between the Irish Circuit Court and High Court), with legal costs awarded in favor of the DPC in 5 proceedings. The DPC also had 4 successful prosecutions involving unsolicited marketing messages under the e-Privacy Regulations.

Child protection remained a priority pillar of the DPC's Regulatory Strategy 2022-2027, reflected in the €345 million fine against a major social media company. The DPC was nominated to represent the EDPB on the new Task Force on Age Verification under the Digital Services Act. By the end of 2023, 3,520 DPOs were notified to the DPC. The DPC's participation in the 2023 Coordinated Enforcement Framework identified three DPO issues: insufficient resources, conflicts of interest, and inappropriate tasks. Of 751 supervision engagements in 2023, 391 were from multinational technology companies.

In February 2024, Helen Dixon stepped down as Data Protection Commissioner after 10 years, with Dr. Des Hogan (Chairperson) and Dale Sunderland taking over their new roles. The DPC continues to focus on systemic non-compliance and children's data protection rights in 2024.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The DPC fines account for 87% of the GDPR fines issued by EU data protection authorities last year."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:

This webpage from PrivacyTerms.io presents a ranked list of the 50 biggest GDPR fines of all time (as of July 2026), with detailed analysis of the top 10 fines, the regulators involved, appeal status, and underlying trends.

**Key Facts and Data:**

- **The biggest GDPR fine ever**: EUR 1.2 billion against Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, issued by Ireland's Data Protection Commission on 22 May 2023, over unlawful EU-to-US data transfers following the CJEU's invalidation of the Privacy Shield framework. This fine has held the record for over three years and is roughly 60% larger than the next-highest figure.

- **Top 10 GDPR fines (ranked)**: 
  1. Meta Platforms Ireland — EUR 1.2 billion (Ireland DPC, 2023)
  2. Amazon Europe Core (disputed) — EUR 746 million (Luxembourg CNPD, 2021)
  3. TikTok — EUR 530 million (Ireland DPC, 2025)
  4. Instagram (Meta) — EUR 405 million (Ireland DPC, 2022)
  5. Meta Platforms Ireland — EUR 390 million (Ireland DPC, 2023)
  6. TikTok — EUR 345 million (Ireland DPC, 2023)

  8. Uber — EUR 290 million (Netherlands AP, 2024)
  9. Meta Platforms Ireland — EUR 265 million (Ireland DPC, 2022)

Chapter V is complementary to Article 3, preventing circumvention of EU data protection law. The DPA also rejected the WTO agreement argument.
2. **The processing constituted a transfer**: Applying the EDPB Guidelines 05/2021's three cumulative criteria, the DPA found all criteria met. The DPA rejected Uber's argument that drivers themselves were the exporters, finding instead that UBV was the exporter because drivers have little influence over processing purposes and means (terms are pre-drafted and non-negotiable).
3. **No valid transfer mechanism**: From 6 August 2021 to 27 November 2023, Uber had no lawful transfer mechanism. The DPA rejected Uber's interpretation of the European Commission's FAQ statements regarding SCCs.

**Fine details:** The DPA imposed a €290,000,000 administrative fine on the joint controllers due to the seriousness of the violation. --- SOURCE 7: Into the Data Transfer Thicket: The Dutch Uber Decision and the Relationship Between GDPR Article 3 and Chapter V – European Law Blog ---
URL: https://europeanlawblog.eu/1xjmngct

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an opinion/analysis article from the European Law Blog (22 October 2024) by E J Kyriakides examining the Dutch DPA's enforcement decision against Uber and the legal relationship between GDPR Article 3 (territorial scope) and Chapter V (data transfer safeguards).

KEY ISSUE: The article addresses a lingering legal ambiguity: under what circumstances are GDPR data transfer safeguards required when a foreign firm is already subject to the GDPR. The classic transfer scenario involves a foreign company NOT governed by GDPR receiving EU data. But GDPR has extraterritorial effect (Article 3(2)), meaning foreign companies targeting the EU can also be subject to it.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:
- Article 3(1): Entities with an EU "establishment" are subject to GDPR
- Article 3(2): Entities without EU establishment are subject if they (a) offer goods/services to EU data subjects, or (b) monitor EU data subject behavior
- Chapter V (Articles 44-47) requires transfer safeguards including adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses (SCCs), binding corporate rules, etc.
- Under Schrems II, firms must independently assess whether transfer tools ensure "essentially equivalent" protection, potentially requiring supplementary measures
- Chapter V applies only to a "transfer" — a term the GDPR does not define

EDPB GUIDELINES (05/2021):
- Defined "transfer" as occurring when: (1) a controller/processor (exporter) is subject to GDPR; (2) the exporter discloses personal data to another controller/processor (importer); (3) the importer is in a third country (regardless of whether importer is subject to GDPR)
- Critically concluded NO transfer occurs when data is directly disclosed by an individual in the EU to a firm in a third country
- Companies subject to GDPR must still assess third country government access risks under other GDPR obligations (Articles 32, 33, 35)
- Not binding but highly authoritative

THE DUTCH DPA UBER DECISION (August 2024):
- Dutch DPA fined Uber €290 million — the largest fine ever from the Dutch DPA — for transferring French Uber drivers' data to the US without Chapter V safeguards
- Fine originated from an NGO (Ligue Des Droits De L'homme) complaint to the French CNIL
- Transfer involved Uber B.V. (UBV, Netherlands) and Uber Technologies Inc (UTI, US parent)
- Uber relied on SCCs until August 2021, then determined SCCs were unnecessary because Article 3 directly applied to UTI's US processing; Uber had NO transfer mechanism from August 2021 until relying on the Data Privacy Framework in November 2023
- Two scenarios found to involve transfers: (1) EU drivers' data sent directly via Uber app to UTI for US storage; (2) data relating to GDPR rights requests where UBV and UTI collaborated
- Dutch DPA rejected Uber's defenses (direct collection, joint controllership, Article 49 derogations), holding transfers between joint controllers subject to GDPR in different countries are governed by Chapter V
- DPA departed from EDPB guidance by finding scenario one (direct collection from EU data subjects) constituted a "transfer," relying on the employment relationship between UBV and drivers and the asymmetry of power
- DPA argued Chapter V should be read broadly to counterbalance risks of diminished protection when data is processed abroad and difficulty enforcing against foreign entities
- DPA found Article 49(b-c) derogations inapplicable because transfers were ongoing, not "incidental" or "necessary"

ANALYSIS/NEXT STEPS:
- Uber is appealing; Dutch courts are likely to refer questions to the CJEU on the Article 3/Chapter V relationship
- The Dutch decision failed to articulate a clear legal standard for when direct collection by foreign providers subject to GDPR triggers Chapter V
- The article recommends that EU entities subject to GDPR under Article 3(2) in doubt apply Chapter V safeguards until the issue is settled
- European Commission has not yet issued SCCs for scenarios where the importer is subject to GDPR (current SCCs only apply when importer is NOT subject to GDPR)
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The EDPB concluded that a transfer occurs when: 1) A controller or a processor ('exporter') is subject to the GDPR for the given processing; 2) The exporter discloses by transmission or otherwise makes personal data... available to another controller, joint controller or processor ('importer'); 3) The importer is in a third country, irrespective of whether or not this importer is subject to the GDPR for the given processing in accordance with Article 3"

**GDPR Fine Structure:**
- Tier 1 violations: Up to 2% of annual revenue or €10 million (whichever is greater) — applies to violations related to child data consent, privacy by design, data breach notifications, DPIA requirements, DPO appointments, certification mechanisms, and third-party involvement.
- Tier 2 violations: Up to 4% of annual revenue or €20 million (whichever is greater) — applies to violations of lawful bases for processing, GDPR individual rights, cross-border data transfers, Member State laws, and orders from supervisory authorities.
- Non-monetary actions may include processing bans, data deletion orders, and transfer restrictions.
- Under Art. 82, affected individuals can claim compensation in court.

**Criteria for Fines:** Nature/severity of violation, number affected, negligence vs. intent, preventive measures, security protocols, prior violations, cooperation with authorities, type of data affected, notification practices, and financial benefits gained from the violation.

**The 20 Biggest GDPR Fines (2018-2024):**
1. Meta (Facebook) — €1.2 billion (May 22, 2023, Irish DPC): EU-to-US data transfers without adequate safeguards using SCCs.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 13 March 2025, the Irish Court of Appeal (COA) delivered its judgment in Data Protection Commission (DPC) v Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, upholding the DPC's appeal and refusing to stay (adjourn) the Meta Proceedings. The background involves a DPC decision on 25 November 2022 finding that Meta violated Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR after third parties 'scraped' personal data from Meta's platforms between May 2018 and September 2019. The DPC issued an order to comply, a reprimand, and two fines totalling €165 million. In December 2022, Meta brought both a statutory appeal and judicial review proceedings in the High Court.

The case related to separate "WhatsApp Proceedings": on 20 August 2021 the DPC fined WhatsApp €225 million for GDPR infringements (Articles 5, 12, 13, 14). WhatsApp's challenge to the EDPB's Article 65 decision was dismissed by the EU General Court as inadmissible (WhatsApp not directly concerned), and an appeal to the Court of Justice was pending (Advocate General's opinion due 27 March 2025). In July 2023, Meta sought to adjourn its High Court proceedings pending the outcome of the WhatsApp Proceedings; the High Court (Simons J) granted this, adjourning the Meta Proceedings in their entirety.

The COA set aside the High Court decision, emphasizing that challenges to decisions of public bodies should be prosecuted with "economy and celerity." The COA identified two scenarios following the upcoming CJEU decision in the WhatsApp case: (1) if the CJEU upholds the General Court's inadmissibility dismissal, unresolved EU law issues could delay Meta Proceedings by ~24 months; (2) if the CJEU allows the appeal, the case returns to the General Court, potentially delaying Meta Proceedings by a further ~40 months. The COA held that the GDPR requires challenges to DPC decisions to be brought in Irish courts, with Article 267 TFEU preliminary references as the exclusive mechanism to resolve GDPR interpretation doubts. The COA found no reason to delay requesting such a reference, and noted parties could later seek stays of the WhatsApp Proceedings if needed. The DPC's appeal was allowed and Meta's adjournment motions were dismissed.
</summary>

The GDPR requires that any challenge to a decision of the DPC be brought before the courts in Ireland. The exclusive mechanism to resolve any doubts as to the interpretation of the GDPR in the context of the Meta Proceedings is therefore by way of a reference for a preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU.

--- SOURCE 3: Meta's €1.2 Billion GDPR Fine: Why It Still Matters in 2025 ---
URL: https://gdprlocal.com/metas-e1-2-billion-gdpr-fine-why-it-still-matters-in-2025

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from GDPRLocal examines Meta's record-breaking €1.2 billion GDPR fine, imposed on May 12, 2023 by Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC), and explores its ongoing significance for international data transfers.

**The Core Violation:** Meta was fined for illegally transferring European users' personal data to the United States, directly breaching the international transfer rules in Chapter V of the GDPR. The conflict stems from U.S. surveillance laws (particularly Section 702 of FISA) clashing with EU privacy rights. The €1.2 billion penalty specifically covers transfers that continued after the landmark Schrems II ruling on July 16, 2020. The case originated from a complaint filed by privacy activist Max Schrems.

**Enforcement Actions:** Regulators ordered Meta to (1) suspend all future transfers of EU data to the U.S. within five months, and (2) bring all previously transferred data into compliance within six months (effectively deleting it or moving it back to the EU). These operational orders were deemed a greater threat to business than the fine itself.

**The Enforcement Journey:** Ireland's DPC initially declined to fine Meta, deeming a penalty "disproportionate" and citing Meta's "good faith" use of SCCs. However, other European data protection authorities objected, escalating the case to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) under Article 65. In Binding Decision 1/2023 (April 13, 2023), the EDPB overruled the DPC, declaring the infringement "highly serious" and mandating a fine with a starting point between 20-100% of the legal maximum, calculated on Meta's worldwide turnover. The fine was based on Article 83(5) of the GDPR, allowing penalties up to 4% of global annual turnover due to aggravating factors including: systematic/repetitive/continuous transfers over nearly three years, involvement of special category data (Article 9), and Meta acting with "at least the highest degree of negligence."

**Why SCCs Were Not Enough:** While Meta used Standard Contractual Clauses, regulators found that U.S. surveillance laws like FISA 702 could legally compel Meta to hand over both encrypted data and the cryptographic keys, rendering encryption ineffective. The EDPB concluded Meta's SCCs were "mere contractual promises" with no practical effect against U.S. surveillance law.

**History of EU-US Transfer Mechanisms:** The article details the evolution from Safe Harbour (invalidated in 2015 by Schrems I) to Privacy Shield (invalidated in 2020 by Schrems II) to SCCs (still valid but requiring Transfer Impact Assessments) to the new EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF, adopted July 10, 2023, valid but contested - NOYB has signaled a potential "Schrems III" challenge, and FISA 702 was only reauthorized until April 2026).

**The Schrems II Ruling Explained:** The 2020 CJEU ruling invalidated Privacy Shield and established new obligations for companies using SCCs, requiring case-by-case Transfer Impact Assessments (TIAs) before transfers and supplementary measures (including encryption with EU-controlled keys) when risks are identified.

**Industry Reactions:** Meta called the fine "flawed, unjustified and unnecessary" and is appealing (case T-325/23), while simultaneously adopting the new DPF. Forrester called the fine a "wake-up call" proving regulators now have the "power and the guts to dismantle a company's business model." EDPB Chair Andrea Jelinek stated the "unprecedented fine is a strong signal to organisations that serious infringements have far-reaching consequences." Other companies like Amazon Web Services quickly self-certified under the DPF for legal certainty. Ireland later fined Microsoft's LinkedIn €310 million in October 2024 for similar processing violations.

**Lessons for Businesses:** The article concludes that "set it and forget it" compliance is no longer viable. Companies must: (1) document every Transfer Impact Assessment, (2) encrypt or pseudonymise by default with keys controlled exclusively by the EU data exporter, (3) diversify legal bases (BCRs for corporate groups, Article 49 derogations only for one-off situations), and (4) continuously monitor legal changes. Boards must treat cross-border data transfers as a dynamic, strategic, multi-jurisdictional risk integrated into products, contracts, and technical architecture from day one.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The largest fine, a record-breaking €1.2 billion, was imposed back in May 2023. That penalty was for one specific reason: unlawfully transferring the personal data of European Facebook users to the United States."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 13 March 2025, the Irish Court of Appeal (COA) delivered its judgment in Data Protection Commission (DPC) v Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, upholding the DPC's appeal and refusing to stay (adjourn) the Meta Proceedings. The background involves a DPC decision on 25 November 2022 finding that Meta violated Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR after third parties 'scraped' personal data from Meta's platforms between May 2018 and September 2019. The DPC issued an order to comply, a reprimand, and two fines totalling €165 million. In December 2022, Meta brought both a statutory appeal and judicial review proceedings in the High Court.

The case related to separate "WhatsApp Proceedings": on 20 August 2021 the DPC fined WhatsApp €225 million for GDPR infringements (Articles 5, 12, 13, 14). WhatsApp's challenge to the EDPB's Article 65 decision was dismissed by the EU General Court as inadmissible (WhatsApp not directly concerned), and an appeal to the Court of Justice was pending (Advocate General's opinion due 27 March 2025). In July 2023, Meta sought to adjourn its High Court proceedings pending the outcome of the WhatsApp Proceedings; the High Court (Simons J) granted this, adjourning the Meta Proceedings in their entirety.

The COA set aside the High Court decision, emphasizing that challenges to decisions of public bodies should be prosecuted with "economy and celerity." The COA identified two scenarios following the upcoming CJEU decision in the WhatsApp case: (1) if the CJEU upholds the General Court's inadmissibility dismissal, unresolved EU law issues could delay Meta Proceedings by ~24 months; (2) if the CJEU allows the appeal, the case returns to the General Court, potentially delaying Meta Proceedings by a further ~40 months. The COA held that the GDPR requires challenges to DPC decisions to be brought in Irish courts, with Article 267 TFEU preliminary references as the exclusive mechanism to resolve GDPR interpretation doubts. The COA found no reason to delay requesting such a reference, and noted parties could later seek stays of the WhatsApp Proceedings if needed. The DPC's appeal was allowed and Meta's adjournment motions were dismissed.
</summary>

The exclusive mechanism to resolve any doubts as to the interpretation of the GDPR in the context of the Meta Proceedings is therefore by way of a reference for a preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU.

  - **Opinion 08/2024** (April): "Consent or Pay" models by large online platforms — concluded most current implementations are unlikely to meet GDPR's valid consent requirements; platforms should offer free alternatives without behavioural advertising, ensure transparency, and avoid excessive fees
  - **Opinion 11/2024** (May): Use of facial recognition at airports — only storage solutions with biometric data held by the individual or central storage with encryption key solely in the individual's hands were found compatible with data protection principles
  - **Opinion 22/2024** (Oct): Obligations regarding processors and sub-processors under Art. 28 GDPR — controllers must have identity information on all processors readily available; verification obligations apply regardless of risk level but extent varies by risk; controller retains ultimate decision on engaging sub-processors
  - **Opinion 28/2024** (Dec): Processing personal data to train AI models — confirmed legitimate interest can serve as legal basis under certain conditions, with a three-step test proposed; EDPB consulted the EU AI Office before adoption

**Statements on Legislative Developments (6 in 2024):**
Covered the child sexual abuse regulation proposal, the financial data access and payments package, DPA roles in the AI Act framework, GDPR procedural rules draft regulation, High-Level Group on Access to Data recommendations, and the Second Report on GDPR Application.

**Enforcement and Litigation:**
- No Art. 65 binding decisions issued in 2024 (first year since 2020)
- EDPB involved as main party in 13 cases before the CJEU (2 new in 2024), mostly annulment applications against binding decisions, plus 1 case as intervener
- Sharp increase in Art. 64(2) opinion requests

**New Roles and Cross-Regulatory Cooperation:**
- EDPB became a member of the DMA High-Level Group and the European Data Innovation Board (EDIB)
- Cooperated with the European Board for Digital Services (EBDS) and the EU AI Office
- New digital legislation (DMA, DSA, AI Act, Governance Act, Data Act) expanded DPA responsibilities — DPAs designated as Market Surveillance Authorities for certain high-risk AI systems under the AI Act

**Secretariat Operations:**
- Budget of €8.36 million (part of EDPS budget)
- Team of 395 professionals across five sectors (legal affairs, litigation/international affairs, IT, information/communications, administrative)
- Organised over 530 meetings in 2024 (up from 360+ in 2023)
- Managed over 4,200 IT assistance requests and queries (up from 3,400 in 2023)
- IMI system facilitated over 5,644 procedures; 907 support requests handled
- EDPB HUB content grew 64% (12,307 content pieces); user base exceeded 1,500 members (7% increase)
- Website received 329,432 visits
- Received 38 access-to-documents requests; handled 18 individual rights requests and 6 data breaches (1 notified to EDPS)
- Coordinated Supervision Committee (CSC) extended to Visa Information System (VIS); work on ETIAS supervision ongoing

**Outreach:**
- Data Protection Guide for Small Business made available in 18 languages
- Launched series of summaries of EDPB guidelines for non-experts
- Two stakeholder events held (AI models and "Consent or Pay")
- First meeting of EDPB with DPAs of countries with an adequacy decision (October 2024)
</summary>

</key_excerpts>

# [Privacy & Cybersecurity Law Blog](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/)

Global Privacy and Cybersecurity Law Updates and Analysis

Meta Fined €390 Million by Irish DPC for Alleged Breaches of GDPR, Including in Behavioral Advertising Context

3 Minute Read

Categories: [Behavioral Advertising](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/behavioral-advertising), [Enforcement](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/enforcement9), [European Union](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/european-union), [International](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/international), [Security Breach](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/security-breach)

On January 4, 2023, the Irish Data Protection Commission (“DPC”) [announced](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/data-protection-commission-announces-conclusion-two-inquiries-meta-ireland) the conclusion of two inquiries into the data processing practices of Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) with respect to the company’s Instagram and Facebook platforms. As a result of the investigations, the DPC fined Meta a combined €390 million for breaches of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (“GDPR”) and, following consultation with the European Data Protection Board (“EDPB”), notably held that Meta can no longer rely on the GDPR’s “performance of a contract” legal basis for processing personal data in the behavioral advertising context, a decision that has broad implications for publishers engaged in behavioral advertising in the EU.

The DPC’s investigation began after None of Your Business (“NOYB”), a non-governmental organization co-founded by privacy activist Max Schrems, submitted complaints alleging that Facebook and Instagram “forced” users to consent to the processing of personal data for behavioral advertising and other services. In anticipation of the GDPR entering into force, Meta updated its Terms of Service and asked its users to accept the new terms before continuing to access its services. Meta asserted that when users accepted the new terms, they entered into a contract with the company that allowed the company to rely on the “performance of a contract” legal basis under the GDPR for the company’s processing of personal data. NOYB argued that, by requiring users to accept the updated Terms of Service as a condition to use Facebook and Instagram, Meta “forced” its users to provide consent, and therefore could not rely on the “performance of a contract” legal basis for processing.

The DPC’s investigation held that, although the GDPR does not preclude Meta’s reliance on the “performance of a contract” legal basis asserted by Meta, the company’s practices breached Article 5(1)(a), which requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly, and in a transparent manner. In particular, the DPC held that Meta’s Terms of Use did not clearly disclose the company’s data processing activities,  or the purposes and legal basis for the processing.

Following consultations with peer regulators in the European Union, the DPC submitted its findings to the EDPB. The EDPB agreed that Meta’s practices breached Article 5(1)(a), and, contrary to the DPC’s findings, notably  held that the company could not continue to rely on the “performance of a contract” legal basis to support its behavioral advertising activities. In addition, the EDPB directed the DPC to conduct a separate investigation into how Facebook and Instagram process special categories of data.

The DPC adopted the EDPB’s findings, issued a €390 million fine, and directed Meta to bring its data processing activities into compliance with the GDPR within three months.

args.summary:
On January 4, 2023, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) concluded two inquiries into Meta Platforms, Inc.'s data processing practices on its Instagram and Facebook platforms, fining Meta a combined €390 million for breaches of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The investigation began following complaints from NOYB (None of Your Business), an NGO co-founded by privacy activist Max Schrems, alleging that Facebook and Instagram "forced" users to consent to personal data processing for behavioral advertising. Meta had updated its Terms of Service and asserted it could rely on the GDPR's "performance of a contract" legal basis for processing.

Key findings of the investigation:
- The DPC held that while GDPR does not preclude Meta's reliance on the "performance of a contract" legal basis, Meta's practices breached Article 5(1)(a), which requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently, because its Terms of Use did not clearly disclose data processing activities, purposes, or legal basis.
- Following consultations with EU peer regulators, the findings were submitted to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), which notably held that Meta could no longer rely on the "performance of a contract" legal basis for behavioral advertising activities—a decision with broad implications for publishers engaged in behavioral advertising in the EU.
- The EDPB also directed the DPC to conduct a separate investigation into how Facebook and Instagram process special categories of data.
- The DPC adopted the EDPB's findings, issued the €390 million fine, and directed Meta to bring its data processing activities into compliance with GDPR within three months.

# Meta Ireland's €1.2bn GDPR fine takes them to €2.5bn in total

##### May's record GDPR fine of €1.2bn means Ireland's DPC has now fined Meta more than the entire aggregate GDPR fines in either 2021 or 2022!

![DPC fines Meta 1.2 billion](http://keepabl.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Ireland-1_2-image-for-blog_400x200_acf_cropped.png)

[Facebook (OK, Meta) just lost out big time](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/Data-Protection-Commission-announces-conclusion-of-inquiry-into-Meta-Ireland) with a fine of €1.2bn and orders to suspend transfers of personal data on EEA users to the USA within 5 months and stop processing (even just storing) previously transferred data within 5 months. This is part of the painfully slow but hugely important race between:

* the Irish DPC’s investigation into Facebook’s use of SCCs, and
* the US-EU efforts to replace Privacy Shield.

#### Just to put that €1.2bn single fine and €2.5bn aggregate number into perspective: [the UK’s Defence budget](https://obr.uk/forecasts-in-depth/brief-guides-and-explainers/public-finances/#:~:text=In%202023%2D24%2C%20we%20expect%20central%20government%20departments%20to%20spend,defence%20(%C2%A332.4%20billion)) in 2023 is £32.4 billion.

In this post we’re focussing on the DPC’s history of fining Meta – to the tune of €2.5bn over the last 3 years – **why those fines have been issued**, and how this immense €1.2bn decision published on 22 May 2023 (and it is physically immense, 222 pages) fits in.

We’ll also look at how European GDPR fines compare to the USA Privacy regime, and how GDPR fines compare to the Finance sector.

See the sister blog with our CEO’s article for Thomson Reuters on the context of the decision and [key takeaways for practitioners](http://keepabl.com/news/meta-ireland-billion-euro-fine-key-takeaways/).

## Ireland fines Meta €2.5bn in 3 years

Taken together, the DPC’s fines on Meta due to GDPR infringements by WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook total a whopping €2.5bn in the last 3 years alone. And other EEA data protection authorities (DPAs) argue Ireland isn’t doing enough enforcement.

Here’s how those fines break down. It’s interesting to note the range of topics as well as how the inquiries originally started:

* **August 2021: WhatsApp – Transparency – €225m.** One of the largest GDPR fines until overtaken by Luxembourg’s €746m Amazon fine. Another [very long decision](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/data-protection-commission-announces-decision-whatsapp-inquiry) at 266 pages focussed on use of phone numbers and transparency in the information given to users in their Privacy Notices, Policies and other documents.
* **March 2022: Facebook – Breach – €17m.** [The smaller fine](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/data-protection-commission-announces-decision-meta-facebook-inquiry) (can one say €17m is in any way small?) followed an inquiry by the DPC into a series of 12 data breach notifications it received in the six-month period between 7 June 2018 and 4 December 2018.
* **September 2022: Instagram – Children – €405m.** [This massive fine](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/data-protection-commission-announces-decision-instagram-inquiry) followed an own-volition inquiry by the DPC (and the May 2023 €1.2 Bn fines was also after an own-volition inquiry) into children’s ability to open personal and business Instagram accounts and how their data was made public and otherwise processed.
* **November 2022: Facebook – Data Scraping – €265m.** [Another huge fine](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/data-protection-commission-announces-decision-in-facebook-data-scraping-inquiry). The inquiry here started because of media reports of “a collated dataset of Facebook personal data that had been made available on the internet”. The DPC examined Facebook Search, Facebook Messenger Contact Importer and Instagram Contact Importer tools in the period from 25 May 2018 to 2019.
* **December 2022: Instagram – ‘Forced Consent’ – €180m.** Issued on 31 December 2022 and [published by the DPC](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/data-protection-commission-announces-conclusion-two-inquiries-meta-ireland) in January 2023 together with the Facebook fine below for the same thing, so they’re often reported together as a €390m fine. This was based on a complaint made by Max Schrems’s organisation [NOYB](https://noyb.eu/en) to the Belgian DPA on 25 May 2018, the day GDPR took effect, and it was referred to the DPC as lead Supervisory Authority (SA). Both decisions were about legal basis: could Instagram switch from using consent for eg targeted advertising and instead make that necessary for the contract with its users. DPC said yes, EDPB said no, DPC had to say no.
* **December 2022: Facebook – ‘Forced Consent’ – €210m.** Published with the Insta decision, this was based on a complaint out of Austria (the DPC notes that Max Schrems / NOYB was a representative of the complainant) and referred by the Austrian DPA on 30 May 2018 just days after GDPR took effect. Same as Insta above, all about legal basis and swapping consent with contract, same result.
* **January 2023: WhatsApp – Legal Basis – €5.5m.** That’s not a typo, it was [“only” €5.5m](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/data-protection-commission-announces-conclusion-inquiry-whatsapp). The decision is still 112 pages long. The fine was “small” as the Privacy Policy and time period were the same as for the Transparency Decision in August 2021, and WhatsApp had already moved that processing into compliance. This inquiry was based on a complaint out of Hamburg, again with Max Schrems / NOYB as a representative, and again referred to the DPC as lead SA. It was also partly a transparency decision, but mainly held that ‘necessary for contract’ wasn’t an available legal basis for “*processing of personal data for the purposes of service improvement and security features (excluding processing for the purpose of “IT Security” as defined by paragraph 90 of the Article 65 Decision)*“.
* **May 2023: Facebook – Transfers – €1.2bn**. And now we come to this month’s immense fine. This was another own-volition inquiry by the DPC started in August 2020, just one month after the [Schrems II decision](http://keepabl.com/news/what-is-schrems-ii/). The inquiry focussed on Meta Ireland’s use of the standard EU SCCs (both the 2010 and 2021 versions) to transfer personal data of EEA Facebook users to the USA. The DPC decided that the SCCs, even combined with the extensive supplemental measures that Meta IE put in place, did not compensate for US surveillance laws to provide an adequate level of protection.

In a separate post, first published on Thomson Reuters and which we’ll post here shortly, we dig into the key takeaways from the decision, and how this might impact your own Privacy Governance at your organisation. But now, let’s see how Ireland fares against the rest of the EEA – it’s a rather ‘intense’ relationship – and then how Europe’s GDPR fines compare to the USA and to fines under the Finance regs.

## Only 0.7% was about Security

Looking at the figures, you can see only €17m was about breaches, or 0.67% of the fines. Over €2.4bn of this €2.5bn total, or more than 99.3%, had nothing to do with Security.

Yes, Security is 1 of [GDPR’s 7 Principles](http://keepabl.com/news/7-principles-of-gdpr/), but it is only 1 of 7 and Privacy is about more than Security – indeed, more than GDPR.

## Ireland vs the rest of the EEA

According to DLA Piper’s [GDPR fines and data breach survey: January 2023](https://www.dlapiper.com/en-ae/insights/publications/2023/01/dla-piper-gdpr-fines-and-data-breach-survey-january-2023) (which starts the year at 28 January):

> 2022 was another record year with an aggregate of EUR1.64bn (USD1.74bn/ GBP1.43bn) GDPR fines reported across Europe [EEA 30 + UK]. The aggregate value of fines issued in 2022 was 50% more than the value of fines reported in 2021.

And remember, we’ve just seen that €390m of that 2022 figure was the DPC ‘forced consent’ fines on Facebook and Instagram.

These numbers mean that:

* the DPC’s single May 2023 fine on Meta IE was **bigger than all GDPR fines** in the EEA 30 + UK in 2021 ,
* the DPC’s aggregate fines on Meta across all services are **twice as big as all 2021 GDPR fines** in the EEA 30 + UK, and
* the DPC’s aggregate fines on Meta across all services are **50% bigger than all 2022 GDPR fines** in the EEA 30 + UK.

You can’t argue that the DPC isn’t fining! But a lot of the decisions above were the result of the Article 60 cooperation procedure in which several other DPAs disagreed with the DPC and, in the end, so did the EDPB, ordering the DPC to increase fines, give fines, or make orders such as the order not to process historically transferred data in the May 2023 decision.

A close read of the decisions is needed to fully understand the DPC’s reasons and what the objections by other DPAs and the EDPB were based on.

But one thing is certain, these are immense numbers.

## Europe v the USA

How about comparing the EEA with the USA? Well, we have a pretty good comparator as Facebook was [fined $5bn by the FTC](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2019/07/ftc-imposes-5-billion-penalty-sweeping-new-privacy-restrictions-facebook) over the Cambridge Analytica matter in 2019. As well as the record-breaking penalty, Facebook had to “*submit to new restrictions and a modified corporate structure that will hold the company accountable for the decisions it makes about its users’ privacy, to settle Federal Trade Commission charges that the company violated a 2012 FTC order by deceiving users about their ability to control the privacy of their personal information*“.

Admittedly that size of fine is rare in the USA as well, but the FTC is taking a much more proactive approach on Privacy violations in recent months.

## GDPR v Financial Regs

As further perspective on GDPR fines, let’s look at 2022’s fines under Finance regulations.

* The [UK FCA states](https://www.fca.org.uk/news/news-stories/2022-fines) that it issued fines totalling £215m (that’s £0.215bn) in 2022, with the biggest being £107m against Santander UK for “*weaknesses in its AML framework [which] meant that Santander UK failed to manage adequately the money laundering risks presented by its Business Banking customers*.”
* Germany’s financial regulators are [reported](https://www.financemagnates.com/institutional-forex/regulators-slapped-industry-with-record-fines-in-2022-sec-in-the-lead/) to have issued €25m of fines in 2022, France’s €95m and the Dutch £900k.

And in the USA, in [December 2022](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/danske-bank-pleads-guilty-fraud-us-banks-multi-billion-dollar-scheme-access-us-financial), the US Department of Justice (DoJ) came out with this headline: “*Danske Bank Pleads Guilty to Fraud on U.S. Banks in Multi-Billion Dollar Scheme to Access the U.S. Financial System*“. Danske Bank plead **guilty to defrauding** US banks. The penalty? Just over $2bn. That’s less than the DPC has fined Meta in aggregate in the last 3 years and not far off the DPC penalty on Meta this month.

args.summary:
This article from Keepabl (a privacy management software company) covers Meta Ireland's record-breaking €1.2bn GDPR fine issued by Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) in May 2023, which brought Meta's total GDPR fines to €2.5bn over three years. The decision, published on 22 May 2023 (222 pages), ordered Meta to suspend transfers of personal data on EEA users to the USA within 5 months and stop processing previously transferred data within 5 months. The fine resulted from an own-volition DPC inquiry starting in August 2020 (one month after the Schrems II decision) examining Meta's use of standard EU SCCs to transfer EEA Facebook user data to the USA; the DPC found SCCs plus supplemental measures did not compensate for US surveillance laws.

A breakdown of Meta fines shows: August 2021 WhatsApp transparency €225m; March 2022 Facebook breach €17m; September 2022 Instagram children's data €405m; November 2022 Facebook data scraping €265m; December 2022 Instagram 'forced consent' €180m; December 2022 Facebook 'forced consent' €210m; January 2023 WhatsApp legal basis €5.5m; May 2023 Facebook transfers €1.2bn. Notably, only 0.67% of the €2.5bn total (€17m) related to security/breaches—over 99.3% concerned other GDPR areas.

The article provides perspective: the DPC's single May 2023 fine was bigger than all GDPR fines in the EEA 30 + UK combined in 2021, and the aggregate Meta fines were 50% bigger than all 2022 GDPR fines (which totaled €1.64bn per DLA Piper's survey). For comparison, Facebook was fined $5bn by the FTC in 2019 over Cambridge Analytica, the UK FCA issued £215m in fines in 2022, and Danske Bank's US penalty was just over $2bn. The article concludes with a promotional section for Keepabl's privacy management software.

DUBLIN, Sept 5 (Reuters) - Ireland's data privacy regulator has agreed to levy a record fine of 405 million euros ($402 million) against social network Instagram following an investigation into its handling of children's data, a spokesperson for the watchdog said.

Instagram plans to appeal against the fine, a spokesperson for parent Meta Platforms Inc [(META.O), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/companies/META.O/) said in an emailed statement.

The investigation, which started in 2020, focused on child users between the ages of 13 and 17 who were allowed to operate business accounts, which facilitated the publication of the user's phone number and/or email address.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

"We adopted our final decision last Friday and it does contain a fine of 405 million euro," said the spokesperson for Ireland's Data Protection Commissioner (DPC), the lead regulator of Instagram's parent company Meta Platforms Inc [(META.O), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/companies/META.O/).

Full details of the decision will be published next week, he said.

Instagram updated its settings over a year ago and has since released new features to keep teens safe and their information private, the Meta spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said Instagram disagrees with how the fine was calculated and is carefully reviewing the decision.

The DPC regulates Facebook, Apple, Google and other technology giants due to the location of their EU headquarters in Ireland. It has opened over a dozen investigations into Meta companies, including Facebook and WhatsApp.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

WhatsApp was last year fined a record 225 million euros for failing to conform with EU data rules in 2018.

The Irish regulator completed a draft ruling in the Instagram investigation in December and shared it with other European Union regulators under the bloc's "one stop shop" system of regulating large multinationals.

args.summary: Reuters article (September 5, 2022) reporting that Ireland's data privacy regulator, the Data Protection Commissioner (DPC), agreed to levy a record fine of 405 million euros ($402 million) against Instagram following an investigation into its handling of children's data. The investigation, started in 2020, focused on child users aged 13-17 who were allowed to operate business accounts, which facilitated the publication of users' phone numbers and/or email addresses. Instagram plans to appeal the fine, with parent company Meta Platforms Inc. spokesperson stating Instagram disagrees with how the fine was calculated. Instagram updated its settings over a year ago and has since released new features to keep teens safe and their information private. The DPC regulates Facebook, Apple, Google, and other tech giants due to their EU headquarters being located in Ireland, and has opened over a dozen investigations into Meta companies, including Facebook and WhatsApp. WhatsApp was fined a record 225 million euros the previous year for failing to conform with EU data rules. The Irish regulator completed a draft ruling in December and shared it with other EU regulators under the bloc's "one stop shop" system. Full details of the decision are scheduled to be published the following week.

# Instagram faces $402 million fine for alleged mishandling of children’s data

News

Sep 6, 20223 mins

## Parent company Meta said that it plans to appeal the decision by the Irish Data Protection Commissioner, which is the second-largest, privacy-based fine on record.

![instagram app login](https://www.csoonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/instagram-app-login-100643660-orig.jpg?quality=50&strip=all&w=1024)

The Irish Data Protection Commissioner will fine Instagram $402 million for allegedly mishandling the personal data of children, specifically through default settings that left phone numbers and email addresses for users between the ages of 13 and 17 exposed via Instagram business accounts, according to published reports.

It’s the second-largest fine ever handed out by EU-based regulators, behind only the $739 million that Luxembourg authorities levied against Amazon last year. A spokesperson for the Irish DPC said that full details on the decision will be published next week, according to the reports.

The decision stems from a 2019 study by data protection scientist David Stier, who found that a large part of the 60 million Instagram users who were under 18 at the time changed their personal accounts into business accounts, in order to gain insight into view numbers for particular posts and numbers of personal profile views, [according to the Washington Post.](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2022/09/06/ireland-instagram-fine-dpc-meta/)

By default, those business accounts made email and phone numbers available publicly. Instagram has since updated its privacy settings, and said that it had “engaged fully” with the Irish DPC’s investigation, though it disagreed with the way the fine was calculated and stated that it plans to appeal.

## More regulatory actions on privacy expected

According to Rob Shavell, co-founder and CEO of online privacy protection firm DeleteMe, companies should expect further regulatory action in the future, unless their privacy systems are already functioning at a particularly high level. Trust and control over personally identifiable information are both at a premium in the current era, and the popular conception of shadowy cybercriminals being most responsible for invasions of privacy is rarely accurate.

“This is not a classic data breach, this is information exposed by willful neglect of preferences and settings and things like that that leaves the door open for information like this to leak out to anyone,” he said. “Businesses, particularly if they have any customers in California, should be concerned that California regulators [are close to implementing] regulations that basically mirror the data protection acts in European countries.”

Both data brokers and holders of personally identifiable information (PII) should be concerned about the coming wave of regulation, noted Shavell. And PII holders, specifically, should be aware that the major threat to their customer data isn’t a malicious attack by hackers, but a simple configuration mistake that allows data to be scraped from the web and sold by brokers.

“Are you exposing the data about the customer in ways that they don’t want, or in ways that could have negative ramifications for their privacy rights?” he urged businesses to ask themselves. “Every organization has to think about a different kind of data breach that could result in a huge fine or real harm to the organization.”

# Irish High Court Upholds TikTok's €530 Million Fine Over Transfers to China

The Irish High Court has upheld the Data Protection Commission's €530 million fine against TikTok over the transfer of EEA user data to China and related transparency failures, confirming one of the largest GDPR penalties on record while allowing a narrow appeal on the size of the fine to proceed.

ABy **Acompli Editorial**

#TikTok#InternationalTransfers#DPC#GDPREnforcement

Share[X/Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Facompli.ie%2Fnews%2Ftiktok-530-million-fine-upheld-2026%2F&text=Irish%20High%20Court%20Upholds%20TikTok's%20%E2%82%AC530%20Million%20Fine%20Over%20Transfers%20to%20China&hashtags=TikTok%2CInternationalTransfers%2CDPC%2CGDPREnforcement)[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Facompli.ie%2Fnews%2Ftiktok-530-million-fine-upheld-2026%2F)[Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Facompli.ie%2Fnews%2Ftiktok-530-million-fine-upheld-2026%2F)[Email](mailto:?subject=Irish%20High%20Court%20Upholds%20TikTok's%20%E2%82%AC530%20Million%20Fine%20Over%20Transfers%20to%20China&body=Irish%20High%20Court%20Upholds%20TikTok's%20%E2%82%AC530%20Million%20Fine%20Over%20Transfers%20to%20China%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Facompli.ie%2Fnews%2Ftiktok-530-million-fine-upheld-2026%2F)

On **3 June 2026**, the Irish High Court upheld the Data Protection Commission's (DPC) findings against TikTok and the **€530 million** fine imposed following the regulator's inquiry into transfers of EEA user data to the People's Republic of China. The penalty - among the largest ever issued under the GDPR - comprised **€485 million** for unlawful data transfers and **€45 million** for transparency failures. The DPC acted in its role as lead supervisory authority for TikTok under the GDPR's one-stop-shop mechanism.

The inquiry examined the lawfulness of TikTok's transfers of EEA users' personal data to China, focusing on whether the company could guarantee a level of protection essentially equivalent to that required within the EU when data was remotely accessible from a third country without an adequacy decision. The transparency component concerned the adequacy of the information TikTok provided to users about those transfers. The High Court's decision confirms that the substantive findings and the fine stand, although the court directed the DPC to reconsider its order suspending further transfers to China and has indicated it will consider TikTok's appeal regarding the **amount** of the penalty - leaving both the corrective measures and the quantum open to further argument even as the underlying liability is settled.

The decision lands at a moment when international data transfers remain one of the most contested areas of GDPR enforcement. The absence of an adequacy decision for China means that transfers rely on safeguards such as standard contractual clauses, supplemented by transfer impact assessments that must account for the legal environment in the destination country - including the prospect of government access to data. The TikTok case turns precisely on whether those safeguards were sufficient given the access risks identified, and the High Court's endorsement of the DPC's core reasoning reinforces the bar that controllers must clear.

For organisations transferring personal data outside the EEA, the ruling is a reminder that the mechanism chosen - SCCs, binding corporate rules, or a certification - is only the starting point. The substantive question is whether the data, once transferred, enjoys protection equivalent to that guaranteed within the Union, and whether the organisation can evidence the assessment that led it to that conclusion.

**Acompli perspective:** The TikTok decision confirms that international transfers remain a primary enforcement target, and that the size of the penalties reflects how seriously regulators treat them. A transfer mechanism on paper is not a defence on its own; what matters is the documented assessment behind it. Organisations moving data outside the EEA should ensure their [records of processing](/ropa/) capture every transfer and its legal basis, that their [risk management](/risk/) framework includes transfer impact assessments that genuinely engage with destination-country access risks, and that their [data mapping](/data-mapping/) reflects where data can be accessed from - not merely where it is nominally stored.

# Verify, guarantee, demonstrate: The TikTok decision and what it means for international data transfers

On 3 June 2026, the Irish High Court delivered its judgment on the appeal by TikTok Technology Limited (“TikTok”) against the decision of the Irish Data Protection Commission (“DPC”) dated 30 April 2025 finding that TikTok had infringed international transfer and transparency requirements under the GDPR.

19/06/2026

Briefing

For organisations operating across borders, the outcome of this appeal, which rejected most grounds of TikTok’s appeal against the DPC’s Inquiry Decision, is a significant reminder that compliance with international transfer requirements under the GDPR requires substantively more than identifying an appropriate transfer mechanism.

## DPC Decision – Inquiry IN-21-9-2

In May 2025, the DPC announced its final decision in an own-volition inquiry into transfers of EEA user data to China. The own-volition inquiry arose from supervisory interactions with TikTok, where the DPC was informed that personal data stored by TikTok outside China was remotely accessed by employees in China, constituting an international transfer for the purpose of Chapter V GDPR. The DPC identified infringements of Article 46 GDPR (transfers subject to appropriate safeguards) and Article 13(1)(f) GDPR (transparency relating to international transfers) and imposed corrective actions comprising administrative fines totalling €530 million and an order requiring TikTok to bring its processing into compliance.

TikTok appealed the DPC Inquiry Decision on 11 grounds, including breaches of fair procedures, errors of assessment, errors of law and failures to correctly apply Article 83 GDPR.

## High Court Judgment – TikTok Technology Limited v Data Protection Commission [2026] IEHC 347

The High Court did not accept most of TikTok’s grounds of appeal and upheld the findings in the DPC Inquiry Decision in relation to the identified infringements of Article 46 GDPR and Article 13(1)(f) GDPR.

### Article 46 GDPR – Demonstrating Adequate Protection

TikTok argued that, following *Schrems II,* it was sufficient for a controller to satisfy itself that adequate protection of transferred data exists. The Court rejected that interpretation, stating that it would be unworkable in practice. Instead, the Court found that the obligation in Article 46(1) GDPR – that international transfers of personal data are permitted only where the controller has provided appropriate safeguards – and its interpretation by the CJEU in *Schrems II* should be read in light of the general principle of accountability contained in Article 5(2) GDPR and the general obligation contained in Article 24(1) GDPR that a controller must implement appropriate measures to demonstrate compliance with the requirements of the GDPR.

Noting the interpretation of Article 46(1) GDPR by the CJEU in *Schrems II* as requiring verification that adequate levels of protection exist in the third country to which personal data is transferred, the Court found that *“[i]f there is a requirement to carry out such a prior assessment … it must be a requirement to carry out an adequate assessment*”. On this basis, the Court concluded that it is open to a supervisory authority “*to examine the assessment carried out by a controller and consider whether it was adequate, and whether it in fact demonstrates what it purports to demonstrate*”.

The Court found it was not necessary for the supervisory authority to conduct an independent examination of the laws of the third country and that identifying a gap or shortcoming in the assessment by the controller was sufficient to ground a conclusion that the controller had failed to comply with its obligations under Article 46 GDPR.

### Article 13(1)(f) GDPR – Transparency

TikTok argued that Article 13(1)(f) GDPR did not contain a specific obligation to name third countries to which personal data was transferred and that the DPC’s argument in favour of doing so would be inconsistent with the requirement in Article 12(1) GDPR for information to be provided to data subjects in concise and easily accessible form.

The Court did not accept TikTok’s argument and affirmed the DPC’s view that identification of the third country to which personal data is transferred by the controller is required by Article 13(1)(f) GDPR. As TikTok’s October 2021 EEA privacy policy did not identify China as a destination country, the Court upheld the DPC’s finding that Article 13(1)(f) had been infringed. The Court also rejected TikTok’s argument based on Article 12(1) GDPR, noting that the December 2022 Privacy Policy showed that this information could readily be provided in clear language.

### Outcome and corrective orders

While most appeal grounds raised by TikTok were not upheld, the Court found that the DPC erred in refusing to consider a third expert opinion on Chinese law provided by TikTok and in concluding, without stating the basis for its conclusion, that TikTok’s Project Clover pseudonymisation and privacy measures, did not justify a different corrective approach.

While the Court found that these errors did not affect the findings of infringement in relation to either Article 46 GDPR or Article 13(1)(f) GDPR, it considered that the corrective orders may have been affected by these errors. On this basis, the Court was satisfied that the appropriate resolution was to make an order vacating the corrective orders and remitting the question of what corrective orders should have been made in light of the Article 46 infringement finding to the DPC for further consideration.

## Key takeaway

The High Court’s decision is an important reminder that organisations transferring personal data outside the EEA must be able to not only identify an appropriate transfer mechanism, but must also be in a position to adequately document its assessment that the transferred data benefits from a level of protection essentially equivalent to that guaranteed under the GDPR. The High Court judgment reaffirms organisations must “*verify, guarantee and demonstrate*” that they have conducted a robust and detailed assessment of the protection afforded to personal data in third countries and that such assessments must be capable of withstanding scrutiny as to their adequacy and sufficiency from supervisory authorities such as the DPC.

args.summary:
This webpage from Arthur Cox (an Irish law firm) publishes a legal briefing on the Irish High Court's judgment in TikTok Technology Limited v Data Protection Commission [2026] IEHC 347, delivered on 3 June 2026. The case concerned TikTok's appeal against a DPC decision dated 30 April 2025, which found that TikTok had infringed international transfer and transparency requirements under the GDPR.

Key facts: The DPC's original inquiry (IN-21-9-2) found that personal data stored by TikTok outside China was remotely accessed by employees in China, constituting an international transfer under Chapter V GDPR. The DPC identified infringements of Article 46 GDPR (transfers subject to appropriate safeguards) and Article 13(1)(f) GDPR (transparency), and imposed fines totaling €530 million plus a compliance order.

The High Court rejected most of TikTok's 11 grounds of appeal and upheld the Article 46 and Article 13(1)(f) infringement findings. Key rulings: (1) Under Article 46 GDPR, controllers must not only identify a transfer mechanism but also carry out an adequate, documented assessment of the protection in the third country—the supervisory authority can examine whether the assessment adequately demonstrates what it purports to demonstrate, without needing an independent examination of third-country laws. (2) Under Article 13(1)(f) GDPR, controllers must specifically identify the third countries to which personal data is transferred; TikTok's October 2021 privacy policy failed to name China as a destination.

The Court did find the DPC erred in refusing to consider a third expert opinion on Chinese law and in not stating the basis for concluding that TikTok's "Project Clover" pseudonymisation measures did not justify a different corrective approach. While these errors did not affect the infringement findings, the corrective orders were vacated and remitted to the DPC for further consideration.

Key takeaway: Organisations transferring data outside the EEA must "verify, guarantee and demonstrate" robust, documented, and defensible assessments of third-country data protection, capable of withstanding supervisory scrutiny.

# Irish High Court upholds DPC's TikTok decision, orders review of corrective measures

##### Published: 11/06/2026

##### | Irish High Court

On Thursday, the Irish High Court largely upheld the Irish Data Protection Commission's (DPC) decision against TikTok for violations of Articles 46 and 13 of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The ruling means that the DPC's [€530 million in administrative fines](https://www.freevacy.com/news/data-protection-commission/irish-dpc-issues-eur530m-gdpr-fine-to-tiktok/6354) remain valid, although the court has indicated that it will consider TikTok's appeal regarding the amount of the fines imposed.

While the court agreed with the DPC that pseudonymised data can still constitute personal data under the GDPR if a person remains identifiable, it disagreed with its conclusions about TikTok's technical measures under 'Project Clover'. The court found that instead of focusing on whether "the data in question can relate to an identifiable person directly or indirectly," it should have addressed "whether, in fact, data subjects can be identified." As a result, the court ruled that the DPC must reconsider its corrective order suspending future transfers to China.

The Irish High Court just upheld a €530 million GDPR fine against TikTok. But they also tore up the DPC's order to suspend their data transfers. Who actually won this case? In the latest episode of the Privacy Partnership Podcast, I look at the significant new judgment in TikTok v DPC. To recap: TikTok allowed personnel in China to remotely access European user data. TikTok's primary defence was data localisation. They argued the data sat safely on servers in the US and Singapore, outside the jurisdiction of Chinese intelligence laws. But the DPC looked right down to the endpoint devices. When an engineer in Beijing remotely opens a file, that data is transmitted across the internet and temporarily loaded into the RAM of their local laptop. -- The court upheld the view that this temporary caching constitutes processing in China. Because TikTok’s Transfer Impact Assessments completely ignored this local processing, their assessments were found to be fundamentally flawed. The court also upheld the DPC's finding that TikTok's privacy notice should have explicitly named China as the possible destination of EEA users' personal data. -- But while the DPC secured its €530 million penalty, it botched the suspension order. Late in the inquiry, TikTok submitted new expert evidence and accelerated "Project Clover", a massive engineering effort to build a secure European data enclave with advanced pseudonymisation. The DPC essentially waved this away and ordered the data flows suspended anyway, without providing detailed technical reasoning for why Project Clover's mitigations were ineffective. The High Court ruled this a procedural failure. The court will gladly defer to a regulator's technical expertise, but the regulator actually has to show its working. -- So, TikTok takes a half-billion-euro hit for historic violations, but they get to keep their data flows running... for now. The case now goes back to the DPC to properly assess TikTok's new technical mitigations.

So there is a partial victory for TikTok at the Irish High Court. While the court largely agreed with the DPC's finding that TikTok violated Chapter V GDPR, it was not satisfied that the regulator took TikTok's expert evidence seriously enough. I spent a lot of time with this DPC decision last year, so here are some thoughts. -- In case you have missed or forgotten the abundant commentary on this case (much of it coming from me)... TikTok is appealing a significant decision made by the Irish DPC about the transfer of EEA user data to China. The DPC had investigated TikTok's "remote access solution," whereby TikTok personnel based in China were allowed to remotely access EEA user data for engineering and maintenance purposes. TikTok's efforts to assuage EU data transfer concerns included "Project Clover", a data security initiative to limit remote access from China and apply privacy-enhancing techniques (PETs). - The appeal judge agreed with the DPC's legal premise that pseudonymised data can still constitute personal data under the GDPR if a person remains identifiable. But the judge criticises the DPC for failing to properly explain WHY TikTok's technical measures failed. The court focuses on two pieces of evidence seen by the DPC in support of TikTok's PETs: 1. The "Mittal Report": A report by a Princeton professor, who concluded "an adversary would not be able to determine with a reliable level of confidence... any incremental information about any attribute of any single individual..." (Para 88) 2. The "NCC Group Report": A security audit which concluded that "the solution does not enable reidentification of an EEA User." (Para 458) There is some further analysis a Chinese legal opinion but I'll stick to the above. -- The court's conclusion initially struck me as odd and potentially unfair towards the DPC. Last year's 194-page decision was hardly light on detail. The DPC spent dozens of pages summarising the technical changes TikTok brought in under Project Clover and explicitly acknowledged the Mittal Report. But actually, re-reading it, I guess I can see why the court thinks this part of the decision is somewhat under-developed. "Following Project Clover, the EEA User Data... still constitutes personal data... because the data in question can relate to an identifiable person directly or indirectly." (Para 690 in the 2025 decision). The judge agrees with TikTok: "...this analysis simply begs the question... The question the DPC should have addressed is whether, in fact, data subjects can be identified. The DPC’s conclusion that TikTok has not demonstrated that they cannot be identified is not explained." (Para 461) -- The court concludes that TikTok DID violate Chapter V GDPR, but vacates the DPC's corrective orders, meaning TikTok does not currently have to suspend transfers. The issue is now sent back to the DPC to properly assess Project Clover. I guess we need a couple hundred more pages to be sure.

[Lena Hornkohl](https://at.linkedin.com/in/lena-hornkohl-59803b135?trk=public_post-text)**Lena Hornkohl** ([Ius Omnibus](https://pt.linkedin.com/company/associa%C3%A7%C3%A3o-ius-omnibus?trk=public_post-text)**Ius Omnibus**&[Universität Wien | University of Vienna](https://at.linkedin.com/school/seema-shiksha-shastri-and-b.ed-college/?trk=public_post-text)**Universität Wien | University of Vienna**) cuts to the heart of the search click-and-query data anonymization debate in four words: unique doesn't mean identifiable. It's the distinction the whole search data-sharing question turns on. A query can be one-of-a-kind simply because language has limitless variations. As such, that tells you nothing about who typed it. Recital 26 GDPR doesn't ask whether re-identification is conceivable in the abstract; it asks whether it is "reasonably likely" given real-world cost, time and technology. The CJEU's SRB ruling reinforces the point: identifiability is contextual and recipient-relative, not absolute. Treating uniqueness as an automatic disqualifier isn't a privacy safeguard. It strips out exactly the less-common queries that smaller search engines need to compete, while doing little for actual user protection — and it assesses anonymization in isolation, ignoring the contractual, security and audit layers that are an integral part of the real risk picture. 🇨🇳 TikTok told regulators European user data wasn’t stored in China. It was. In May 2025, Ireland’s Data Protection Commission fined TikTok €530 million — the third-largest GDPR fine in history — for illegally transferring personal data of European users to China, where it could potentially be accessed by Chinese authorities under local law. But the fine wasn’t the worst part. During the four-year investigation, TikTok explicitly told the DPC that no European user data was stored on servers in China. In February 2025 — mid-investigation — it quietly admitted that actually, yes, a “limited amount” of data had ended up on Chinese servers. They told regulators one thing. The reality was another. And this is not just a TikTok problem. This is a structural problem with any platform whose parent company, infrastructure, or staff operate under the jurisdiction of a government with conflicting surveillance laws. Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) — the legal fig leaf most platforms use to justify international transfers — were found insufficient here. The DPC was explicit: TikTok failed to “verify, guarantee and demonstrate” that EU-equivalent protections were in place in China. SCCs are not a shield. They are paperwork. When we built [XeniaCloud](https://nl.linkedin.com/company/xeniacloud?trk=public_post-text) , we made one foundational choice: EU-only infrastructure, under EU jurisdiction, with no parent company in a third country. No China clause. No FISA clause. No “trust us” clause. Because €530 million fines are not the problem. On this warm end of June Saturday, let's remind folks a few things people tend to confuse about data protection: - the GDPR is a data protection law (that's the second and third letter of GDPR for those who hadn't noticed), protecting the fundamental rights of people when their personal data is processed. - fundamental rights are defined in the EU in a Charter of Fundamental Rights - the GDPR is not a privacy law, although the right to privacy is within the EU Charter, but when assessing risks, privacy isn't the only one to consider. - privacy is subjective. Data protection is objective with 6 principles for handling + 1 for demonstrating - data protection by design and by default is a GDPR requirement, privacy by design isn't, see previous point. Most organisations don't understand the difference. - when you see what the EU parliement votes sometimes, you may wonder if fundamental rights matter to them, but that's another story, and you vote to elect MEP. Cookies may be placed on a browser: sometimes to help the user, sometimes to help tracking the user (Bigtech is about forcing selling things people don't need). Placement of cookies is governed by another piece of legislation, the ePrivacy directive written in 2002, amended in 2006 and 9. The cookie placement is subject to consent unless the cookies are technically needed (sessions for instance). Legitimate interest is not an option and all those cookie banners that offer the option are flawed. IAB had a major role on the issue as they had released incorrect information, which was natural given who backs them. When GDPR came, it said cookie consent should be aligned with the way GDPR consent was obtained, but didn't say cookie were subject to GDPR. Cookies are placed before the processing of personal data, and have their own legal basis for processing. Once the cookie has been placed, processing of personal data may start. If such processing is subject to personal data, it also needs its own lawful basis for processing. Luckily for many, cookie consent hasn't been enforced much in the EU. There was even a stage when some EU supervisory authorities gave wrong advice for cookie consent, so it would be hard for them to enforce since their guidance was incorrect and they didn't do anything for years (not to forget Bigtech doesn't want them to enforce ;)).
