Know your Privacy Policy and Notice. Most people have clicked "I agree" on a privacy policy without reading a single line of it. It is one of the most common habits on the internet, and one of the most consequential. So what exactly is a privacy policy? A privacy policy is a statement that explains how an organisation collects, uses, stores, and shares your personal information. Most organisations that collect personal data provide one explaining how that information is handled. A privacy notice goes one step further. It is the information provided directly to you at the point your data is collected, or when there is a significant change in how that data is processed. Under the NDPA 2023, you have the right to know what is being collected, why it is being collected, who it is shared with, and how long it will be kept. That is not a formality. That is your right. Here is a real example of what happens when people ignore it. In September 2025, [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/linkedin?trk=public_post-text) notified users about changes that allowed certain profile information and public content to be used to improve generative AI systems. For affected users, the setting was enabled by default unless they chose to opt out. The notice existed. Most people scrolled past it. By the time the policy took effect, many had already been opted in simply because nobody read the update carefully enough to act on it. That is the risk of ignoring a privacy notice. You lose the chance to make an informed choice about your own data. Before you agree to anything online, look for three things: • What exactly are they collecting? • Who are they sharing it with? • How do you opt out? Those three questions take two minutes. They are also the three questions most people never ask. Your data has value. The organisations collecting it know that. The question is whether you do too. Review your app permissions today. The webpage features a LinkedIn post by Robert Bateman (privacy influencer) analyzing the Irish High Court judgment in TikTok v. Data Protection Commission (DPC), including a full podcast transcript and related commentary.

Key facts of the judgment:
- The Irish High Court upheld the €530 million GDPR fine against TikTok (issued by the DPC in April 2025, covering July 2020–May 2023), making it among the largest GDPR fines.
- The court also upheld a €45 million portion of the fine related to TikTok's 2021 privacy policy, ruling that organizations must explicitly name specific third countries involved in data transfers (generic boilerplate language is insufficient).
- TikTok personnel in China (Bytedance Group entities) remotely accessed European user data. The court agreed that temporary caching of data in RAM/CPU of devices in China constitutes processing in China, even though data was stored on servers in the US and Singapore. Because TikTok's Transfer Impact Assessments ignored this local processing, they were found fundamentally flawed.
- The court confirmed that failing to properly verify and document specific technical risks is itself an infringement under Article 46 GDPR, read with accountability principles in Articles 5 and 24. The threshold for negligence is very low—a sophisticated controller cannot avoid liability by relying on incomplete external legal advice.
- However, the court vacated the DPC's order to suspend TikTok's ongoing data transfers to China due to procedural unfairness. The DPC allegedly failed to provide detailed technical reasoning for why TikTok's "Project Clover" (a European data enclave with advanced pseudonymization and privacy-enhancing techniques) mitigations were ineffective, and previously promised to consider all submissions. The case is sent back to the DPC to properly reassess Project Clover.

Evidence referenced in related posts:
- The "Mittal Report" (Princeton professor) concluded an adversary could not reliably determine incremental information about any individual.
- The "NCC Group Report" concluded the solution does not enable reidentification of EEA users.
- A related commentary notes the DPC decision was 194 pages and the High Court ruling was 185 pages.

Related content includes discussion of unique-doesn't-mean-identifiable in anonymization debates, cookie/ePrivacy law distinctions, and the newly formed European CMP Association. One commentator (Peter Borner) noted the split outcome points to a regulatory capacity problem—EU regulators may lack engineering depth to evaluate sophisticated technical mitigations.

Industry News – Data Privacy and Protection Beat

### Implications of the €310 Million LinkedIn Fine for GDPR Compliance

*ComplexDiscovery Staff*

In a recent landmark decision, Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC) imposed a substantial fine of €310 million on LinkedIn, a Microsoft Corp.-owned career platform, for infringing the stringent European Union data privacy and security regulations. The ruling stemmed from an investigation initiated back in 2018 after a complaint lodged by the French non-profit organization La Quadrature Du Net highlighted potential violations of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This substantial penalty epitomizes the EU’s vigorous enforcement of data protection laws and signals a stern warning to other technology giants operating within its jurisdiction.

The investigation revealed that LinkedIn’s processing of users’ personal data for behavioral analysis and targeted advertising breached fundamental GDPR principles. Specifically, the company was found lacking in areas of lawfulness, transparency, and the provision of adequate consent for processing personal data. “The lawfulness of processing is a fundamental aspect of data protection law and the processing of personal data without an appropriate legal basis is a clear and serious violation of a data subjects’ fundamental right to data protection,” stated Graham Doyle, Deputy Commissioner of the Irish Data Protection Commission, emphasizing the gravity of LinkedIn’s oversight.

The scrutiny focused intensely on LinkedIn’s practices concerning the handling of personal data obtained both directly from users and indirectly through third-party partners. The commission observed that LinkedIn had failed to demonstrate legitimate interest, contractual necessity, or obtain explicit consent from users regarding the data processed for targeted advertisements. Such oversights breach the GDPR mandates, which aim to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals in relation to data processing.

As part of the regulatory decision, LinkedIn has been directed to bring its data processing operations into full compliance with GDPR guidelines. The company acknowledged the findings and while it maintained that its practices aligned with regulatory requirements, LinkedIn expressed commitment to modifying its advertising policies to meet the commission’s directives. Responding to the commission’s ruling, LinkedIn indicated that revisions would be implemented by the stipulated deadline.

The repercussions of this decision expand beyond the immediate monetary penalty. For Microsoft, already embroiled in the competitive dynamics of the gaming industry with the upcoming launch of “Call of Duty: Black Ops 6,” this ruling reiterates the critical importance of adherence to local data protection standards. While LinkedIn’s penalties fell short of the $425 million initially anticipated by Microsoft in its 10-K filings, the broader impact reverberates through heightened awareness and regulatory compliance demands across their technological endeavors, including the adoption of their Copilot AI by enterprise clients.

The DPC’s enforcement action underscores the GDPR’s role as a pivotal tool in fortifying data protection within the EU, establishing a paradigm where companies are held accountable for their digital advertising practices. This case exemplifies the ongoing challenges facing multinational corporations as they navigate complex legal landscapes to ensure compliance with local and international regulations. With the GDPR setting a rigorous benchmark, companies must continuously evolve their data handling frameworks to mitigate potential legal and financial risks associated with non-compliance.

This decision also illuminates the active role of regional regulatory authorities, such as the Irish Data Protection Commission, in scrutinizing and curbing unlawful data practices across the European Union. As regulatory bodies proceed with heightened vigilance, the need for robust data protection protocols becomes increasingly imperative for companies to preserve consumer trust and uphold their operational integrity within the European market.

This article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ reports on Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) imposing a €310 million fine on LinkedIn (owned by Microsoft Corp.) for breaches of the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The ruling resulted from an investigation initiated in 2018 following a complaint by the French non-profit La Quadrature Du Net.

Key facts:
- The investigation found LinkedIn's processing of users' personal data for behavioral analysis and targeted advertising breached fundamental GDPR principles, specifically lacking in lawfulness, transparency, and adequate consent.
- The DPC found LinkedIn failed to demonstrate legitimate interest, contractual necessity, or obtain explicit consent regarding data processed for targeted advertisements.
- LinkedIn was directed to bring its data processing into full GDPR compliance and expressed commitment to modifying its advertising policies, while maintaining its practices aligned with regulatory requirements.
- The €310 million penalty fell short of the $425 million Microsoft initially anticipated in its 10-K filings.
- The ruling has broader implications for Microsoft, including its gaming industry activities (Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 launch) and adoption of Copilot AI by enterprise clients.
- The case underscores GDPR's role as a pivotal tool in EU data protection enforcement and highlights the active role of regional regulatory authorities like the Irish DPC.
- The fine signals a stern warning to other technology giants operating within the EU.

The article is part of ComplexDiscovery OÜ's "Industry News – Data Privacy and Protection Beat" and includes an editor's note highlighting compliance considerations for cybersecurity, data governance, and eDiscovery professionals. Additional content on the page includes related articles on eDiscovery market sizing, marketing strategies, vendor viability tools, pricing surveys, business confidence surveys, M&A activity, and 2026 event outlooks.

# LinkedIn fined $335 million in EU for tracking ads privacy breaches

[Natasha Lomas](https://techcrunch.com/author/natasha-lomas/)

Bad news for LinkedIn in Europe, where the Microsoft-owned social network has been reprimanded and fined €310 million for privacy violations related to its tracking ads business.

The administrative penalties, which are worth around $335 million at current exchange rates, have been issued by Ireland’s [Data Protection Commission](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/irish-data-protection-commission-fines-linkedin-ireland-eu310-million) (DPC) under the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The regulator found a raft of breaches, including breaches to the lawfulness, fairness and transparency of its data processing in this area.

The GDPR requires that uses of people’s information have a proper legal basis. In this case, the justifications LinkedIn had relied upon to run its tracking ads business were found to be invalid. It also did not properly inform users about its uses of their information, per the DPC’s decision.

LinkedIn had sought to claim (variously) “consent”-, “legitimate interests”-, and “contractual necessity”-based legal bases for processing people’s information — when obtained directly and/or from third parties — to track and profile its users for behavioral advertising. However, the DPC found none were valid. LinkedIn also failed to comply with the GDPR principles of transparency and fairness.

Commenting in a statement, DPC deputy commissioner Graham Doyle said: “The lawfulness of processing is a fundamental aspect of data protection law and the processing of personal data without an appropriate legal basis is a clear and serious violation of a data subjects’ fundamental right to data protection.”

The size of the sanction catapults the professional social network into a mid-table position in [the top 10 biggest GDPR penalties on Big Tech](https://techcrunch.com/2024/08/10/the-10-largest-gdpr-fines-on-big-tech/). And while this is [not the first time LinkedIn has been slapped](https://techcrunch.com/2018/11/24/linkedin-ireland-data-protection/) for regional data protection violations, it is certainly its most significant sanction to date. (Albeit, the company was keen to flag that the size of the fine was less than the amount Microsoft set aside in an earlier 10-K disclosure alerting investors that it expected a sanction.)

The case against LinkedIn originated with a complaint in France in 2018 by the digital rights non-profit La Quadrature Du Net. The country’s data protection authority then passed the complaint to the DPC, on account of its role as lead oversight body for Microsoft’s GDPR compliance.

The DPC instigated a complaint-based investigation in August 2018 before finally going on to submit its draft decision to other interested data protection authorities almost a full six years later (in July 2024). After no objections were raised, the decision was finalized and the enforcement has now been made public.

As well as being fined, LinkedIn has been given three months to bring its European operations into compliance with the GDPR.

LinkedIn spokesman Jonny Wing pointed TechCrunch to a statement put out on the company’s [press room](https://news.linkedin.com/2024/October/Our-Response-to-the-Irish-Data-Protection-Commissions-Decision) regarding the sanction in which it wrote: “Today the Irish Data Protection Commission (IDPC) reached a final decision on claims from 2018 about some of our digital advertising efforts in the EU. While we believe we have been in compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), we are working to ensure our ad practices meet this decision by the IDPC’s deadline.”

*This report was updated with a correction to the currency conversion of the DPC fine*.

LinkedIn, the Microsoft-owned professional social network, has been fined €310 million (approximately $335 million) by Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) under the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) for privacy violations related to its tracking ads business. The DPC found a raft of breaches, including violations of the lawfulness, fairness, and transparency requirements of its data processing in this area. The legal bases LinkedIn had relied upon to run its tracking ads business—claiming variously "consent," "legitimate interests," and "contractual necessity"—were all found to be invalid. LinkedIn also failed to comply with the GDPR principles of transparency and fairness.

The case originated with a complaint in France in 2018 by the digital rights non-profit La Quadrature Du Net, which was passed to the DPC as the lead oversight body for Microsoft's GDPR compliance. The DPC instigated a complaint-based investigation in August 2018, submitted its draft decision to other interested authorities in July 2024 (almost six years later), and after no objections were raised, the decision was finalized and made public. The fine places LinkedIn in a mid-table position among the top 10 biggest GDPR penalties on Big Tech and represents its most significant sanction to date, though the company noted the fine was less than the amount Microsoft had set aside in an earlier 10-K disclosure. LinkedIn has been given three months to bring its European operations into compliance with the GDPR. In a statement, the company said it believes it has been in compliance with GDPR but is working to ensure its ad practices meet the DPC's decision. The article was written by TechCrunch senior reporter Natasha Lomas.

URL: http://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/irish-data-protection-commission-fines-meta-eu251-million

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) announced on 17 December 2024 that it has fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (MPIL) €251 million following two inquiries into a personal data breach reported by MPIL in September 2018. The breach impacted approximately 29 million Facebook accounts globally, including roughly 3 million in the EU/EEA. Affected personal data categories included user full names, email addresses, phone numbers, locations, places of work, dates of birth, religion, gender, timeline posts, group memberships, and children's personal data.

The breach originated from the exploitation of user tokens on Facebook's platform. Specifically, a vulnerability was created when a video upload function was deployed in July 2017. Facebook's 'View As' feature, combined with the 'Happy Birthday Composer' facility, could be exploited to generate fully permissioned user tokens granting full access to other users' profiles. Between 14-28 September 2018, unauthorized persons used scripts to exploit this vulnerability, gaining the ability to log on as account holders for approximately 29 million accounts globally.

The decisions were made by Commissioners for Data Protection Dr. Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland, and included reprimands and administrative fines totaling €251 million. The DPC submitted a draft decision to the GDPR cooperation mechanism under Article 60 in September 2024, with no objections raised by peer EU/EEA supervisory authorities. DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle commented on the enforcement action, emphasizing that the failure to build in data protection requirements throughout the design and development cycle can expose individuals to serious risks and harms, including risks to fundamental rights and freedoms, particularly given that Facebook profiles can contain sensitive information about religious or political beliefs, sexual life, and orientation.
</summary>

Facebook profiles can, and often do, contain information about matters such as religious or political beliefs, sexual life or orientation, and similar matters that a user may wish to disclose only in particular circumstances. By allowing unauthorised exposure of profile information, the vulnerabilities behind this breach caused a grave risk of misuse of these types of data." - DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This GDPRhub page documents the Dutch Data Protection Authority's (AP - Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens) decision to fine Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI) and Uber B.V. (UBV) €290,000,000 for violating Article 44 GDPR. The decision was issued on 22 July 2024 and published on 25 August 2024.

**Key Facts:**
- Uber B.V. (UBV), based in the Netherlands, is part of the Uber group and serves as the EEA representative. Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI), based in San Francisco, US, is the parent company and joint controller for Uber drivers' personal data.
- Uber used a centralized IT infrastructure with servers located in the US. EEA-based drivers' personal data was processed in the US in two situations: (1) data collected through the driver app and stored on US-based servers (including account, location, criminal and health data, identity documents, and taxi licenses), and (2) when drivers exercised their GDPR rights, UTI was responsible for making data available to UBV.
- Uber previously used the European Commission's Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) but removed them from their joint controllership agreement effective 6 August 2021, arguing SCCs could not be used when processing falls directly under GDPR scope.
- The complaint originated from the French human rights group Ligue des droits de l'Homme on behalf of 172 Uber drivers, filed with CNIL (French DPA) on 12 June 2020, and forwarded to the Dutch AP due to Uber's main establishment in the Netherlands.

**Key Holdings:**
1. **Article 3 GDPR and Chapter V can apply simultaneously**: The DPA rejected Uber's argument that the territorial scope (Article 3 GDPR) and Chapter V (international transfers) were mutually exclusive. Chapter V is complementary to Article 3, preventing circumvention of EU data protection law. The DPA also rejected the WTO agreement argument.
2. **The processing constituted a transfer**: Applying the EDPB Guidelines 05/2021's three cumulative criteria, the DPA found all criteria met. The DPA rejected Uber's argument that drivers themselves were the exporters, finding instead that UBV was the exporter because drivers have little influence over processing purposes and means (terms are pre-drafted and non-negotiable).
3. **No valid transfer mechanism**: From 6 August 2021 to 27 November 2023, Uber had no lawful transfer mechanism. The DPA rejected Uber's interpretation of the European Commission's FAQ statements regarding SCCs.
4. **Article 49 GDPR exceptions did not apply**: The transfers were systematic, repetitive, and ongoing (not incidental per Recital 111). The transfers were not "necessary" for contract performance per C-252/21 (Meta Platforms), as there were practicable, less intrusive alternatives (e.g., processing on EU servers).

**Fine details:** The DPA imposed a €290,000,000 administrative fine on the joint controllers due to the seriousness of the violation. This is the third fine the Dutch DPA has issued against Uber: €600,000 in 2018 for a data breach notification violation, €10 million in 2023 for a nontransparent privacy policy (which Uber has appealed), and this €290 million fine.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: Into the Data Transfer Thicket: The Dutch Uber Decision and the Relationship Between GDPR Article 3 and Chapter V – European Law Blog ---
URL: https://europeanlawblog.eu/1xjmngct

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an opinion/analysis article from the European Law Blog (22 October 2024) by E J Kyriakides examining the Dutch DPA's enforcement decision against Uber and the legal relationship between GDPR Article 3 (territorial scope) and Chapter V (data transfer safeguards).

KEY ISSUE: The article addresses a lingering legal ambiguity: under what circumstances are GDPR data transfer safeguards required when a foreign firm is already subject to the GDPR. The classic transfer scenario involves a foreign company NOT governed by GDPR receiving EU data. But GDPR has extraterritorial effect (Article 3(2)), meaning foreign companies targeting the EU can also be subject to it.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:
- Article 3(1): Entities with an EU "establishment" are subject to GDPR
- Article 3(2): Entities without EU establishment are subject if they (a) offer goods/services to EU data subjects, or (b) monitor EU data subject behavior
- Chapter V (Articles 44-47) requires transfer safeguards including adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses (SCCs), binding corporate rules, etc.
- Under Schrems II, firms must independently assess whether transfer tools ensure "essentially equivalent" protection, potentially requiring supplementary measures
- Chapter V applies only to a "transfer" — a term the GDPR does not define

EDPB GUIDELINES (05/2021):
- Defined "transfer" as occurring when: (1) a controller/processor (exporter) is subject to GDPR; (2) the exporter discloses personal data to another controller/processor (importer); (3) the importer is in a third country (regardless of whether importer is subject to GDPR)
- Critically concluded NO transfer occurs when data is directly disclosed by an individual in the EU to a firm in a third country
- Companies subject to GDPR must still assess third country government access risks under other GDPR obligations (Articles 32, 33, 35)
- Not binding but highly authoritative

THE DUTCH DPA UBER DECISION (August 2024):
- Dutch DPA fined Uber €290 million — the largest fine ever from the Dutch DPA — for transferring French Uber drivers' data to the US without Chapter V safeguards
- Fine originated from an NGO (Ligue Des Droits De L'homme) complaint to the French CNIL
- Transfer involved Uber B.V. (UBV, Netherlands) and Uber Technologies Inc (UTI, US parent)
- Uber relied on SCCs until August 2021, then determined SCCs were unnecessary because Article 3 directly applied to UTI's US processing; Uber had NO transfer mechanism from August 2021 until relying on the Data Privacy Framework in November 2023
- Two scenarios found to involve transfers: (1) EU drivers' data sent directly via Uber app to UTI for US storage; (2) data relating to GDPR rights requests where UBV and UTI collaborated
- Dutch DPA rejected Uber's defenses (direct collection, joint controllership, Article 49 derogations), holding transfers between joint controllers subject to GDPR in different countries are governed by Chapter V
- DPA departed from EDPB guidance by finding scenario one (direct collection from EU data subjects) constituted a "transfer," relying on the employment relationship between UBV and drivers and the asymmetry of power
- DPA argued Chapter V should be read broadly to counterbalance risks of diminished protection when data is processed abroad and difficulty enforcing against foreign entities
- DPA found Article 49(b-c) derogations inapplicable because transfers were ongoing, not "incidental" or "necessary"

ANALYSIS/NEXT STEPS:
- Uber is appealing; Dutch courts are likely to refer questions to the CJEU on the Article 3/Chapter V relationship
- The Dutch decision failed to articulate a clear legal standard for when direct collection by foreign providers subject to GDPR triggers Chapter V
- The article recommends that EU entities subject to GDPR under Article 3(2) in doubt apply Chapter V safeguards until the issue is settled
- European Commission has not yet issued SCCs for scenarios where the importer is subject to GDPR (current SCCs only apply when importer is NOT subject to GDPR)
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The EDPB concluded that a transfer occurs when: 1) A controller or a processor ('exporter') is subject to the GDPR for the given processing; 2) The exporter discloses by transmission or otherwise makes personal data... available to another controller, joint controller or processor ('importer'); 3) The importer is in a third country, irrespective of whether or not this importer is subject to the GDPR for the given processing in accordance with Article 3"
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On August 26, 2024, the Dutch Data Protection Authority (Dutch DPA) fined Uber Technologies, Inc. and Uber B.V. €290 million for violating the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The fine stems from Uber's failure to implement appropriate safeguards for transferring EEA-based drivers' personal data to the United States over a 27-month period, during which Uber removed Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) from its data-sharing agreements between EEA and U.S. entities.

The investigation originated from complaints by drivers to the French data protection authority and was transferred to the Dutch DPA since Uber's European headquarters are in the Netherlands. Uber's personal data transfers included special category and criminal record data, and were directed to Uber's centralized IT infrastructure in the United States.

Key findings of the Decision:
- **Adequate safeguards required for intra-group transfers**: Uber argued both its U.S. and EEA entities were subject to GDPR under Article 3 as joint controllers, making Chapter V compliance unnecessary. The Dutch DPA rejected this, stating the data transfer requirements in Chapter V place a direct obligation on parties processing personal data in third countries. The DPA also determined an "onward transfer" occurred from Uber EEA (data exporter) to Uber U.S. (data importer), even though drivers entered data directly into the Uber platform.
- **Article 49 derogations limited**: Uber argued the transfers were lawful under Article 49 as necessary for contract performance. The DPA rejected this, finding the transfers were systematic, repetitive, and ongoing rather than incidental, and that contract existence alone does not constitute "necessity." The DPA was unconvinced that centralized U.S. processing was crucial to Uber's services, suggesting efficiency motives were insufficient.
- **Fine proportionality**: The DPA considered the violation serious, given the sensitive nature of drivers' personal data (including criminal data) and the 27-month duration. The fine was evaluated under the maximum parameters (higher of €20 million or 4% annual turnover). The DPA determined Uber "could have known" the transfer would require additional safeguards based on GDPR, CJEU case law, and prior regulator decisions.

The Dutch DPA coordinated its decision with other EU data protection authorities, meaning similar determinations could follow. Uber is expected to appeal. The Decision's biggest takeaway is the added uncertainty to the international data transfer landscape, particularly casting doubt on whether companies can rely on European Commission Q&A guidance for compliance or penalty mitigation purposes. The article was authored by attorneys at Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP and published in The Computer & Internet Lawyer, Volume 42, Number 1, January 2025.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) imposed a record-breaking fine of EUR 290 million on Uber for violating Article 44 GDPR by unlawfully transferring personal data of EU-based drivers to the United States. This is the AP's highest-ever fine.

Background: The AP's investigation began in April 2021 after the French DPA (CNIL) forwarded a complaint from the French NGO Ligue des droits de l'Homme (LDH) on behalf of 172 Uber drivers. Following the ECJ's Schrems II ruling in 2020, the EU-US Privacy Shield was invalidated, but Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) remained a valid transfer mechanism, potentially with supplementary measures. The AP acted as the lead Supervisory Authority since Uber's EMEA HQ is established in the Netherlands.

Investigation findings: The AP found Uber processed sensitive data including location data, photos, payment details, ID records, and criminal and health records of drivers. This data was collected through Uber's EU entity (UBV) and transferred to its US-based entity (UTI). Uber stopped using SCCs in August 2021 and continued data transfers without adequate safeguards until November 2023, when it certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.

Uber's defense arguments included: (i) Chapter V GDPR was not applicable since Article 3 already applied (UBV and UTI as joint controllers); (ii) Chapter V was subordinate to Article 3; (iii) "data transfer" was undefined in the GDPR; (iv) no "data transfer" occurred since drivers provided data directly to UTI; and (v) exceptions under Article 49(1)(b) and (c) GDPR applied. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from CookieYes (dated December 17, 2025) provides a comprehensive guide to GDPR fines and penalties, including the 20 largest fines imposed since the regulation took effect on May 25, 2018.

**GDPR Fine Structure:**
- Tier 1 violations: Up to 2% of annual revenue or €10 million (whichever is greater) — applies to violations related to child data consent, privacy by design, data breach notifications, DPIA requirements, DPO appointments, certification mechanisms, and third-party involvement.
- Tier 2 violations: Up to 4% of annual revenue or €20 million (whichever is greater) — applies to violations of lawful bases for processing, GDPR individual rights, cross-border data transfers, Member State laws, and orders from supervisory authorities.
- Non-monetary actions may include processing bans, data deletion orders, and transfer restrictions.
- Under Art. 82, affected individuals can claim compensation in court.

**Criteria for Fines:** Nature/severity of violation, number affected, negligence vs. intent, preventive measures, security protocols, prior violations, cooperation with authorities, type of data affected, notification practices, and financial benefits gained from the violation.

**The 20 Biggest GDPR Fines (2018-2024):**
1. Meta (Facebook) — €1.2 billion (May 22, 2023, Irish DPC): EU-to-US data transfers without adequate safeguards using SCCs.

URL: https://www.uniconsent.com/blog/gdpr-enforcement-fines-2026

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from UniConsent provides a comprehensive overview of GDPR enforcement and fines as of 2026, with a specific focus on the ad tech sector. Key statistics include: over 2,500 fines totaling 7.1 billion euros issued since 2018, with approximately 1.2 billion euros issued in 2025 alone; an average fine of 2.4 million euros; and the largest fine ever being 1.2 billion euros against Meta Platforms Ireland (May 2023) for unlawful EU-US data transfers.

**Top 10 Largest GDPR Fines of All Time:**
1. Meta Platforms Ireland — 1.2B euros (Irish DPC, May 2023) — unlawful EU-US data transfers
2. Amazon Europe Core — 746M euros (Luxembourg CNPD, July 2021) — ad targeting without valid consent (annulled on procedural grounds in March 2026)
3. TikTok — 530M euros (Irish DPC, May 2025) — unlawful EU-China data transfers
4. Meta (Instagram) — 405M euros (Irish DPC, Sept 2022) — mishandling of children's data
5. Meta (Facebook + Instagram) — 390M euros (Irish DPC, Jan 2023) — invalid legal basis for behavioural ads
6. TikTok — 345M euros (Irish DPC, Sept 2023) — children's data processing failures
7. Google — 325M euros (French CNIL, Sept 2025) — Gmail inbox ads + invalid signup consent
8. LinkedIn Ireland — 310M euros (Irish DPC, Oct 2024) — invalid legal basis for behavioural ads
9. Uber — 290M euros (Dutch AP, Aug 2024) — unlawful EU-US data transfers
10. Meta (Facebook) — 265M euros (Irish DPC, Nov 2022) — inadequate protection against data scraping

Eight of the ten largest fines were issued by Ireland's DPC due to Dublin being the European HQ for most major tech companies. Ireland accounts for 4.04 billion euros (~57%) of all GDPR fine value, while Spain has issued the most fines by count (nearly 1,000). Ireland and France together account for ~70% of all GDPR fine value.

**Key structural insights:** The Media, Telecoms and Broadcasting sector accounts for ~70% of all corporate fine value, and "insufficient legal basis for data processing" is the most common violation. Ad tech is uniquely exposed due to: (1) data being the product itself, (2) opaque programmatic supply chains, and (3) consent being the only realistic legal basis for targeted advertising. Ad tech-driven fines approach 5 billion euros — well over half of all GDPR fines ever issued.

**Notable ad tech cases include:** Criteo (40M euros, 2023, for unverified partner consent), Google (50M euros, 2019, first major fine), Google + Amazon (100M + 35M euros, 2020, cookies before consent), Google + Facebook (150M + 60M euros, 2022, dark-pattern banners), Shein (150M euros, Sept 2025, cookie practices), Optimove (1M euros, Dec 2025, processor obligations), and Quantcast (ongoing DPC investigation).

**Critical finding on payment:** Of Ireland's 4.04 billion euros in fines, only ~20 million euros (0.5%) has actually been collected, as most major fines are under appeal. The conflict stems from U.S. surveillance laws (particularly Section 702 of FISA) clashing with EU privacy rights. **Enforcement Actions:** Regulators ordered Meta to (1) suspend all future transfers of EU data to the U.S. within five months, and (2) bring all previously transferred data into compliance within six months (effectively deleting it or moving it back to the EU). These operational orders were deemed a greater threat to business than the fine itself.

**The Enforcement Journey:** Ireland's DPC initially declined to fine Meta, deeming a penalty "disproportionate" and citing Meta's "good faith" use of SCCs. However, other European data protection authorities objected, escalating the case to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) under Article 65. The fine was based on Article 83(5) of the GDPR, allowing penalties up to 4% of global annual turnover due to aggravating factors including: systematic/repetitive/continuous transfers over nearly three years, involvement of special category data (Article 9), and Meta acting with "at least the highest degree of negligence."

**Why SCCs Were Not Enough:** While Meta used Standard Contractual Clauses, regulators found that U.S. surveillance laws like FISA 702 could legally compel Meta to hand over both encrypted data and the cryptographic keys, rendering encryption ineffective. The COA set aside the High Court decision, emphasizing that challenges to decisions of public bodies should be prosecuted with "economy and celerity." The COA identified two scenarios following the upcoming CJEU decision in the WhatsApp case: (1) if the CJEU upholds the General Court's inadmissibility dismissal, unresolved EU law issues could delay Meta Proceedings by ~24 months; (2) if the CJEU allows the appeal, the case returns to the General Court, potentially delaying Meta Proceedings by a further ~40 months. The COA held that the GDPR requires challenges to DPC decisions to be brought in Irish courts, with Article 267 TFEU preliminary references as the exclusive mechanism to resolve GDPR interpretation doubts. The COA found no reason to delay requesting such a reference, and noted parties could later seek stays of the WhatsApp Proceedings if needed. The DPC's appeal was allowed and Meta's adjournment motions were dismissed.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The COA referred to the "critical function" of legal certainty regarding decisions of bodies exercising a public power and stated that challenges to any such decisions should be prosecuted with "economy and celerity". The GDPR requires that any challenge to a decision of the DPC be brought before the courts in Ireland. The exclusive mechanism to resolve any doubts as to the interpretation of the GDPR in the context of the Meta Proceedings is therefore by way of a reference for a preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Meta's €1.2 Billion GDPR Fine: Why It Still Matters in 2025 ---
URL: https://gdprlocal.com/metas-e1-2-billion-gdpr-fine-why-it-still-matters-in-2025

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from GDPRLocal examines Meta's record-breaking €1.2 billion GDPR fine, imposed on May 12, 2023 by Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC), and explores its ongoing significance for international data transfers.

**The Core Violation:** Meta was fined for illegally transferring European users' personal data to the United States, directly breaching the international transfer rules in Chapter V of the GDPR. The conflict stems from U.S. surveillance laws (particularly Section 702 of FISA) clashing with EU privacy rights. The €1.2 billion penalty specifically covers transfers that continued after the landmark Schrems II ruling on July 16, 2020. The case originated from a complaint filed by privacy activist Max Schrems.

**Enforcement Actions:** Regulators ordered Meta to (1) suspend all future transfers of EU data to the U.S. within five months, and (2) bring all previously transferred data into compliance within six months (effectively deleting it or moving it back to the EU). These operational orders were deemed a greater threat to business than the fine itself.

**The Enforcement Journey:** Ireland's DPC initially declined to fine Meta, deeming a penalty "disproportionate" and citing Meta's "good faith" use of SCCs. However, other European data protection authorities objected, escalating the case to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) under Article 65. In Binding Decision 1/2023 (April 13, 2023), the EDPB overruled the DPC, declaring the infringement "highly serious" and mandating a fine with a starting point between 20-100% of the legal maximum, calculated on Meta's worldwide turnover. The fine was based on Article 83(5) of the GDPR, allowing penalties up to 4% of global annual turnover due to aggravating factors including: systematic/repetitive/continuous transfers over nearly three years, involvement of special category data (Article 9), and Meta acting with "at least the highest degree of negligence."

**Why SCCs Were Not Enough:** While Meta used Standard Contractual Clauses, regulators found that U.S. surveillance laws like FISA 702 could legally compel Meta to hand over both encrypted data and the cryptographic keys, rendering encryption ineffective. The EDPB concluded Meta's SCCs were "mere contractual promises" with no practical effect against U.S. surveillance law.

**History of EU-US Transfer Mechanisms:** The article details the evolution from Safe Harbour (invalidated in 2015 by Schrems I) to Privacy Shield (invalidated in 2020 by Schrems II) to SCCs (still valid but requiring Transfer Impact Assessments) to the new EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF, adopted July 10, 2023, valid but contested - NOYB has signaled a potential "Schrems III" challenge, and FISA 702 was only reauthorized until April 2026).

**The Schrems II Ruling Explained:** The 2020 CJEU ruling invalidated Privacy Shield and established new obligations for companies using SCCs, requiring case-by-case Transfer Impact Assessments (TIAs) before transfers and supplementary measures (including encryption with EU-controlled keys) when risks are identified.

**Industry Reactions:** Meta called the fine "flawed, unjustified and unnecessary" and is appealing (case T-325/23), while simultaneously adopting the new DPF. Forrester called the fine a "wake-up call" proving regulators now have the "power and the guts to dismantle a company's business model." EDPB Chair Andrea Jelinek stated the "unprecedented fine is a strong signal to organisations that serious infringements have far-reaching consequences." Other companies like Amazon Web Services quickly self-certified under the DPF for legal certainty. Ireland later fined Microsoft's LinkedIn €310 million in October 2024 for similar processing violations.

**Lessons for Businesses:** The article concludes that "set it and forget it" compliance is no longer viable. Companies must: (1) document every Transfer Impact Assessment, (2) encrypt or pseudonymise by default with keys controlled exclusively by the EU data exporter, (3) diversify legal bases (BCRs for corporate groups, Article 49 derogations only for one-off situations), and (4) continuously monitor legal changes. Boards must treat cross-border data transfers as a dynamic, strategic, multi-jurisdictional risk integrated into products, contracts, and technical architecture from day one.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The largest fine, a record-breaking €1.2 billion, was imposed back in May 2023. That penalty was for one specific reason: unlawfully transferring the personal data of European Facebook users to the United States."
</key_excerpts>

On 4 January 2023, Ireland's data protection authority (DPC) announced its final decision fining Meta Ireland €210 million for GDPR breaches regarding its Facebook services and €180 million for breaches regarding its Instagram services, totaling €390 million. The decisions center on the legal basis Meta used for processing personal data for personalised advertising.

Key events in the timeline:
- The DPC launched an investigation into Meta on 25 May 2018, following complaints about Facebook and Instagram. Meta had previously relied on user consent but shifted to the 'performance of a contract' legal basis after the GDPR took effect on 25 May 2018, arguing that processing personal data (including for personalised ads) was necessary to fulfil its contractual obligations under its terms of service.

SUMMARY:

On 13 March 2025, the Irish Court of Appeal (COA) delivered its judgment in Data Protection Commission (DPC) v Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, upholding the DPC's appeal and refusing to stay (adjourn) the Meta Proceedings. The background involves a DPC decision on 25 November 2022 finding that Meta violated Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR after third parties 'scraped' personal data from Meta's platforms between May 2018 and September 2019. The DPC issued an order to comply, a reprimand, and two fines totalling €165 million. In December 2022, Meta brought both a statutory appeal and judicial review proceedings in the High Court.

The case related to separate "WhatsApp Proceedings": on 20 August 2021 the DPC fined WhatsApp €225 million for GDPR infringements (Articles 5, 12, 13, 14). WhatsApp's challenge to the EDPB's Article 65 decision was dismissed by the EU General Court as inadmissible (WhatsApp not directly concerned), and an appeal to the Court of Justice was pending (Advocate General's opinion due 27 March 2025). In July 2023, Meta sought to adjourn its High Court proceedings pending the outcome of the WhatsApp Proceedings; the High Court (Simons J) granted this, adjourning the Meta Proceedings in their entirety.

The COA set aside the High Court decision, emphasizing that challenges to decisions of public bodies should be prosecuted with "economy and celerity." The COA identified two scenarios following the upcoming CJEU decision in the WhatsApp case: (1) if the CJEU upholds the General Court's inadmissibility dismissal, unresolved EU law issues could delay Meta Proceedings by ~24 months; (2) if the CJEU allows the appeal, the case returns to the General Court, potentially delaying Meta Proceedings by a further ~40 months. The COA held that the GDPR requires challenges to DPC decisions to be brought in Irish courts, with Article 267 TFEU preliminary references as the exclusive mechanism to resolve GDPR interpretation doubts. The COA found no reason to delay requesting such a reference, and noted parties could later seek stays of the WhatsApp Proceedings if needed. The DPC's appeal was allowed and Meta's adjournment motions were dismissed.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On January 4, 2023, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) concluded two inquiries into Meta Platforms, Inc.'s data processing practices on its Instagram and Facebook platforms, fining Meta a combined €390 million for breaches of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The investigation began following complaints from NOYB (None of Your Business), an NGO co-founded by privacy activist Max Schrems, alleging that Facebook and Instagram "forced" users to consent to personal data processing for behavioral advertising. Meta had updated its Terms of Service and asserted it could rely on the GDPR's "performance of a contract" legal basis for processing.

Key findings of the investigation:
- The DPC held that while GDPR does not preclude Meta's reliance on the "performance of a contract" legal basis, Meta's practices breached Article 5(1)(a), which requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently, because its Terms of Use did not clearly disclose data processing activities, purposes, or legal basis.
- Following consultations with EU peer regulators, the findings were submitted to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), which notably held that Meta could no longer rely on the "performance of a contract" legal basis for behavioral advertising activities—a decision with broad implications for publishers engaged in behavioral advertising in the EU.
- The EDPB also directed the DPC to conduct a separate investigation into how Facebook and Instagram process special categories of data.
- The DPC adopted the EDPB's findings, issued the €390 million fine, and directed Meta to bring its data processing activities into compliance with GDPR within three months.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined Meta €251 million on Tuesday, 17 December 2024, for failure to comply with the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The fine relates to a security breach on Facebook that began in July 2017 and affected close to three million accounts in the European Economic Area.

The breach was a bug in Facebook's design that allowed unauthorized users exploiting a vulnerability to view profiles they should not have been able to see. Affected personal data included users' full names, gender, religion, phone numbers, location, and place of work.

The fine was split into two parts: €11 million for Meta's failure to notify and fully document the breach to regulatory authorities, and €240 million for the nature of the personal data breach itself. Irish DPC deputy commissioner Graham Doyle said the bulk of the fine related to a "failure to build in data protection requirements throughout the design" of the affected system.

Meta is expected to appeal the decision. A Meta spokesperson said, "We took immediate action to fix the problem." Meta discovered the security issue in September 2018, fixed the vulnerability, and informed law enforcement authorities at that time.

This is the third fine issued by the DPC under GDPR since Des Hogan became Commissioner for Data Protection in February 2024. The final decision followed the DPC's submission of its draft ruling for review under the GDPR cooperation mechanism, which received no objections from peer EU data protection authorities. The DPC had previously fined Meta €91 million for a password management lapse in September and fined LinkedIn €310 million over targeted advertising in October.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Meta Ireland fined €390 million for unlawful legal basis ---
URL: https://www.stibbe.com/publications-and-insights/meta-ireland-fined-eu390-million-for-unlawful-legal-basis

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 4 January 2023, Ireland's data protection authority (DPC) announced its final decision fining Meta Ireland €210 million for GDPR breaches regarding its Facebook services and €180 million for breaches regarding its Instagram services, totaling €390 million. The decisions center on the legal basis Meta used for processing personal data for personalised advertising.

Key events in the timeline:
- The DPC launched an investigation into Meta on 25 May 2018, following complaints about Facebook and Instagram. Meta had previously relied on user consent but shifted to the 'performance of a contract' legal basis after the GDPR took effect on 25 May 2018, arguing that processing personal data (including for personalised ads) was necessary to fulfil its contractual obligations under its terms of service.
- The DPC published a draft decision on 6 October 2021 proposing fines of up to €23 million for Instagram and €36 million for Facebook, finding that personalised advertising was a core element of Meta's services and that Meta had breached transparency obligations.
- Ten European supervisory authorities (including the Dutch DPA) disagreed with the DPC's draft, arguing personalised ads are not a core element of Meta's services. This triggered the European Consistency Mechanism, and the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) issued a binding decision on 5 December 2022.
- The EDPB upheld the DPC's position on transparency breaches but found that 'performance of a contract' was not a lawful basis for processing personal data for personalised advertising. The EDPB reasoned that: (1) Meta is not contractually obligated to offer personalised ads to users (the obligation exists with advertisers instead); (2) transparency requirements are indispensable to the contract basis; and (3) under Article 21(2)-(3) GDPR, users can object to direct marketing processing at any time without reason, meaning such processing is not "necessary" for the contract. The EDPB also ordered significantly increased fines.
- The DPC adopted the EDPB's binding decision on 31 December 2022, finding breaches of Article 6(1) GDPR from the GDPR's entry into force. Meta was given three months to bring its data processing into compliance.

Impact: The decisions strike at Meta's core business model, which relies on personalised advertising. Meta announced it would appeal, and the case may ultimately be referred to both the Irish Supreme Court and the CJEU. The decision also highlights significant disagreement between the DPC and other European supervisory authorities, with the DPC claiming the EDPB exceeded its powers. The ruling may affect other platforms relying on personalised ads, and preliminary questions on the 'legitimate interest' legal basis are pending before the CJEU (Case C-621/22). Meta is also facing revenue loss from Apple's iOS opt-out tracking feature.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The EDPB upheld the DPC's position regarding breaches of transparency obligations but – unlike the DPC – found that the 'performance of a contract' was not a lawful basis for the processing of personal data for the purpose of personalised advertisements."

--- SOURCE 5: EU & Ireland: Meta’s legal basis for targeted ads found to breach GDPR | Privacy Matters ---
URL: https://privacymatters.dlapiper.com/2023/01/eu-ireland-metas-legal-basis-for-targeted-ads-found-to-breach-gdpr

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a DLA Piper "Privacy Matters" blog post (authors: James Sullivan, John Magee & David Brazil) analyzing Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) decisions announced January 4, 2023, fining Meta €390 million for breaching GDPR by using 'contractual necessity' as the legal basis for processing millions of Europeans' personal data for targeted advertising on Facebook and Instagram.

**Key Background:**
- Prior to GDPR's effective date (May 25, 2018), Meta changed its Terms of Service to rely on 'contractual necessity' instead of consent as the lawful basis for processing user data for personalized advertising.
- Two EU complainants argued Meta was "forcing" users to consent by conditioning services on accepting updated Terms of Service.
- The DPC initially sided with Meta, concluding 'contractual necessity' was a valid legal basis for personalized ads, while also finding transparency violations (with proposed fines understood to be €28-36 million).

**The Dispute:**
- 10 DPAs from across Europe contested the DPC's draft decision, arguing personalized advertising was not necessary to perform the core contract with users.
- On December 5, 2022, the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) issued a binding determination partially reversing the DPC, finding Meta was NOT entitled to rely on 'contractual necessity.' The EDPB also ordered the DPC to conduct a new investigation into ALL of Facebook's and Instagram's data processing operations.
- The DPC's final decisions on December 31, 2022 incorporated the EDPB's ruling, and were announced January 4, 2023.

**Disagreements Among Regulators:**
The decisions reflect two growing divisions among European DPAs: (1) whether 'contractual necessity' is an appropriate GDPR legal basis for personalized advertising, and (2) whether the EDPB has legal authority to order DPAs to bring new investigations. The DPC characterized the EDPB's order as an "open-ended and speculative investigation" and overreach, and indicated it will bring an annulment action before the Court of Justice of the EU—the DPC's first legal challenge of the EDPB's directions.

**Next Steps & Implications:**
- Meta announced its intention to appeal both the substance and the fines, meaning the 'contractual necessity' issue will be litigated for years.
- The DPC required Meta to bring processing into compliance within three months, but Meta's appeal may allow it to continue its current approach pending appellate outcomes.
- The decisions did not prohibit personalized advertising; Meta could pivot to 'consent' or 'legitimate interest' as legal bases, though 'legitimate interest' gives users a right to object that could undermine personalized advertising at scale.
- A third DPC decision regarding Meta's WhatsApp service was due imminently, though that inquiry concerned processing for service improvement purposes.
- Commercial implications are significant: Meta's share price fell 6.2% on the day the EDPB's position was reported. The business model of providing personalized ads without an opt-out option is increasingly difficult to justify.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Arthur Cox (an Irish law firm) publishes a legal briefing on the Irish High Court's judgment in TikTok Technology Limited v Data Protection Commission [2026] IEHC 347, delivered on 3 June 2026. The case concerned TikTok's appeal against a DPC decision dated 30 April 2025, which found that TikTok had infringed international transfer and transparency requirements under the GDPR.

Key facts: The DPC's original inquiry (IN-21-9-2) found that personal data stored by TikTok outside China was remotely accessed by employees in China, constituting an international transfer under Chapter V GDPR. The DPC identified infringements of Article 46 GDPR (transfers subject to appropriate safeguards) and Article 13(1)(f) GDPR (transparency), and imposed fines totaling €530 million plus a compliance order.

The High Court rejected most of TikTok's 11 grounds of appeal and upheld the Article 46 and Article 13(1)(f) infringement findings. Key rulings: (1) Under Article 46 GDPR, controllers must not only identify a transfer mechanism but also carry out an adequate, documented assessment of the protection in the third country—the supervisory authority can examine whether the assessment adequately demonstrates what it purports to demonstrate, without needing an independent examination of third-country laws. (2) Under Article 13(1)(f) GDPR, controllers must specifically identify the third countries to which personal data is transferred; TikTok's October 2021 privacy policy failed to name China as a destination.

The Court did find the DPC erred in refusing to consider a third expert opinion on Chinese law and in not stating the basis for concluding that TikTok's "Project Clover" pseudonymisation measures did not justify a different corrective approach. While these errors did not affect the infringement findings, the corrective orders were vacated and remitted to the DPC for further consideration.

Key takeaway: Organisations transferring data outside the EEA must "verify, guarantee and demonstrate" robust, documented, and defensible assessments of third-country data protection, capable of withstanding supervisory scrutiny.

--- SOURCE 27: Meta Platforms Ireland v Data Protection Commission ---
URL: https://www.mccannfitzgerald.com/knowledge/disputes/meta-platforms-ireland-v-data-protection-commission-importance-of-expediency-in-challenges-to-decisions-of-public-bodies

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 13 March 2025, the Irish Court of Appeal (COA) delivered its judgment in Data Protection Commission (DPC) v Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, upholding the DPC's appeal and refusing to stay (adjourn) the Meta Proceedings. The background involves a DPC decision on 25 November 2022 finding that Meta violated Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR after third parties 'scraped' personal data from Meta's platforms between May 2018 and September 2019. The DPC issued an order to comply, a reprimand, and two fines totalling €165 million. In December 2022, Meta brought both a statutory appeal and judicial review proceedings in the High Court.

The case related to separate "WhatsApp Proceedings": on 20 August 2021 the DPC fined WhatsApp €225 million for GDPR infringements (Articles 5, 12, 13, 14). WhatsApp's challenge to the EDPB's Article 65 decision was dismissed by the EU General Court as inadmissible (WhatsApp not directly concerned), and an appeal to the Court of Justice was pending (Advocate General's opinion due 27 March 2025). In July 2023, Meta sought to adjourn its High Court proceedings pending the outcome of the WhatsApp Proceedings; the High Court (Simons J) granted this, adjourning the Meta Proceedings in their entirety.

The COA set aside the High Court decision, emphasizing that challenges to decisions of public bodies should be prosecuted with "economy and celerity." The COA identified two scenarios following the upcoming CJEU decision in the WhatsApp case: (1) if the CJEU upholds the General Court's inadmissibility dismissal, unresolved EU law issues could delay Meta Proceedings by ~24 months; (2) if the CJEU allows the appeal, the case returns to the General Court, potentially delaying Meta Proceedings by a further ~40 months. The COA held that the GDPR requires challenges to DPC decisions to be brought in Irish courts, with Article 267 TFEU preliminary references as the exclusive mechanism to resolve GDPR interpretation doubts. The COA found no reason to delay requesting such a reference, and noted parties could later seek stays of the WhatsApp Proceedings if needed. The DPC's appeal was allowed and Meta's adjournment motions were dismissed.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The COA referred to the "critical function" of legal certainty regarding decisions of bodies exercising a public power and stated that challenges to any such decisions should be prosecuted with "economy and celerity". The GDPR requires that any challenge to a decision of the DPC be brought before the courts in Ireland. The exclusive mechanism to resolve any doubts as to the interpretation of the GDPR in the context of the Meta Proceedings is therefore by way of a reference for a preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU.
</key_excerpts>

# Meta fined €265 million for Facebook GDPR breaches

#### ON THIS PAGE

Facebook parent Meta was fined by the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) €265 million fine on 28 November 2022, for the period of 2018 and 2019.

## The Reasons for the €265 Million Fine

Facebook’s owner Meta has been fined €265 million by the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) for breaching [European data protection law](https://cookie-script.com/blog/cookie-law "European data protection law"). The breach resulted in more than 500 million users' details being published online.  **The data was hacked and included names, Facebook IDs, mobile phone numbers, real addresses, birth dates, and email addresses of people from more than 100 countries.** The Irish watchdog said a “significant” number of these users were from the EU.

Details of Facebook users were scraped from public profiles in 2018 and 2019. According to Meta, the data had been scraped from the Facebook platform using tools designed to find friends through phone numbers using search and contact import features.

An inquiry for the Meta investigation was opened by the Irish DPC on April 14, 2021, following media reports.

The DPC confirmed that the decision is based on the infringement of Articles 25(1) and 25(2) of the General Data Protection Regulation ([GDPR](https://cookie-script.com/gdpr-and-e-privacy-regulation-compliance.html "GDPR")). These articles deal with data protection by design and default.

In addition to the fine, the DPC also imposed various corrective measures. The Irish watchdog requires Meta to “*bring its processing into compliance by taking a range of specified remedial actions within a particular timeframe*”.

args.summary:
On 28 November 2022, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined Facebook parent company Meta €265 million for breaches of European data protection law (GDPR) relating to a data breach affecting more than 500 million users. The breach, which occurred when user details were scraped from public Facebook profiles in 2018 and 2019, exposed names, Facebook IDs, mobile phone numbers, real addresses, birth dates, and email addresses of people from more than 100 countries, with a "significant" number of EU users affected.

The DPC's decision was based on infringements of Articles 25(1) and 25(2) of the GDPR, which deal with data protection by design and default. The inquiry was opened on April 14, 2021, following media reports. In addition to the fine, the DPC imposed corrective measures requiring Meta to bring its processing into compliance through specified remedial actions within a particular timeframe.

Meta downplayed the breach, claiming the data was "old data" and that it was scraped illegally, stating "unauthorized data scraping is unacceptable and against our rules." Meta subsequently fixed the issue by removing the ability to scrape features using phone numbers.

This is part of a series of fines against Meta by the DPC totaling nearly €1 billion, including a €225m fine for WhatsApp in September 2021 over privacy notice failures, a €17m fine in March 2022, and a €405m fine in September 2022 for allowing teenagers to create Instagram accounts that publicly displayed personal data. The DPC has 40 ongoing inquiries into big tech companies, including 13 involving Meta. DECISION OF THE IRISH DPC / 25 NOVEMBER 2022 / ANNOUNCED 28 NOVEMBER 2022

# Meta €265 Million DPC Fine, 2022 Facebook Data-Scraping Decision Explained

The Irish Data Protection Commission fined Meta Platforms Ireland €265 million over the Facebook data-scraping incident, finding that the contact-import and search tools breached the Data Protection by Design and Default obligations in Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR.

Fine amount

Issuing DPA

Irish DPC

Decision date

25 Nov 2022

Status

Final

Articles cited

25(1), 25(2)

EDUCATIONAL ONLY

This page is a reference summary of a published regulator decision. It is not legal advice. Consult a qualified data protection lawyer for advice on your specific situation. The UK GDPR is a separate regime from the EU GDPR following Brexit. Always read the source decision in full before relying on any figure or quote.

DECISION SUMMARY

## What happened

On 28 November 2022, Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) announced a final decision, adopted on 25 November 2022, imposing a €265 million administrative fine on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (MPIL). The decision concluded an inquiry into the Facebook "data scraping" incident, opened after a collated dataset of Facebook user data was found published on the internet in April 2021. The inquiry examined whether Meta had complied with its obligation to build data protection into the design of the affected features.

The scope of the inquiry covered the Facebook Search, Facebook Messenger Contact Importer and Instagram Contact Importer tools, and the processing carried out by MPIL between 25 May 2018 (the date the GDPR took effect) and September 2019. During that period, third parties abused those tools to match very large lists of phone numbers against user profiles, enabling them to compile personal data on more than 500 million users from over 100 countries. The compiled dataset included names, Facebook IDs, phone numbers, locations, dates of birth and email addresses.

The incident was not a conventional security breach in which an attacker penetrated Facebook's systems. The data was assembled by exploiting features working as built, at scale, because those features lacked adequate safeguards against enumeration and bulk matching. The DPC's inquiry therefore centred on Data Protection by Design and Default rather than on the security-of-processing obligation in Article 32.

## What the DPC found

The decision recorded findings of infringement of Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR. Article 25(1) requires a controller, both at the time of determining the means of processing and at the time of processing itself, to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures designed to implement the data-protection principles effectively and to integrate the necessary safeguards into the processing. Article 25(2) requires that, by default, only personal data necessary for each specific purpose is processed, including limits on the amount of data collected, the extent of processing, the storage period and accessibility.

The DPC concluded that Meta's contact-import and search features did not meet either obligation. The features allowed identifiers such as phone numbers to be matched to profiles at a scale and with a default accessibility that exposed large volumes of personal data to collection by third parties. Effective measures, such as default-private settings, rate limiting and controls on bulk enumeration, were not built in by design or applied by default during the relevant period. Because the deficiencies were in the design and default configuration of the processing, they fell squarely within Article 25.

## The corrective measures and the fine

Alongside the €265 million fine, the DPC imposed a reprimand and an order requiring MPIL to bring its processing into compliance by taking a range of specified remedial actions within a set timeframe. Article 25 infringements are assessed under the lower tier of Article 83(4), which caps fines at €10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Given Meta's scale, the 2% turnover ceiling sat well above €265 million, so the amount reflects the DPC's Article 83(2) assessment of the gravity and duration of the infringement and the very large number of affected data subjects, rather than the statutory cap.

## Where this sits among the Meta decisions

The data-scraping fine is one of a series of large DPC decisions against Meta entities. It is distinct from the WhatsApp transparency fine (€225 million, 2021), the Instagram children's-data fine (€405 million, 2022), the contractual-basis fines on Facebook and Instagram (€390 million combined, 2023) and the €1.2 billion transfers fine (2023). The data-scraping case is the leading Article 25 decision in that group: it is about how a product is built, rather than the lawful basis for advertising or the legality of international transfers. Each of these prior decisions counts as a relevant previous infringement under Article 83(2)(e) when later Meta fines are assessed.

## What this decision tells controllers

The practical lesson is that Data Protection by Design and Default is an enforceable obligation with nine-figure exposure, not an aspirational principle. Any feature that lets a user look up, match or enumerate other people by an identifier (phone number, email, user ID) must be designed against abuse from the outset: default-private visibility, rate limiting, anomaly detection and minimisation of the data returned. Controllers should treat adversarial misuse of legitimate features as a foreseeable risk that Article 25 makes them responsible for, and should document the by-design and by-default safeguards as part of the data-protection impact assessment for any such feature.

FREQUENTLY ASKED

## About the Meta €265 million data-scraping fine

Why was Meta fined €265 million?+

The Irish Data Protection Commission fined Meta Platforms Ireland €265 million on 25 November 2022 over the Facebook data-scraping incident. The DPC found that Meta had failed to implement Data Protection by Design and Default as required by Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR, so that contact-import and search tools could be abused to compile a dataset of more than 500 million users' personal data, which was later published online.

What was the Facebook data-scraping incident?+

Between May 2018 and September 2019, third parties abused Facebook's search, Facebook Messenger Contact Importer and Instagram Contact Importer tools to match large lists of phone numbers to user profiles, scraping data on more than 500 million users. The compiled dataset, which included names, Facebook IDs, phone numbers, locations, birth dates and email addresses, was found published on a hacking forum in April 2021. The breach was not a system hack but the abuse of features that lacked adequate safeguards by design.

Which GDPR articles did the fine concern?+

The decision recorded infringements of Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR, the Data Protection by Design and by Default obligations. Article 25(1) requires controllers to build appropriate technical and organisational measures into processing from the design stage; Article 25(2) requires that, by default, only personal data necessary for each specific purpose is processed. The DPC found Meta's contact-import and search features did not meet either obligation.

Did the EDPB get involved in the €265 million fine?+

The DPC submitted a draft decision to the other concerned supervisory authorities under Article 60, and the matter was resolved through that cooperation process. The €265 million figure reflects the DPC's own assessment of the Article 83(2) factors. This distinguishes it from the Meta €1.2 billion transfers fine, where the European Data Protection Board issued an Article 65 binding decision instructing the DPC to raise the amount.

What does the data-scraping decision mean for product design?+

The decision establishes that scraping enabled by a product's own features is a Data Protection by Design failure, not merely third-party misconduct. Controllers offering contact-matching, search-by-identifier or enumeration features must build in rate limiting, default-private settings, and abuse monitoring from the design stage. Article 25 makes the controller responsible for foreseeable misuse of its own tools, so privacy-by-design reviews need to model adversarial use, not just intended use.

Irish Data Protection Commission Fines Meta €265 Million for Privacy Violations

1 Minute Read

Categories: [Enforcement](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/enforcement9), [European Union](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/european-union), [Information Security](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/information-security), [International](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/international), [Online Privacy](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/online-privacy)

On November 25, 2022, Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (“DPC”) released a [decision](https://www.dataprotection.ie/sites/default/files/uploads/2022-12/Final%20Decision_IN-21-4-2_Redacted.pdf) fining Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) €265 million for a 2019 data leak involving the personal information of approximately 533 million Facebook users worldwide.

In the decision, the DPC argued that Meta failed to comply with the GDPR’s requirement of providing privacy “by design and default” when it failed to prevent the disclosure of users’ phone numbers, email addresses, full names, dates of birth and other personal information on an online hacking forum. The leak was a result of a hacking group exploiting a weakness in Facebook’s data processing measures to scrape public profiles and connect user profiles with email addresses.

In September, the DPC [fined](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/2022/09/07/irish-data-protection-commissioner-fines-instagram-for-children-privacy-violations/) Meta €405 million for allowing minors to operate business accounts on Instagram, which led to the disclosure of affected users’ contact information. Meta says it plans to appeal both of the DPC’s decisions.

# Data Protection Commission announces decision in Facebook “Data Scraping” Inquiry

28th November 2022

The Data Protection Commission (DPC) has today announced the conclusion to an inquiry into Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (MPIL), data controller of the “Facebook” social media network, imposing a fine of €265 million and a range of corrective measures.

The DPC commenced this inquiry on 14 April 2021, on foot of media reports into the discovery of a collated dataset of Facebook personal data that had been made available on the internet. The scope of the inquiry concerned an examination and assessment of Facebook Search, Facebook Messenger Contact Importer and Instagram Contact Importer tools in relation to processing carried out by Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (‘MPIL’) during the period between 25 May 2018 and September 2019. The material issues in this inquiry concerned questions of compliance with the GDPR obligation for **Data Protection by Design and Default**.  The DPC examined the implementation of technical and organisational measures pursuant to Article 25 GDPR (which deals with this concept).

There was a comprehensive inquiry process, including cooperation with all of the other data protection supervisory authorities within the EU. Those supervisory authorities agreed with the decision of the DPC.

The decision, which was adopted on Friday, 25 November 2022, records findings of infringement of Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR. The decision imposed a reprimand and an order requiring MPIL to bring its processing into compliance by taking a range of specified remedial actions within a particular timeframe. In addition, the decision has imposed administrative fines totalling €265 million on MPIL.

# Facebook: Meta fined €265m by Irish Data Protection Commission

![](https://static.files.bbci.co.uk/bbcdotcom/web/20260729-174851-148577b706-web-3.17.0-2/grey-placeholder.png)![Getty Images A person walks past the Meta logo](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/17378/production/_127569059_gettyimages.jpg.webp)Getty Images

**Meta, the company which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, has been fined €265m (£228m) by the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC).**

The fine is over a data breach that saw the personal details of hundreds of millions of Facebook users published online.

Phone numbers and email addresses of up to 533m users appeared on an online hacking forum.

The DPC [launched an investigation in April 2021](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/technology-56745734).

Facebook said at the time that the information, some of which had already appeared online a number of years ago, was "scraped", but not hacked, by malicious actors through a vulnerability in its tools prior to September 2019.

"Scraping" uses automated software to lift public information from the internet that can then end up being distributed in online forums.

## 'Considerable risks'

However, the DPC found that Meta was in breach of Article 25 of General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) rules.

"Because this data set was so large, because there had been previous instances of scraping on the platform, where the issues could have been identified in a more timely way, we ultimately imposed a significant sanction," Data Protection Commissioner Helen Dixon said.

"The risks are considerable for individuals in terms of scamming, spamming, smishing, phishing and loss of control over their personal data so we imposed a fine of €265m in total."

As well as the fine, Meta has been issued with a reprimand and an order requiring it to bring its processing into compliance by taking a range of specified remedial actions within a particular timeframe.

A spokesman for the company said: "Protecting the privacy and security of people's data is fundamental to how our business works. That's why we have cooperated fully with the Irish Data Protection Commission on this important issue.

"We made changes to our systems during the time in question, including removing the ability to scrape our features in this way using phone numbers.

"Unauthorised data scraping is unacceptable and against our rules and we will continue working with our peers on this industry challenge. We are reviewing this decision carefully."

In September, Meta lodged an appeal in the High Court against a record fine of €405m imposed on Instagram by the DPC.

It was the largest fine ever handed down by the Irish data watchdog and was issued for breaches relating to the processing of children's data.
