The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined video-sharing platform TikTok €345 million for breaches related to the processing of children's data. The investigation began in September 2021 and focused on the period from July to December 2020, examining TikTok's settings as they related to child users and the processing of personal data of children under 13 for age verification purposes during registration.

The DPC found that "public-by-default" settings caused child accounts to be automatically set to public rather than private. It also found that in the "family pairing" feature, a child's account could be paired with a non-child user who was not necessarily a parent or guardian. Additionally, TikTok failed to properly consider risks posed to children under 13 who gained access to the platform, which the DPC deemed a clear breach of the data protection by design and by default principle.

The DPC ordered TikTok to bring its data processing into compliance within three months and fined it a total of €345 million. TikTok stated it respectfully disagrees with the decision, particularly the level of the fine, and argued the DPC's criticisms focus on features and settings that were in place three years ago, noting changes were made well before the investigation began, such as setting all under-16 accounts to private by default. However, child online protection experts considered the fine appropriate and proportionate. TikTok had approximately 2 million users in Ireland out of over 1 billion globally. An appeal has not been ruled out.

# Irish Data Protection Commission announces €345 million fine of TikTok

15th September 2023

The Data Protection Commission (**DPC**) adopted its final decision regarding its inquiry into TikTok Technology Limited (**TTL**) on 1 September 2023.

This own-volition inquiry sought to examine the extent to which, during the period between 31 July 2020 and 31 December 2020 (the **Relevant Period**), TTL complied with its obligations under the GDPR in relation to its processing of personal data relating to child users of the TikTok platform in the context of:

As part of the inquiry, the DPC also examined certain of TTL’s transparency obligations, including the extent of information provided to child users in relation to default settings.

At the conclusion of its investigation, the DPC submitted a draft decision to all Supervisory Authorities Concerned (**CSAs**), for the purpose of Article 60(3) GDPR, on 13 September 2022. The DPC’s draft decision proposed findings of infringement of Articles 5(1)(c), 5(1)(f), 24(1), 25(1), 25(2), 12(1) and 13(1)(e) GDPR, in relation to the above processing. While there was broad consensus on the DPC’s proposed findings, objections to the draft decision were raised by the Supervisory Authorities (each an **SA**, collectively **SAs**) of Italy and Berlin (acting on behalf of itself and the Baden-Württemberg SA).

The objection raised by the Berlin SA sought the inclusion of an additional finding of infringement of the Article 5(1)(a) GDPR principle of fairness as regards ‘dark patterns’ while the objection raised by the Italian SA sought to reverse the DPC’s proposed finding of compliance with Article 25 GDPR, as regards TTL’s approach to age verification during the Relevant Period. The DPC was unable to reach consensus with the CSAs on the subject-matter of the objections and, in the circumstances, decided to refer the objections to the EDPB for determination pursuant to the Article 65 GDPR dispute resolution mechanism.

The European Data Protection Board adopted its binding decision on the subject matter of the objections on 2 August 2023 with a direction that the DPC must amend its draft decision to include a new finding of infringement of the Article 5(1)(a) GDPR principle of fairness, further to the objection raised by the Berlin SA, and to extend the scope of the existing order to bring processing into compliance, to include reference to the remedial work required to address this new finding of infringement.

The DPC’s decision, which was adopted on 1 September 2023, records findings of infringement of Articles 5(1)(c), 5(1)(f), 24(1), 25(1), 25(2), 12(1), 13(1)(e) and 5(1)(a) GDPR. The decision further exercises the following corrective powers:

args.summary:
On 1 September 2023, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) adopted its final decision in its own-volition inquiry into TikTok Technology Limited (TTL), imposing a €345 million fine. The inquiry examined TTL's compliance with the GDPR regarding processing of personal data relating to child users of the TikTok platform during the period from 31 July 2020 to 31 December 2020, as well as certain transparency obligations, including information provided to child users about default settings.

On 13 September 2022, the DPC submitted a draft decision to all Supervisory Authorities Concerned (CSAs) under Article 60(3) GDPR, proposing findings of infringement of Articles 5(1)(c), 5(1)(f), 24(1), 25(1), 25(2), 12(1) and 13(1)(e) GDPR. While there was broad consensus, objections were raised by the SAs of Italy and Berlin (the latter acting on behalf of itself and the Baden-Württemberg SA). The Berlin SA sought an additional finding of infringement of the Article 5(1)(a) GDPR principle of fairness regarding 'dark patterns,' while the Italian SA sought to reverse the DPC's proposed finding of compliance with Article 25 GDPR regarding age verification. The DPC referred the objections to the EDPB under the Article 65 GDPR dispute resolution mechanism.

The EDPB adopted its binding decision on 2 August 2023, directing the DPC to amend its draft decision to include a new finding of infringement of the Article 5(1)(a) fairness principle and to extend the scope of the existing order regarding remedial work. The DPC's final decision, adopted on 1 September 2023, records findings of infringement of Articles 5(1)(c), 5(1)(f), 24(1), 25(1), 25(2), 12(1), 13(1)(e) and 5(1)(a) GDPR, and exercises corrective powers. The fine of €345 million represents one of the largest GDPR penalties issued against a major tech platform.

The EDPB wants to make GDPR compliance "easy" in 2026. The 2025 annual report shows how they are rolling out helpful new templates, and also fighting a massive multi-front war at the CJEU. In the latest episode of the Privacy Partnership Podcast, I dig into the EDPB's newly published Annual Report, with a focus on what's coming down the pipeline. Following last year's Helsinki Statement, the EDPB has seemingly realised that GDPR compliance is quite hard, particularly for smaller businesses. (I maintain that this is true. It's doable, of course, but it's complicated, and there are a lot of moving targets) So, early this year we are getting a harmonised DPIA template, followed by a pan-European data breach notification template. They are also launching a web form allowing stakeholders to signal inconsistencies between national DPA guidance and EDPB guidance. -- But it's not all peace and harmonisation. The EDPB is has been juggling 15 cases before the CJEU. Meta is practically single-handedly testing the EDPB's litigation defence, fighting binding decisions on children's data, behavioural advertising, and "consent or pay". TikTok and WhatsApp are also in the mix. The Board also spent time fighting off annulment actions from the Irish DPC over jurisdictional competence, and is currently entangled in an appeal brought by the European Commission itself. Nobody, it seems, likes being told what to do by the EDPB. -- Looking ahead, we can expect joint EDPB-Commission guidelines on the interplay between the AI Act and the GDPR later this year. We are also watching the brewing battle over the Digital Omnibus. I break down the EDPB's litigation troubles and the 2026 regulatory pipeline in this week's episode.

🤖🇦🇹The Austrian Federal Administrative Court dealt with the scope of Article 15(1)(h) [#GDPR](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fgdpr&trk=public_post-text) in a case concerning credit scoring by a commercial credit reference agency. The data subject requested access to her personal data. It claimed that the controller’s response was incomplete, in particular as to the source of the data and the manner in which her creditworthiness scores were generated. The Austrian DPA partially upheld the complaint and ordered the controller to provide meaningful information about the logic underlying the creditworthiness assessment. The controller challenged that decision, arguing that Article 15(1)(h) GDPR did not apply because no decision solely based on automated processing within the meaning of Article 22(1) GDPR had been taken. In particular, the scores had not been disclosed to third parties and had not produced legal effects or similarly significant effects for the data subject. The Court found that the controller operated as a credit reference agency and used automated processing to calculate scores predicting the probability of payment default or payment irregularities. In its access response, the controller had informed the data subject that it processed three creditworthiness values: a RiskIndicator, a WirtschaftlichkeitsIndex and a KKE score. The Court accepted that these scores had not been disclosed to third parties and had not otherwise affected the data subject. The data subject’s assertion that there had only “allegedly” been no disclosure was considered speculative, as she did not provide substantiated information or evidence despite being invited to do so. The Court read Article 15(1)(h) GDPR together with Articles 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g) and 22 GDPR. It held that the additional right of access to meaningful information about the logic involved applies where there is automated decision-making within the meaning of Article 22 of the GDPR. The phrase “at least in those cases” was not interpreted as imposing the same obligation on all automated processing outside Article 22 of the GDPR. Relying on CJEU judgments C-634/21 and C-203/22, and Austrian Supreme Administrative Court case law, the Court recalled that Article 22(1) GDPR requires three cumulative conditions: a decision; a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling; and legal effects or similarly significant effects for the data subject. The Court accepted that the automated creditworthiness assessment could constitute a decision and that it was based solely on automated processing. The decisive issue was the third condition, i.e. the impact. In this case, the scores remained internal: they were not transmitted to potential contractual partners, were not relied on by any third party, and were not shown to have influenced the data subject’s housing search or any other decision concerning her. The Court therefore found that the required effect on the data subject was missing.

Double standards: On the Digital Omnibus re GDPR, the EDPB & EDPS claim the Commission shouldn't have the power to adopt implementing acts to "specify means and criteria to determine whether data resulting from pseudonymisation no longer constitutes personal data for certain entities". Yet under the Digital Markets Act, no problem at all. The situations are "firmly different", said the EDPB & EDPS, because under the [#DMA](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fdma&trk=public_post-text) the Commission is empowered "as enforcer of the DMA to specify the measures that the gatekeeper concerned is to implement in order to effectively comply with the obligations laid down in the DMA", while under the Digital Omnibus re GDPR, the proposed Article 41a [#GDPR](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fgdpr&trk=public_post-text) would allow the Commission "to set out general means and criteria applicable to all controllers for assessing whether data resulting from pseudonymisation no longer constitutes personal data". This is a bit of a fallacy. Where a term is not made specific in law, it is not meant to be an autonomous concept. "Anonymisation" is not defined in the DMA or in the GDPR, so it should be interpreted the same way. This means that "anonymisation of personal data" under the DMA (= an obligation as far as search query data is concerned) is not supposed to be any different from the idea of anonymisation of personal data (to which Recital 26 GDPR refers). As a result, Commission requirements for anonymisation will be at least indirectly relevant for *all* controllers, as they tell us what is deemed "anonymous". Pretending that the search context makes them irrelevant is unhelpful to everyone, from businesses who need rules to be clear and workable, to data subjects who need enforceable rules. Different standards don't make rules enforceable, clear or workable. In this context, the EDPB/EDPS fear that an implementing act pursuant to the Digital Omnibus "could de facto affect the material scope of EU data protection law, effectively redefining the scope of when and for whom information is considered personal data" is not a great excuse, as this has *already materialised* - based on a power foreseen by law since over 3 years. In practice, this is a turf war born out of bad law. We need *one* authority to be able to tell us what is or is not / no longer personal data - and for that authority's positions to be clearly challengeable. Accountability and consistency, to allow for greater legal certainty and foreseeability. Perhaps then what we really need out of the Digital Omnibus is a change to Article 70 of the GDPR? Or a de-coupling of the power to dictate interpretation and the power of enforcement? More on the Commission's approach to anonymisation of personal data under Art. 6(11) DMA and some of the issues it raises in [#dataprotection](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fdataprotection&trk=public_post-text) terms: [https://lnkd.in/euu2b9es](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2Feuu2b9es&urlhash=BhvQ&trk=public_post-text)

One GDPR question. 28 articles. Most compliance advice covers 7. Here's the question: "I have a platform in the EU. Minors and adults can both access it. I need to collect and process data. Which legal basis should I use, what obligations do I have, and what case law should I know?" Looks like a single question. It isn't. A complete answer requires 28 GDPR articles across 7 distinct clusters: 1. Legal basis Art. 6 (legal bases), Art. 7 (consent conditions), Art. 8 (children's consent), Art. 9 (special categories) 2. Core principles Art. 5 - lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimisation, storage limitation, accountability. Everything else is downstream of this. 3. Transparency Arts. 12, 13, 14 - what you tell users, when, and how 4. Data subject rights Arts. 15-22 - access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection, automated decisions 5. Controller obligations Arts. 24, 25, 26, 28, 30 - responsibility, privacy by design, joint controller agreements, processor contracts, records of processing 6. Security infrastructure Arts. 32-35, 37-39 - security measures, DPIAs, breach notification, DPO appointment 7. Transfers and remedies Arts. 44-49, 77-79, 82, 83 Then case law on top: C-252/21 (Meta - when a dominant market position undermines consent), C-446/21 (data minimisation - sexual orientation data inferred from platform behaviour). And primary law underneath all of it: Art. 7/8/24 of the EU Charter, Art. 16 TFEU. The constitutional layer that most GDPR advice doesn't reference at all. Most answers to this question stop at cluster 1. Maybe cluster 2. Clusters 4-7 are where enforcement actually happens. Save this. It's the scope of analysis the question actually requires.

Most organizations transferring data outside the EU are doing it wrong. They’re working from a mental model that is outdated. The GDPR says: “Any processing of personal data is prohibited but subjected to the possibility of authorization. In addition to consent, Art. 6 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) sets forth further authorization reasons, such as fulfilling a contract or protecting vital interests. For special personal data which requires a higher level of protection, the Art. 9 of the GDPR provides separate legal requirements. If the intended data transfer meets the general requirements, one must check in a second step whether transfer to the third country is permitted. One must differentiate between secure and unsecure third countries. Secure third countries are those for which the European Commission has confirmed a suitable level of data protection on the basis of an adequacy decision.” ([https://lnkd.in/dCEtbG2v](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FdCEtbG2v&urlhash=Mwu3&trk=public_post-text)) In 2026, the gap between what organizations think is compliant and what is really compliant significantly widened. The fundamental rule is the following: Transferring personal data outside the EU is prohibited by default, unless a specific legal basis exists that makes it permissible. Most organizations understand this in theory, but they still haven’t built the two-stage verification process that, in practice, GDPR actually requires. These stages are the following: 1. Is the transfer itself legal? An organization must ask whether the transfer is lawful at all. Article 6 of the GDPR requires a lawful basis for any processing, and data transfer is also processing. From contract performance to consent, each aspect is subject to specific conditions that must be met. Special category data, like health, is the subject of Article 9 of GDPR. Most organizations check this stage loosely and go straight to stage two. That means going backwards. 2. Is the destination country safe? Only when the first stage is cleared can the second stage begin. Here, most organizations are working from outdated information. GDPR states: “The third countries which ensure an adequate level of protection are: Andorra, Argentina, Canada (only commercial organizations), Faroe Islands, Guernsey, Israel, Isle of Man, Jersey, New Zealand, Switzerland, Uruguay , Japan, the United Kingdom and South Korea. Data transfer to these countries is expressly permitted.” ([https://lnkd.in/dCEtbG2v](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FdCEtbG2v&urlhash=Mwu3&trk=public_post-text)) This is the complete list. And the US is not on it! Since July 2023, there has been an adequacy decision covering the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. It applies only to US companies and organizations formally certified under that framework. In other cases, you need another legal mechanism. Now, the question is: Did your organization conduct both of these phases thoroughly? args.summary:
This is a LinkedIn post and podcast episode by Robert Bateman (Privacy Partnership Podcast) analyzing the EDPB's newly published 2025 Annual Report, focusing on the regulator's 2026 priorities and its extensive litigation before the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU).

**Compliance Simplification Initiatives (2026):**
- Following the July 2025 Helsinki Statement, the EDPB acknowledged that GDPR compliance is difficult, especially for small and medium-sized businesses.
- Early 2026: A harmonised Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) template is expected.
- Later in 2026: A pan-European data breach notification template is expected.
- A new web form will allow stakeholders to signal inconsistencies between national DPA guidance and EDPB guidelines.

**Litigation at the CJEU:**
- The EDPB was a party to 15 cases before the CJEU in 2025, with many continuing into 2026.
- Meta is challenging EDPB binding decisions on children's data (Instagram), behavioural advertising, data transfers outside the EU, and the "consent or pay" model.
- TikTok and WhatsApp also have ongoing annulment actions against EDPB decisions.
- In January 2025, the General Court closed three cases where the Irish DPC sued the EDPB over jurisdictional competence.
- The European Commission is currently appealing a General Court ruling related to accessing an EDPB case file.

**2026 Regulatory Pipeline:**
- Joint EDPB and European Commission guidelines on the interplay between the AI Act and GDPR are expected later in 2026 (following a similar DMA-GDPR collaboration).
- There is a brewing battle over the Digital Omnibus proposed in November 2025. The EDPB and EDPS pushed back hard against the Commission's proposal to alter the definition of personal data, arguing it would significantly narrow the concept and ignore CJEU jurisprudence. The EDPB did support other omnibus elements like increasing the risk threshold for data breach notification.
- The EDPB has secured a staff increase for 2026 despite tight budget constraints.

The page also includes several related posts flagged by LinkedIn's algorithm, including: an Austrian case on automated credit scoring under Art. 15(1)(h) GDPR, GDPR enforcement trends (€7.1 billion in fines, 60% targeting transparency), a critique of EDPB/EDPS positions on the Digital Omnibus pseudonymisation provisions, and a discussion on whether data protection law is entering a phase of recalibration (featuring Professor Herke Kranenborg and Case C-492/23 Russmedia).

# CNIL fines Google and Facebook over cookie consent

[Home](https://www.activemind.legal/) » [Guides](https://www.activemind.legal/guides/) » CNIL fines Google and Facebook over cookie consent

[![Klaus Foitzick](https://storage.activemind.legal/wp-am-legal-cdn/wp-content/uploads/activeMind-Klaus-Foitzick-1024x768.jpg)](https://www.activemind.legal/office/experts/klaus-foitzick/)

### [Klaus Foitzick](https://www.activemind.legal/office/experts/klaus-foitzick/)

[Lawyer / Managing Director](https://www.activemind.legal/office/experts/klaus-foitzick/)

* Last update:
* Reading time: 2 minutes

The French data protection authority (CNIL) recently fined [Google](https://www.cnil.fr/en/cookies-cnil-fines-google-total-150-million-euros-and-facebook-60-million-euros-non-compliance) and [Facebook](https://www.cnil.fr/en/cookies-facebook-ireland-limited-fined-60-million-euros) with high fines for failing to obtain cookie consent in compliance with French data protection law. Both companies did not ensure that refusing cookies is as simple as accepting them. In this article we will show you what this means for your company.

## High fines for insufficient cookie consent

CNIL issued a combined fine of EUR 150 million against two Google subsidiaries and a EUR 60 million fine against Facebook. CNIL based its decisions on the fact that users are not able to reject cookies on some of Googles’ and Facebooks’ websites as easily as they can accept them.

In Google’s case, on the websites google.fr and youtube.com, cookies could be accepted with just one click, but several clicks were necessary to reject them. Also in Facebook’s case, on facebook.com, several clicks were necessary to refuse cookies. Moreover, users had to click on a button titled “Accept cookies” to refuse cookies, which is also misleading.

Based on this, CNIL argued that Google and Facebook violated Article 82 of the French Data protection Act, which implements Art. 5 (3) of the ePrivacy Directive into French national law. Hence, similar provisions exist in all EU countries. Art 5 (3) stipulates that cookies or similar technologies may only be used with prior consent of the data subject.

Google and Facebook now have to adjust their websites in order to comply with French law within three months. For each day of delay they will have to pay EUR 100,000.

## Importance of obtaining cookie consent in compliance with data protection law

The decision by the French data protection authority sets an important precedent. Hence, it becomes even more important for your company to ensure that you obtain valid user consent, if you use cookies. This is especially the case as consumer associations are issuing more and more complaints against companies with non-compliant cookie banners ([e.g. privacy advocate Max Schrems’ organisation noyb](https://www.activemind.legal/guides/complaints-cookie-banners/)) and are also increasingly bringing cases on behalf of individuals to supervisory authorities and courts.

## Valid consent for the use of cookies

Art. 5 (3) ePrivacy Directive stipulates that cookies or similar technologies may only be used with prior consent of the data subject. Exceptions exist only for cookies that are strictly necessary for the operation of the respective website, e.g. session cookies. For all other cookies, like advertising cookies or analysis cookies, website operators must obtain the informed consent of the users.

For consent to be valid, it has to be obtained before you collect any data through cookies and in compliance with the standard set out in [Art. 4 (11) GDPR.](https://www.activemind.legal/legislation/gdpr/article-4/) Hence, it must be “freely given, specific and informed”. Therefore, information on the tracked data and the purposes of the tracking has to be provided in an easily understandable way. Moreover, as the CNIL fines showed again, it must be possible to reject and withdraw cookie as easily as accepting them.

More detailed information on how cookie consent can be validly obtained and how respective cookie banners should be designed [can be found here.](https://www.activemind.legal/guides/complaints-cookie-banners/)

# FRANCE: Cookies – new record sanctions for tech giants – CNIL fines Facebook Ireland 60 million euros and Google 150 million euros.

By [yaelhirsch](https://privacymatters.dlapiper.com/author/yaelhirsch/) on

Posted in [Uncategorized](https://privacymatters.dlapiper.com/category/uncategorized/)

**On 31 December 2021, the restricted committee of the French Data Protection Supervisory Authority (“CNIL”) (i) fined [Facebook Ireland](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/cnil/id/CNILTEXT000044840532?isSuggest=true) 60 million euros and [Google](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/cnil/id/CNILTEXT000044840062) a total of 150 million euros (i.e., 90 million euros for Google LLC and 60 million euros for Google Ireland Limited) for failing to allow the users of facebook.com, google.fr and youtube.com to reject cookies as easily as they may accept them and (ii) issued an injunction to remedy to such infringement within 3 months under penalty of 100,000 euros per day of delay.**

**Regardless of the very substantial amount of fines applied, in a context where the CNIL’s issues several formal notices for non-compliances with cookies regulations since the end of March 2021, these decisions give an opportunity to analyze what are the CNIL’s expectations and what sanctions may be anticipated for companies targeting French users through their websites.**

***1. Context of the infringements sanctioned***

The CNIL’s decisions were taken further to:

* several complaints lodged with the CNIL regarding **Facebook Ireland, Google LLC and Google Ireland Limited (“the Companies”)** practices with respect to their use of cookies, between October 2020 and July 2021, respectively four complaints against Facebook and two against Google; and
* online investigations conducted by the CNIL onto the Companies’ websites, which revealed that they were failing to comply with the requirements governing cookies under Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act.

Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act and the CNIL guidelines dated and [17 September 2020](https://www.cnil.fr/sites/default/files/atoms/files/lignes_directrices_de_la_cnil_sur_les_cookies_et_autres_traceurs.pdf), require that the Website cookies banner offers users the option to reject cookies as easily as they may accept them. However, although the Companies banner displayed a button allowing to immediately accept cookies, it does not offer an equivalent solution (button or other) enabling the user to reject the deposit of cookies as easily. Several clicks were necessary to reject all cookies (3 for Facebook and 5 for Google), when only one click was necessary to accept them all.

The restricted committee, which is the body responsible for issuing sanction within the CNIL, ruled that such a method affected the users’ freedom of consent and thus an infringement of Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act, as the several steps implemented to refuse cookies was a way to discourage users from rejecting them while favoring an opt-in which is more easy to choose.

The restricted committee does not challenge the fact that the Companies offer a choice to accept or refuse cookies but more the practical implementation of the refusal mechanism which is either complex (for Google where the user has to click on a “personalize button” and to go through a detailed page presenting cookies to make his choice) or unclear (notably for Facebook where the “cookies set up page” was leading to an acceptance button which was confusing regarding the nature of cookies accepted). The restricted committee reminds that next to an “Accept all” Button, a “Refusal all” button must be implemented.

***2. Justification of the sanctions level***

Based on the above infringement, the restricted committee issued:

* two fines against Google for a total amount of 150 million euros (i.e., 90 million euros for Google LLC and 60 million euros for Google Ireland Limited); and
* one fine against Facebook Ireland of 60 million euros

Such fines are based on the following considerations:

* the scope of the processing;
* the high number of data subjects;
* the substantial profits generated by the Companies from advertising, using the data collected through cookies placed with a biased consent whereas other companies which have duly offered users the opportunity to reject all cookies as easily as to accept them have seen a decrease in the number of consents and thus their advertising revenues;
* the fact that the Companies were already made aware of their lack of compliance with Article 82 of the French Data protection Act, by the CNIL; and
* the continuous CNIL’s communication on the necessity to ensure that refusal of cookies should be as easy of their acceptance

It is interesting to note that while the fine issued against Facebook was applied to Facebook Ireland Limited considered as the sole data controller, Facebook France being the “establishment” of the Facebook group in France, the fine against Google was applied to both Google LLC based in California and Google Ireland Limited considered as joint controllers.

In addition, the CNIL issued an injunction for each Company to remedy to their practices in order to guarantee the users’ freedom of consent within three months as from the notification of the CNIL’s decision, subject to a late payment penalty of 100.000 EUR per day.

These sanctions fall within the global conformity strategy regarding cookies that the CNIL started about 2 years ago. Since 31 March 2021, the CNIL has issued almost 100 formal notices related to cookies infringements of French and Foreign websites (including order to comply with the Cookies regulation and sanctions).

***3. CNIL remains competent even if a Lead Authority has been appointed***

The Companies attempted to challenge the CNIL’s competence as they appointed a Lead Authority which is the Irish Data Protection Commissioner.

The restricted committee decision is grounded on the following considerations:

a. Material competence

The CNIL remains materially competent to investigate and sanction operations related to cookies deposited by the company on the terminals of Internet users located in France. The CNIL used the same rationale as in previous decisions regarding the use of cookies (notably, [sanction pronounced on 7 December 2020 against Google](https://blogs.dlapiper.com/privacymatters/europe-cookies-heavy-sanction-by-the-cnil-in-france-for-google-llc-and-google-ireland/)) to challenge Google’s defense arguing that the French data protection authority was not competent to control cookies policies.

The CNIL held that the “one stop shop” mechanism set forth in the GDPR does not apply to the extent its action was related to Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act, which transposes the provisions of the “e-Privacy” directive into French law.

According to the restricted committee:

* a distinction has to be made between *on the one hand, the operations consisting in depositing and reading cookies in a user’s terminal and, on the other hand, the subsequent use made of the data generated by these cookies, for example for profiling purposes, referred to as “subsequent processing” (also known as “post processing”).*
* Each of these two successive stages is subject to a different legal regime*: while read and/or write operations are governed by special rules, set out in Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive* and thus to the CNIL’s competence*, further processing is subject to the GDPR and, as such, may be subject to the “one-stop shop” mechanism, if they relate to transborder data processing activities.*

Therefore, as the present procedure related only to the reading and/or writing operations in the terminal of users located in France, the CNIL’s competence is confirmed.

b. Territorial competence

The CNIL remains also territorially competent pursuant to Article 3 of the French Data Protection Act since the use of cookies is carried out within the “framework of the activities” of the French local companies (Facebook France and Google France), which constitutes the respective “establishment” of the Companies on French territory.

Each Company has the opportunity to lodge an appeal against the CNIL decisions before the Council of State, highest French Administrative Court.

Google already appealed the previous CNIL’s decision on cookies dated December 2020 but such appeal was rejected by the Council of State in March 2021.

For any question related to this decision, please contact [Denise Lebeau-Marianna](mailto:Denise.Lebeau-Marianna@dlapiper.com), Partner or [Yaël Hirsch](mailto:yael.hirsch@dlapiper.com), senior associate – Data Protection – IPT Department DLA Piper France LLP.

Authors: Denise Lebeau-Marianna,  Yaël Hirsch, Paul Sierzputowski

On 31 December 2021, the French data protection authority (CNIL) imposed record cookie fines: 60 million euros on Facebook Ireland and a total of 150 million euros on Google (90 million for Google LLC and 60 million for Google Ireland Limited). The companies failed to allow users of facebook.com, google.fr, and youtube.com to reject cookies as easily as they could accept them. While banners displayed a button for immediate cookie acceptance, users needed several clicks to reject all cookies (3 for Facebook, 5 for Google). The CNIL also issued injunctions requiring remediation within 3 months under penalty of 100,000 euros per day of delay.

The fines were based on several factors: the scope of processing, the high number of data subjects, substantial advertising profits generated through biased consent, the companies' prior awareness of non-compliance, and ongoing CNIL communications about cookie refusal requirements. Facebook Ireland was treated as sole data controller, while Google LLC and Google Ireland were considered joint controllers.

The decisions stemmed from complaints lodged between October 2020 and July 2021 (four against Facebook, two against Google) and online CNIL investigations. The rulings were grounded in Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (transposing Article 5(3) of the e-Privacy Directive) and CNIL guidelines of 17 September 2020. The CNIL maintained jurisdiction despite the companies' Lead Authority (the Irish DPC), arguing the "one-stop shop" GDPR mechanism does not apply to cookie read/write operations, which fall under the e-Privacy Directive and CNIL competence. The CNIL also asserted territorial competence since cookies were used within the activities of French establishments (Facebook France and Google France). This action is part of a broader CNIL cookies enforcement strategy; since March 2021, it has issued nearly 100 formal notices about cookie infringements. The companies may appeal to the Council of State.

PARIS, Jan 6 (Reuters) - France's data privacy watchdog CNIL said on Thursday it had fined Alphabet's Google [(GOOGL.O), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/companies/GOOGL.O/) a record 150 million euros ($169 million) for making it difficult for internet users to refuse online trackers known as cookies.

Meta Platforms' Facebook [(FB.O), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/companies/FB.O/) was also fined 60 million euros for the same reason, the CNIL said.

Internet users' prior consent for the use of cookies -- tiny snippets of data that help build targeted digital ad campaigns -- is a key pillar of the European Union's data privacy regulation and a top priority for the CNIL.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

"When you accept cookies, it's done in just one click," said Karin Kiefer, CNIL's head for data protection and sanctions. "Rejecting cookies should be as easy as accepting them".

In its statement, the watchdog said it had found that the facebook.com, google.fr and youtube.com websites didn't allow the refusal of cookies easily, citing Google's video-streaming platform.

The CNIL said the two companies had three months to comply with its orders or face an extra penalty payment of 100,000 euros per day of delay.

These include the obligation for Google and Facebook to provide French internet users simpler tools for refusing cookies, in order to guarantee their consent.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

The CNIL said that while Google and Facebook provided a virtual button to allow the immediate acceptance of cookies, there was no equivalent to refuse them as easily.

"People trust us to respect their right to privacy and keep them safe. We understand our responsibility to protect that trust and are committing to further changes and active work with the CNIL in light of this decision," a Google spokesperson said.

Facebook did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

CNIL's previous record fine in 2020 also targeted Google and amounted to 100 million euros.

At the time, the CNIL found that Google's French websites didn't seek the prior consent of visitors before advertising cookies were saved on computers and failed to provide clear information about how it intended to make use of them. [read more](https://www.reuters.com/world/french-watchdog-fines-google-amazon-breaching-cookies-rules-2020-12-10/)

Kiefer said the issues have been resolved since then.

In 2020, the CNIL strengthened consent rights over ad trackers, saying websites operating in France should keep a register of internet users' refusal to accept cookies for at least six months.

It also said internet users should be able to easily reconsider any initial agreement concerning cookies via a web link or an icon that should be visible on all the website pages.

args.summary:
On January 6, 2022, France's data privacy watchdog CNIL fined Alphabet's Google a record 150 million euros ($169 million) and Meta Platforms' Facebook 60 million euros for making it difficult for internet users to refuse online cookies (tracking snippets used for targeted digital advertising). The decision stemmed from findings that facebook.com, google.fr, and youtube.com websites did not allow easy refusal of cookies - both companies provided a one-click button to accept cookies but no equivalent to reject them.

The CNIL gave both companies three months to comply with orders to provide French internet users simpler tools for refusing cookies, or face additional penalty payments of 100,000 euros per day of delay. This was a second fine for Google over cookie breaches - the CNIL's previous record fine in 2020 also targeted Google for 100 million euros over failing to seek prior consent for advertising cookies, although CNIL noted those earlier issues had since been resolved.

A Google spokesperson said the company understood its responsibility to protect user trust and was committing to further changes and active work with the CNIL. Facebook did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The enforcement reflects that prior consent for cookie use is a key pillar of EU data privacy regulation and a top priority for the CNIL. Earlier 2020 CNIL actions also strengthened consent rights by requiring websites operating in France to keep registers of users' cookie refusals for at least six months and to allow users to easily reconsider cookie agreements via visible web links or icons on all website pages.

# CNIL fines Google and Facebook a total of €210 million over cookies

In 2021, CNIL fined Facebook €60 million and Google €150 million for making it harder to refuse cookies than to accept them, violating the French Data Protection Act and ePrivacy requirements.

### Tags

[GDPR fines](https://legit.eu/tag/gdpr-fines/)

The French Data Protection Authority – **CNIL** (**[Commission Nationale de l’Informatique et des Libertés](https://www.cnil.fr/en/cnils-missions)**) fined **Facebook €60 million** and **Google €150 million** for non-compliance with the French Data Protection Act.

Facebook is a social media giant with over **[2.895 billion monthly active users](https://www.wallstreetzen.com/stocks/us/nasdaq/meta/statistics)**, and at least 1.908 billion people use Facebook every day.

**Google**, on the other hand, is the most visited website in the whole world, with over **92 billion visits** last March of 2021. And did you know that 92.41% of the search engine segment is controlled by Google?

After numerous complaints and online investigations, CNIL concluded that both Facebook and Google failed to make it as easy to reject cookies as it is to accept them.

While websites offer a button allowing a **single click to accept cookies,** they do not provide an equivalent solution that would allow users to **refuse cookies just as easily**.

The fine was issued by French CNIL rather than the Irish Data Protection Commission (lead supervisory authority for Facebook and Google) as cookies fall under the **[ePrivacy Directive](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32002L0058#PP1Contents),** which is embedded into French Data Protection Act and not GDPR.

However, GDPR still regulates consent, and therefore, fines can qualify as a GDPR fine.

## Facebook **€60 million fine**

On the last day of 2021, **[CNIL issued a €60 million fine to Facebook](https://www.cnil.fr/en/cookies-facebook-ireland-limited-fined-60-million-euros)** Ireland Limited.

The investigation, which started in April, uncovered that, as opposed to a **single button to accept cookies**, Facebook requires several clicks to refuse cookies.

In addition, the button to refuse cookies is **located at the bottom of a second page** and was labeled “Accept cookies,” which was not only confusing but also misleading.

## Google **€150 million fine**

In June 2021, the CNIL carried out an **online investigation** on websites google.fr and youtube.com and found that, while Google offers a button allowing users to immediately accept cookies, to reject them, they have to go through at least five different actions.

Following the investigation, the **[CNIL issued a €150 million fine to Google](https://www.cnil.fr/en/cookies-google-fined-150-million-euros)** (€90 million fine to Google LLC and €60 million for Google Ireland Limited) on account of their findings.

The restricted committee, the **CNIL body in charge of issuing sanctions**, stated that “*making the refusal mechanism more complex actually discourages users from refusing cookies and encourages them to opt for the ease of the “I accept” button*“.

## Conclusion

Both Google and Facebook ignored cookie recommendations and cookie guidelines that clearly state that organizations must offer to users the possibility to accept or refuse online trackers with the same degree of simplicity.

The CNIL ordered the companies to provide users in France with a means of refusing cookies as simple as the existing means of accepting them **within three months**.

If they fail to do so within three-months time, the companies will have to pay a penalty of **€100 thousand per day of delay**.

The amount of the fine is determined considering the number of data subjects involved, the scope of processing, and the profits of companies, which are mostly generated through the company’s advertising streams based on cookies.

args.summary:
In 2021, the French Data Protection Authority (CNIL) fined Facebook €60 million and Google €150 million (totaling €210 million) for violating the French Data Protection Act and ePrivacy requirements by making it harder to refuse cookies than to accept them. CNIL found that while both companies offered a single-click button to accept cookies, they did not provide an equivalent easy solution to refuse them. The fines were issued by CNIL rather than the Irish DPC (the lead supervisory authority for these companies) because cookie requirements fall under the ePrivacy Directive embedded in French law, though GDPR still regulates consent and fines can qualify as GDPR fines.

Facebook's €60 million fine (issued December 31, 2021, after an investigation starting in April) stemmed from its refusal mechanism requiring several clicks, with the refusal button located at the bottom of a second page and misleadingly labeled "Accept cookies." Google's €150 million fine (split €90 million for Google LLC and €60 million for Google Ireland Limited) resulted from a June 2021 investigation of google.fr and youtube.com, which found that rejecting cookies required at least five actions versus one click to accept.

CNIL's restricted committee stated that "making the refusal mechanism more complex actually discourages users from refusing cookies and encourages them to opt for the ease of the 'I accept' button." The CNIL ordered both companies to provide French users with a means of refusing cookies as simple as accepting them within three months, with a penalty of €100 thousand per day of delay for non-compliance. Fine amounts were determined considering the number of data subjects, scope of processing, and company profits largely derived from cookie-based advertising.

--- SOURCE 1: Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) GDPR Fines ---
URL: https://gdprfine.com/dpa/ireland-dpc

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a reference profile of the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC), the most-fined GDPR regulator by cumulative amount. Ireland is the EU establishment of choice for US Big Tech, making the DPC the lead supervisory authority (under Article 56 GDPR) for the largest single-issuer fines on the register. ~25 headline decisions are indexed, with the largest single fine being €1.2 billion (Meta 2023) and 5+ EDPB Article 65 cases since 2021. The DPC has been active since 1989 (GDPR: 2018).

**Mandate and constitution:** The DPC is designated under Article 51 GDPR, and as lead authority for controllers with main EU establishment in Ireland. Established under the Data Protection Act 1988, modernised under the Data Protection Act 2018. It reports to the Oireachtas through the Minister for Justice, with headquarters in Dublin (Fitzwilliam Square) and a satellite office in Portarlington. Staff grew from ~110 in 2018 to more than 230 by 2026.

**Fining philosophy:** Characterised by long inquiry timelines (3-5 years), detailed factual analysis, and rigorous Article 83(2) factor-by-factor weighting. Critics accuse the DPC of being insufficiently aggressive; the EDPB Article 65 mechanism has repeatedly recalibrated fines upward (WhatsApp: €30-50M draft to €225M final; Meta Chapter V case).

**Headline decisions:** WhatsApp €225M (Sept 2021, following EDPB BD 1/2021, first ever Article 65 decision); Instagram €405M children's data (Sept 2022, EDPB BD 2/2022); two Meta Ireland decisions totalling €390M (Jan 2023, contractual lawful basis for personalised advertising); Meta €1.2B Chapter V transfer decision (May 2023, largest GDPR fine to date, following EDPB BD 1/2023); TikTok €345M children's data (Sept 2023, EDPB BD 2/2023); TikTok €530M Chapter V China transfers (May 2025, second-largest single GDPR fine).

**Statistical record:** Cumulative DPC fines exceed €3 billion. Distribution is highly skewed; Big Tech share is ~95% of total in years with major decisions, and median annual fine count is in the tens. Complaint volumes rose steadily, exceeding 11,000 in 2024. --- SOURCE 2: Meta €265 Million DPC Fine: 2022 Facebook Data-Scraping Decision Explained | GDPRFine.com ---
URL: https://gdprfine.com/cases/meta-265-million-dpc-2022

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 25 November 2022 (announced 28 November 2022), the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) imposed a €265 million administrative fine on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (MPIL) over the Facebook "data scraping" incident, concluding an inquiry opened after a dataset of Facebook user data was published online in April 2021.

The inquiry covered Facebook Search, Facebook Messenger Contact Importer, and Instagram Contact Importer tools, and processing between 25 May 2018 and September 2019. During that period, third parties abused these tools to match large lists of phone numbers against user profiles, compiling personal data on more than 500 million users from over 100 countries (including names, Facebook IDs, phone numbers, locations, dates of birth, and email addresses). The incident was not a conventional security breach; the data was assembled by exploiting features working as built because they lacked safeguards against enumeration and bulk matching. The DPC therefore centered the inquiry on Data Protection by Design and Default rather than Article 32 security of processing.

The DPC found infringements of Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR (Data Protection by Design and by Default), concluding that Meta's contact-import and search features did not meet either obligation. Effective measures such as default-private settings, rate limiting, and controls on bulk enumeration were not built in by design or applied by default. Alongside the fine, the DPC imposed a reprimand and an order requiring MPIL to take specified remedial actions within a set timeframe. Article 25 infringements fall under the lower tier of Article 83(4), capped at €10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover; given Meta's scale the 2% ceiling sat well above €265 million, so the amount reflects the DPC's Article 83(2) assessment of gravity, duration, and the very large number of affected data subjects.

This fine is one of a series of large DPC decisions against Meta, distinct from the WhatsApp transparency fine (€225 million, 2021), the Instagram children's-data fine (€405 million, 2022), the contractual-basis fines (€390 million combined, 2023), and the €1.2 billion transfers fine (2023). It is the leading Article 25 decision in that group. The EDPB was involved through the Article 60 cooperation process (but not via a binding Article 65 decision, unlike the €1.2 billion transfers fine).

The practical lesson: Data Protection by Design and Default is an enforceable obligation with nine-figure exposure. Any feature allowing lookup, matching, or enumeration by identifier must be designed against abuse from the outset, and controllers are responsible for foreseeable misuse of their own tools under Article 25.
</summary>

The Irish Data Protection Commission fined Meta Platforms Ireland €265 million over the Facebook data-scraping incident, finding that the contact-import and search tools breached the Data Protection by Design and Default obligations in Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR.

# Cybersecurity Policy Report, Instagram Faces Fine in Ireland Over Handling of Children's Data, (Sep 15, 2022)

By [R. Jason Howard, J.D.](mailto:robert.howard@wolterskluwer.com)

The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) announced that it had reached a decision following an inquiry into Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd. concerning the processing of personal data relating to child users of the Instagram social networking service.

Ac ...

By [R. Jason Howard, J.D.](mailto:robert.howard@wolterskluwer.com)

The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) announced that it had reached a decision following an inquiry into Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd. concerning the processing of personal data relating to child users of the Instagram social networking service.

According to the DPC [press release](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/data-protection-commission-announces-decision-instagram-inquiry), the inquiry into Instagram was initiated by the DPC on Sept. 21, 2020, in response to information provided by a U.S. data scientist and findings by DPC following an examination of the Instagram user registration process. In particular, the DPC examined the "public disclosure of email addresses and/or phone numbers of children using the Instagram business account feature and a public-by-default setting for personal Instagram accounts of children."

In December 2021, the DPC submitted a draft decision to all European Union "concerned supervisory authorities" (CSAs) pursuant to Article 60 of the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Six of those regulators raised objections to the draft decision, and the DPC was unable to reach a consensus with those CSAs on the subject matter of the objections. The case was thereafter referred to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), pursuant to Article 65 of the GDPR concerning the dispute-resolution process.

In late July 2022, the EDPB adopted its binding [decision](https://edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/binding-decision-board-art-65/binding-decision-22022-dispute-arisen_en) that rejected a "considerable quantity" of the objections but upheld certain objections requiring that the DPC amend its draft decision to include a finding of infringement of Article 6(1) of the GDPR. The DPC, therefore, had to reassess its proposed administrative fines based on the inclusion of the infringement finding. Following incorporation of the amendments, the DPC's decision was adopted on Sept. 2.

The original DPC draft decision recommended a fine of up to 405 million euros ($404 million) and, "having taken account of the EDPB's binding decision, the fine imposed on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Instagram) totals €405 million (over $404 million), including a fine of €20 million (over $19 million) for the infringement of Article 6(1)."

In addition to the administrative fines, Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd. was reprimanded by the DPC and ordered to bring its processing into compliance by taking remedial actions.

args.summary:
The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) announced its decision following an inquiry into Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd. regarding the processing of personal data relating to child users of Instagram. The inquiry, initiated on Sept. 21, 2020, was triggered by information from a U.S. data scientist and DPC findings from examining the Instagram user registration process. The DPC specifically examined "the public disclosure of email addresses and/or phone numbers of children using the Instagram business account feature and a public-by-default setting for personal Instagram accounts of children."

In December 2021, the DPC submitted a draft decision to EU concerned supervisory authorities per Article 60 of the GDPR. Six regulators raised objections, and the case was referred to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) under Article 65 dispute-resolution. In late July 2022, the EDPB adopted a binding decision rejecting many objections but upholding certain objections requiring the DPC to amend its draft to include an infringement finding under Article 6(1) of the GDPR. Following the amendments, the DPC's final decision was adopted on Sept. 2, 2022.

The DPC imposed a total fine of €405 million ($404 million) on Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd. (Instagram), including €20 million ($19 million) specifically for the Article 6(1) infringement. Additionally, Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd. was reprimanded and ordered to bring its processing into compliance through remedial actions. # Instagram is under investigation over handling of children’s data

![Instagram under investigation](https://www.gdprregister.eu/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/instagram-children-data-1-900x600.jpg)

# **Instagram is being investigated by Ireland’s Data Protection Commissioner (DPC) over its handling of children’s personal data on the platform.**

The social media app’s owner Facebook could face a large fine if Instagram is found to have broken privacy laws.

The investigations stem from complaints that Instagram made contact information on business accounts publicly visible to anyone accessing the app.

The BBC has approached Facebook for comment.

A number of US tech giants have their European headquarters in Ireland, and the DPC is the lead European Union regulator under the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which came into force in 2018.

The DPC is responsible for protecting individuals’ right to online privacy, and has the power to issue large fines.

The Irish regulator is investigating whether Facebook has a [legal basis](/?p=1426) for processing children’s personal data and if it employs adequate protections and restrictions on Instagram for children.

Separately, it is also looking at whether Facebook has adhered with GDPR requirements in relation to Instagram’s profile and account settings. It is inquiring into whether Facebook is adequately protecting the data protection rights of children as vulnerable persons.

The minimum age for having an Instagram account is 13.

“Instagram is a social media platform which is used widely by children in Ireland and across Europe,” said Graham Doyle, a deputy commissioner with DPC.

“The DPC has been actively monitoring complaints received from individuals in this area and has identified potential concerns in relation to the processing of children’s personal data on Instagram which require further examination.”

## A parent’s worries

In February 2019, data scientist David Stier analysed profiles of almost 200,000 Instagram users across the world. He estimated that for over a year, at least 60 million users under the age of 18 were given the option to easily change their profiles into business accounts.

Instagram business accounts require users to display their phone numbers and email addresses publicly, meaning that personal data belonging to many users is visible to other Instagram users.

The same personal information was also contained in the HTML source code of web pages accessed when using Instagram on a computer, meaning that it could be “scraped” by hackers.

Mr Stier reported his findings to Facebook, but [he wrote in a Medium blog](https://medium.com/@davidjstier/instagram-shows-kids-phone-num-in-plain-sight-d03c8ab9d168) that Instagram had refused to mask the email addresses and phone numbers for business accounts.

However, Facebook did decide to remove the contact information from the source code of Instagram pages.

Despite this, Mr Stier believes that hackers might have succeeded in stealing the personal information from Instagram’s website, after it was revealed in May 2019 that [contact details relating to 49 million users were stored online in an unguarded database](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-asia-india-48347592) owned by a firm in India.

“Do we have a responsibility to keep kids’ phone numbers and emails hidden so that strangers can’t find them just by clicking a button?” wrote Mr Stier.

“Speaking as a parent, I want to be assured that the experience Instagram offers to teens is as ‘adult-overseen’ as possible.”

Irish Data Protection Commissioner Fines Instagram for Children's Privacy Violations

1 Minute Read

Categories: [Children’s Privacy](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/childrens-privacy), [European Union](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/european-union), [International](/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/category/international)

On September 5, 2022, the Irish Data Protection Commissioner (the “DPC”) imposed a €405,000,000 fine on Instagram (a Meta-owned social media platform) for violations of the EU General Data Protection Regulation’s (“GDPR’s”) rules on the processing of children’s personal data.

The fine is the result of an investigation that began in 2020 and focused on the company’s processing of children’s personal data. Based on press reports, the investigation focused on children between the ages of 13 and 17 who were allowed to operate business or creator Instagram accounts. As a result, children’s phone numbers and email addresses were publicly accessible.

The fine is the second-largest fine imposed by an EU regulator for GDPR violations. According to online sources, Meta plans to appeal the fine.

The DPC has not yet published an official statement about the fine.

args.summary:
This is a post from the Privacy & Cybersecurity Law Blog (a global privacy and cybersecurity law updates publication) reporting on the Irish Data Protection Commissioner's (DPC) actions against Instagram.

Key facts:
- On September 5, 2022, the Irish Data Protection Commissioner imposed a €405,000,000 (405 million euro) fine on Instagram, a Meta-owned social media platform.
- The fine was levied for violations of the EU General Data Protection Regulation's (GDPR) rules on the processing of children's personal data.
- The fine resulted from an investigation that began in 2020, focused on the company's processing of children's personal data.
- The investigation focused on children between the ages of 13 and 17 who were allowed to operate business or creator Instagram accounts, which resulted in children's phone numbers and email addresses being publicly accessible.
- This fine was the second-largest fine imposed by an EU regulator for GDPR violations at the time.
- Meta planned to appeal the fine.
- The DPC had not yet published an official statement about the fine at the time of writing.

Categories for the post include Children's Privacy, European Union, and International. It is a short article (1 Minute Read). The blog also lists recent posts and extensive archive/category/tag navigation for its content spanning from 2008 to 2026.

The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) found that Meta Platforms (formerly known as Facebook) violated the GDPR due to continuing to transfer personal information from the European Union to the United States following the *Schrems II* decision of the CJEU in reliance on the Standard Contractual Clauses (SCC). The fine, 1.2 billion Euros, is the largest fine imposed to date under the GDPR. The Irish Data Protection Commission also prohibited Meta from using SCC as a basis for transferring information from the EU to the United States.

The DPC found that the SCCs do not mitigate the risks to the fundamental rights and freedoms of EU data subjects, such as the possibility of US security and intelligence agencies collecting and monitoring extensive personal information of EU users on Facebook. While the decision specifically refers to Meta, it has direct implications for all information transfers from the EU to the United States.

In its initial draft decision, the DPC found that Meta violated the GDPR and, therefore, ordered Meta to cease the transfer of personal data from the EU to the United States. EU data protection authorities discussed this draft but failed to reach an agreement regarding the measures to be taken against Meta. Therefore, the DPC referred the matter to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) to resolve the dispute.

A few weeks ago, the EDPB reached its binding decision, which instructed the DPC to impose a fine in the range of 20% to 100% of the highest fine permitted under the GDPR and to change the processing and transfer of personal data. Following the EDPB decision, The Irish Data Protection Commission decided on a 1.2 billion Euro fine. It also ordered Meta to suspend all future transfers of personal information to the United States within five months from the date of the DPC’s notification to Meta Ireland. Finally, it requires Meta to suspend the unlawful processing and storage in the United States of existing personal data within six months.

Meta plans to appeal the decision of the DPC. It also indicated that it relied on the validity of the SCCs like thousands of other companies.

[Click here](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/Data-Protection-Commission-announces-conclusion-of-inquiry-into-Meta-Ireland) to read the press release of the Ireland Data Protection Commission.

[Click here](https://edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2023-05/edpb_bindingdecision_202301_ie_sa_facebooktransfers_redacted.pdf) to read the decision of the EDPB on the dispute submitted by the Irish SA on data transfers by Meta Platforms Ireland Limited for its Facebook service (Art. 65 GDPR).

[Click here](https://edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2023-05/final_for_issue_ov_transfers_decision_12-05-23.pdf) to read the final decision of the Irish Data Protection Commission in the matter of Meta Platforms.

# Irish Data Protection Commission Fines Meta €251 Million

The Irish DPC fined Meta €251 million for a 2018 breach exposing 29 million users’ data, highlighting GDPR violations and the need for robust privacy solutions like DPM.

### Tags

[GDPR fines](https://legit.eu/tag/gdpr-fines/)

The **[Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC)](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/who-we-are)** has issued a **€251 million fine to Meta Platforms** Ireland Limited following investigations into a significant data breach that occurred in 2018.

The breach exposed the personal information of **29 million Facebook users worldwide**, including three million within the European Union (EU) and European Economic Area (EEA).

The breach involved unauthorized **third parties exploiting user tokens** on the Facebook platform, granting access to a wide range of personal data.

The categories of personal data compromised included users’ full names, email addresses, phone numbers, locations, dates of birth, places of work, religion, gender, timeline posts, group memberships, and even data about children.

**Key GDPR Infringements and Fines**

The DPC identified multiple violations of GDPR:

* **Failure to Notify Adequately**: Meta did not provide all required information in its breach notification, resulting in a **€8 million fine** under **Article 33(3) GDPR**.
* **Inadequate Documentation**: Meta failed to properly document the breach and remediation efforts, leading to a **€3 million fine** under **Article 33(5)**.
* **Poor System Design**: Meta was found to have violated **Article 25(1) GDPR** by not integrating data protection principles in the design of its processing systems, resulting in a **€130 million fine**.
* **Default Data Protection Lapses**: Under **Article 25(2)**, Meta failed to ensure that only necessary personal data was processed by default, leading to a **€110 million fine**.

DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle emphasized the serious risks posed by such breaches, highlighting the exposure of sensitive information, including religious and political beliefs, and the potential for misuse of such data.

**Broader Implications**

This latest fine adds to Meta’s growing list of penalties from the DPC, including a €91 million fine earlier this year and a **[record €1.2 billion fine](https://legit.eu/resources/blog/meta-hit-with-record-e1-2b-gdpr-fine/)** last year for transferring EU user data to the US.

As the lead privacy regulator for many tech giants based in Ireland, the **DPC continues to play a pivotal role** in the EU’s crackdown on big tech.

Meta has announced plans to appeal the decision, reiterating its commitment to data security and its industry-leading measures to protect users.

The DPC has confirmed that it will publish the full decision and related information in due course.

**Ensure Compliance with DPM**

This case serves as a critical reminder for organizations to **prioritize compliance** with data protection regulations like GDPR.

Businesses can significantly **reduce privacy-related risks** and ensure adherence to these stringent standards by leveraging solutions like [Data Privacy Manager (DPM)](https://legit.eu/solutions/data-privacy-manager/).

Designed as an innovative SaaS platform, DPM automates privacy processes and fosters cross-departmental collaboration, offering a visual dashboard to provide continuous insights into all processing activities.

With its comprehensive suite of products and modules, **DPM simplifies the complexities of compliance**, helping organizations safeguard their data and maintain trust.

args.summary:
The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited €251 million for a significant data breach that occurred in 2018, which exposed the personal information of 29 million Facebook users worldwide, including three million within the EU and EEA. The breach involved unauthorized third parties exploiting user tokens on the Facebook platform, granting access to personal data including full names, email addresses, phone numbers, locations, dates of birth, places of work, religion, gender, timeline posts, group memberships, and children's data.

The DPC identified multiple GDPR violations with corresponding fines:
- Failure to notify adequately (Article 33(3) GDPR): €8 million
- Inadequate documentation (Article 33(5)): €3 million
- Poor system design (Article 25(1)): €130 million
- Default data protection lapses (Article 25(2)): €110 million

DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle emphasized the serious risks posed by breaches exposing sensitive information. This fine adds to Meta's other penalties, including a €91 million fine and a record €1.2 billion fine for transferring EU user data to the US. Meta has announced plans to appeal the decision. The article concludes by promoting Data Privacy Manager (DPM), a SaaS platform that automates privacy processes and helps organizations maintain GDPR compliance. The page also lists several related GDPR fine articles, including fines against TikTok (€530M), LinkedIn (€310M), Uber (€290M), Netflix (€4.75M), Clearview AI (€30.5M), and a Croatian telecom (€4.5M).

# EU privacy regulator fines Meta 251 million euros for 2018 breach

By Reuters

December 17, 2024 3:42 PM UTC Updated December 17, 2024

REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/illustration-shows-eu-flag-and-meta-logo/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjM6bmV3c21sX1JDMlIzMUFUTE1VNA%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

DUBLIN, Dec 17 (Reuters) - The lead European Union data privacy regulator for Meta [(META.O), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/META.O) fined the social media giant 251 million euros ($263.5 million) on Tuesday for a 2018 Facebook security breach that affected 29 million users.

Meta notified Ireland's Data Protection Commission at the time that cyber attackers had exploited a vulnerability in Facebook's code that impacted the "View As" feature that lets users see what their own profile looks like to someone else.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

That led to a breach in personal data including users' full name, contact details, location, place of work, date of birth, religion, gender and their children's personal data, the DPC said.

"By allowing unauthorised exposure of profile information, the vulnerabilities behind this breach caused a grave risk of misuse of these types of data," DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle said in a statement.

Meta remedied the breach shortly after its discovery, the DPC said. Of the 29 million Facebook accounts impacted globally, about 3 million were based in the EU and European Economic Area.

The DPC is the lead EU regulator for most of the top U.S. internet firms due to the location of their EU operations in Ireland.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

It has so far fined Meta almost 3 billion euros for breaches under the bloc's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) introduced in 2018, including a record 1.2 billion euro fine in 2023 that Meta is appealing.

Meta said it will also appeal Tuesday's decision and that it has a wide range of measures in place to protect users across its platforms.

"We took immediate action to fix the problem as soon as it was identified, and we proactively informed people impacted as well as the Irish Data Protection Commission," a spokesperson for Meta said in a statement.

args.summary:
On December 17, 2024, the lead European Union data privacy regulator for Meta — Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) — fined the social media giant 251 million euros ($263.5 million) for a 2018 Facebook security breach that affected 29 million users worldwide, including about 3 million in the EU and European Economic Area.

The 2018 breach stemmed from cyber attackers exploiting a vulnerability in Facebook's code that impacted the "View As" feature, which allows users to see how their profile appears to others. The breach exposed personal data including users' full names, contact details, locations, places of work, dates of birth, religion, gender, and children's personal data. Meta remedied the breach shortly after its discovery and notified the DPC at the time.

The DPC has now fined Meta almost 3 billion euros total for breaches under the GDPR, including a record 1.2 billion euro fine in 2023 that Meta is appealing. Meta said it will also appeal Tuesday's decision, stating it took immediate action to fix the problem and proactively informed affected users and the Irish regulator.

# Irish Data Protection Commission fines Meta €251 Million

17th December 2024

The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) has today announced its final decisions following two inquiries into Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (‘MPIL’). These own-volition inquiries were launched by the DPC following a personal data breach, which was reported by MPIL in September 2018.

This data breach impacted approximately 29 million Facebook accounts globally, of which approximately 3 million were based in the EU/EEA. The categories of personal data affected included: user’s full name; email address; phone number; location; place of work; date of birth; religion; gender; posts on timelines; groups of which a user was a member; and children’s personal data. The breach arose from the exploitation by unauthorised third parties of user tokens[[1]](#_ftn1) on the Facebook platform.  The breach was remedied by MPIL and its US parent company shortly after its discovery.

The decisions, which were made by the Commissioners for Data Protection, Dr. Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland, included a number of reprimands and an order to pay administrative fines totalling €251 million.

The DPC submitted a draft decision to the GDPR cooperation mechanism in Sept 2024, as required under Article 60 of the GDPR[[2]](#_ftn2). No objections to the DPC’s draft decision were raised. The DPC is grateful for the cooperation and assistance of its peer EU/EEA supervisory authorities in this case.

The DPC’s final decisions record the following findings of infringement of the GDPR:

DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle commented:

*“This enforcement action highlights how the failure to build in data protection requirements throughout the design and development cycle can expose individuals to very serious risks and harms, including a risk to the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals. Facebook profiles can, and often do, contain information about matters such as religious or political beliefs, sexual life or orientation, and similar matters that a user may wish to disclose only in particular circumstances. By allowing unauthorised exposure of profile information, the vulnerabilities behind this breach caused a grave risk of misuse of these types of data.”*

[Read the full decision and further related information.](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/dpc-guidance/decisions/inquiries-meta-platforms-ireland-limited-token-breach)

![Irish Data Protection Commission fines Meta Ireland €251 million](/sites/default/files/uploads/inline-images/20241217_Meta%20Decision%20Infographic%2017%20December%202024%20Final.png)

![Irish Data Protection Commission fines Meta Ireland €251 million](/sites/default/files/uploads/inline-images/20241217_Meta%20Decision%20Infographic%2017%20December%202024%20Final.png)

### Further information

[[1]](#_ftnref1)User tokens are coded identifiers that can be used to verify the user of a platform or utility, and to control access to particular platform features and to personal data of the user and their contacts.

[[2]](#_ftnref2)Article 60 of the GDPR regulates the cooperation procedure between the Lead Supervisory Authority and the other Concerned Supervisory Authorities.

### Background

The breach that gave rise to the DPC’s Decisions arose from the deployment of a video upload function on the Facebook platform in July 2017. Facebook’s ‘View As’ feature allowed a user to see their own Facebook page as it would be seen by another user. A user making use of this feature could invoke the video uploader in conjunction with Facebook’s ‘Happy Birthday Composer’ facility. The video uploader would then generate a fully permissioned user token that gave them full access to the Facebook profile of that other user. A user could then use that token to exploit the same combination of features on other accounts, allowing them to access multiple users’ profiles and the data accessible through them. Between 14 and 28 September 2018 unauthorised persons used scripts to exploit this vulnerability and gained the ability to log on as the account holder to approximately 29 million Facebook accounts globally, of which approximately 3 million were based in the EU/EEA. Facebook security personnel were alerted to the vulnerability by an anomalous increase in video upload activity and removed the functionality that caused the vulnerability shortly thereafter.

The decisions, made by Commissioners Dr. Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland, included reprimands and an order to pay administrative fines totalling €251 million. The final decisions recorded findings of infringement of the GDPR related to the failure to build data protection requirements throughout the design and development cycle.
