# Meta appeal against €265m DPC fine adjourned until after EU decision

[by Vish Gain](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/author/vish-gain/)

10 May 2024

![The Meta logo in front of silhouettes of people using media devices.](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/AdobeStock_490145103_Editorial_Use_Only-718x523.jpeg)

Image: © kovop58/Stock.adobe.com

The fine in question was imposed by the DPC on Meta in November 2022 following a massive data breach that affected more than 500m Facebook users.

An appeal made by Meta against a €265m fine has been adjourned by the High Court until a related case is resolved in the EU courts.

In a judgement published today (10 May), Justice Garrett Simons of the High Court said that [the €265m fine imposed by the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC)](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/business/meta-fine-dpc-ireland-data-scraping-facebook) in November 2022 will not be legally effective until the EU Court of Justice resolves another appeal made by Meta against a €225m fine imposed by the DPC on WhatsApp.

Simons noted that the corrective measures prescribed in the fine had been complied with by Meta to the satisfaction of the DPC and that there was no ongoing breach of any data subject’s rights.

The fine in question was imposed by the DPC on Meta following a [data breach that affected millions of Facebook users](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/enterprise/facebook-leak-explained-have-i-been-affected).

In April 2021, the DPC [commenced an inquiry](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/enterprise/facebook-data-leak-data-protection-commission) into Meta after a database of information on 533m Facebook users emerged on a hacking forum. This scraped data included phone numbers, Facebook IDs, names, locations, birthdates and email addresses.

At the time, the DPC said it believed that “one or more provisions” of GDPR and the 2018 Data Protection Act could have been infringed in relation to Facebook users’ personal data.

Now, while the DPC and Meta agree that the fine cannot be paid until domestic proceedings have concluded, Simons noted that there was a disagreement over whether an interim trial could be held in which some of the specific issues could be determined.

Simons said that the issues in the domestic proceedings “cannot sensibly be separated out”.

“This is because the question of liability and sanction are inextricably bound up together. Meta had strongly contended that the conduct complained of did not involve any infringement of the GDPR,” Simons said.

“For example, Meta placed emphasis on the limited categories of information which had been disclosed as a result of the (alleged) infringement. In particular, the point was made that the disclosed material included information which would have been publicly viewable on the affected users’ Facebook profiles.”

Last month, Meta reported that its latest quarterly revenue [grew by 27pc](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/business/meta-earnings-revenue-ai-threads-reality-labs-shares-outlook) compared to last year as its family of apps now has more than 3.2bn daily active users.

Earlier this year, Dr Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland [took over](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/business/dpc-data-protection-commissioners-ireland-helen-dixon) as the two new data protection commissioners, replacing [outgoing commissioner Helen Dixon](https://www.siliconrepublic.com/business/helen-dixon-dpc-ireland-data-protection-commissioner).

# GDPR Enforcement in 2026: What Record Fines Mean for Your Business (italy)

By Global Law Experts

– posted 2 months ago

* [Legal](https://globallawexperts.com/lawyer_specialism/legal/?term_type=news)
* [Italy](https://globallawexperts.com/lawyer_region/italy/?term_type=news)
* [Data Protection](https://globallawexperts.com/lawyer_practice_area/data-protection/?term_type=news)

GDPR enforcement in 2026 has entered uncharted territory, with record fines reshaping how European supervisory authorities punish non-compliance and how businesses across Italy must respond. Cumulative penalties issued under the General Data Protection Regulation since 2018 have now surpassed the €7 billion mark, according to leading enforcement trackers, and the pace of high-value decisions accelerated sharply through 2025 and into the first half of 2026. The simultaneous enforcement of the EU Data Act, which entered into force in September 2025, has added a new layer of data-sharing and access obligations that regulators are scrutinising alongside GDPR compliance.  
 For in-house counsel, DPOs and compliance officers at Italian businesses, these developments demand immediate, structured action: the gap between regulatory expectation and operational reality has never been more consequential.

Executive Summary: What 2026 Record GDPR Fines Mean for Italian Businesses

The enforcement landscape for [data privacy laws](https://globallawexperts.com/data-privacy-laws-evolving-worldwide/) has shifted fundamentally. Regulators are no longer issuing symbolic penalties; they are deploying fines calibrated to global turnover, targeting systemic failures and holding both controllers and processors directly accountable. For businesses operating in or processing the personal data of individuals in Italy, three realities now define the compliance environment:

* Scale of financial exposure. Upper-tier fines under Article 83 GDPR reach up to €20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Multiple decisions in 2025–2026 have pushed individual penalties well into the hundreds of millions of euros, demonstrating that supervisory authorities will apply these ceilings to major infringements.
* Broadened enforcement scope. Regulators are pursuing not only consent failures and security breaches but also unlawful international transfers, inadequate Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), insufficient record-keeping under Article 30, and, increasingly, failures to comply with new EU Data Act obligations around data access and sharing.
* Immediate action required. Italian businesses should prioritise a comprehensive data-processing audit, a lawful-basis review across all processing activities, an overhaul of consent mechanisms and transfer safeguards, and an incident response plan aligned to the 72-hour breach notification rule under Article 33.

2026 GDPR Enforcement Snapshot: Numbers, Trends and Who Is Fining

The numbers tell a stark story. Data compiled by the GDPR Enforcement Tracker and analysed in the CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report confirms that GDPR fines 2026 have continued the steep upward trajectory that began around 2021. Aggregate fines imposed since the GDPR took effect in May 2018 now exceed €7.1 billion, with a significant proportion of that total concentrated in decisions handed down during 2024, 2025 and the first half of 2026.

Several national supervisory authorities have driven this trend. The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC), acting as lead supervisory authority for many of the world’s largest technology platforms under the One-Stop-Shop mechanism, has been responsible for some of the highest individual penalties. Authorities in Luxembourg, France (CNIL) and Italy’s own Garante per la protezione dei dati personali have also issued substantial fines targeting adtech, financial services and telecommunications companies.

The sectors most heavily affected reflect where large-scale personal data processing is most concentrated: technology platforms and social-media companies, advertising technology and real-time bidding ecosystems, financial institutions and payment processors, and healthcare providers handling sensitive data at scale.

Notable Recent Record GDPR Fines (2024–2026)

Regulator

Irish DPC

Luxembourg (CNPD)

Industry observers expect this trajectory to continue, with DPC decisions in 2026 alone accounting for a disproportionate share of total enforcement value across the EU. For Italian businesses, particularly those with cross-border operations or that rely on third-party processors headquartered in other EU member states, these decisions are directly applicable and set binding precedents for how obligations are interpreted.

Why GDPR Fines Are Bigger Now: Legal and Policy Drivers

Understanding why record GDPR fines have escalated requires examining both the statutory framework and the evolving policy posture of European supervisory authorities.

Article 83 of the GDPR establishes two tiers of administrative fines. The lower tier, up to €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover, applies to infringements of obligations related to controllers and processors (Articles 8, 11, 25–39, 42 and 43). The upper tier, up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, applies to infringements of the basic principles of processing, conditions for consent, data subject rights and rules governing international transfers.

Article 83(2) then lists the factors supervisory authorities must weigh when setting fine amounts. These include the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement; whether the infringement was intentional or negligent; actions taken to mitigate damage; the degree of responsibility and any previous infringements; the categories of personal data affected; how the authority learned of the infringement; and any aggravating or mitigating factors such as financial benefits gained. Crucially, regulators in 2025–2026 have given significant weight to the global turnover of the undertaking, meaning that companies with large market capitalisation face proportionally larger fines, even for infringements similar to those committed by smaller entities.

The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) has issued harmonisation guidelines encouraging consistent application of these factors across all EU supervisory authorities, and early indications suggest that these guidelines have emboldened smaller national DPAs, including the Garante, to align their penalty calculations more closely with the aggressive approach seen in Irish and French decisions.

The Role of the EU Data Act in GDPR Enforcement

The EU Data Act, which entered into force in September 2025, introduces new obligations around data sharing, data access and portability that sit alongside, and sometimes intersect with, GDPR requirements. While the Data Act is primarily concerned with non-personal and IoT-generated data, its provisions on data access rights and fair contractual terms apply in contexts where personal data is also processed. Industry observers expect supervisory authorities to treat compliance failures under the Data Act as an aggravating factor when assessing GDPR penalties, particularly in sectors such as connected devices, cloud services and platform economies where the two regulatory regimes overlap. For Italian businesses, this means that lawful basis assessments and data-sharing architectures must now account for both frameworks simultaneously.

Most Common GDPR Enforcement Triggers (Italy and EU)

Enforcement actions are not random. Across the decisions catalogued in the GDPR Enforcement Tracker, several recurring triggers account for the majority of fines and corrective orders issued in 2025–2026:

* Unlawful international transfers. Transferring personal data outside the EEA without adequate safeguards, particularly to the US, remains the single highest-value enforcement trigger. Despite the EU-US Data Privacy Framework adopted in 2023, transfers to processors or sub-processors that fall outside its scope, or transfers relying on outdated Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) without supplementary measures, continue to attract severe penalties.
* Consent failures. Supervisory authorities are scrutinising consent mechanisms with increasing granularity. Dark patterns, pre-ticked boxes, bundled consents and consent walls that force users to accept tracking as a condition of service have all resulted in enforcement. Consent under GDPR must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and regulators are now auditing the user experience (UX) implementation, not just the legal text.
* Inadequate security measures. Failures to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures under Article 32 remain a persistent trigger, particularly following data breaches that expose personal data. The Garante has been especially active in this area, issuing guidance and corrective orders where Italian organisations lacked encryption, access controls, pseudonymisation or regular security testing.
* Large-scale profiling without DPIAs. Processing operations that involve systematic monitoring of individuals or large-scale profiling, including behavioural advertising, credit scoring and employee surveillance, require a DPIA under Article 35. Failure to conduct or properly document a DPIA is treated as a standalone infringement and has featured in several high-value decisions.
* Insufficient record-keeping. Article 30 requires both controllers and processors to maintain records of processing activities. While this may appear administrative, regulators treat missing or incomplete records as evidence of broader governance failures and often use record-keeping deficiencies to widen the scope of investigations.

International Transfers: SCCs and Residual Schrems II Risk

The legacy of the Court of Justice’s Schrems II decision continues to shape international transfers under GDPR. Although the EU-US Data Privacy Framework provides a legal basis for transfers to certified US organisations, many Italian businesses transfer data to recipients in jurisdictions without an adequacy decision or to US entities not certified under the framework. In these cases, SCCs supplemented by Transfer Impact Assessments (TIAs) remain the primary mechanism, and regulators are now reviewing whether businesses have genuinely assessed the legal framework of the recipient country, implemented effective supplementary technical measures, and documented their reasoning. Failure to do so has been the basis of several record GDPR fines.

Legal Basis for the Largest 2026 GDPR Penalties

The penalty reasoning in the largest decisions of 2025–2026 reveals a consistent analytical framework that supervisory authorities are applying with increasing rigour. In the most significant DPC decisions, the authority cited infringements of Articles 44–49 (international transfers), Article 6 (lawful basis for processing), Article 5(1)(a) (lawfulness, fairness and transparency) and Article 7 (conditions for consent). In each case, the DPC applied the Article 83(2) factors methodically, giving particular weight to the duration of the infringement, in some cases spanning several years, and the number of data subjects affected, often running into hundreds of millions.

The CNIL’s decisions against adtech operators similarly focused on Article 5(1)(a) and Article 7, but additionally cited Article 25 (data protection by design and by default) where companies had built tracking architectures without adequate privacy safeguards from inception. The Italian Garante’s own enforcement decisions have cited Articles 5, 6, 13 and 14 (transparency obligations) and have placed emphasis on the inadequacy of privacy notices and the failure to provide data subjects with meaningful control over their data.

For Italian businesses, the practical effect of these decisions is that penalties are no longer limited to clear-cut breaches such as data leaks. Systemic governance failures, poorly drafted privacy policies, untested consent flows, legacy transfer mechanisms, and absent DPIAs, now expose organisations to upper-tier fines.

Practical Action Plan for Legal Teams: GDPR Enforcement 2026 Checklist and Timeline

Given the scale and velocity of GDPR enforcement in 2026, legal teams at Italian businesses should adopt a structured, time-bound remediation programme. The following 30/60/90-day plan provides a prioritised framework:  
 Days 1–30: Foundation audit and risk assessment

- Conduct a comprehensive data-processing inventory, map all processing activities, data categories, purposes, legal bases, data flows and third-party processors.
- Perform a lawful basis assessment for each processing activity. Verify that consent, where relied upon, meets the GDPR standard (freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous) and is documented.
- Review and update Article 30 records of processing activities for completeness and accuracy.
- Identify all international transfers and verify the legal mechanism in use (adequacy decision, SCCs, binding corporate rules). Flag any transfer relying on outdated SCCs or lacking a TIA.

Days 31–60: Remediation and mechanism overhaul

- Overhaul consent mechanisms, redesign cookie banners, consent forms and preference centres to eliminate dark patterns and ensure genuine choice.
- Conduct or update DPIAs for all high-risk processing, including profiling, large-scale processing of special categories and systematic monitoring.
- Review and strengthen technical and organisational security measures under Article 32: encryption at rest and in transit, access controls, pseudonymisation, regular penetration testing and vulnerability assessments.
- Update transfer safeguards: execute new-form SCCs where necessary, complete Transfer Impact Assessments, implement supplementary technical measures.

Days 61–90: Incident response, training and governance

- Build or refresh a documented incident response plan aligned to the 72-hour breach notification requirement (see below).
- Deliver training for all employees who handle personal data, with role-specific modules for IT, marketing, HR and customer service teams.
- Establish or strengthen internal governance: ensure DPO reporting lines, board-level accountability, and documented policies for data retention, subject access requests and data-sharing under the EU Data Act.
- Schedule regular compliance reviews, quarterly internal audits and annual external assessments, and document findings.

Reporting Obligations by Entity Type

Obligation  
 Controller  
 Processor

Breach notification to DPA  
 Must notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware (Article 33) and document the reasoning for the notification or for not notifying.  
 Must notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a breach; the controller decides whether DPA notification is required.

Record-keeping (Article 30)  
 Must maintain full records of all processing activities, including purposes, categories of data subjects, recipients, transfers and retention periods.  
 Must maintain records of all categories of processing carried out on behalf of each controller.

Direct enforcement risk  
 Directly subject to fines under Article 83; fine quantum may reflect market power, turnover and the systemic nature of the infringement.  
 Can be fined directly under Article 83 depending on role, culpability and whether processing exceeded the controller’s instructions; must document compliance measures.

Incident Response and 72-Hour Breach Notification

Article 33 of the GDPR requires controllers to notify the competent supervisory authority, in Italy, the Garante, within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. Processors must notify controllers without undue delay. Meeting this deadline requires a pre-built, tested response protocol:

- Detection and escalation. Implement automated monitoring and detection systems. Define clear internal escalation pathways so that IT, legal and the DPO are alerted immediately upon identification of a potential breach.
- Evidence preservation. Secure logs, access records, system snapshots and communications relevant to the breach before any remediation that might alter the evidence.
- Impact assessment. Within the first hours, assess the nature of the personal data compromised, the number of data subjects affected, the likely consequences for those individuals, and whether the data was encrypted or pseudonymised.
- Supervisory authority notification. Prepare the notification to the Garante including: a description of the nature of the breach; the categories and approximate number of data subjects and records concerned; the name and contact details of the DPO; a description of the likely consequences; and the measures taken or proposed to address the breach and mitigate its effects.
- Data subject notification. Where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to rights and freedoms, controllers must also notify affected individuals directly, in clear and plain language, without undue delay (Article 34).

Compliance Checklist for International Transfers and EU Data Act Interplay

Cross-border privacy compliance requires a dual-track approach in 2026. For international transfers under GDPR, legal teams should verify the following:

* All transfers are mapped and the legal basis for each is documented (adequacy decision, new-form SCCs, binding corporate rules, or a specific derogation under Article 49).
* Transfer Impact Assessments have been completed for every transfer relying on SCCs, evaluating the legal framework of the recipient country and the effectiveness of supplementary measures.
* Supplementary technical measures, such as encryption where the keys are retained within the EEA, pseudonymisation, or split processing, are implemented where the TIA identifies residual risk.
* Sub-processor chains are reviewed to ensure that all onward transfers by processors are covered by equivalent safeguards and documented in sub-processing agreements.

For the EU Data Act overlay, Italian businesses should additionally confirm that data-sharing architectures comply with new access-right obligations, that contracts with cloud and IoT service providers incorporate fair data-access terms as required by the Act, and that any refusal to share data can be justified under the Act’s exemptions. Failure to meet EU Data Act obligations is increasingly likely to compound GDPR enforcement risk where the same data-processing activities are involved.

What to Expect If Investigated: Process, Remedies and Mitigation

An investigation by the Garante, or, in cross-border cases, by a lead supervisory authority under the One-Stop-Shop mechanism, typically follows a structured lifecycle. The authority may act on the basis of a complaint, a notified breach, a media report, or its own monitoring and audit programme. The investigation stage involves information requests, on-site inspections and technical audits. The authority then issues a preliminary assessment, giving the organisation an opportunity to respond before a final decision.

Businesses under investigation should take immediate steps to cooperate fully and transparently with the authority, preserve all relevant records and communications, implement remedial measures as soon as deficiencies are identified (even before a final decision), and prepare detailed mitigation submissions demonstrating good-faith efforts, the scope and speed of remediation, and any investments in improved governance. Article 83(2) expressly lists cooperation with the supervisory authority and measures taken to mitigate damage as factors that can reduce fine amounts. Appeals against Garante decisions can be brought before the Italian courts, and in cross-border cases, the consistency mechanism under the EDPB provides an additional procedural layer.

Italy-Specific Considerations: Garante Practice and Enforcement Posture

The Garante per la protezione dei dati personali has established itself as one of the more active national supervisory authorities in the EU, with a particular focus on transparency, security and the lawful use of emerging technologies. Italian Garante fines have targeted organisations for insufficiently detailed privacy notices, the use of analytics tools that transfer data to the US without adequate safeguards, and the processing of biometric and location data without a valid DPIA.

The Garante has also issued specific guidance on the use of cookies and tracking technologies, aligning Italian practice with the EDPB’s recommendations, and has intervened in cases involving artificial intelligence and automated decision-making where transparency and lawful basis requirements were not met. For companies with a main establishment outside Italy but processing Italian residents’ data, coordinating with both the Garante and the lead supervisory authority under the One-Stop-Shop is essential to avoid parallel enforcement actions and inconsistent outcomes. Early engagement with the Garante, including voluntary compliance audits and proactive breach notifications, is widely recognised as a mitigating factor in Italian enforcement practice.

Conclusion: GDPR Enforcement 2026 Record Fines, Priority Actions and Final Checklist

The message from GDPR enforcement in 2026 is unambiguous: supervisory authorities have the tools, the mandate and the willingness to impose penalties that materially affect even the largest organisations. For Italian businesses, the path forward is structured compliance, not reactive firefighting. What record GDPR fines mean, in practical terms, is that organisations can no longer treat data protection as a secondary governance function.

The following seven-point checklist summarises the priority actions every Italian business should take immediately:

- Audit all processing activities, map data flows, purposes, legal bases and third-party processors comprehensively.
- Review and secure international transfers, execute new-form SCCs, complete TIAs and implement supplementary technical measures.
- Overhaul consent mechanisms, eliminate dark patterns, ensure genuine choice and document valid consent.
- Strengthen security, implement encryption, access controls, pseudonymisation and regular testing aligned to Article 32.
- Build a 72-hour breach notification plan, pre-draft templates, define escalation pathways and test the response protocol.
- Train all staff, deliver role-specific [compliance training](https://globallawexperts.com/pay-transparency-italy/) covering GDPR and EU Data Act obligations.
- Engage specialist legal counsel, secure expert guidance on cross-border privacy compliance, Garante engagement and enforcement risk assessment.

## FAQs

What are the GDPR fines in 2026?

   

GDPR uses two penalty tiers: up to €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover for procedural infringements, and up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover for substantive breaches such as unlawful processing, consent failures or transfer violations. Cumulative fines issued since 2018 have exceeded €7 billion.

   

How high can a GDPR fine be?

   

The maximum fine under Article 83 is €20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. For the largest technology companies, this has translated into individual penalties exceeding €1 billion in recent enforcement actions.

   

What triggers a GDPR investigation?

   

Common triggers include data breaches, complaints from data subjects, unlawful international transfers, consent mechanism failures, large-scale profiling without a DPIA, and inadequate security measures. Supervisory authorities also initiate investigations based on their own monitoring programmes.

   

How quickly must data breaches be reported under GDPR?

   

Controllers must notify the competent supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach, unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms. Processors must notify their controllers without undue delay.

   

What immediate steps should an Italian business take after receiving a penalty notice?

   

Engage in-house counsel and external data protection specialists immediately, preserve all relevant evidence and records, begin implementing remedial measures, prepare detailed mitigation submissions for the supervisory authority, and assess whether to appeal the decision through the Italian courts.

   

Can the EU Data Act affect GDPR enforcement?

   

Yes. The EU Data Act, in force since September 2025, creates new data-sharing and access obligations. Regulators are increasingly scrutinising compliance with both frameworks simultaneously, and failures under the Data Act can compound enforcement risk under GDPR.

   

Who is liable in cross-border data processing?

   

Both controllers and processors can face direct enforcement action depending on their respective roles and culpability. In cross-border cases, the One-Stop-Shop mechanism designates a lead supervisory authority, but concerned authorities, including the Garante, retain the ability to act in certain circumstances.

   

How can companies reduce GDPR fine amounts?

   

Cooperate promptly and transparently with the supervisory authority, implement remedial measures as soon as deficiencies are identified, demonstrate robust security and governance frameworks, document all mitigation steps, and show evidence of good-faith compliance efforts. Article 83(2) expressly lists these factors as relevant to fine calculation.

   

How do supervisory authorities calculate fine amounts?

   

Authorities apply the criteria in Article 83(2) GDPR, weighing the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement; the number of data subjects affected; intentional or negligent character; mitigation measures taken; previous infringements; categories of personal data; cooperation with the authority; and any financial benefit derived from the infringement.

   

Are small businesses exempt from GDPR fines?

   

No. The GDPR applies to all organisations processing personal data of individuals in the EU, regardless of size. However, Article 83(2) requires that fines be “effective, proportionate and dissuasive,” meaning that fine amounts should reflect the size and resources of the organisation. Smaller businesses may face lower absolute penalties, but the proportional impact can be equally significant.

**Key facts and statistics:**
- Cumulative GDPR fines since May 2018 have surpassed €7.1 billion, with acceleration through 2025 and into the first half of 2026.
- The EU Data Act entered into force in September 2025, adding new data-sharing/access obligations that regulators scrutinize alongside GDPR.
- GDPR has two fine tiers under Article 83: up to €10 million or 2% of global turnover (procedural infringements) and up to €20 million or 4% of global turnover (substantive breaches).

**Notable record fines (2024–2026):**
- Irish DPC: €1.2 billion+ (unlawful international transfers to the US)
- Irish DPC: €390 million+ (invalid legal basis for behavioural advertising, consent failures)
- Luxembourg CNPD: €746 million (issued 2021, overturned on appeal March 2026 and referred back)

The EDPB has issued harmonisation guidelines that emboldened smaller DPAs like the Garante. The Schrems II legacy continues to make SCCs with Transfer Impact Assessments essential for transfers outside the EEA.

**Practical 30/60/90-day action plan:**
- Days 1–30: data-processing inventory, lawful basis assessment, Article 30 record updates, identify international transfers.
- Days 31–60: overhaul consent mechanisms, conduct DPIAs, strengthen Article 32 security, update transfer safeguards/SCCs/TIAs.
- Days 61–90: build 72-hour incident response plan, staff training, governance/DPO reporting, regular compliance reviews.

**Reporting obligations:** Controllers must notify the Garante within 72 hours of a breach (Article 33); processors notify controllers without undue delay. Data subjects must be notified where high risk exists (Article 34).

**Italy-specific considerations:** The Garante is one of the EU's most active DPAs, focusing on transparency, security, and emerging tech (biometric/location data, AI, cookies). Early engagement with the Garante is recognised as a mitigating factor.

**Seven-point final checklist** covering: audits, transfer safeguards, consent overhaul, security strengthening, breach notification plans, staff training, and engaging specialist legal counsel.

# GDPR Fines Hit €7.1 Billion: What the 2026 Enforcement Patterns Tell You

Eight years of GDPR enforcement have produced €7.1 billion in cumulative fines, 2,800+ documented decisions, and a pattern that is no longer confined to Big Tech.

![](https://flashsip.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Blog-18-6.img_.cover_-1024x585.png)

Eight years of GDPR enforcement have produced €7.1 billion in cumulative fines, 2,800+ documented decisions, and a pattern that is no longer confined to Big Tech. This analysis breaks down the 2026 DPA enforcement data to show which regulators are most active, which violations are most penalised, and what the trajectory means for mid-market businesses.

## **From Sporadic to Systemic**

GDPR enforcement began slowly. The first two years after the regulation took effect in May 2018 produced relatively few fines – regulators were building capacity, investigating backlogs, and establishing precedent. The €50 million fine against Google in France (January 2019) and the €35.3 million H&M fine in Hamburg (November 2020) were outliers, not patterns.

What the 2026 data shows is a different regime entirely. According to the [DLA Piper GDPR Fines and Data Breach Survey published in January 2026](https://www.dlapiper.com/en/insights/publications/2026/01/dla-piper-gdpr-fines-and-data-breach-survey-january-2026),  cumulative administrative penalties since May 2018 have passed €7.1 billion across more than 2,800 enforcement actions. More than 60% of that total landed after January 2023. A 22% year-on-year increase in breach notifications – reaching an average of 443 notifications per day – signals that regulators are receiving more actionable intelligence, not just issuing more fines arbitrarily.

This is what systemic enforcement looks like.

## **The Distribution That Matters More Than the Total**

The €7.1 billion headline number is accurate. It is also, in isolation, misleading. Two countries – Ireland and France – account for approximately 70% of all GDPR fine value. Understanding why tells you more about the current enforcement environment than the total does.

### Ireland

**Ireland** holds the top position because of a jurisdictional quirk: Google, Meta, Apple, LinkedIn, TikTok, and most major US technology platforms established their EU headquarters in Dublin. The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) is therefore the lead supervisory authority for all of them. The consequences: Meta’s €1.2 billion fine for unlawful EU–US data transfers (May 2023, the largest single GDPR fine ever issued), TikTok’s €530 million penalty for sending European user data to China without adequate safeguards (May 2025), and LinkedIn’s €310 million fine for consent and legal basis violations. Ireland’s cumulative fine total sits at approximately €4.04 billion- about 57% of the global total – almost entirely driven by decisions involving US tech platforms.

### France

**France** is the second-largest enforcer by fine value and, according to multiple analyst rankings, one of the most prolific by volume. The CNIL has been particularly focused on cookie consent manipulation, advertising technology, and – as covered in our previous analysis – the use of US-hosted analytics tools including Google Analytics.

### Spain

**Spain** leads by sheer number of enforcement decisions, with nearly 1,000 documented actions since 2018, according to the CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report 2025/2026. Spanish fines are typically smaller in individual amount, targeting direct marketing violations, video surveillance without adequate notice, and unsolicited commercial calls. But the volume signals something important: GDPR is enforced at every level of the economy in Spain, not just against large operators.

### Italy

**Italy** sits between the two poles – high volume and meaningful fine amounts. The Garante has been among the most active regulators in AI-related enforcement, acting ahead of the EU AI Act’s August 2026 enforcement date. Its €5 million fine against Replika chatbot maker Luka Inc. in 2025 signalled that AI systems’ data processing practices are already subject to GDPR enforcement, not just the incoming AI Act.

### Germany

**Germany** produces hundreds of fines distributed across 16 state-level DPAs plus the federal BfDI. Hamburg’s €35.3 million H&M penalty remains its single largest, but German enforcement tends to focus on technical security failures and vendor risk – particularly inadequate data processing agreements and insufficient sub-processor oversight.

## **What DPAs Are Actually Penalising**

[The CMS Enforcement Tracker data](https://cms.law/en/int/publication/GDPR-Enforcement-Tracker-Report/numbers-and-figures) shows that violations of general data processing principles – Articles 5 and 6 of the GDPR – account for the largest category of fines across all member states. These are not obscure technical infractions. They include processing data without a valid legal basis, collecting more data than necessary, and retaining data beyond declared retention periods.

The five largest GDPR fines to date all involve either unlawful international data transfers (Article 46) or invalid legal basis for processing. Cross-border transfers remain the highest-value enforcement territory because they affect the largest operators – US tech platforms routing EU data to non-adequate third countries.

But the 2024–2026 enforcement period has expanded well beyond that population. Cookie consent remains a major enforcement focus, with the EDPB’s 2026 coordinated enforcement action on transparency and information obligations adding scrutiny pressure across all member states. The Belgian DPA, Spanish AEPD, Italian Garante, and German DPAs have all issued enforcement actions against organisations running non-compliant cookie banners – pre-ticked boxes, obscured rejection options, and consent bundled with terms of service.

## **The SME Problem the Headlines Don’t Cover**

A persistent misconception holds that GDPR enforcement targets only large enterprises. The enforcement tracker data contradicts this clearly. A significant share of all documented fines involve organisations with fewer than 250 employees – regional service providers, local agencies, small SaaS companies.

SMEs face lower absolute penalties. They face penalties nonetheless. And the Belgian DPA’s published 2026–2028 strategy makes the trajectory explicit: fewer reactive complaint-driven investigations, more proactive inspections targeting sectors the authority has identified as systemically high-risk. Retail loyalty programmes, direct marketing operations, and organisations handling health or financial data at scale are explicitly in scope.

The average GDPR fine across all documented decisions sits at approximately €2.4 million. That number is heavily skewed by the Meta, TikTok, and Amazon decisions. The median – the fine amount a typical penalised organisation actually pays – is considerably lower. But even fines in the €10,000–€50,000 range carry reputational consequences and operational disruption that mid-market businesses are poorly equipped to absorb.

## **The Enforcement Acceleration Nobody Expected**

The 2023–2026 period produced more fines than the preceding five years combined. Three factors drove this acceleration.

First, coordination. The European Data Protection Board’s Coordinated Enforcement Framework (CEF) has been running since 2023, focusing national DPAs on common themes: cookies in 2023, children’s data in 2024, transparency in 2026. A violation that once triggered a single national fine now risks coordinated actions from multiple DPAs, reaching penalties in the €15–25 million range across jurisdictions.

Second, expansion into new sectors. Finance, healthcare, telecommunications, and public sector organisations that were largely outside the early enforcement wave are now firmly in scope. AI-driven processing, audience modelling, and automated bidding systems are all under active scrutiny.

Third, political will. Data protection has become a consumer-facing political issue across European member states. DPAs face institutional pressure to demonstrate enforcement effectiveness – which means fines are increasingly likely to be made public, detailed, and proportionally significant.

## **What to do with this before your next audit**

Three things the 2026 enforcement pattern tells you to prioritize:

**1. Map your sub-processors before your auditor does.** The 2026 CEF is specifically targeting whether organizations know – and have documented – every entity that touches their data. If your analytics vendor’s DPA lists sub-processors in generic categories rather than named entities, that’s an Article 13 gap.

**2. Establish the jurisdiction of every tool in your stack, not just the server location.** Country of incorporation governs CLOUD Act exposure. Country of server location governs data residency. These are different questions. Both require an answer.

**3. Audit your data retention schedule.** This is about data that should have been deleted years earlier still sitting in the system when the breach occurred. Retention policy failures are amplifiers – they turn security incidents into maximum-penalty events.

For organizations that don’t have a dedicated DPO or internal compliance team, working through a digital transformation partner with cybersecurity expertise – like [Neotiq](https://www.neotiq.com/cyber-securite/) and compliance teams such as [Flashsip analytics | Alternative GA4 France](https://flashsip.com/)– are often the most practical way to run that audit without pulling engineering resources off the product.

The €7.1 billion didn’t accumulate because organizations were reckless. It accumulated because 2,245 enforcement actions’ worth of organizations assumed someone upstream had sorted the compliance side. In 2026, that assumption has a documented cost.

--- SOURCE 1: Irish Data Protection Commission fines Meta €251 Million ---
URL: http://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/irish-data-protection-commission-fines-meta-eu251-million

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) announced on 17 December 2024 that it has fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (MPIL) €251 million following two inquiries into a personal data breach reported by MPIL in September 2018. The breach impacted approximately 29 million Facebook accounts globally, including roughly 3 million in the EU/EEA. Affected personal data categories included user full names, email addresses, phone numbers, locations, places of work, dates of birth, religion, gender, timeline posts, group memberships, and children's personal data.

The breach originated from the exploitation of user tokens on Facebook's platform. Specifically, a vulnerability was created when a video upload function was deployed in July 2017. Facebook's 'View As' feature, combined with the 'Happy Birthday Composer' facility, could be exploited to generate fully permissioned user tokens granting full access to other users' profiles. Between 14-28 September 2018, unauthorized persons used scripts to exploit this vulnerability, gaining the ability to log on as account holders for approximately 29 million accounts globally.

The decisions were made by Commissioners for Data Protection Dr. Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland, and included reprimands and administrative fines totaling €251 million. The DPC submitted a draft decision to the GDPR cooperation mechanism under Article 60 in September 2024, with no objections raised by peer EU/EEA supervisory authorities. DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle commented on the enforcement action, emphasizing that the failure to build in data protection requirements throughout the design and development cycle can expose individuals to serious risks and harms, including risks to fundamental rights and freedoms, particularly given that Facebook profiles can contain sensitive information about religious or political beliefs, sexual life, and orientation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This enforcement action highlights how the failure to build in data protection requirements throughout the design and development cycle can expose individuals to very serious risks and harms, including a risk to the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals. Facebook profiles can, and often do, contain information about matters such as religious or political beliefs, sexual life or orientation, and similar matters that a user may wish to disclose only in particular circumstances. By allowing unauthorised exposure of profile information, the vulnerabilities behind this breach caused a grave risk of misuse of these types of data." - DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle

URL: https://gdprhub.eu/index.php?title=AP_%28The_Netherlands%29_-_Uber

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This GDPRhub page documents the Dutch Data Protection Authority's (AP - Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens) decision to fine Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI) and Uber B.V. (UBV) €290,000,000 for violating Article 44 GDPR. The decision was issued on 22 July 2024 and published on 25 August 2024.

**Key Facts:**
- Uber B.V. (UBV), based in the Netherlands, is part of the Uber group and serves as the EEA representative. Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI), based in San Francisco, US, is the parent company and joint controller for Uber drivers' personal data.
- Uber used a centralized IT infrastructure with servers located in the US. EEA-based drivers' personal data was processed in the US in two situations: (1) data collected through the driver app and stored on US-based servers (including account, location, criminal and health data, identity documents, and taxi licenses), and (2) when drivers exercised their GDPR rights, UTI was responsible for making data available to UBV.
- Uber previously used the European Commission's Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) but removed them from their joint controllership agreement effective 6 August 2021, arguing SCCs could not be used when processing falls directly under GDPR scope.
- The complaint originated from the French human rights group Ligue des droits de l'Homme on behalf of 172 Uber drivers, filed with CNIL (French DPA) on 12 June 2020, and forwarded to the Dutch AP due to Uber's main establishment in the Netherlands.

**Key Holdings:**
1. **Article 3 GDPR and Chapter V can apply simultaneously**: The DPA rejected Uber's argument that the territorial scope (Article 3 GDPR) and Chapter V (international transfers) were mutually exclusive. Chapter V is complementary to Article 3, preventing circumvention of EU data protection law. The DPA also rejected the WTO agreement argument.
2. **The processing constituted a transfer**: Applying the EDPB Guidelines 05/2021's three cumulative criteria, the DPA found all criteria met. The DPA rejected Uber's argument that drivers themselves were the exporters, finding instead that UBV was the exporter because drivers have little influence over processing purposes and means (terms are pre-drafted and non-negotiable).
3. **No valid transfer mechanism**: From 6 August 2021 to 27 November 2023, Uber had no lawful transfer mechanism. The DPA rejected Uber's interpretation of the European Commission's FAQ statements regarding SCCs.
4. **Article 49 GDPR exceptions did not apply**: The transfers were systematic, repetitive, and ongoing (not incidental per Recital 111). --- SOURCE 7: Into the Data Transfer Thicket: The Dutch Uber Decision and the Relationship Between GDPR Article 3 and Chapter V – European Law Blog ---
URL: https://europeanlawblog.eu/1xjmngct

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an opinion/analysis article from the European Law Blog (22 October 2024) by E J Kyriakides examining the Dutch DPA's enforcement decision against Uber and the legal relationship between GDPR Article 3 (territorial scope) and Chapter V (data transfer safeguards).

KEY ISSUE: The article addresses a lingering legal ambiguity: under what circumstances are GDPR data transfer safeguards required when a foreign firm is already subject to the GDPR. The classic transfer scenario involves a foreign company NOT governed by GDPR receiving EU data. But GDPR has extraterritorial effect (Article 3(2)), meaning foreign companies targeting the EU can also be subject to it.

LEGAL BACKGROUND:
- Article 3(1): Entities with an EU "establishment" are subject to GDPR
- Article 3(2): Entities without EU establishment are subject if they (a) offer goods/services to EU data subjects, or (b) monitor EU data subject behavior
- Chapter V (Articles 44-47) requires transfer safeguards including adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses (SCCs), binding corporate rules, etc.
- Under Schrems II, firms must independently assess whether transfer tools ensure "essentially equivalent" protection, potentially requiring supplementary measures
- Chapter V applies only to a "transfer" — a term the GDPR does not define

EDPB GUIDELINES (05/2021):
- Defined "transfer" as occurring when: (1) a controller/processor (exporter) is subject to GDPR; (2) the exporter discloses personal data to another controller/processor (importer); (3) the importer is in a third country (regardless of whether importer is subject to GDPR)
- Critically concluded NO transfer occurs when data is directly disclosed by an individual in the EU to a firm in a third country
- Companies subject to GDPR must still assess third country government access risks under other GDPR obligations (Articles 32, 33, 35)
- Not binding but highly authoritative

THE DUTCH DPA UBER DECISION (August 2024):
- Dutch DPA fined Uber €290 million — the largest fine ever from the Dutch DPA — for transferring French Uber drivers' data to the US without Chapter V safeguards
- Fine originated from an NGO (Ligue Des Droits De L'homme) complaint to the French CNIL
- Transfer involved Uber B.V. (UBV, Netherlands) and Uber Technologies Inc (UTI, US parent)
- Uber relied on SCCs until August 2021, then determined SCCs were unnecessary because Article 3 directly applied to UTI's US processing; Uber had NO transfer mechanism from August 2021 until relying on the Data Privacy Framework in November 2023
- Two scenarios found to involve transfers: (1) EU drivers' data sent directly via Uber app to UTI for US storage; (2) data relating to GDPR rights requests where UBV and UTI collaborated
- Dutch DPA rejected Uber's defenses (direct collection, joint controllership, Article 49 derogations), holding transfers between joint controllers subject to GDPR in different countries are governed by Chapter V
- DPA departed from EDPB guidance by finding scenario one (direct collection from EU data subjects) constituted a "transfer," relying on the employment relationship between UBV and drivers and the asymmetry of power
- DPA argued Chapter V should be read broadly to counterbalance risks of diminished protection when data is processed abroad and difficulty enforcing against foreign entities
- DPA found Article 49(b-c) derogations inapplicable because transfers were ongoing, not "incidental" or "necessary"

ANALYSIS/NEXT STEPS:
- Uber is appealing; Dutch courts are likely to refer questions to the CJEU on the Article 3/Chapter V relationship
- The Dutch decision failed to articulate a clear legal standard for when direct collection by foreign providers subject to GDPR triggers Chapter V
- The article recommends that EU entities subject to GDPR under Article 3(2) in doubt apply Chapter V safeguards until the issue is settled
- European Commission has not yet issued SCCs for scenarios where the importer is subject to GDPR (current SCCs only apply when importer is NOT subject to GDPR)
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The EDPB concluded that a transfer occurs when: 1) A controller or a processor ('exporter') is subject to the GDPR for the given processing; 2) The exporter discloses by transmission or otherwise makes personal data... available to another controller, joint controller or processor ('importer'); 3) The importer is in a third country, irrespective of whether or not this importer is subject to the GDPR for the given processing in accordance with Article 3"
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On August 26, 2024, the Dutch Data Protection Authority (Dutch DPA) fined Uber Technologies, Inc. and Uber B.V. €290 million for violating the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The fine stems from Uber's failure to implement appropriate safeguards for transferring EEA-based drivers' personal data to the United States over a 27-month period, during which Uber removed Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) from its data-sharing agreements between EEA and U.S. entities.

The investigation originated from complaints by drivers to the French data protection authority and was transferred to the Dutch DPA since Uber's European headquarters are in the Netherlands. Uber's personal data transfers included special category and criminal record data, and were directed to Uber's centralized IT infrastructure in the United States.

Key findings of the Decision:
- **Adequate safeguards required for intra-group transfers**: Uber argued both its U.S. and EEA entities were subject to GDPR under Article 3 as joint controllers, making Chapter V compliance unnecessary. The Dutch DPA rejected this, stating the data transfer requirements in Chapter V place a direct obligation on parties processing personal data in third countries. The DPA also determined an "onward transfer" occurred from Uber EEA (data exporter) to Uber U.S. (data importer), even though drivers entered data directly into the Uber platform.

The DPA rejected this, finding the transfers were systematic, repetitive, and ongoing rather than incidental, and that contract existence alone does not constitute "necessity." The DPA was unconvinced that centralized U.S. processing was crucial to Uber's services, suggesting efficiency motives were insufficient.
- **Fine proportionality**: The DPA considered the violation serious, given the sensitive nature of drivers' personal data (including criminal data) and the 27-month duration. The fine was evaluated under the maximum parameters (higher of €20 million or 4% annual turnover). The DPA determined Uber "could have known" the transfer would require additional safeguards based on GDPR, CJEU case law, and prior regulator decisions.

The Dutch DPA coordinated its decision with other EU data protection authorities, meaning similar determinations could follow. Uber is expected to appeal. The Decision's biggest takeaway is the added uncertainty to the international data transfer landscape, particularly casting doubt on whether companies can rely on European Commission Q&A guidance for compliance or penalty mitigation purposes. The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) imposed a record-breaking fine of EUR 290 million on Uber for violating Article 44 GDPR by unlawfully transferring personal data of EU-based drivers to the United States. This is the AP's highest-ever fine.

Background: The AP's investigation began in April 2021 after the French DPA (CNIL) forwarded a complaint from the French NGO Ligue des droits de l'Homme (LDH) on behalf of 172 Uber drivers. Following the ECJ's Schrems II ruling in 2020, the EU-US Privacy Shield was invalidated, but Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) remained a valid transfer mechanism, potentially with supplementary measures. This article from CookieYes (dated December 17, 2025) provides a comprehensive guide to GDPR fines and penalties, including the 20 largest fines imposed since the regulation took effect on May 25, 2018.

**GDPR Fine Structure:**
- Tier 1 violations: Up to 2% of annual revenue or €10 million (whichever is greater) — applies to violations related to child data consent, privacy by design, data breach notifications, DPIA requirements, DPO appointments, certification mechanisms, and third-party involvement.
- Tier 2 violations: Up to 4% of annual revenue or €20 million (whichever is greater) — applies to violations of lawful bases for processing, GDPR individual rights, cross-border data transfers, Member State laws, and orders from supervisory authorities.
- Non-monetary actions may include processing bans, data deletion orders, and transfer restrictions.
- Under Art. 82, affected individuals can claim compensation in court.

**Criteria for Fines:** Nature/severity of violation, number affected, negligence vs. intent, preventive measures, security protocols, prior violations, cooperation with authorities, type of data affected, notification practices, and financial benefits gained from the violation.

**The 20 Biggest GDPR Fines (2018-2024):**
1. Meta (Facebook) — €1.2 billion (May 22, 2023, Irish DPC): EU-to-US data transfers without adequate safeguards using SCCs.

Key takeaways: (1) TRAs must be substantively robust with detailed analysis of local law measured against European Essential Guarantees; (2) supplementary measures must meaningfully address specific government access risks rather than being generic security controls; (3) Article 83(2) factors serve as a useful framework for organisations' own risk management, with high-risk transfers requiring enhanced scrutiny and stronger measures.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 13 March 2025, the Irish Court of Appeal (COA) delivered its judgment in Data Protection Commission (DPC) v Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, upholding the DPC's appeal and refusing to stay (adjourn) the Meta Proceedings. The background involves a DPC decision on 25 November 2022 finding that Meta violated Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR after third parties 'scraped' personal data from Meta's platforms between May 2018 and September 2019. The DPC issued an order to comply, a reprimand, and two fines totalling €165 million. In December 2022, Meta brought both a statutory appeal and judicial review proceedings in the High Court.

The case related to separate "WhatsApp Proceedings": on 20 August 2021 the DPC fined WhatsApp €225 million for GDPR infringements (Articles 5, 12, 13, 14). WhatsApp's challenge to the EDPB's Article 65 decision was dismissed by the EU General Court as inadmissible (WhatsApp not directly concerned), and an appeal to the Court of Justice was pending (Advocate General's opinion due 27 March 2025). In July 2023, Meta sought to adjourn its High Court proceedings pending the outcome of the WhatsApp Proceedings; the High Court (Simons J) granted this, adjourning the Meta Proceedings in their entirety.

The COA set aside the High Court decision, emphasizing that challenges to decisions of public bodies should be prosecuted with "economy and celerity." The COA identified two scenarios following the upcoming CJEU decision in the WhatsApp case: (1) if the CJEU upholds the General Court's inadmissibility dismissal, unresolved EU law issues could delay Meta Proceedings by ~24 months; (2) if the CJEU allows the appeal, the case returns to the General Court, potentially delaying Meta Proceedings by a further ~40 months. The COA held that the GDPR requires challenges to DPC decisions to be brought in Irish courts, with Article 267 TFEU preliminary references as the exclusive mechanism to resolve GDPR interpretation doubts. The COA found no reason to delay requesting such a reference, and noted parties could later seek stays of the WhatsApp Proceedings if needed. The DPC's appeal was allowed and Meta's adjournment motions were dismissed.
</summary>

The GDPR requires that any challenge to a decision of the DPC be brought before the courts in Ireland. The exclusive mechanism to resolve any doubts as to the interpretation of the GDPR in the context of the Meta Proceedings is therefore by way of a reference for a preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU.

--- SOURCE 3: Meta's €1.2 Billion GDPR Fine: Why It Still Matters in 2025 ---
URL: https://gdprlocal.com/metas-e1-2-billion-gdpr-fine-why-it-still-matters-in-2025

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from GDPRLocal examines Meta's record-breaking €1.2 billion GDPR fine, imposed on May 12, 2023 by Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC), and explores its ongoing significance for international data transfers.

**The Core Violation:** Meta was fined for illegally transferring European users' personal data to the United States, directly breaching the international transfer rules in Chapter V of the GDPR. The conflict stems from U.S. surveillance laws (particularly Section 702 of FISA) clashing with EU privacy rights. The €1.2 billion penalty specifically covers transfers that continued after the landmark Schrems II ruling on July 16, 2020. The case originated from a complaint filed by privacy activist Max Schrems.

**Enforcement Actions:** Regulators ordered Meta to (1) suspend all future transfers of EU data to the U.S. within five months, and (2) bring all previously transferred data into compliance within six months (effectively deleting it or moving it back to the EU). These operational orders were deemed a greater threat to business than the fine itself.

**The Enforcement Journey:** Ireland's DPC initially declined to fine Meta, deeming a penalty "disproportionate" and citing Meta's "good faith" use of SCCs. However, other European data protection authorities objected, escalating the case to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) under Article 65. In Binding Decision 1/2023 (April 13, 2023), the EDPB overruled the DPC, declaring the infringement "highly serious" and mandating a fine with a starting point between 20-100% of the legal maximum, calculated on Meta's worldwide turnover. The fine was based on Article 83(5) of the GDPR, allowing penalties up to 4% of global annual turnover due to aggravating factors including: systematic/repetitive/continuous transfers over nearly three years, involvement of special category data (Article 9), and Meta acting with "at least the highest degree of negligence."

**Why SCCs Were Not Enough:** While Meta used Standard Contractual Clauses, regulators found that U.S. surveillance laws like FISA 702 could legally compel Meta to hand over both encrypted data and the cryptographic keys, rendering encryption ineffective. The EDPB concluded Meta's SCCs were "mere contractual promises" with no practical effect against U.S. surveillance law.

**History of EU-US Transfer Mechanisms:** The article details the evolution from Safe Harbour (invalidated in 2015 by Schrems I) to Privacy Shield (invalidated in 2020 by Schrems II) to SCCs (still valid but requiring Transfer Impact Assessments) to the new EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF, adopted July 10, 2023, valid but contested - NOYB has signaled a potential "Schrems III" challenge, and FISA 702 was only reauthorized until April 2026).

**The Schrems II Ruling Explained:** The 2020 CJEU ruling invalidated Privacy Shield and established new obligations for companies using SCCs, requiring case-by-case Transfer Impact Assessments (TIAs) before transfers and supplementary measures (including encryption with EU-controlled keys) when risks are identified.

**Industry Reactions:** Meta called the fine "flawed, unjustified and unnecessary" and is appealing (case T-325/23), while simultaneously adopting the new DPF. Forrester called the fine a "wake-up call" proving regulators now have the "power and the guts to dismantle a company's business model." EDPB Chair Andrea Jelinek stated the "unprecedented fine is a strong signal to organisations that serious infringements have far-reaching consequences." Other companies like Amazon Web Services quickly self-certified under the DPF for legal certainty. Ireland later fined Microsoft's LinkedIn €310 million in October 2024 for similar processing violations.

**Lessons for Businesses:** The article concludes that "set it and forget it" compliance is no longer viable. Companies must: (1) document every Transfer Impact Assessment, (2) encrypt or pseudonymise by default with keys controlled exclusively by the EU data exporter, (3) diversify legal bases (BCRs for corporate groups, Article 49 derogations only for one-off situations), and (4) continuously monitor legal changes. Boards must treat cross-border data transfers as a dynamic, strategic, multi-jurisdictional risk integrated into products, contracts, and technical architecture from day one.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The largest fine, a record-breaking €1.2 billion, was imposed back in May 2023. That penalty was for one specific reason: unlawfully transferring the personal data of European Facebook users to the United States."
</key_excerpts>

On 13 March 2025, the Irish Court of Appeal (COA) delivered its judgment in Data Protection Commission (DPC) v Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, upholding the DPC's appeal and refusing to stay (adjourn) the Meta Proceedings. The background involves a DPC decision on 25 November 2022 finding that Meta violated Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR after third parties 'scraped' personal data from Meta's platforms between May 2018 and September 2019. The DPC issued an order to comply, a reprimand, and two fines totalling €165 million. In December 2022, Meta brought both a statutory appeal and judicial review proceedings in the High Court.

The case related to separate "WhatsApp Proceedings": on 20 August 2021 the DPC fined WhatsApp €225 million for GDPR infringements (Articles 5, 12, 13, 14). WhatsApp's challenge to the EDPB's Article 65 decision was dismissed by the EU General Court as inadmissible (WhatsApp not directly concerned), and an appeal to the Court of Justice was pending (Advocate General's opinion due 27 March 2025). In July 2023, Meta sought to adjourn its High Court proceedings pending the outcome of the WhatsApp Proceedings; the High Court (Simons J) granted this, adjourning the Meta Proceedings in their entirety.

The COA set aside the High Court decision, emphasizing that challenges to decisions of public bodies should be prosecuted with "economy and celerity." The COA identified two scenarios following the upcoming CJEU decision in the WhatsApp case: (1) if the CJEU upholds the General Court's inadmissibility dismissal, unresolved EU law issues could delay Meta Proceedings by ~24 months; (2) if the CJEU allows the appeal, the case returns to the General Court, potentially delaying Meta Proceedings by a further ~40 months. The COA held that the GDPR requires challenges to DPC decisions to be brought in Irish courts, with Article 267 TFEU preliminary references as the exclusive mechanism to resolve GDPR interpretation doubts. The COA found no reason to delay requesting such a reference, and noted parties could later seek stays of the WhatsApp Proceedings if needed. The DPC's appeal was allowed and Meta's adjournment motions were dismissed.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A LinkedIn post by Matthew Newman reports on a major decision by the EU Court of Justice regarding WhatsApp's challenge against the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). The EU's top court ruled that WhatsApp can directly challenge a binding decision of the EDPB before the EU courts (a "direct action" at the General Court), rather than being limited to national courts. This ruling potentially shortens judicial proceedings and reshapes how companies appeal GDPR enforcement actions, and it unlocks six pending appeals by Meta in similar cases against the board.

The case arose after WhatsApp appealed a December 2022 General Court decision that found its original action inadmissible because the EDPB's binding decision did not directly affect the company's legal position. WhatsApp argued the EDPB's decision was binding on Ireland's Data Protection Commission, leaving it no discretion on finding data protection violations and forcing it to substantially raise a data-privacy penalty. The court ruled the EDPB's decision "was of direct concern to WhatsApp, since it brought about a distinct change in the legal position of that undertaking, without leaving any discretion to its addressees." The top court sent the case back to the EU's General Court to rule on the substance.

A WhatsApp spokesperson welcomed the judgment, stating: "The EDPB is an unelected authority whose decisions can directly impact businesses and people across the EU. We welcome the Court's final judgment on the matter which upholds our argument that those businesses and people should be able to challenge decisions the EDPB makes against them, so that it can be held fully accountable by the EU courts." Comments on the post noted this exposes a "giant flaw in the EDPB system" and that litigation can presumably still occur at a national level as well, potentially leading to more "lawfare."
</summary>

### Key Highlights of 2024

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On January 4, 2023, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) concluded two inquiries into Meta Platforms, Inc.'s data processing practices on its Instagram and Facebook platforms, fining Meta a combined €390 million for breaches of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The investigation began following complaints from NOYB (None of Your Business), an NGO co-founded by privacy activist Max Schrems, alleging that Facebook and Instagram "forced" users to consent to personal data processing for behavioral advertising. Meta had updated its Terms of Service and asserted it could rely on the GDPR's "performance of a contract" legal basis for processing.

Key findings of the investigation:
- The DPC held that while GDPR does not preclude Meta's reliance on the "performance of a contract" legal basis, Meta's practices breached Article 5(1)(a), which requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently, because its Terms of Use did not clearly disclose data processing activities, purposes, or legal basis.
- Following consultations with EU peer regulators, the findings were submitted to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), which notably held that Meta could no longer rely on the "performance of a contract" legal basis for behavioral advertising activities—a decision with broad implications for publishers engaged in behavioral advertising in the EU.
- The EDPB also directed the DPC to conduct a separate investigation into how Facebook and Instagram process special categories of data.
- The DPC adopted the EDPB's findings, issued the €390 million fine, and directed Meta to bring its data processing activities into compliance with GDPR within three months.
</summary>

Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined Meta €251 million on Tuesday, 17 December 2024, for failure to comply with the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The fine relates to a security breach on Facebook that began in July 2017 and affected close to three million accounts in the European Economic Area.

Meta is expected to appeal the decision. A Meta spokesperson said, "We took immediate action to fix the problem." Meta discovered the security issue in September 2018, fixed the vulnerability, and informed law enforcement authorities at that time.

This is the third fine issued by the DPC under GDPR since Des Hogan became Commissioner for Data Protection in February 2024. The final decision followed the DPC's submission of its draft ruling for review under the GDPR cooperation mechanism, which received no objections from peer EU data protection authorities. --- SOURCE 4: Meta Ireland fined €390 million for unlawful legal basis ---
URL: https://www.stibbe.com/publications-and-insights/meta-ireland-fined-eu390-million-for-unlawful-legal-basis

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 4 January 2023, Ireland's data protection authority (DPC) announced its final decision fining Meta Ireland €210 million for GDPR breaches regarding its Facebook services and €180 million for breaches regarding its Instagram services, totaling €390 million. The decisions center on the legal basis Meta used for processing personal data for personalised advertising.

Key events in the timeline:
- The DPC launched an investigation into Meta on 25 May 2018, following complaints about Facebook and Instagram. Meta had previously relied on user consent but shifted to the 'performance of a contract' legal basis after the GDPR took effect on 25 May 2018, arguing that processing personal data (including for personalised ads) was necessary to fulfil its contractual obligations under its terms of service.
- The DPC published a draft decision on 6 October 2021 proposing fines of up to €23 million for Instagram and €36 million for Facebook, finding that personalised advertising was a core element of Meta's services and that Meta had breached transparency obligations.
- Ten European supervisory authorities (including the Dutch DPA) disagreed with the DPC's draft, arguing personalised ads are not a core element of Meta's services. This triggered the European Consistency Mechanism, and the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) issued a binding decision on 5 December 2022.
- The EDPB upheld the DPC's position on transparency breaches but found that 'performance of a contract' was not a lawful basis for processing personal data for personalised advertising. The EDPB reasoned that: (1) Meta is not contractually obligated to offer personalised ads to users (the obligation exists with advertisers instead); (2) transparency requirements are indispensable to the contract basis; and (3) under Article 21(2)-(3) GDPR, users can object to direct marketing processing at any time without reason, meaning such processing is not "necessary" for the contract. The EDPB also ordered significantly increased fines.
- The DPC adopted the EDPB's binding decision on 31 December 2022, finding breaches of Article 6(1) GDPR from the GDPR's entry into force. Meta was given three months to bring its data processing into compliance.

Impact: The decisions strike at Meta's core business model, which relies on personalised advertising. Meta announced it would appeal, and the case may ultimately be referred to both the Irish Supreme Court and the CJEU. The decision also highlights significant disagreement between the DPC and other European supervisory authorities, with the DPC claiming the EDPB exceeded its powers. The ruling may affect other platforms relying on personalised ads, and preliminary questions on the 'legitimate interest' legal basis are pending before the CJEU (Case C-621/22). Meta is also facing revenue loss from Apple's iOS opt-out tracking feature.
</summary>

URL: https://privacymatters.dlapiper.com/2023/01/eu-ireland-metas-legal-basis-for-targeted-ads-found-to-breach-gdpr

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a DLA Piper "Privacy Matters" blog post (authors: James Sullivan, John Magee & David Brazil) analyzing Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) decisions announced January 4, 2023, fining Meta €390 million for breaching GDPR by using 'contractual necessity' as the legal basis for processing millions of Europeans' personal data for targeted advertising on Facebook and Instagram.

**Key Background:**
- Prior to GDPR's effective date (May 25, 2018), Meta changed its Terms of Service to rely on 'contractual necessity' instead of consent as the lawful basis for processing user data for personalized advertising.
- Two EU complainants argued Meta was "forcing" users to consent by conditioning services on accepting updated Terms of Service.
- The DPC initially sided with Meta, concluding 'contractual necessity' was a valid legal basis for personalized ads, while also finding transparency violations (with proposed fines understood to be €28-36 million).

**The Dispute:**
- 10 DPAs from across Europe contested the DPC's draft decision, arguing personalized advertising was not necessary to perform the core contract with users.
- On December 5, 2022, the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) issued a binding determination partially reversing the DPC, finding Meta was NOT entitled to rely on 'contractual necessity.' The EDPB also ordered the DPC to conduct a new investigation into ALL of Facebook's and Instagram's data processing operations.
- The DPC's final decisions on December 31, 2022 incorporated the EDPB's ruling, and were announced January 4, 2023.

**Disagreements Among Regulators:**
The decisions reflect two growing divisions among European DPAs: (1) whether 'contractual necessity' is an appropriate GDPR legal basis for personalized advertising, and (2) whether the EDPB has legal authority to order DPAs to bring new investigations. The DPC characterized the EDPB's order as an "open-ended and speculative investigation" and overreach, and indicated it will bring an annulment action before the Court of Justice of the EU—the DPC's first legal challenge of the EDPB's directions.

**Next Steps & Implications:**
- Meta announced its intention to appeal both the substance and the fines, meaning the 'contractual necessity' issue will be litigated for years.
- The DPC required Meta to bring processing into compliance within three months, but Meta's appeal may allow it to continue its current approach pending appellate outcomes.
- The decisions did not prohibit personalized advertising; Meta could pivot to 'consent' or 'legitimate interest' as legal bases, though 'legitimate interest' gives users a right to object that could undermine personalized advertising at scale.
- A third DPC decision regarding Meta's WhatsApp service was due imminently, though that inquiry concerned processing for service improvement purposes.
- Commercial implications are significant: Meta's share price fell 6.2% on the day the EDPB's position was reported. The business model of providing personalized ads without an opt-out option is increasingly difficult to justify.
</summary>
