--- SOURCE 17: TikTok Decision: Impact on International Data Transfers | Arthur Cox LLP ---
URL: https://www.arthurcox.com/knowledge/the-tiktok-decision-what-it-means-for-international-data-transfers

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Arthur Cox (an Irish law firm) publishes a legal briefing on the Irish High Court's judgment in TikTok Technology Limited v Data Protection Commission [2026] IEHC 347, delivered on 3 June 2026. The case concerned TikTok's appeal against a DPC decision dated 30 April 2025, which found that TikTok had infringed international transfer and transparency requirements under the GDPR.

Key facts: The DPC's original inquiry (IN-21-9-2) found that personal data stored by TikTok outside China was remotely accessed by employees in China, constituting an international transfer under Chapter V GDPR. The DPC identified infringements of Article 46 GDPR (transfers subject to appropriate safeguards) and Article 13(1)(f) GDPR (transparency), and imposed fines totaling €530 million plus a compliance order.

The High Court rejected most of TikTok's 11 grounds of appeal and upheld the Article 46 and Article 13(1)(f) infringement findings. Key rulings: (1) Under Article 46 GDPR, controllers must not only identify a transfer mechanism but also carry out an adequate, documented assessment of the protection in the third country—the supervisory authority can examine whether the assessment adequately demonstrates what it purports to demonstrate, without needing an independent examination of third-country laws. (2) Under Article 13(1)(f) GDPR, controllers must specifically identify the third countries to which personal data is transferred; TikTok's October 2021 privacy policy failed to name China as a destination.

The Court did find the DPC erred in refusing to consider a third expert opinion on Chinese law and in not stating the basis for concluding that TikTok's "Project Clover" pseudonymisation measures did not justify a different corrective approach. While these errors did not affect the infringement findings, the corrective orders were vacated and remitted to the DPC for further consideration.

Key takeaway: Organisations transferring data outside the EEA must "verify, guarantee and demonstrate" robust, documented, and defensible assessments of third-country data protection, capable of withstanding supervisory scrutiny.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 13 March 2025, the Irish Court of Appeal (COA) delivered its judgment in Data Protection Commission (DPC) v Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, upholding the DPC's appeal and refusing to stay (adjourn) the Meta Proceedings. The background involves a DPC decision on 25 November 2022 finding that Meta violated Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR after third parties 'scraped' personal data from Meta's platforms between May 2018 and September 2019. The DPC issued an order to comply, a reprimand, and two fines totalling €165 million. In December 2022, Meta brought both a statutory appeal and judicial review proceedings in the High Court.

The case related to separate "WhatsApp Proceedings": on 20 August 2021 the DPC fined WhatsApp €225 million for GDPR infringements (Articles 5, 12, 13, 14). WhatsApp's challenge to the EDPB's Article 65 decision was dismissed by the EU General Court as inadmissible (WhatsApp not directly concerned), and an appeal to the Court of Justice was pending (Advocate General's opinion due 27 March 2025). In July 2023, Meta sought to adjourn its High Court proceedings pending the outcome of the WhatsApp Proceedings; the High Court (Simons J) granted this, adjourning the Meta Proceedings in their entirety.

The COA set aside the High Court decision, emphasizing that challenges to decisions of public bodies should be prosecuted with "economy and celerity." The COA identified two scenarios following the upcoming CJEU decision in the WhatsApp case: (1) if the CJEU upholds the General Court's inadmissibility dismissal, unresolved EU law issues could delay Meta Proceedings by ~24 months; (2) if the CJEU allows the appeal, the case returns to the General Court, potentially delaying Meta Proceedings by a further ~40 months. The COA held that the GDPR requires challenges to DPC decisions to be brought in Irish courts, with Article 267 TFEU preliminary references as the exclusive mechanism to resolve GDPR interpretation doubts. The COA found no reason to delay requesting such a reference, and noted parties could later seek stays of the WhatsApp Proceedings if needed. The DPC's appeal was allowed and Meta's adjournment motions were dismissed.
</summary>

On August 26, 2024, the Dutch Data Protection Authority (Dutch DPA) fined Uber Technologies, Inc. and Uber B.V. €290 million for violating the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The fine stems from Uber's failure to implement appropriate safeguards for transferring EEA-based drivers' personal data to the United States over a 27-month period, during which Uber removed Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) from its data-sharing agreements between EEA and U.S. entities.

Key findings of the Decision:
- **Adequate safeguards required for intra-group transfers**: Uber argued both its U.S. and EEA entities were subject to GDPR under Article 3 as joint controllers, making Chapter V compliance unnecessary. The Dutch DPA rejected this, stating the data transfer requirements in Chapter V place a direct obligation on parties processing personal data in third countries. The DPA also determined an "onward transfer" occurred from Uber EEA (data exporter) to Uber U.S. (data importer), even though drivers entered data directly into the Uber platform.
- **Article 49 derogations limited**: Uber argued the transfers were lawful under Article 49 as necessary for contract performance. The DPA rejected this, finding the transfers were systematic, repetitive, and ongoing rather than incidental, and that contract existence alone does not constitute "necessity." The DPA was unconvinced that centralized U.S. processing was crucial to Uber's services, suggesting efficiency motives were insufficient.
- **Fine proportionality**: The DPA considered the violation serious, given the sensitive nature of drivers' personal data (including criminal data) and the 27-month duration. The fine was evaluated under the maximum parameters (higher of €20 million or 4% annual turnover). The DPA determined Uber "could have known" the transfer would require additional safeguards based on GDPR, CJEU case law, and prior regulator decisions.

The Dutch DPA coordinated its decision with other EU data protection authorities, meaning similar determinations could follow. Uber is expected to appeal. The Decision's biggest takeaway is the added uncertainty to the international data transfer landscape, particularly casting doubt on whether companies can rely on European Commission Q&A guidance for compliance or penalty mitigation purposes. **List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

The researcher conducted three rounds of web searches via the Tavily search tool (each round combining multiple queries):
- Round 1: "largest GDPR fines 2024 2025 over 50 million euros list"; "Irish DPC Meta Platforms Ireland fine November 2024 251 million euro final decision"; "Dutch AP Uber fine 290 million euros August 2024 GDPR"; "LinkedIn Irish DPC fine 310 million euros October 2024 GDPR"
- Round 2: "biggest GDPR fines 2025 imposed DPA over 50 million"; "TikTok 530 million euro fine Irish DPC GDPR 2025"; "Meta draft fine 2.5 billion euro DPC Ireland status 2026"; "Instagram draft fine 520 million DPC 2026 status"; "Meta 1.2 billion GDPR fine appeal General Court ruling 2025"
- Round 3: "Meta 2.5 billion fine draft DPC GDPR 2025 status Facebook advertising"; "Instagram 520 million euro draft fine DPC Meta status 2026"; "CNIL Google 325 million euros fine September 2025 Gmail GDPR"; "Enel Energia multa 79 milioni Garante privacy 2024 telemarketing"; "Meta 1.2 billion euro fine General Court T-325/23 judgment appeal 2025"
- Round 4: "DPC inquiry Meta behavioural advertising draft fine 2.5 billion 2025 status"; "Instagram fine 520 million DPC draft children data 2025 2026"; "GDPR fines 2026 new impositions above 50 million Garante AEPD Bundesdatenschutz"; "TikTok €530 million appeal Irish High Court judgment June 2026"; "LinkedIn DPC 310 million fine appeal notice 2025"; "Meta 1.2 billion GDPR fine appeal General Court T-325/23 hearing 2026"
- Round 5: "DPC inquiry Instagram children data proposed fine 520 million draft 2025 status news"; "Meta behavioural advertising inquiry DPC draft decision proposed fine billion euro status 2026"; "Meta 251 million fine appeal Irish High Court 2025 Uber 290 million appeal Amsterdam court"; "GDPR fine 2026 imposed DPC Garante AEPD over 50 million news July August 2026"

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

---

## A. Scope Determination and Summary of Qualifying Fines

The user asked for final GDPR enforcement fines strictly greater than €50,000,000 imposed by EU/EEA DPAs in calendar years 2024, 2025, and January–24 August 2026. Based on all sources gathered, the fines that **qualify** as imposed within the window (with caveats on appeal status and legal basis noted below) are:

1. **Enel Energia S.p.A.** – €79,107,101 – Italian Garante per la protezione dei dati personali – February 2024
2. **Uber Technologies Inc. / Uber B.V.** – €290,000,000 – Dutch Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP) – 26 August 2024
3. **LinkedIn Ireland Unlimited Company** – €310,000,000 – Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) – 24 October 2024
4. **Meta Platforms Ireland Limited** – €251,000,000 – Irish DPC – 17 December 2024
5. **TikTok Technology Limited** – €530,000,000 – Irish DPC – 2 May 2025
6. **Google LLC / Google Ireland Limited** – €325,000,000 – French CNIL – 1 September 2025 – **FLAGGED: this fine was imposed under the ePrivacy Directive (French CPCE and Data Protection Act), not under the GDPR, although it is often listed among GDPR fine rankings. It is included for completeness but must be flagged as not a GDPR fine.**

Out-of-scope but verified for context:
- **Meta Platforms Ireland Limited** – €1.2 billion – Irish DPC – 22 May 2023 (before the window; still the largest GDPR fine ever; under appeal with payment suspended)
- **Amazon Europe Core** – €746 million – Luxembourg CNPD – 2021 (annulled on procedural grounds by Luxembourg's Administrative Court on 12 March 2026)

No search results confirmed any other final GDPR fine above €50 million imposed between 1 January 2025 and 24 August 2026 besides the TikTok and Google fines. DLA Piper's January 2026 survey confirms approximately €1.2 billion in fines issued in 2025, with the €530 million TikTok fine as the largest of 2025 [46].

---

## B. Fines Within Scope – Detailed Findings

### 1. Meta Platforms Ireland Limited – €251 million (Irish DPC, 17 December 2024)

**Final amount:** €251,000,000 total (four administrative fines: €8M + €3M + €130M + €110M) [1][3][5].
**Date:** Final decisions adopted 12 December 2024; announced 17 December 2024 [1][5]. The DPC press release is dated 17 December 2024 [1][17].
**Issuing DPA:** Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC), Commissioners for Data Protection Dr. Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland [1][5].

**Article breakdown:**
- Decision 1 (inquiry IN-18-10-1): €8 million for infringement of Article 33(3) GDPR (failure to include necessary details in breach notification – nature of breach, categories of data subjects, categories of personal data records, likely consequences); €3 million for infringement of Article 33(5) GDPR (failure to create a contemporaneous documentary record of breach facts and remedial steps) [3][5].
- Decision 2 (inquiry IN-18-11-1): €130 million for infringement of Article 25(1) GDPR (failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures ensuring data protection by design); €110 million for infringement of Article 25(2) GDPR (failure to ensure data protection by default – tokens gave unnecessarily broad access to personal data) [3][5].
- Corrective measures included reprimands under Article 58(2)(b) GDPR and fines under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83 GDPR [1][5].

**Factual summary of conduct:** The fines stem from a personal data breach reported by Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (MPIL, formerly Facebook Ireland Ltd) in September 2018, impacting approximately 29 million Facebook accounts globally, including roughly 3 million in the EU/EEA [1][3][4]. The breach originated from a vulnerability created when a video upload function was deployed on Facebook in July 2017: Facebook's 'View As' feature combined with the 'Happy Birthday Composer' facility could be exploited to generate fully permissioned user tokens (coded identifiers) granting full access to other users' profiles [3][5]. Between 14 and 28 September 2018, unauthorized persons used scripts to exploit this vulnerability, gaining the ability to log on as account holders for approximately 29 million accounts globally [1][4][5]. Affected personal data categories included user full names, email addresses, phone numbers, locations, places of work, dates of birth, religion, gender, timeline posts, group memberships, and children's personal data [1][3][4]. Facebook security personnel were alerted by anomalous video upload activity and removed the vulnerable functionality; MPIL notified the DPC on 28 September 2018 [3][5].

**Procedure:** The DPC submitted a draft decision to the GDPR cooperation mechanism under Article 60 in September 2024; no objections were raised by peer EU/EEA supervisory authorities, though three comments per decision were received and considered [1][5]. Euractiv reports the fine was split as €11 million for failure to notify/full document the breach and €240 million for the nature of the breach itself [16]. Reuters reported the fine as 251 million euros ($263.5 million) on 17 December 2024 [17].

**Appeal status (as of August 2026):** Meta said "We took immediate action to fix the problem" and announced it would appeal (per Reuters: "Meta said it will also appeal Tuesday's decision") [16][17]. The Legit.eu summary also states "Meta has announced plans to appeal the decision" [18]. No court judgment confirming the finality of this specific €251M fine was found in the searches. Flag as **under appeal / appeal expected; final amount not yet confirmed by a court**.

**DPC Deputy Commissioner statement (verbatim):** "This enforcement action highlights how the failure to build in data protection requirements throughout the design and development cycle can expose individuals to very serious risks and harms, including a risk to the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals. Facebook profiles can, and often do, contain information about matters such as religious or political beliefs, sexual life or orientation, and similar matters that a user may wish to disclose only in particular circumstances. By allowing unauthorised exposure of profile information, the vulnerabilities behind this breach caused a grave risk of misuse of these types of data." – DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle [1][3][4].

**Off-DPA URL:** https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/dpc-guidance/decisions/inquiries-meta-platforms-ireland-limited-token-breach (full redacted decisions available as PDFs) [5]. Press release: https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/irish-data-protection-commission-fines-meta-eu251-million [1].
**Independent tracker URL:** GDPRhub case page: https://gdprhub.eu/index.php?title=DPC_%28Ireland%29_-_Meta_%22View-as%22_feature [3].

---

### 2. LinkedIn Ireland Unlimited Company – €310 million (Irish DPC, 24 October 2024)

**Final amount:** €310,000,000 (approximately $335 million) – three administrative fines totalling €310 million [11][14][17].
**Date:** Decision notified to LinkedIn on 22 October 2024; announced 24 October 2024; Pinsent Masons states the decision was published 25 October 2024 [13][14][17].
**Issuing DPA:** Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC); Commissioners Dr. Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland [14].

**Articles infringed:**
- Article 6(1)(a) GDPR – invalid reliance on consent for third-party data (consent was not "freely given, sufficiently informed, specific, and unambiguous") [11][13][14].
- Article 6(1)(f) GDPR – unlawful reliance on legitimate interests (rights and freedoms of members outweighed LinkedIn's commercial interests) [11][13][14].
- Article 6(1)(b) GDPR – unlawful reliance on contractual necessity [11][13][14].
- Article 5(1)(a) GDPR – breach of the principle of fairness [11][13][14].
- Articles 13(1)(c) and 14(1)(c) GDPR – transparency failures (failure to provide clear, transparent information about the lawful bases relied upon) [11][14].

**Factual summary of conduct:** The inquiry examined LinkedIn's processing of personal data of its registered members (data provided directly by members and data obtained via third-party partners) for behavioural analysis and targeted advertising. The DPC found LinkedIn lacked a valid lawful basis for these processing activities [11][13][14]. The complaint-based inquiry commenced 20 August 2018 following a complaint made by the French non-profit organisation La Quadrature Du Net to the French DPA [14][17]; the matter was redirected to the DPC as lead supervisory authority for LinkedIn (EU operations headquartered in Ireland) [13][14].

**Corrective measures:** A reprimand under Article 58(2)(b); three administrative fines totalling €310 million under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83; an order under Article 58(2)(d) to bring processing into compliance within three months [14][17][44].

**Procedure:** The DPC submitted its draft decision to the GDPR cooperation mechanism in July 2024 under Article 60; no objections were raised by peer EU/EEA supervisory authorities [13][14]. TechCrunch notes the fine is less than the amount Microsoft had set aside in an earlier 10-K disclosure [78].

**Appeal status (as of August 2026):** Goodwin states "It is unclear whether LinkedIn will appeal" [12]. Measured Collective's January 2026 ranking lists LinkedIn as "Under appeal" [39]. TechCrunch quotes LinkedIn: "While we believe we have been in compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), we are working to ensure our ad practices meet this decision by the IDPC's deadline" [78]. **Flag as: appeal status uncertain per Goodwin; listed as under appeal by Measured Collective; no final court judgment on a challenge found.**

**DPC Deputy Commissioner statement (verbatim):** "The lawfulness of processing is a fundamental aspect of data protection law and the processing of personal data without an appropriate legal basis is a clear and serious violation of a data subject's fundamental right to data protection." – DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle [14][17][44].

**Off-DPA URL:** http://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/irish-data-protection-commission-fines-linkedin-ireland-eu310-million [14].
**Independent tracker URL:** No GDPRhub page was captured in searches; the fine is tracked in the CookieYes list (ranked #6 among biggest fines) [42], Legit.eu list [43], PrivacyTerms.io list [41], and UniConsent list [40].

---

### 3. Uber Technologies Inc. and Uber B.V. – €290 million (Dutch AP, 26 August 2024)

**Final amount:** €290,000,000 [6][9][10]. This was the largest fine ever imposed by the Dutch DPA [7][10].
**Date:** GDPRhub records the decision date as 22 July 2024, published 25 August 2024 [6]. The AP press release and Willkie article state the fine was imposed/announced on 26 August 2024 [8][9].
**Issuing DPA:** Dutch Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP, Dutch Data Protection Authority), acting as lead supervisory authority because Uber's European headquarters are in the Netherlands [6][9][10].

**Article infringed:** Article 44 GDPR – transfer of personal data to a third country without appropriate safeguards under Chapter V (the AP found no valid transfer mechanism from 6 August 2021 to 27 November 2023) [6][10]. The AP rejected Uber's defenses under Article 3 (territorial scope), Article 49(1)(b) and (c) derogations, and arguments that no "transfer" occurred because drivers provided data directly [6][7][10].

**Factual summary of conduct:** Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI, San Francisco) and Uber B.V. (UBV, Netherlands) were found to be joint controllers for Uber drivers' personal data. Uber used a centralized IT infrastructure with servers in the US; EEA drivers' data was processed in the US in two situations: (1) data collected through the driver app and stored on US servers (including account details, taxi licences, location data, photos, payment details, identity documents, and in some cases criminal and medical data of drivers), and (2) when drivers exercised GDPR rights, UTI made data available to UBV [6][9]. Uber had used the European Commission's Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) but removed them from its joint controllership agreement effective 6 August 2021, arguing SCCs could not be used when processing falls directly under GDPR scope [6][8]. The violation lasted approximately 27 months, until Uber certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework in November 2023 [8][10]. The investigation began after more than 170 French drivers complained to the French human rights group Ligue des droits de l'Homme (LDH), which submitted a complaint to the French DPA (CNIL) on 12 June 2020; it was forwarded to the Dutch AP under the one-stop-shop mechanism [6][9][10].

**Key legal holdings:** The AP rejected Uber's argument that Article 3 and Chapter V are mutually exclusive, holding Chapter V is complementary and prevents circumvention; applied the EDPB Guidelines 05/2021's three cumulative criteria to find a "transfer" (including finding UBV was the exporter because drivers have little influence over processing purposes/means); rejected Uber's claim that drivers themselves were exporters; and rejected Article 49 derogations because transfers were systematic, repetitive, and ongoing, not incidental [6][7].

**Fine calculation:** The fine represents up to 4% of worldwide annual turnover; Uber reported approximately €34.5 billion in worldwide turnover in 2023 [9]. The fine was calculated per EDPB guidelines considering gravity and duration, Uber's global scale and financial capacity, the two-year period of non-compliance, the exposure of sensitive driver data, and insufficient mitigation measures; the AP determined Uber "could have known" the transfer would require additional safeguards based on GDPR, CJEU case law, and prior regulator decisions [8][10].

**Appeal status (as of August 2026):** Uber has indicated its intention to object/appeal the fine [9][10]. ### 4. TikTok Technology Limited – €530 million (Irish DPC, 2 May 2025)

**Final amount:** €530,000,000 total – €485 million for infringement of Article 46(1) GDPR (transfers of EEA user data to China without appropriate safeguards) and €45 million for infringement of Article 13(1)(f) GDPR (transparency failure) [19][21][22].
**Date:** Final decision announced 2 May 2025 [19][20]; some sources date the DPC's decision 30 April 2025 [22][25]. Draft decision submitted to the GDPR cooperation mechanism on 21 February 2025 under Article 60; no objections raised [19][20].
**Issuing DPA:** Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC), Commissioners Dr. Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland, as Lead Supervisory Authority for TikTok [19][20].

**Factual summary of conduct:** The inquiry (IN-21-9-2) examined TikTok's transfers of EEA user personal data to China, including remote access by ByteDance personnel in China to data stored in Singapore and the US (and Malaysia per one source) [19][22]. The DPC found TikTok failed to verify, guarantee, and demonstrate that EEA users' data remotely accessed by staff in China was afforded a level of protection essentially equivalent to EU standards; TikTok's own assessment of Chinese law identified material divergences from EU standards under the Anti-Terrorism Law, Counter-Espionage Law, Cybersecurity Law, and National Intelligence Law [19][21]. The DPC rejected TikTok's reliance on SCCs plus supplementary measures, finding its Transfer Risk Assessments were not substantively robust, and found Article 49 derogations inapplicable because transfers were systematic, repetitive and continuous [22].

**Transparency finding:** TikTok's October 2021 EEA Privacy Policy failed to name third countries (including China) to which data was transferred and failed to explain the processing operations (remote access by personnel in China to data stored in Singapore and the US). The infringement period ran from 29 July 2020 to 1 December 2022; the December 2022 privacy policy was deemed compliant [19][21].

**Notable aggravating disclosure:** Throughout the inquiry TikTok claimed it did not store EEA user data on servers in China, but in April 2025 disclosed that limited EEA user data had in fact been stored on servers in China (discovered in February 2025), meaning TikTok had provided inaccurate information to the inquiry. The DPC stated it is considering further regulatory action regarding this [19][21][23].

**Corrective measures:** TikTok was ordered to bring processing into compliance within 6 months; if not compliant, transfers to China would be suspended [19][21].

**Appeal and litigation timeline (crucial for finality):**
- 27 May 2025: TikTok filed an appeal at the Irish High Court against the fine and suspension order [20][83].
- 14 July 2025: High Court granted TikTok leave to proceed with the legal challenge [20][83].
- 13/14 November 2025: High Court granted TikTok's application to stay (suspend) the data transfer suspension order [20][22][83].
- 30 April 2026: Supreme Court dismissed the DPC's appeal against the High Court ruling [20][83].
- 3 June 2026: Irish High Court (judgment [2026] IEHC 347) largely upheld the DPC's decision: rejected most of TikTok's 11 grounds of appeal; upheld the Article 46 and Article 13(1)(f) infringement findings and the €530 million fine [20][24][25][26][83]. Freevacy: "The DPC's €530 million in administrative fines remain valid, although the court has indicated that it will consider TikTok's appeal regarding the amount of the fines imposed" [26].
- 30 June 2026: High Court of Ireland upheld the DPC's decision to impose the fine [20][83].
- **However**: The High Court found the DPC erred in refusing to consider a third expert opinion on Chinese law and in not stating the basis for concluding that TikTok's "Project Clover" measures (a €12 billion data security initiative with advanced pseudonymisation/encryption) did not justify a different corrective approach; the corrective orders (suspension/compliance) were **vacated and remitted to the DPC for reconsideration** [25][26][27]. The fine amount remains subject to TikTok's appeal regarding quantum [26].

**Bottom line on finality:** The €530 million fine was upheld by the Irish High Court on 3 June 2026 (with quantum still open to argument), and the corrective/suspension orders were remitted. So as of August 2026, the fine amount stands but remains under appeal regarding its amount. **Flag as: upheld at first instance but not fully final (quantum under appeal).**

**Quote (verbatim), DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle:** "The GDPR requires that the high level of protection provided within the European Union continues where personal data is transferred to other countries. TikTok's personal data transfers to China infringed the GDPR because TikTok failed to verify, guarantee and demonstrate that the personal data of EEA users, remotely accessed by staff in China, was afforded a level of protection essentially equivalent to that guaranteed within the EU." [19]

### 6. Google LLC / Google Ireland Limited – €325 million (CNIL, 1 September 2025) – FLAGGED AS ePrivacy, NOT GDPR

**Final amount:** €325,000,000 total – €200 million against GOOGLE LLC and €125 million against GOOGLE IRELAND LIMITED [55][56][57].
**Date:** Deliberation NoSAN-2025-004 of 1 September 2025; Reuters reported 3 September 2025 [55][57][59][58].
**Issuing DPA:** Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL), France – restricted committee [57].

**Important classification flag:** The CNIL explicitly stated these proceedings fall under the **ePrivacy Directive** (transposed into French law as Article L.34-5 of the French Postal and Electronic Communications Code and Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act), NOT the GDPR, and therefore the GDPR "one-stop shop" mechanism did not apply [56][57]. Several trackers nonetheless rank it among GDPR fines (e.g., UniConsent lists it at #7 of largest fines) [40]. **This fine must be EXCLUDED from a strict list of final GDPR fines, but is reported here because the user asked about CNIL fines above €50M and it is frequently miscategorized.**

**The two violations:**
1. Displaying advertisements in the form of emails inserted between private emails in Gmail users' "Promotions" and "Social" tabs without prior consent, violating Article L.34-5 CPCE (direct electronic marketing). The CNIL, citing CJEU judgment of 25 November 2021 (Case C-102/20), held these ads required consent [55][56][57].
2. Collecting invalid consent for advertising cookies/trackers during Google account creation until October 2023 – consent was not freely given (harder to refuse than accept – "dark patterns") and not informed (users were not told service access was conditional on tracker placement), violating Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act [55][56][57].

**Scale:** The cookie breach affected more than 74 million accounts; 53 million individuals in France illegally saw the ads in their Gmail tabs [55][56][57]. Aggravating factors: Google's central position in the online advertising market, Gmail's global scale, and Google having been sanctioned twice before by the CNIL (€100 million in 2020 and €150 million in 2021 for cookie-related breaches) [56][57].

**Compliance order:** Google must cease displaying ads between emails without prior consent and obtain valid consent for advertising trackers within six months, with a penalty of €100,000 per day of delay per company [55][56][57].

**Appeal status:** A Google spokesperson said the company was reviewing the decision and noted users have always been able to control ads; Google pointed to updates made over the prior two years [59]. **Under review; no court ruling found.**

## C. Verified Out-of-Window Fines and Status of the Meta €1.2 Billion Fine (2023)

**Meta Platforms Ireland Limited – €1.2 billion (Irish DPC/EDPB, 22 May 2023):**
- The largest GDPR fine ever imposed. Imposed 22 May 2023 following the EDPB's Binding Decision 1/2023 (13 April 2023), which overruled the Irish DPC's initial draft decision not to fine Meta [28][30][33][41]. One source (GDPRLocal) states "imposed on May 12, 2023" [28]; the DPC announcement and majority of sources date it 22 May 2023 [30][33][34].
- Conduct: unlawful transfers of EU users' personal data to the US after the Schrems II ruling (16 July 2020), using SCCs that the EDPB found did not adequately address US surveillance laws (FISA Section 702); the EDPB described the infringement as "systematic, repetitive and continuous" involving "massive" volumes of data, with Meta acting with "at least the highest degree of negligence" [28][30][33].
- Alongside the fine, Meta was ordered to suspend EU-US transfers within five months and to cease unlawful processing/storage in the US within six months [30][33][34].
- **Appeal status as of August 2026:** Under appeal (case T-325/23 before the EU General Court) with payment suspended [28][38][39][40]. GDPR Local (2025): "Meta called the fine 'flawed, unjustified and unnecessary' and is appealing (case T-325/23)"; Measured Collective (Jan 2026): "Under appeal with payment suspended"; Meta's total penalties documented by Tech Fines lists the €1.2B as "under appeal" [38]. **This fine is outside the 2024–2026 window; it remains the largest GDPR fine ever, but is not a "final" in-effect fine as of August 2026 (under appeal, payment suspended).**
- The maximum possible fine was over €4 billion (4% of global turnover) [30].
- NOYB (Max Schrems) stated: "We are happy to see this decision after ten years of litigation. The fine could have been much higher, given that the maximum fine is more than 4 billion and Meta has knowingly broken the law to make a profit for ten years." [30]

**Amazon Europe Core – €746 million (Luxembourg CNPD, 2021):**
- Per PrivacyTerms.io and UniConsent (as of July 2026): the €746 million Amazon fine was **annulled by Luxembourg's Administrative Court on 12 March 2026 on procedural grounds** (the CNPD did not properly assess intentionality/negligence or weigh a more lenient measure); the case was remanded to the CNPD for reassessment; the underlying violation was not overturned [40][41]. An earlier appeal had been dismissed in March 2025 [39][41]. **Excluded from the final list – annulled.**

**WhatsApp CJEU ruling (context):** The EU Court of Justice ruled (decision reported in 2026) that WhatsApp can directly challenge a binding EDPB decision before the EU courts; the top court sent the case back to the General Court on substance. This "unlocks six pending appeals by Meta in similar cases against the board" [82]. The Irish Court of Appeal judgment of 13 March 2025 (DPC v Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd) refused to stay Meta proceedings pending the WhatsApp CJEU case, emphasizing challenges to DPC decisions must be prosecuted with "economy and celerity" [36].

## On 26 June 2023, Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (**Meta**), the owner of Facebook, appealed a recent decision of the Data Protection Commission of Ireland (**DPC**) in the Irish High Court.

While not central to the appeal, submissions made to the High Court indicate that certainty for EU-US data transfers may come by mid-July 2023 when the European Commission is expected to determine “US adequacy” under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (**DPF**).

### Background

On 22 May 2023, the DPC issued a decision against Meta. The DPC’s decision had three parts:

1. An administrative fine of €1.2 billion (as directed by the European Data Protection Board (**EDPB**));
2. An order for Meta to suspend all transfers of European-based Facebook user data from Europe to the US to take effect 12 weeks after the period of appeals was allowed; and
3. An order for Meta to bring its transfers of European-based Facebook user data into compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (**GDPR**) within six months from the date of the decision (as directed by the EDPB).

### Context of Decision for EU-US Data Transfers

The context of the second and third limb to the DPC’s decision is important for businesses transferring personal data from the European Union (**EU**) to the US who eagerly await a solution to EU-US transfers (see our previous article [here](https://www.williamfry.com/knowledge/christmas-comes-early-for-eu-us-data-transfers/)).

The European Commission’s draft US adequacy decision under the DPF was expected by the end of the Summer – meaning that Meta’s EU-US transfers of European Facebook user data could be brought into compliance from the date the DPF takes effect.

### Decision on DPF Expected in July 2023

Meta appealed the DPC’s decision in the Irish High Court on various grounds under Section 150 of the Irish Data Protection Act 2018. On 26 June 2023, Meta was granted an extension of an interim stay on the decision until 31 July 2023.

This period of extension is significant because counsel for the DPC submitted to the Court that the European Commission would make its decision regarding the DPF in mid-July, indicating that:

* A decision about the DPF will be issued before 31 July 2023; and
* Meta’s appeal to this element of the DPC’s decision may be unnecessary for the Court to hear.

### Impact for Businesses

While Meta’s appeal remains on hold, the update about the possible timing of the European Commission’s draft US decision under the DPF is a welcome development. For many European businesses doing business in and through the US, the long-standing complexity and uncertainty for EU-US transfers have resulted in elevated compliance obligations to transfer personal data from Europe to the US. The impact of the DPF, if passed, is hoped to bring business-critical certainty (once it is fully operational), at least for a time.

In the meantime, European businesses must continue to rely on the GDPR’s other transfer mechanisms for EU-US data transfers (such as the standard contractual clauses).

If you have any queries about these developments, please contact [Leo Moore](https://www.williamfry.com/people/leo-moore/) or [Rachel Hayes](https://www.williamfry.com/people/rachel-hayes/).

args.summary:
This is a William Fry law firm knowledge article (dated June 29, 2023) about the anticipated EU-US data transfer adequacy decision under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF). It was authored by partners Rachel Hayes, Paul Convery, and Leo Moore.

BACKGROUND: On 22 May 2023, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) issued a decision against Meta Platforms Ireland (Facebook's owner) with three parts: (1) an administrative fine of €1.2 billion (as directed by the European Data Protection Board/EDPB); (2) an order to suspend all transfers of European-based Facebook user data from Europe to the US, effective 12 weeks after the appeal period; and (3) an order to bring those transfers into GDPR compliance within six months (as directed by the EDPB).

KEY DEVELOPMENTS: On 26 June 2023, Meta appealed the DPC's decision in the Irish High Court under Section 150 of the Irish Data Protection Act 2018. Meta was granted an extension of an interim stay on the decision until 31 July 2023. DPC counsel told the Court that the European Commission was expected to make its DPF adequacy decision in mid-July 2023, indicating a decision would be issued before 31 July 2023 and that Meta's appeal on this element might not need to be heard. The DPF would allow Meta's EU-US transfers to come into compliance once it takes effect.

IMPACT FOR BUSINESSES: The anticipated DPF decision was seen as a welcome development for European businesses transferring personal data from the EU to the US, promising to reduce the long-standing complexity and uncertainty that have resulted in elevated compliance obligations. However, until the DPF is fully operational, businesses must continue relying on GDPR's other transfer mechanisms, such as standard contractual clauses. Contact persons for queries: Leo Moore and Rachel Hayes.

# Irish data watchdog fines Instagram €405 million

![Instagram's parent, Meta, intends to file an appeal against the fine](./media_1ca2803e87b38f0ffe8c707ec5fab441b1a353539.jpeg?width=750&format=jpeg&optimize=medium)

![Instagram's parent, Meta, intends to file an appeal against the fine](./media_1ca2803e87b38f0ffe8c707ec5fab441b1a353539.jpeg?width=750&format=jpeg&optimize=medium)

#### It is the second-largest GDPR fine to-date, and deals with Instragram's failure to protect children.

Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) has fined Instagram a record €405 million for violating the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and failing to protect children's data.

The DPC's fine comes after a two-year investigation into the social media platform, which is owned by Meta.

The probe covered complaints that Instagram set all users' accounts to public settings by default, including those of users between the ages of 13 and 17. The probe also dealt with how teenagers with Instagram business accounts - many of them aspiring influencers - were allowed to make their email addresses and phone numbers public.

A spokesperson for the regulator told *BBC* that the [decision to impose a fine against Instagram](https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-62800884) under the GDPR was made on the 2nd September.

The specifics of the ruling will be made public next week.

Meta disagreed with the decision and said it intended to file an appeal against the fine.

The company said the probe centred on old settings that had been updated more than a year ago, and that it has subsequently introduced additional protections to keep teenagers secure and their information private.

'Anyone under 18 automatically has their account set to private when they join Instagram, so only people they know can see what they post, and adults can't message teens who don't follow them,' Meta said.

The firm disagrees with how the fine was calculated and said it was reviewing the ruling.

Commenting on the DPC's decision, Andy Burrows, head of child-safety-online policy for the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC), called it a "major breach" that had "significant safeguarding implications" and "the potential to cause real harm to children using Instagram."

He added that the ruling highlights how effective enforcement of regulations can safeguard children on social media.

"It's now over to the new Prime Minister to keep the promise to give children the strongest possible protections by delivering the Online Safety Bill in full and without delay."

The fine, the third the Irish regulator has imposed on a Meta-owned firm, is the second-highest imposed under the GDPR after a €746 million penalty against Amazon last year.

Also last year, the DPC fined Meta €225 million in relation to its messaging app WhatsApp; and in March, a penalty of €17 million after the DPC held an inquiry into [data breach notifications on Facebook](https://www.computing.co.uk/news/4029906/irish-regulator-gdpr-inquiry-facebook-leak).

The Instagram fine is the latest in a series of steps taken by regulators in the US and Europe to limit what data is gathered and shared by companies on [teens online](https://www.computing.co.uk/news/4037782/facebook-shelves-plans-instagram-kids).

The data children generate on social networking platforms, online video games, and other internet services are the focus of policymakers' efforts to improve data protection.

European legislators this year introduced more regulations pertaining to children. This includes the [Digital Services Act](https://www.computing.co.uk/news/4048581/eu-law-force-big-tech-regulate-online-content-update), which bars companies from using specific data to personalise ads shown to under-18s.

Last week, the Californian state senate approved a law, which could go into effect in 2024, which would require many online services to bolster child safety measures.

In the UK, changes to social networking sites were brought in to safeguard childrens' privacy after the Children's Code, also known as an age-appropriate design code, was passed into law last year.

# Instagram owner Meta fined €405m over handling of teens’ data

This article is more than 3 years old

Penalty follows investigation into Instagram setting that allowed teenagers to set up accounts that displayed contact details

Instagram owner Meta has been fined €405m (£349m) by the Irish data watchdog for letting teenagers set up accounts that publicly displayed their phone numbers and email addresses.

The Data Protection Commission confirmed the penalty after a two-year investigation into potential breaches of the European Union’s general data protection regulation (GDPR).

Instagram had allowed users aged between 13 and 17 to operate business accounts on the platform, which showed the users’ phone numbers and email addresses. The DPC also found the platform had operated a user registration system whereby the accounts of 13-to-17-year-old users were set to “public” by default.

The DPC regulates Meta – which is also the owner of Facebook and WhatsApp – on behalf of the entire EU because the company’s European headquarters are in [Ireland](https://www.theguardian.com/world/ireland).

The penalty is the highest imposed on Meta by the watchdog, after a [€225m fine imposed in September 2021](https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2022/jun/30/uk-data-watchdog-to-scale-back-fines-for-public-bodies) for “severe” and “serious” infringements of GDPR at WhatsApp and a €17m fine in March this year.

The fine is the second largest under GDPR, behind the €746m levied on Amazon in July 2021.

A DPC spokesperson said: “We adopted our final decision last Friday and it does contain a fine of €405m. Full details of the decision will be published next week.”

Caroline Carruthers, a UK data consultancy owner, said Instagram had not thought through its privacy responsibilities when letting teenagers set up business accounts and had shown an “obvious lack of care” in users’ privacy settings.

“GDPR has special provisions to make sure any service which targets children are living up to a high standard of transparency. Instagram fell foul of this when accounts of children were set to open by default rather than private.”

Last year [Meta](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/meta) suspended work on a version of Instagram for children following revelations about the app’s impact on teen mental health.

Instagram said it was [“pausing”](https://about.instagram.com/blog/announcements/pausing-instagram-kids) work to address concerns raised by parents, experts and regulators. The move followed revelations from a whistleblower, Frances Haugen, that Facebook’s own research showed Instagram [could affect girls’ mental health](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2021/sep/18/teenage-girls-body-image-and-instagrams-perfect-storm) on issues such as body image and self-esteem.

Instagram has said that prior to September 2019, it had put user contact details on business accounts and had informed users during the setup process. Under-18s now have their account set to private automatically when they join the platform.

Andy Burrows, head of child safety online policy at NSPCC, said: “This was a major breach that had significant safeguarding implications and the potential to cause real harm to children using Instagram.

“The ruling demonstrates how effective enforcement can protect children on social media and underlines how regulation is already making children safer online.”

A Meta spokesperson said: “This inquiry focused on old settings that we updated over a year ago, and we’ve since released many new features to help keep teens safe and their information private*.*

“Anyone under 18 automatically has their account set to private when they join Instagram, so only people they know can see what they post, and adults can’t message teens who don’t follow them.

“While we’ve engaged fully with the DPC throughout their inquiry, we disagree with how this fine was calculated and intend to appeal it. We’re continuing to carefully review the rest of the decision.”

### TikTok Fined €345m, Appeals Data Privacy Fine Imposed by DPC

[![tiktok fined](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7)](https://www.sovy.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/tiktokfined-1.jpeg)

Tiktok was fined a hefty €345 million for violation of the GDPR (The General Data Protection Regulation) requirements. The fine was a consequence of TikTok's mishandling of personal information, particularly that of children.

The Data Protection Commission is investigating TikTok, a popular social media platform with over 1.6 billion users worldwide. The Chinese company ByteDance owns it, and it's particularly popular among young people.

In 2020, accounts of users under 16 were automatically set to "public" by default allowing anyone to view.

Another concern revolves around the "family pairing" feature, which allows a teenager to link their TikTok account with a parent's. According to the [DPC,](https://edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2023-09/final_decision_tiktok_in-21-9-1_-_redacted_8_september_2023.pdf) TikTok failed to verify the identity of the associated user as the minor user's parent or guardian during this pairing process, and when posting videos.

In response, TikTok said in a statement that it strongly disagrees with the decision. Especially in terms of the substantial fine imposed. TikTok stressed that the fine doesn't match the alleged infractions.

 TikTok said the DPC criticized old features and settings, but they have made important changes. Now, all users under 16 have their accounts set to "private" automatically.

The Ireland's Data Protection Commission has issued a significant directive concerning the social media platform TikTok. The Commission stated that TikTok must pay €345 million in fines and ensure compliance with general data protection regulation, gdpr for its data processing operations.

This move reflects the Commission's commitment to enforcing data privacy and security standards within the digital landscape.

Moreover, the Data Protection Commission emphasized the urgency of this matter by setting a tight deadline. TikTok has only three months to make required changes and meet GDPR compliance.

This development signals a significant step in upholding data privacy and accountability in the realm of social media platforms. It underlines the growing importance of safeguarding user data, especially with a focus on child user protection, within the digital sphere.

## TikTok has appealed the fine to the European Union court

TikTok has taken legal action in Ireland's High Court, targeting both the DPC and Ireland's Attorney General in a parallel legal move. The platform vehemently opposes the penalties, and this legal challenge is a significant move in the dispute. The platform is doing everything it can to protect its position.

TikTok claims that the DPC's judgments and conclusions against the social media platform are invalid and should overturn them. The Commission will address the matter in October 2023.

# Inquiry into TikTok Technology Limited

**Area:** [Cross Border Private Company](/dpc-guidance/decisions?decision_tags=88&decision_category=All&decision_articles=All)

**Topic:** [Transfers](/dpc-guidance/decisions?decision_tags=All&decision_category=99&decision_articles=All)

**Articles:** [46](/dpc-guidance/decisions?decision_tags=All&decision_category=All&decision_articles=97), [13](/dpc-guidance/decisions?decision_tags=All&decision_category=All&decision_articles=98)

**DPC Reference:** IN-21-9-2

**Decision Date:** 30 April 2025

On 30 April 2025, the Irish Data Protection Commission (the ‘**DPC’**) adopted a final decision in an own-volition statutory inquiry, concerning TikTok Technology Limited’s (‘**TikTok’**) transfers of EEA User Data to China. The inquiry was carried out in accordance with the Data Protection Act 2018 and Article 60 of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The DPC was competent to act as lead supervisory authority for the processing at issue, pursuant to Article 56 GDPR. Prior to its adoption, the DPC submitted a draft of its decision to the Concerned Supervisory Authorities in February 2025, as required under Article 60(3) of the GDPR. The Concerned Supervisory Authorities did not raise any objections (for the purpose of Article 60(4) GDPR) to the draft decision.

### **Background to the Inquiry Process**

The transfers of personal data considered in the Decision consisted of TikTok’s transfers of EEA User Data to China by way of remote access to that personal data by personnel of the ByteDance group of companies in China. The Decision considered whether those transfers complied with Chapter V of the GDPR. The Decision also considered whether TikTok’s provision of information to users in relation to such transfers met TikTok’s transparency requirements as required by the GDPR.

### **Summary of Findings**

The decision concluded that:

* The DPC found that TikTok infringed Article 46(1) GDPR during the temporal scope of the Inquiry by carrying out the Data Transfers while failing to verify, guarantee and demonstrate that that the personal data of EEA users subject to the Data Transfers was afforded a level of protection essentially equivalent to that guaranteed within the European Union.
* The DPC found that TikTok infringed Article 13(1)(f) GDPR from 29 July 2020 to 1 December 2022 by failing to provide data subjects with required information on the Data Transfers and information on how the processing concerned remote access to personal data stored in Singapore and the United States by personnel based in China.

### **Corrective Measures**

Having considered the infringements of the GDPR as set out above, the DPC decided to exercise the following corrective powers, in accordance with Article 58(2) GDPR:

* An order pursuant to Article 58(2)(j) GDPR requiring TikTok Ireland to suspend the Data Transfers.
* An order pursuant to Article 58(2)(d) GDPR requiring TikTok Ireland to bring the processing into compliance. This requires TikTok to ensure that any EEA User Data located in China, as a result of the Remote Access Solution, when the order takes effect must cease being processed in China immediately at that point in time.
* Two administrative fines pursuant to Article 58(2)(i) GDPR as follows:

In respect of TikTok’s infringement of Article 46(1) GDPR, a fine of €485million.

In respect of TikTok’s infringement of Article 13(1)(f) GDPR, a fine of €45million.

---

For more information, you can download:

* A complete summary of the decision at this link: [Summary of inquiry into TikTok Technology Limited 30 April 2025](https://www.dataprotection.ie/sites/default/files/uploads/2025-11/TikTok-IN-21-9-2-Summary-EN.pdf)
* The full decision at this link: [Full decision into TikTok Technology Limited 30 April 2025](https://www.dataprotection.ie/sites/default/files/uploads/2025-10/Inquiry%20into%20TikTok%20Technology%20Limited%20April%202025.pdf)

# Meta fined $275 million over data scraping practices that violated GDPR

Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC) has fined Meta €265 million (about $275 million) after a year-long inquiry into the company's data protection practices.

The fines stem from Facebook’s practice of making personal data accessible by default through search functions and concern Facebook Contact Importer, Messenger Contact Importer, Instagram Contact Importer and Messenger Search and its variant Messenger Contact Creator features.

The DPC said on Monday the features violated General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [rules around Data Protection by Design and Default](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-25-gdpr/).

The features allowed anyone to scrape the social media giant — a process where bots are able to gather data online automatically. Typically, the bots are used to scan social media sites like Facebook and copy whatever information is available.

The investigation began in April 2021 after media reports emerged of a “collated dataset of Facebook personal data that had been made available on the internet” following an instance of scraping. According to the ruling, the issues occurred between May 2018 and September 2019.

The DPC noted that it worked with “all of the other data protection supervisory authorities within the EU” – which were in agreement with its decision.

In addition to the fine, the DPC is ordering a range of corrective measures that need to be taken, including remedying the practices within three months of the ruling’s release.

A DPC spokesperson told The Record that the order requires the company to “implement appropriate technical and organizational measures” that ensure “by default personal data are not made accessible without the individual’s intervention to an indefinite number of natural persons.”

In a statement to The Record, a Meta spokesperson said the company has “cooperated fully with the Irish Data Protection Commission on this important issue.”

“We made changes to our systems during the time in question, including removing the ability to scrape our features in this way using phone numbers,” the spokesperson said.

“Unauthorized data scraping is unacceptable and against our rules and we will continue working with our peers on this industry challenge. We are reviewing this decision carefully.”

In September, Meta [said it was appealing](https://therecord.media/instagram-appealing-400-million-fine-from-ireland-data-privacy-org-over-gdpr-violations/) another fine, worth $400 million, for violations related to Instagram allowing children as young as 13 to operate business accounts. Last year, the DPC also [fined Meta $267 million](https://therecord.media/whatsapp-hit-with-giant-e225-million-267m-million-gdpr-fine/) for GDPR violations related to data processing done by WhatsApp.

# Amazon's €746M GDPR Fine Annulled in 2026, But Legitimate Interest Still Lost

Luxembourg's Administrative Court annulled Amazon's record €746 million GDPR fine on March 12, 2026, but not because the underlying violations were wrong. It did not agree that Amazon's data practices were lawful.

![Secure Privacy Logo](/_next/image?url=%2FLogo%2BSecure%2BPrivacy.avif&w=3840&q=75)

Secure Privacy Team

Privacy Experts

·9 min read

Share:

![Amazon's €746M GDPR Fine Annulled in  2026, But Legitimate Interest Still Lost](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.prismic.io%2Fsecure-privacy%2FdfWYzN6XwffLe_KW_Gemini_Generated_Image_hgf3crhgf3crhgf3.png%3Fauto%3Dformat%2Ccompress&w=3840&q=75)

Luxembourg's Administrative Court annulled Amazon's record €746 million GDPR fine on March 12, 2026, but not because the underlying violations were wrong. The court found Luxembourg's CNPD skipped a fault analysis that EU case law now requires before any fine issues, and sent the case back to the regulator to redo that step. Everything else the CNPD found in 2021, including that Amazon could not rely on legitimate interest for behavioral advertising and that its transparency notices fell short, was left standing.

If your organization runs ad-targeting or profiling on a legitimate interest basis, the headline "Amazon's fine got thrown out" is not the takeaway you want to carry into your next documentation review. The court agreed with Amazon on how the fine was calculated. It did not agree that Amazon's data practices were lawful.

## Key Takeaways

* The Administrative Court's March 12, 2026 judgment (case no. 52757C) annulled the CNPD's July 2021 decision in full, but on procedural grounds only: the regulator never assessed whether Amazon acted with fault (intent or negligence) before fining it, a step the Court of Justice of the EU made mandatory in its December 5, 2023 rulings in *Deutsche Wohnen* (C-807/21) and the Lithuanian *"Nacionalinis"* case (C-683/21).
* The court separately confirmed the CNPD's substantive findings: Amazon's reliance on legitimate interest as the legal basis for its behavioral advertising was not justified, and its information practices did not meet GDPR's transparency requirements under Articles 12-14.
* At a January 8, 2026 hearing, both sides told the court that Amazon had already brought its practices into compliance with the CNPD's original order, which is why the coercive daily penalty attached to the case became moot before the ruling even came down.

## What actually changed on March 12, 2026

The CNPD opened its investigation into Amazon Europe Core in 2018 after a coordinated complaint campaign by La Quadrature du Net on behalf of roughly 10,000 individuals, and issued its decision in July 2021: a €746 million fine, at the time the largest in GDPR history, plus a coercive penalty of €746,000 per day for continued non-compliance. Amazon appealed to Luxembourg's Administrative Court.

The appeal sat for years while a separate strand of EU law caught up with it. On December 5, 2023, the CJEU ruled in *Deutsche Wohnen* and the parallel Lithuanian case that GDPR fines cannot be imposed on a strict-liability basis. A regulator has to establish that the controller acted with intent or negligence before a fine is even on the table; a bare finding of infringement is not enough on its own.

That doctrine did not exist when the CNPD wrote its 2021 decision, and the regulator never went back to retrofit it. At the January 8, 2026 hearing, the CNPD's own counsel conceded the point: the fault inquiry required by the 2023 CJEU judgments had not been attempted. The Administrative Court treated that gap as fatal to the fine itself, not fixable by the appellate court patching in a fault finding after the fact, and annulled the decision in full, sending the case back to the CNPD to redo the fault and sanction-selection analysis from scratch.

## What the court left standing: legitimate interest and transparency violations

This is the part that gets flattened in headline coverage and in AI-generated summaries of the ruling: annulling the fine is not the same as clearing Amazon.

The Administrative Court reviewed the CNPD's substantive violations on the merits and did not disturb them. It confirmed that Amazon's use of legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f) to justify behavioral advertising and cross-service profiling did not hold up, the same conclusion the CNPD reached in 2021. It also confirmed the CNPD's finding that Amazon's disclosures to users about how their data was used for ad-targeting did not satisfy the transparency obligations in Articles 12 through 14.

In other words, the court split the case cleanly into two questions and answered them differently. Were the violations real? Yes, mostly. Was the fine issued the right way? No, because the CNPD skipped a procedural step. Amazon won on the second question, not the first, which is exactly why the CNPD's own statement on the ruling describes it as having secured "effective data-processing compliance by Amazon" with its "key findings confirmed," rather than framing the outcome as a loss.

Amazon's own public statement on the case leans on the procedural win rather than disputing the substance: the company said it "worked in good faith to give customers control over whether they see personalised advertising based on their interests" after the 2018 rollout of GDPR left ad-targeting rules unclear. That framing is notably different from arguing the CNPD's legitimate-interest and transparency findings were mistaken, because the court did not find them mistaken.

### Annulled vs. upheld, at a glance

| Element of the case | Outcome after the March 2026 ruling |
| --- | --- |
| €746 million fine | Annulled — CNPD must redo the fault (intent/negligence) analysis before any fine can be reimposed |
| €746,000/day coercive penalty | Moot — both parties confirmed at the January 2026 hearing that Amazon had already complied |
| Legitimate interest for behavioral advertising | Upheld against Amazon — rejected as a valid legal basis, same as the CNPD's original finding |
| Transparency notices (Articles 12-14) | Upheld against Amazon — found deficient, same as the CNPD's original finding |
| Underlying data practices at issue | Still non-compliant as found; Amazon's subsequent remediation is what resolved the compliance order, not the court reversing the finding |

If a table like this one is the first place you're seeing your own legitimate-interest use cases laid out this plainly, that's worth fixing before a regulator does it for you.

## Why this is a procedural win, not a substantive one

A narrowing of a regulator's internal process is not a legal theory a defendant can lean on twice. The fault-requirement doctrine from *Deutsche Wohnen* controls how the CNPD (and every other EU data protection authority) must build the record before issuing a fine going forward. It does not change what counts as a valid legal basis for advertising, and it does not retroactively bless legitimate interest as sufficient for profiling.

That distinction matters directly for anyone using [legitimate interest as a lawful basis for marketing or ad-targeting](https://secureprivacy.ai/blog/legitimate-interest-vs-consent-gdpr), because the substantive bar the CNPD applied to Amazon, and that the court left untouched, is now a live precedent for how any legitimate interest assessment for advertising gets tested. The EDPB's own October 2024 Guidelines 1/2024 already pushed toward stricter necessity and balancing criteria; this ruling is a concrete enforcement example of that standard being applied to one of the largest ad-tech operations in the world and holding up on appeal.

If your program relies on legitimate interest for any advertising, profiling, or cross-service tracking use case, the operational lesson is not "wait and see if the fine survives." It's to pressure-test the documentation now: does your legitimate interest assessment show a real, specific interest (not "we want to market effectively"), a genuine necessity analysis with alternatives considered, and a balancing test that actually weighs the intrusiveness of the profiling against what a user would reasonably expect? A [legitimate interests assessment built on a worked example](https://secureprivacy.ai/blog/legitimate-interests-assessment-gdpr-guide) walks through exactly that three-part test, and it is worth rerunning against your current ad-targeting setup rather than assuming last year's version still clears this bar.

This is also where documentation gaps get expensive twice over: once if a regulator finds the legal basis itself doesn't hold, and again if you can't produce a contemporaneous record showing when and how the assessment was done. Secure Privacy's Data Map & ROPA module ties legal bases, data categories, and retention periods directly to each processing activity in one record, so a legitimate-interest justification for an advertising use case is documented at the point it's relied on rather than reconstructed after a regulator asks. The Assessments module runs LIAs alongside DPIAs and AIAs from the same workflow, with approval routing, so the balancing test itself has a timestamped, audit-ready trail if a DPA ever asks to see it.

## What to do before your next audit

Audit every processing activity currently justified on legitimate interest grounds where the underlying purpose is advertising, profiling, or personalization. For each one, confirm the LIA was completed before processing started, not after, and that it names a specific alternative the organization considered and rejected, not a generic "no other option was viable" line. If any of those assessments were written before October 2024, treat them as due for a refresh against the EDPB's current guidance, not just this ruling.

None of that has to live in spreadsheets scattered across legal, marketing, and IT. Secure Privacy's [Privacy & AI Governance Platform](https://secureprivacy.ai/privacy-governance) puts Data Map & ROPA and the Assessments module in one place, so every legitimate-interest basis for advertising is tied to a documented, approved LIA before processing starts, not reconstructed under pressure after a regulator opens a file.

## FAQ

### Was Amazon's GDPR fine overturned because it did nothing wrong?

No. Luxembourg's Administrative Court confirmed that Amazon's legitimate interest basis for behavioral advertising was invalid and that its transparency notices fell short. The €746 million fine was annulled only because the CNPD failed to first establish that Amazon acted with fault, a step EU case law made mandatory after the CNPD's original decision was issued.

### What is the fault requirement that got the fine annulled?

It's a threshold condition from the CJEU's December 5, 2023 judgments in *Deutsche Wohnen* (C-807/21) and a related Lithuanian case (C-683/21): a data protection authority must show a controller acted with intent or negligence before imposing an administrative fine. Strict liability, fining based on the violation alone, is no longer sufficient.

### Does this ruling mean legitimate interest can be used for ad-targeting now?

No. The court upheld the CNPD's finding that legitimate interest did not justify Amazon's behavioral advertising and profiling. That substantive rejection was not part of what got annulled.

### What happened to the €746,000-per-day coercive fine?

It became moot before the ruling. At a January 8, 2026 hearing, both Amazon and the CNPD told the court Amazon had already complied with the underlying corrective order, so the coercive penalty tied to non-compliance no longer applied.

### Can the CNPD fine Amazon again for the same conduct?

The case was remanded to the CNPD to redo its fault and sanction-selection analysis. If the CNPD completes that analysis and finds fault, it can issue a new fine on the same substantive findings the court already upheld, though it must do so through the corrected procedure this ruling requires.

### What should privacy teams take from this if they don't use legitimate interest for advertising?

The fault-requirement doctrine applies to how any DPA builds a fine, not just this case. It's relevant background for any organization under active investigation, but it is a process safeguard for regulators to follow, not a substantive defense a controller can raise to justify its own processing.

### How is this different from Amazon's 2020 French fine over cookies?

That was a separate, earlier CNIL enforcement action in France concerning cookie consent practices, unrelated to this CNPD case, which concerns the lawful basis for behavioral advertising and profiling rather than cookie banners specifically.

# Amazon vs CNPD (12/03/2026): fine annulled, fine methodology reset

On 12 March 2026, Luxembourg’s Administrative Court annulled Amazon’s €746m fine while upholding core findings. Key takeaway: apply CJEU (Deutsche Wohnen/Nacionalinis) and robustly justify the GDPR fine methodology.

By **Expertise Luxgap** 06/08/2026

**12 March 2026 — Amazon vs CNPD**. Luxembourg’s Administrative Court (judgment No 52757C) annulled the €746m fine imposed on Amazon in 2021, while upholding core findings on processing activities. Key takeaway: GDPR fine methodology must reflect CJEU case law (Deutsche Wohnen and Nacionalinis) and the fault requirement. Official sources: [Luxembourg Justice portal](https://justice.public.lu/fr/actualites/2026/03/arret-cour-administrative-amazon.html), [CNPD (FR)](https://cnpd.public.lu/fr/actualites/national/2026/03/arret-ca-amazon-cnpd.html), [CNPD (EN)](https://cnpd.public.lu/en/actualites/national/2026/03/arret-ca-amazon-cnpd.html).

## The case

The Court noted that orders and the penalty payment became moot because Amazon had brought its processing into compliance. However, the fine was annulled due to a *subsequent* change in CJEU case law (5/12/2023) governing sanction powers and the need to establish at least negligent *fault*. References: [C‑807/21 Deutsche Wohnen](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=celex%3A62021CJ0807) and [C‑683/21 Nacionalinis](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/FR/CASE/?uri=CELEX%3A62021CJ0683). See also the [CJEU flash (Decisions of interest to the Union, 2026/2)](https://curia.europa.eu/site/upload/docs/application/pdf/2026-06/flash_interet_n2-26.pdf).

## Legal reasoning

### 1) Article 83 GDPR and judicial review

Article 83 GDPR requires effective, proportionate and dissuasive fines, reasoned against specific factors (gravity, duration, intent/negligence, cooperation, corrective measures, past infringements, etc.). Text: [EUR‑Lex, GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?%3Btid=+111270262&uri=celex%3A32016R0679). The CJEU (5/12/2023) clarified: (i) the entity as controller may be directly fined; (ii) the authority must establish fault (at least negligence) and respect the autonomous framework of Article 83(2). The Administrative Court applied this framework and remitted the fine calculation/method.

### 2) Right to object (Article 21) and scope

The CJEU flash notes the Court dismissed an *independent* Article 21 violation in this case, without undermining the right to object to interest‑based marketing. It stresses specificity of charges and burden of proof. Framework: [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN-DE/TXT/?from=EN&uri=CELEX%3A32016R0679) and [European Commission guidance](https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/information-business-and-organisations/dealing-requests-individuals_en).

### 3) Fine calculation: EDPB expectations

EDPB Guidelines 04/2022 (24/05/2023) set five steps: starting point (gravity/category), number of infringements, aggravating/mitigating factors, legal caps, and final check (effective, proportionate, dissuasive). Refs.: [EDPB 04/2022](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/documents/guideline/guidelines-042022-on-the-calculation-of-administrative-fines-under-the-gdpr_en) and [EDPB news](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/news/2023/edpb-adopts-final-version-guidelines-calculation-administrative-fines-following_en).

## What changes in practice

* **Executives, in‑house counsel and DPOs in Luxembourg**: fines will remain high where fault is evidenced and the EDPB method is robustly reasoned. Conversely, weak reasoning can lead to annulment or recalibration even if non‑compliance persists. To secure your [DPO mandate](/services/dpo/) and sanction governance, structure evidence under Article 83(2) and EDPB steps.
* **Marketing and CISOs**: material compliance comes first. Fix quickly and log remediation (decision logs, change logs, CMP, ID deactivation, new legal bases, updated DPAs, Article 32 controls). An independent [security audit](/services/audit-cybersecurite/) helps substantiate these controls.
* **Advertising and legitimate interest**: document the balancing test (Art. 6(1)(f)), offer a frictionless objection (Art. 21) and keep execution evidence; clarify roles/contracts (Arts. 26–28) per [EDPB 8/2020](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/documents/guideline/guidelines-82020-on-the-targeting-of-social-media-users_en). For local implementation, see [GDPR Luxembourg compliance with the CNPD](/rgpd-luxembourg/).

*Example*: a banner relying on legitimate interest for marketing must provide a simple, enforceable objection, truly disable tags/IDs, and show the controller’s interests do not override data subjects’ interests. Otherwise: investigation, orders, then a fine under a methodology now tested against the 05/12/2023 CJEU rulings.

## Common pitfalls

1. **Incomplete fine methodology**: failure to align with EDPB 04/2022’s five steps (gravity/duration, number of infringements, factors, caps, proportionality) risks partial/total annulment. Ref.: [EDPB 04/2022](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/documents/guideline/guidelines-042022-on-the-calculation-of-administrative-fines-under-the-gdpr_en).
2. **Underestimating the fault requirement**: since C‑807/21 and C‑683/21, provide concrete elements (known inadequate procedures, lack of controls, ignored warnings, etc.). Refs.: [C‑807/21](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=celex%3A62021CJ0807), [C‑683/21](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/FR/CASE/?uri=CELEX%3A62021CJ0683).
3. **Equating remediation with no liability**: later compliance affects penalty payments and quantum but does not erase past infringements. Refs.: [official summary](https://justice.public.lu/fr/actualites/2026/03/arret-cour-administrative-amazon.html), [CNPD position](https://cnpd.public.lu/en/actualites/national/2026/03/arret-ca-amazon-cnpd.html).
4. **Poorly implemented right to object**: a non‑functional opt‑out, inconsistent request handling, or mis‑mapped legal bases triggers focused allegations. Framework: [European Commission](https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/information-business-and-organisations/dealing-requests-individuals_en).
5. **Weak adtech governance**: unclear roles/contracts (Arts. 26–28), missing records (Art. 30) and unproven measures (Art. 32). Ref.: [EDPB 8/2020](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/documents/guideline/guidelines-82020-on-the-targeting-of-social-media-users_en).

## Official sources

* [CNPD — compliance achieved (FR)](https://cnpd.public.lu/fr/actualites/national/2026/03/arret-ca-amazon-cnpd.html) — [(EN)](https://cnpd.public.lu/en/actualites/national/2026/03/arret-ca-amazon-cnpd.html)
* [CJEU — C‑807/21 Deutsche Wohnen](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=celex%3A62021CJ0807) — [Press release 184/23](https://curia.europa.eu/jcms/upload/docs/application/pdf/2023-12/cp230184en.pdf)
* [CJEU — C‑683/21 Nacionalinis](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/FR/CASE/?uri=CELEX%3A62021CJ0683)
* [EDPB — Guidelines 04/2022](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/documents/guideline/guidelines-042022-on-the-calculation-of-administrative-fines-under-the-gdpr_en) — [news](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/news/2023/edpb-adopts-final-version-guidelines-calculation-administrative-fines-following_en)
* [GDPR text (Arts. 83, 21)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?%3Btid=+111270262&uri=celex%3A32016R0679)
* [CJEU flash — Decisions of interest to the Union (2026/2)](https://curia.europa.eu/site/upload/docs/application/pdf/2026-06/flash_interet_n2-26.pdf)

## In short

The 12 March 2026 ruling does not loosen Luxembourg enforcement: it raises the bar on reasoning and methodology for GDPR fines under CJEU oversight. Priorities for organisations: remediate fast and document legal basis, objection flows and adtech governance. For local guidance across risk calculation and evidencing, see our [GDPR Luxembourg page](/rgpd-luxembourg/) or [contact us](/contact/).

On March 12, 2026, the Administrative Court ruled on Amazon's appeal against the Administrative Tribunal's judgment of March 18, 2025, in proceedings concerning the CNPD's July 15, 2021, decision which imposed a €746 million fine on Amazon Europe Core S.à rl for violations of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

Key points of the ruling:
- The case concerned the legal basis for processing personal data for interest-based advertising and compliance with GDPR provisions.
- At the pleadings hearing on January 8, 2026, the parties confirmed Amazon had brought the disputed processing into compliance.
- The Court confirmed that reliance on legitimate interest for processing was not justified.
- The €746 million fine was annulled due to developments in case law, and the CNPD must reassess the financial sanction.
- The CNPD stated that the Court confirmed the information modalities were not compliant with GDPR provisions at the time of the CNPD's decision.
- The CNPD will continue its examination of the case to ensure efficient application of the GDPR.

The article also provides practical guidance for companies to review their legal bases for data processing to ensure GDPR compliance and alignment with evolving case law. The content is truncated behind a subscription paywall.
