# Luxembourg court scraps Amazon’s €746m data privacy fine

Published on

by

**Failure by a watchdog to verify the existence of a deliberate act or negligence when evaluating GDPR violations has seen Amazon escape a record fine.**

The Administrative Court of Luxembourg has annulled a €746 million penalty imposed against Amazon by the Luxembourg National Commission for Data Protection (CNPD) in 2021 for [failures to comply with the EU General Data Protection Regulation](https://iclg.com/practice-areas/data-protection-laws-and-regulations) (GDPR). Handing down its judgment on 12 March, the court held that the CNPD had failed to carry out two critical analyses in handing down its decision and returned the case to the watchdog for reconsideration.

### **Record fine**

The penalty had been imposed alongside corrective measures in July 2021 after the CNPD concluded the e-commerce giant had breached the GDPR by processing personal data for targeted advertising purposes without consent.

It had made history at the time as the largest fine ever levied by a European data protection watchdog under the GDPR and remains the second largest penalty to date – surpassed only by a €1.2 billion fine brought by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) against Meta Platforms Ireland in 2023.

La Quadrature du Net, a non-profit which had been involved in a collective legal action relating to Amazon’s targeted advertising systems, had at the time praised the fine as one that “hits straight to the heart of Big Tech’s predatory system, and should be celebrated as such”.

Believing the CNPD’s decision to be without merit, Amazon appealed the penalty but failed to convince the Luxembourg Administrative Tribunal to annul it. In March 2025, the tribunal upheld the CNPD’s original decision but suspended the fine and corrective measures for the duration of the appeal period.

### **The judgment**

This time around, Amazon has seen better success. In annulling the fine, the Administrative Court relied on two decisions handed down by the Court of Justice of the European Union in 2023, *Deutsche Wohnen* and *Nacionalinis,* which established a supervisory authority’s obligation to demonstrate a deliberate act or negligence on the part of the personal data controller.

The court held that the CNPD had failed to analyse the criterion of fault and had not verified an intentional violation of the GDPR by Amazon or, at the very least, the company’s negligence.

The court further found that the CNPD had hastily chosen to impose a fine without first considering whether other measures provided for under the GDPR might be more appropriate.

“Indeed, the supervisory authority had adopted an approach of almost automatically imposing a fine following the identification of GDPR violations,” the court held (*Google translation here and hereafter).*

The case has now been referred to the CNPD so that the two missed analyses can be conducted for the first time.

Critically, while the fine was annulled because of the CNPD’s procedural shortcomings, the Administrative Court largely sided with the watchdog on the various identified GDPR violations.

With Amazon having taken effective steps to come into compliance with the GDPR, a CNPD representative confirmed at a January 2026 hearing that the “aspects of the case relating to coercive measures, under penalty of fines, had […] become moot”.

In a press statement on the ruling, Amazon said it was “pleased” that the court has “overturned the CNPD’s decision and recognised [its] position”.

 “In 2018, when an ambiguous new privacy law came into force in the EU without clear guidance on how to show customers relevant advertising, we worked in good faith to give customers control over whether they see personalised advertising based on their interests,” the company added. “We strongly disagreed with the initial ruling and disproportionate fine that had originally been issued in this case, which is why we appealed.”

Administrative Court ruling in the case between Amazon and the CNPD

# The CNPD has secured effective data-processing compliance by Amazon, has seen its key findings confirmed and pursues its work

• National

The National Commission for Data Protection (CNPD) takes note of the judgment delivered by the Administrative Court on 12 March 2026 in the case between Amazon Europe Core S.à r.l. (Amazon) and the CNPD concerning the decision taken by the latter in the summer of 2021 regarding Amazon.

In this decision, the CNPD issued a compliance order against Amazon for breaching several provisions of the GDPR in relation to its online behavioural advertising practices and imposed a fine in this regard.

The CNPD notes that the main regulatory action it had taken has borne fruit. Indeed, the Administrative Court has endorsed the CNPD’s approach almost in its entirety and, in particular, confirmed that Amazon’s reliance on legitimate interests as the legal basis for the processing operations in question was not justified. The Administrative Court also upheld the CNPD’s analysis that, at the time of its decision, the information procedures did not comply with the relevant provisions of the GDPR.

Finally, the Administrative Court noted that, prior to the date of the hearing in this case, Amazon had complied with the compliance order issued by the CNPD. It therefore concluded that the proceedings had become irrelevant in this respect.

As regards the fine, the Administrative Court annulled it on the basis of a development in the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union that occurred after the CNPD’s decision. Thus, whilst upholding the core work of the CNPD, the judgment nevertheless establishes that the CNPD must analyse the imposition of a financial penalty in the light of this case law, particularly with regard to the question of whether Amazon demonstrated a certain degree of negligence in its practices.

The CNPD notes that its action has led to Amazon’s practices being brought into full compliance with the relevant provisions of the case regarding online behavioural advertising. Building on this progress, it will continue to handle the case in a way to ensure the efficient application of the GDPR.

args.summary:
The Luxembourg National Commission for Data Protection (CNPD) announced that the Administrative Court issued a judgment on 12 March 2026 in the case between Amazon Europe Core S.à r.l. (Amazon) and the CNPD, concerning a CNPD decision from summer 2021. In that decision, the CNPD had issued a compliance order against Amazon for breaching several GDPR provisions related to its online behavioural advertising practices and imposed a fine.

Key outcomes of the Administrative Court ruling:
- The Court endorsed the CNPD's approach almost entirely, confirming that Amazon's reliance on legitimate interests as the legal basis for the processing was not justified.
- The Court upheld the CNPD's analysis that Amazon's information procedures did not comply with GDPR provisions at the time of the decision.
- The Court noted that Amazon had already complied with the compliance order before the hearing, rendering those proceedings irrelevant.
- The Court annulled the fine, based on a development in Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) case law that occurred after the CNPD's decision. It established that the CNPD must analyse financial penalties in light of this new case law, particularly regarding whether Amazon demonstrated a certain degree of negligence.

The CNPD stated that its action successfully brought Amazon's practices into full compliance with relevant GDPR provisions on online behavioural advertising, and it will continue the case to ensure efficient GDPR application.

# GDPR Fines Structure and the Biggest GDPR Fines to Date

* Share

* 8 minutes to read

Table of Contents

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a law enacted by the European Union in 2018 to handle data protection and privacy. This regulation affects all companies that process and hold the personal data of individuals residing in the European Union, regardless of the company’s location. A critical aspect of GDPR is the hefty fines that can be imposed if businesses fail to comply with its regulations. Check out this blog to learn about the impact of [AI in cyber security](https://www.exabeam.com/explainers/ai-cyber-security/ai-cyber-security-securing-ai-systems-against-cyber-threats/).

**About this Explainer:**

This content is part of a series about [GDPR compliance](https://www.exabeam.com/explainers/gdpr-compliance/gdpr-compliance-a-practical-guide/).

---

## Structure of GDPR Fines

### Maximum Fine Limits

The GDPR sets forth maximum limits for fines, which are quite substantial. The upper limit depends on the tier of the violation. For the lower tier, the maximum fine can go up to 10 million Euro or 2% of the company’s global annual turnover of the previous financial year, whichever is higher.

For the upper tier, the maximum fine can reach 20 million Euro or 4% of the company’s global annual turnover of the previous financial year, whichever is higher. These significant amounts underscore the seriousness with which the EU takes data protection and privacy.

It’s worth noting that these are maximum limits. The actual fine will depend on the specific circumstances of each case. Thus, not every infringement will lead to millions of euros in fines. However, the potential for such high fines clearly signifies the importance of complying with the GDPR.

### Two-Tiered Fine System

Here is how the GDPR defines the two tiers:

* **Lower-tier infringements** mostly relate to technical aspects of the GDPR, such as failing to adequately document processing activities, not conducting a required impact assessment, and not designating a data protection officer when required.
* **Upper-tier infringements** pertain to violations of the fundamental principles of the GDPR, such as processing personal data without sufficient legal basis, infringing on the rights of data subjects, and transferring personal data to a third country or an international organization in violation of the GDPR.

The two-tiered system ensures that the fines correspond to the severity of the violation, preventing minor technical infringements from leading to excessive fines.

**Learn more:**

Read our detailed explainer about [GDPR requirements](https://www.exabeam.com/explainers/gdpr-compliance/the-main-gdpr-requirements-in-plain-english/).

---

## Criteria Used to Determine GDPR Fines and Violations

### 1. Nature, Gravity, and Duration of Infringement

The nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement play a significant role in determining the fines. For instance, a minor violation that did not lead to any substantial damage may attract a lesser fine compared to a massive data breach that exposed sensitive personal data of thousands of users. Similarly, the duration of the infringement also matters. A one-off violation might be treated differently from a recurring or persistent breach.

Additionally, the number of people affected by the violation and the level of damage they suffered are also taken into account. If an infringement led to serious damage like identity theft or financial loss, the GDPR fines imposed could be hefty. In contrast, if the breach resulted in minimal harm, the fines may be less severe.

### 2. Intentional or Negligent Character of the Infringement

Another important aspect considered when determining GDPR fines is whether the violation was intentional or due to negligence. If an entity deliberately violated GDPR rules, it would likely face a higher fine. On the other hand, if the breach occurred due to negligence, the fine might be lower, especially if the entity can demonstrate that it took all reasonable measures to prevent such an occurrence.

This aspect of GDPR enforcement emphasizes that organizations must be fully aware of their responsibilities and take appropriate measures to ensure data protection. If negligence leads to a data breach, the organization might still face a significant fine.

### 3. Actions Taken by the Data Controller or Processor to Mitigate Damage

The actions taken by the data controller or processor to mitigate the damage caused by the violation are also taken into account. If the entity took swift and effective measures to contain the breach, notify the affected individuals, and minimize the damage, this could potentially reduce the amount of the fine.

This factor underscores the importance of having a robust data breach response plan in place. By responding promptly and effectively to a breach, organizations can not only limit the harm caused to individuals but also potentially lessen the financial penalties they might face.

### 4. Degree of Responsibility of the Controller or Processor

The degree of responsibility of the data controller or processor is another crucial factor in determining GDPR fines. The GDPR holds controllers and processors accountable for ensuring data protection. If they fail in their responsibilities and it can be proven that they were deliberately negligent, they can face significant fines.

The degree of responsibility is evaluated based on several factors, including the technical and organizational measures implemented by the entity to ensure data protection, the entity’s compliance with its obligations under the GDPR, among others. If the entity can demonstrate that it took all necessary steps to protect personal data and comply with GDPR rules, this could potentially reduce the amount of the fine.

### 5. Relevant Previous Infringements

Previous infringements are also taken into account when determining GDPR fines. If the entity has a history of violations, it could face a higher fine. This is because repeat violations indicate a disregard for data protection rules and a lack of commitment to rectify past mistakes.

However, it’s not just the number of previous violations that matters, but also their nature and severity. A single severe violation could be viewed more seriously than multiple minor infringements. Therefore, organizations should not only strive to prevent violations but also take swift action to rectify any violations that do occur.

### 6. Degree of Cooperation with the Supervisory Authority

The degree of cooperation with the supervisory authority is another factor that can influence GDPR fines. If the entity cooperates fully with the supervisory authority, this could potentially reduce the amount of the fine. Cooperation could include promptly reporting the violation, providing all necessary information to the authority, assisting in the investigation, among others.

By contrast, if the entity tries to conceal the violation or obstruct the investigation, it could face a higher fine. Thus, it’s in the best interest of organizations to cooperate fully with the supervisory authority in the event of a data breach.

### 7. Categories of Personal Data Affected by the Infringement

The categories of personal data affected by the infringement can also influence the amount of the GDPR fines. If sensitive personal data such as financial information, health records, or other special category data are exposed in a data breach, the entity is likely to face a higher fine.

This is because the exposure of such data can lead to serious harm to individuals, including identity theft, financial loss, damage to reputation, among others. Therefore, organizations must take extra care to protect sensitive personal data to avoid hefty fines.

### 8. Manner in Which the Infringement Became Known to the Supervisory Authority

The manner in which the infringement became known to the supervisory authority can also impact the GDPR fines. If the entity reported the violation promptly and voluntarily, this could potentially reduce the amount of the fine. Conversely, if the infringement was discovered through a third-party complaint or an audit, the entity could face a higher fine.

This factor underscores the importance of transparency and prompt reporting in the event of a data breach. By reporting the breach promptly, organizations can not only comply with their legal obligations but also potentially mitigate the financial penalties they might face.

### 9. Compliance with Measures Against the Controller or Processor

Compliance with measures ordered against the controller or processor is another factor that can influence GDPR fines. If the entity complies promptly and fully with the measures ordered by the supervisory authority, this could potentially reduce the amount of the fine. On the other hand, if the entity fails to comply with the measures, it could face a higher fine.

This factor highlights the importance of complying with all legal obligations under the GDPR. By complying with the measures ordered by the supervisory authority, organizations can not only rectify the violation but also potentially lessen the financial penalties they might face.

### 10. Adherence to Codes of Conduct or Approved Certification Mechanisms

Lastly, the adherence to codes of conduct or approved certification mechanisms can also impact GDPR fines. If the entity adheres to such codes or mechanisms, this could potentially reduce the amount of the fine. This is because such adherence demonstrates the entity’s commitment to data protection and compliance with GDPR rules.

Therefore, organizations should strive to adhere to relevant codes of conduct or certification mechanisms to demonstrate their commitment to data protection and potentially mitigate the financial penalties they might face.

---

## Examples of the Biggest GDPR Fines So Far

### Meta

Formerly known as Facebook, Meta was hit with one of the largest GDPR fines to date. In July 2021, Luxembourg’s National Commission for Data Protection (CNPD) fined Meta €746 million for violating GDPR. The fine was levied due to the company’s failure to satisfactorily protect user data and misuse of personal data for advertising purposes.

In 2023, Meta received an even larger fine of €1.2 billion by the Irish Data Protection Commission for transferring personal data of European users to the United States without adequate data protection mechanisms

### Amazon

In July 2021, Amazon received the highest GDPR fine to date. The Luxembourg National Commission for Data Protection (CNPD) fined the e-commerce giant €746 million. The fine was issued due to Amazon’s non-compliance with GDPR regulations in its advertising practices.

### TikTok

Popular, China-owned social media platform TikTok was also on the receiving end of a GDPR fine. In July 2021, the Dutch Data Protection Authority (DPA) fined TikTok €750,000 for violating GDPR regulations. The violation was due to TikTok’s failure to provide a privacy statement in Dutch, leaving many young users unable to understand the company’s data processing methods. Then, in 2023, TikTok received a fine of £12.7 million for illegally processing the data of 1.4 million children under the age of 13 without parental consent

### WhatsApp

WhatsApp, the popular messaging service, was fined €225 million by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC) in September 2021. The fine was issued due to WhatsApp’s lack of transparency about how it processes user data. This case shows that even companies that primarily offer free services can face significant GDPR fines if they fail to comply with data protection laws.

### Google LLC

In March 2020, the Swedish Data Protection Authority (DPA) fined Google LLC €7 million for failing to comply with GDPR’s right to be forgotten. The fine was issued because Google did not adequately remove two search result listings that individuals requested to be deleted, demonstrating the importance of respecting user requests for data deletion.

### CRITEO

In December 2020, The French Data Protection Authority (CNIL) fined CRITEO €225,000 for violating GDPR’s rules on consent for cookies. The company was found guilty of continuing to place advertising cookies on users’ computers after they had refused consent.

### H&M

In one of the largest GDPR fines related to employee data, H&M was fined €35 million by the Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (HmbBfDI) in October 2020. The fine was issued due to H&M’s unlawful surveillance of several hundred employees at its Nuremberg service center.

### Clearview AI

In a landmark case, Clearview AI, a facial recognition company, was fined €20 million by the Italian Data Protection Authority (Garante) in January 2022. The company was found to have violated GDPR by collecting biometric data without users’ consent. This case demonstrates that GDPR fines can be levied against companies that misuse sensitive biometric data.

---

## Are GDPR Fines On the Rise?

In short, yes, GDPR fines have been marked by a gradual escalation in both the frequency and size of penalties.

Initially, after its implementation in May 2018, the focus of GDPR enforcement was more on awareness and compliance. However, by 2019 and 2020, there was a noticeable increase in enforcement actions, highlighted by significant fines such as the €50 million penalty against Google by France’s CNIL for inadequate data consent policies.

This trend continued to accelerate in 2021, exemplified by Amazon’s €746 million fine for non-compliance with data processing standards, and in 2022 with several substantial fines against Meta, including a €225 million penalty for WhatsApp’s privacy policy issues.

The year 2023 marked a turning point in GDPR enforcement, witnessing record-breaking fines that pushed the total to over €1.6 billion. A notable example is the unprecedented €1.2 billion fine imposed on Meta by the Irish Data Protection Commission. This dramatic increase in both the size and total amount of fines underscores a more aggressive approach to GDPR enforcement, signaling the European Union’s strong commitment to data protection.

---

This webpage from Exabeam provides a comprehensive explainer on the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) fines structure and the largest fines imposed to date. The GDPR, enacted by the EU in 2018, applies to all companies processing personal data of EU residents regardless of company location.

**Fines Structure:**
- Two-tiered fine system: Lower-tier infringements (technical aspects like failure to document processing activities) can incur up to €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher). Upper-tier infringements (violations of fundamental principles like processing data without legal basis) can incur up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover.
- Ten criteria determine actual fines: nature/gravity/duration of infringement, intentional vs. negligent character, mitigation actions taken, degree of responsibility, previous infringements, cooperation with supervisory authority, categories of personal data affected, how the infringement became known, compliance with ordered measures, and adherence to codes of conduct/certification mechanisms.

**Biggest GDPR Fines:**
- Amazon: €746 million (July 2021, Luxembourg CNPD, advertising practices)
- Meta/Facebook: €746 million (July 2021, Luxembourg CNPD) and €1.2 billion (2023, Irish DPC, transferring EU user data to US without adequate protection)
- WhatsApp: €225 million (September 2021, Irish DPC, lack of transparency)
- TikTok: €750,000 (2021, Dutch DPA, no Dutch privacy statement) and £12.7 million (2023, processing data of 1.4 million children under 13 without parental consent)
- Google LLC: €7 million (March 2020, Swedish DPA, right to be forgotten violations)
- H&M: €35 million (October 2020, Hamburg, unlawful employee surveillance)
- Clearview AI: €20 million (January 2022, Italian Garante, biometric data collection without consent)
- CRITEO: €225,000 (December 2020, French CNIL, cookie consent violations)

--- SOURCE 1: Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) GDPR Fines ---
URL: https://gdprfine.com/dpa/ireland-dpc

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a reference profile of the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC), the most-fined GDPR regulator by cumulative amount. Ireland is the EU establishment of choice for US Big Tech, making the DPC the lead supervisory authority (under Article 56 GDPR) for the largest single-issuer fines on the register. ~25 headline decisions are indexed, with the largest single fine being €1.2 billion (Meta 2023) and 5+ EDPB Article 65 cases since 2021. The DPC has been active since 1989 (GDPR: 2018).

**Mandate and constitution:** The DPC is designated under Article 51 GDPR, and as lead authority for controllers with main EU establishment in Ireland. Established under the Data Protection Act 1988, modernised under the Data Protection Act 2018. It reports to the Oireachtas through the Minister for Justice, with headquarters in Dublin (Fitzwilliam Square) and a satellite office in Portarlington. Staff grew from ~110 in 2018 to more than 230 by 2026.

**Fining philosophy:** Characterised by long inquiry timelines (3-5 years), detailed factual analysis, and rigorous Article 83(2) factor-by-factor weighting. Critics accuse the DPC of being insufficiently aggressive; the EDPB Article 65 mechanism has repeatedly recalibrated fines upward (WhatsApp: €30-50M draft to €225M final; Meta Chapter V case).

**Headline decisions:** WhatsApp €225M (Sept 2021, following EDPB BD 1/2021, first ever Article 65 decision); Instagram €405M children's data (Sept 2022, EDPB BD 2/2022); two Meta Ireland decisions totalling €390M (Jan 2023, contractual lawful basis for personalised advertising); Meta €1.2B Chapter V transfer decision (May 2023, largest GDPR fine to date, following EDPB BD 1/2023); TikTok €345M children's data (Sept 2023, EDPB BD 2/2023); TikTok €530M Chapter V China transfers (May 2025, second-largest single GDPR fine).

**Statistical record:** Cumulative DPC fines exceed €3 billion. Distribution is highly skewed; Big Tech share is ~95% of total in years with major decisions, and median annual fine count is in the tens. Complaint volumes rose steadily, exceeding 11,000 in 2024. The 2024 annual report was the most recent available, with 2025 report expected mid-2026.

**How to engage:** Data subjects can lodge complaints under Article 77 GDPR via dataprotection.ie; cross-border complaints use the one-stop-shop mechanism (lodged via local DPA, forwarded to DPC as lead, with original DPA as "concerned" authority under Articles 60/65).

**Recent enforcement trends (2024-2026):** Children's data, AI-system processing (intersecting with EU AI Act), DPIA compliance, and continued one-stop-shop relationships. The DPC moved to a three-Commissioner structure in 2024 (Des Hogan, Dale Sunderland, Niamh Sweeney), replacing the single Commissioner model (Helen Dixon, 2014-2024), to handle the workload.

**FAQ highlights:** The DPC issues many large fines because major US tech firms have EU headquarters in Ireland. The EDPB Article 65 mechanism lets concerned authorities refer draft decisions to the EDPB for binding decisions. The Spanish AEPD issues more decisions by count, but the DPC leads in cumulative amount. Fines are imposed on the EU-established subsidiary, not directly on US parents. Decisions are published on dataprotection.ie and EDPB decisions on edpb.europa.eu.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The most-fined GDPR regulator by cumulative amount. Ireland is the EU establishment of choice for US Big Tech, which makes the DPC the lead supervisory authority for the largest single-issuer fines on the register."

URL: https://privacymatters.dlapiper.com/2024/06/ireland-dpc-issues-record-87-of-eu-gdpr-fines-in-2023-breach-reports-increase-by-20

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) published its 2023 Annual Report, highlighting a record year in which DPC fines accounted for 87% of all GDPR fines issued across the EU. The DPC received 6,991 valid personal data breach notifications in 2023 (a 20% increase from the prior year), with unauthorized disclosure being the leading reason for breaches (52% of the total). 146 notifications came under the ePrivacy Regulations (up 42%) and 59 under the Law Enforcement Directive. Most incidents originated from the private sector (3,766), followed by the public sector (2,968) and voluntary/charity sector (275).

In 2023, the DPC concluded 11,147 cases, held 89 statutory inquiries on-hand (including 51 cross-border inquiries), and handled over 25,130 electronic contacts, 7,085 phone calls, and 1,253 postal contacts. The most frequent GDPR topics for queries and complaints were access requests, fair-processing, disclosure, direct marketing, and right to erasure. The DPC concluded 19 inquiries in 2023 resulting in fines totaling €1.55 billion.

Notable cross-border inquiries concluded in 2023 included: two social media fines (€5.5 million for relying on contract as a lawful basis for service improvement, and €1.6 billion for transferring EU data to the US without a lawful basis) and a €345 million fine for processing children's personal data. Notable domestic inquiries included fines for Financial Services (€750,000 for ten data breaches involving unauthorized disclosure on a customer-facing app), Healthcare (€460,000 for a ransomware attack affecting over 70,000 patients), and a County Council (€50,000 for CCTV and car plate reading technology usage).

The DPC pursued 7 national judgments or final orders in 2023 (split between the Irish Circuit Court and High Court), with legal costs awarded in favor of the DPC in 5 proceedings. The DPC also had 4 successful prosecutions involving unsolicited marketing messages under the e-Privacy Regulations.

Child protection remained a priority pillar of the DPC's Regulatory Strategy 2022-2027, reflected in the €345 million fine against a major social media company. The DPC was nominated to represent the EDPB on the new Task Force on Age Verification under the Digital Services Act. By the end of 2023, 3,520 DPOs were notified to the DPC. The DPC's participation in the 2023 Coordinated Enforcement Framework identified three DPO issues: insufficient resources, conflicts of interest, and inappropriate tasks. Of 751 supervision engagements in 2023, 391 were from multinational technology companies.

In February 2024, Helen Dixon stepped down as Data Protection Commissioner after 10 years, with Dr. Des Hogan (Chairperson) and Dale Sunderland taking over their new roles. The DPC continues to focus on systemic non-compliance and children's data protection rights in 2024.
</summary>

The Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) announced on 15 September 2022 the conclusion of an inquiry into Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Instagram), imposing a fine of €405 million and a range of corrective measures.

The inquiry concerned the processing of personal data relating to child users of Instagram. It was initiated by the DPC on 21 September 2020 in response to information provided by David Stier (a US data scientist) and issues identified by the DPC itself following examination of the Instagram user registration process. The inquiry examined the public disclosure of email addresses and/or phone numbers of children using the Instagram business account feature and a public-by-default setting for personal Instagram accounts of children.

Following investigation, the DPC submitted a draft decision to all peer regulators (Concerned Supervisory Authorities) under Article 60 of the GDPR in December 2021. Six national regulators raised objections, and the DPC referred the case to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) under the Article 65 dispute resolution process. On 28 July 2022, the EDPB adopted a binding decision that rejected many objections but upheld objections requiring the DPC to include a finding of infringement of Article 6(1) GDPR and reassess fines. The DPC adopted its decision on 2 September 2022, recording findings of infringement of Articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(c), 6(1), 12(1), 24, 25(1), 25(2) and 35(1) of the GDPR.

The fine totals €405 million, including €20 million specifically for the Article 6(1) infringement. In addition, the DPC imposed a reprimand and an order requiring Meta to bring its processing into compliance through specified remedial actions. The EDPB published the Article 65 decision and final decision on its website.

--- SOURCE 2: Meta €265 Million DPC Fine: 2022 Facebook Data-Scraping Decision Explained | GDPRFine.com ---
URL: https://gdprfine.com/cases/meta-265-million-dpc-2022

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 25 November 2022 (announced 28 November 2022), the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) imposed a €265 million administrative fine on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (MPIL) over the Facebook "data scraping" incident, concluding an inquiry opened after a dataset of Facebook user data was published online in April 2021.

The inquiry covered Facebook Search, Facebook Messenger Contact Importer, and Instagram Contact Importer tools, and processing between 25 May 2018 and September 2019. During that period, third parties abused these tools to match large lists of phone numbers against user profiles, compiling personal data on more than 500 million users from over 100 countries (including names, Facebook IDs, phone numbers, locations, dates of birth, and email addresses). The incident was not a conventional security breach; the data was assembled by exploiting features working as built because they lacked safeguards against enumeration and bulk matching. The DPC therefore centered the inquiry on Data Protection by Design and Default rather than Article 32 security of processing.

The DPC found infringements of Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR (Data Protection by Design and by Default), concluding that Meta's contact-import and search features did not meet either obligation. Effective measures such as default-private settings, rate limiting, and controls on bulk enumeration were not built in by design or applied by default. Alongside the fine, the DPC imposed a reprimand and an order requiring MPIL to take specified remedial actions within a set timeframe. Article 25 infringements fall under the lower tier of Article 83(4), capped at €10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover; given Meta's scale the 2% ceiling sat well above €265 million, so the amount reflects the DPC's Article 83(2) assessment of gravity, duration, and the very large number of affected data subjects.

This fine is one of a series of large DPC decisions against Meta, distinct from the WhatsApp transparency fine (€225 million, 2021), the Instagram children's-data fine (€405 million, 2022), the contractual-basis fines (€390 million combined, 2023), and the €1.2 billion transfers fine (2023). It is the leading Article 25 decision in that group. The EDPB was involved through the Article 60 cooperation process (but not via a binding Article 65 decision, unlike the €1.2 billion transfers fine).

The practical lesson: Data Protection by Design and Default is an enforceable obligation with nine-figure exposure. Any feature allowing lookup, matching, or enumeration by identifier must be designed against abuse from the outset, and controllers are responsible for foreseeable misuse of their own tools under Article 25.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

In September 2023, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) issued a landmark €345 million fine to TikTok Technology Limited for breaching GDPR requirements regarding children's data. This followed a two-year investigation into TikTok's privacy policies and practices covering the period from July 31 to December 31, 2020. The inquiry examined platform settings for child users (including the 'Family Pairing' feature), age verification, and transparency information for child users. The DPC submitted a draft decision to supervisory authorities, after which the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) delivered a 126-page binding decision. Key findings from the DPC investigation included: (1) child user profiles were configured as public by default, allowing anyone to access content posted by children, with an option to 'skip' making accounts private during setup—violating data minimisation, data protection by design, and data protection by default principles; (2) the Family Pairing feature allowed non-child users who couldn't be verified as parents or guardians to pair with child accounts and send direct messages, posing "severe possible risks to child users" and violating the security principle; (3) TikTok failed to provide sufficient transparency information to child users, with ambiguous wording in privacy notices (terms like "public," "anyone," and "everyone" not clearly distinguishing between registered and non-registered users); and (4) TikTok implemented "dark patterns" that nudged users toward more privacy-intrusive options during registration and when posting videos, violating the GDPR fairness principle.

--- SOURCE 1: GDPR Enforcement and Fines 2026: Business Categories, ... ---
URL: https://www.uniconsent.com/blog/gdpr-enforcement-fines-2026

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from UniConsent provides a comprehensive overview of GDPR enforcement and fines as of 2026, with a specific focus on the ad tech sector. Key statistics include: over 2,500 fines totaling 7.1 billion euros issued since 2018, with approximately 1.2 billion euros issued in 2025 alone; an average fine of 2.4 million euros; and the largest fine ever being 1.2 billion euros against Meta Platforms Ireland (May 2023) for unlawful EU-US data transfers.

**Top 10 Largest GDPR Fines of All Time:**
1. Meta Platforms Ireland — 1.2B euros (Irish DPC, May 2023) — unlawful EU-US data transfers
2. Amazon Europe Core — 746M euros (Luxembourg CNPD, July 2021) — ad targeting without valid consent (annulled on procedural grounds in March 2026)
3. TikTok — 530M euros (Irish DPC, May 2025) — unlawful EU-China data transfers
4. Meta (Instagram) — 405M euros (Irish DPC, Sept 2022) — mishandling of children's data
5. Meta (Facebook + Instagram) — 390M euros (Irish DPC, Jan 2023) — invalid legal basis for behavioural ads
6. TikTok — 345M euros (Irish DPC, Sept 2023) — children's data processing failures
7. Google — 325M euros (French CNIL, Sept 2025) — Gmail inbox ads + invalid signup consent
8. LinkedIn Ireland — 310M euros (Irish DPC, Oct 2024) — invalid legal basis for behavioural ads
9. Uber — 290M euros (Dutch AP, Aug 2024) — unlawful EU-US data transfers
10. Meta (Facebook) — 265M euros (Irish DPC, Nov 2022) — inadequate protection against data scraping

Eight of the ten largest fines were issued by Ireland's DPC due to Dublin being the European HQ for most major tech companies. Ireland accounts for 4.04 billion euros (~57%) of all GDPR fine value, while Spain has issued the most fines by count (nearly 1,000). Ireland and France together account for ~70% of all GDPR fine value.

**Key structural insights:** The Media, Telecoms and Broadcasting sector accounts for ~70% of all corporate fine value, and "insufficient legal basis for data processing" is the most common violation. Ad tech is uniquely exposed due to: (1) data being the product itself, (2) opaque programmatic supply chains, and (3) consent being the only realistic legal basis for targeted advertising. Ad tech-driven fines approach 5 billion euros — well over half of all GDPR fines ever issued.

**Notable ad tech cases include:** Criteo (40M euros, 2023, for unverified partner consent), Google (50M euros, 2019, first major fine), Google + Amazon (100M + 35M euros, 2020, cookies before consent), Google + Facebook (150M + 60M euros, 2022, dark-pattern banners), Shein (150M euros, Sept 2025, cookie practices), Optimove (1M euros, Dec 2025, processor obligations), and Quantcast (ongoing DPC investigation).

**Critical finding on payment:** Of Ireland's 4.04 billion euros in fines, only ~20 million euros (0.5%) has actually been collected, as most major fines are under appeal. However, companies almost always implement corrective orders despite appealing headline numbers (e.g., Meta localised EU data infrastructure, LinkedIn rewrote consent flows within three months).

**Five common causes of ad tech fines:** (1) Wrong legal basis for targeted advertising, (2) cookies set before user consent, (3) dark pattern consent banners, (4) unverified partner consent in the supply chain, and (5) GDPR transparency/information failures.

**2026 enforcement trends:** Rising average fine sizes in Media/Telecoms/Broadcasting, more regulators becoming active across all member states, the DSA adding a second penalty layer (first DSA fine: 120M euros against X in December 2025), AI Act enforcement beginning August 2026 (penalties up to 35M euros or 7% of turnover), and decentralising cookie-banner challenges via noyb-style coordinated complaints.

The article concludes that consent management has become core infrastructure rather than optional software, with a compliance checklist for publishers and ad tech vendors covering: defaulting to consent for advertising processing, blocking non-essential tags until consent, making reject equal to accept, recording consent with full audit trails, auditing downstream partners, investing in the information layer, and treating international transfers as a separate compliance domain. The FAQ section clarifies the maximum fine (20M euros or 4% of turnover), extraterritorial reach (Article 3(2)), and the distinction between GDPR and ePrivacy fines (e.g., the Shein fine is technically an ePrivacy fine under French law).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"GDPR enforcement is no longer a theoretical risk that lives in a compliance deck. Based on publicly disclosed enforcement data, regulators across the EU and UK have issued more than 2,500 fines totalling over 7 billion euros since 2018, with approximately 1.2 billion euros of that issued in 2025 alone — and the curve is still climbing."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://iapp.org/news/a/meta-fined-gdpr-record-1-2-billion-euros-in-data-transfer-case

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) issued a record 1.2 billion euro fine against Meta Platforms Ireland — the highest penalty to date under the GDPR — for unlawful transfers of EU/EEA users' personal data to the U.S. via Facebook. The decision ordered Meta to suspend future data transfers to the U.S. within five months and to cease unlawful processing and storage of EU user data in the U.S. within six months. The case stemmed from the July 2020 CJEU ruling that invalidated the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield; Meta subsequently relied on standard contractual clauses (SCCs), including those updated by the European Commission in 2021. The European Data Protection Board completed its binding dispute resolution on April 13, 2023, after supervisory authorities disagreed with the DPC's initial draft. EDPB Chair Andrea Jelinek called the infringement "very serious" given the systematic and continuous transfers of massive volumes of data from Facebook's millions of European users. Meta's Global Affairs President Nick Clegg and Chief Legal Officer Jennifer Newstead called the fine "unjustified and unnecessary" and said the company would appeal, noting a "fundamental conflict of law" between U.S. government data access rules and European privacy rights that policymakers are expected to resolve. NOYB Chairman Max Schrems, who had challenged trans-Atlantic data transfer regimes, said unless U.S. surveillance laws are fixed, Meta will need to "fundamentally restructure its systems." The decision has broad implications beyond Meta — the DPC explicitly noted that any internet platform falling under FISA 702 PRISM could face similar GDPR violations, and experts noted the ruling applies to both old and new SCCs and casts doubt on a risk-based approach to data transfers. The decision also raises questions about U.K. adequacy given the UK's proposed "not materially lower" data protection test. Stakeholders await finalization of the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, with a European Commission spokesperson stating it should be "fully functionable by summer" — though experts anticipate legal challenges similar to its predecessors.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The EDPB found that (Meta's) infringement is very serious since it concerns transfers that are systematic, repetitive and continuous. Facebook has millions of users in Europe, so the volume of personal data transferred is massive. The unprecedented fine is a strong signal to organisations that serious infringements have far-reaching consequences." - EDPB Chair Andrea Jelinek, "This is not about one company's privacy practices — there is a fundamental conflict of law between the U.S. government's rules on access to data and European privacy rights, which policymakers are expected to resolve this summer." - Meta's Nick Clegg and Jennifer Newstead, "We are happy to see this decision after 10 years of litigation. ... Unless U.S. surveillance laws get fixed, Meta will have to fundamentally restructure its systems." - NOYB Chairman Max Schrems, "The impact of this decision is very broad, going vastly beyond Meta and being of concern for all businesses, universities, clinical trials and whomever is transferring personal data from the EU to the U.S. on the basis of SCCs in the absence of an adequacy decision." - Future of Privacy Forum's Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, "This enforcement action puts international data transfers at the top of the list of regulatory priorities by European data protection authorities. However, by focusing entirely on the potential for government access to data rather than on the protections deployed to protect that data from interference, this distorts the aim of data protection law." - Hogan Lovells Partner Eduardo Ustaran

BACKGROUND: On 22 May 2023, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) issued a decision against Meta Platforms Ireland (Facebook's owner) with three parts: (1) an administrative fine of €1.2 billion (as directed by the European Data Protection Board/EDPB); (2) an order to suspend all transfers of European-based Facebook user data from Europe to the US, effective 12 weeks after the appeal period; and (3) an order to bring those transfers into GDPR compliance within six months (as directed by the EDPB).

IMPACT FOR BUSINESSES: The anticipated DPF decision was seen as a welcome development for European businesses transferring personal data from the EU to the US, promising to reduce the long-standing complexity and uncertainty that have resulted in elevated compliance obligations. The fund was deemed necessary due to the wide-ranging impacts of harm and the complex nature of the remedy. The funds will be allocated to the following categories:

- Screening and assessment: $90 million

- Implementation, continuous quality improvement, and evaluation: $9 million

Cybersecurity expert Pawan Duggal commented that this represents a consistent behavioral pattern by Meta, which he characterized as an intermediary acting as if it is "a law unto its own self" by encouraging and promoting CSAM (child sexual abuse material) content. He noted that this judgment is significant because it requires Meta not only to pay penalties for its conduct but also to fund constructive steps to protect the mental health of children and teens, including recurring costs for training and awareness. He also noted that no prosecution has yet begun in India regarding CSAM content promotion, but that this ruling could trigger other events globally.

# [Article](https://www.loc.gov/search/?fa=original_format:web+page) Netherlands: Amsterdam Court of Appeals Orders Meta to Implement Algorithm-Choice Changes for Facebook and Instagram by End of Year

Back to Search Results

On October 28, 2025, the Amsterdam Court of Appeals (Gerechtshof Amsterdam) in the Netherlands [held](https://perma.cc/WDP8-W939) that Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd., a subsidiary of Meta Inc. that operates the social media platforms Facebook and Instagram in Europe, must modify the platforms by December 31, 2025, to comply with the European Union’s [Digital Services Act](https://perma.cc/47KB-A92X) (DSA). The company must allow users to easily choose and retain their choice to display an unprofiled, chronological timeline unaffected by the platforms’ algorithms that determine what content is shown to users.

The appeals court suspended the provisional enforcement of an October 2, 2025, [ruling](https://perma.cc/K84B-DUNM) from the Amsterdam District Court (Rechtbank Amsterdam), which was issued as part of preliminary injunction proceedings. The appeal against the district court’s ruling remains pending.

**Legal Framework**

The Netherlands is a member state of the EU. The DSA, like all EU regulations, applies directly in all member states, is fully binding, and does not require implementation through national legislation. ([Consolidated Version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union](https://perma.cc/3QT7-7T8X), art. 288, para. 2.) It [aims](https://perma.cc/L6Q8-P69C) to “create a safer digital space where the fundamental rights of users are protected and to establish a level playing field for businesses” by regulating online intermediaries and platforms, such as social networks.

The DSA contains special obligations for “[very large online platforms](https://www.loc.gov/item/global-legal-monitor/2023-05-04/european-union-commission-publishes-list-of-very-large-online-platforms-and-search-engines-under-digital-services-act/),” or “VLOPs.” These are platforms that have 45 million or more active monthly users in the EU and are designated by the European Commission as VLOPs. (DSA, art. 33, para. 1.) Facebook and Instagram were both [designated as VLOPs on April 25, 2025](https://perma.cc/24X7-DULD), along with [15 other platforms](https://perma.cc/JQ9N-WAJB).

Article 25 of the DSA prohibits “dark patterns,” requiring online platforms to be designed to make it easy for users to make free and informed decisions and not requiring users to repeatedly confirm a certain choice. According to recital 67 of the DSA, making default settings difficult to change is an example of a dark pattern.

Article 38 of the DSA specifically requires VLOPs to offer users a timeline option without profiling for each of the VLOPs’ recommender systems. A recommender system is defined in the DSA as a “fully or partially automated system used by an online platform to suggest in its online interface specific information to recipients of the service or prioritise that information, including as a result of a search initiated by the recipient of the service or otherwise determining the relative order or prominence of information displayed.” (DSA, art. 3(s).) Profiling is defined in the EU’s [General Data Protection Regulation](https://perma.cc/T5SH-K4RT) as “any form of automated processing of personal data consisting of the use of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person.” (GDPR, art. 4 (4).)

**Facts of the Case**

The plaintiff, a Dutch digital rights organization, brought preliminary injunction proceedings against Meta, claiming that the design of Facebook’s and Instagram’s timelines does not comply with articles 25 and 38 of the DSA. In particular, the plaintiff alleged the platforms make it unreasonably difficult for users to select and maintain a timeline that is not profiled, as they automatically reverted users’ timelines back to algorithmic timelines when users reopened the app or switched sections. ([Rechtbank Amsterdam](https://perma.cc/K84B-DUNM), para. 4.16.)

On October 2, 2025, the first-instance Amsterdam District Court [ruled](https://perma.cc/K84B-DUNM) in favor of the plaintiff and held that the platforms’ current design constituted a prohibited dark pattern because it discouraged users from choosing the “non-profiled” option and undermined their autonomy. The Amsterdam District Court ordered Meta to create a direct and simple mechanism for Facebook and Instagram that enables users to select a chronological timeline that remains active throughout use. It further made the decision provisionally enforceable and ordered Meta to make these changes within two weeks. Meta appealed the decision, and the Amsterdam Court of Appeals reviewed the case. (Paras. 4.33, 4.46, 4.47, 5.1.)

**Court of Appeals’ Decision**

On October 28, 2025, the Amsterdam Court of Appeals, responding to Meta’s request, suspended the provisional enforceability of the first-instance judgment and granted Meta until December 31, 2025, to complete the necessary technical adjustments. In this interim decision, the court emphasized the necessary balancing of interests by weighing Meta’s need for sufficient time to implement the changes against the public’s interest in the prompt enforcement of the injunction. (Paras. 2.6, 3.)

Under Dutch procedural law, courts may attach monetary penalties to ensure compliance with injunctions. ([Wetboek van Burgerlijke Rechtsvordering](https://perma.cc/7YHP-FSPT), art. 611a.) Following the judgment of the court of first instance, the Amsterdam Court of Appeals ruled that if Meta fails to comply by December 31, 2025, financial penalties in the amount of €100,000 (about US$115,000) for each day it fails to comply with the orders up to a maximum of €5 million (about US$5.75 million) will take effect starting January 1, 2026. (Para. 2.1.)

**Original Appeal Still Pending**

Meta has appealed the district court’s ruling that its algorithms constitute a prohibited dark pattern, and a hearing has been scheduled for January 26, 2026. No decision has yet been made on the substance of the appeal.

# GDPR Fines in Numbers: Enforcement and Penalty Statistics

European data protection authorities have issued roughly €6.31 billion in GDPR fines across 3,206 enforcement actions since May 2018, per the CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker as of August 19, 2026. The largest fine remains Meta’s €1.2 billion (Irish DPC, 2023), 2025 added about €1.2 billion more, and the most common grounds are insufficient legal basis (Art. 6), violations of the core processing principles (Art. 5) and insufficient security measures (Art. 32) — failures of exactly the program-and-documentation layer small businesses most often skip.

Reviewed by[Dor Israel, Founder](/about) · Updated

[Free: The GDPR Compliance Checklist for small business (8 steps) →](/resources/gdpr-compliance-checklist)

## Headline enforcement numbers

The figures below come from the two most-cited GDPR enforcement datasets: the CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker (enforcementtracker.com), a continuously updated public database of published fines, and DLA Piper’s annual GDPR fines survey, which also counts non-public authority totals. They use different methodologies, so each figure is labeled with its source and as-of date.

| Metric | Figure | Source, as of |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cumulative fines since May 2018 | ≈ €6.31 billion | CMS Enforcement Tracker, August 19, 2026 |
| Tracked enforcement actions | 3,206 | CMS Enforcement Tracker, August 19, 2026 |
| Cumulative fines (survey basis, incl. non-public totals) | ≈ €7.1 billion | DLA Piper survey, January 2026 |
| Fines issued in 2025 (12 months to Jan 27, 2026) | ≈ €1.2 billion | DLA Piper survey, January 2026 |
| Average fine (all published fines) | €2,277,122 | CMS Enforcement Tracker Report 2026 (cut-off March 1, 2026) |
| Personal-data breach notifications | 443 per day on average, up 22% year over year | DLA Piper survey, January 2026 |
| Ireland alone, cumulative | ≈ €4.04 billion | DLA Piper survey, January 2026 |

Sources: CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker (enforcementtracker.com), retrieved August 19, 2026; DLA Piper GDPR Fines and Data Breach Survey, January 2026 (dlapiper.com). The average is heavily skewed by a handful of Big Tech mega-fines — the typical published fine is far smaller.

## The largest GDPR fines on record

All of the largest fines were issued against large technology platforms, and the two biggest both punish unlawful international data transfers (Art. 46). One long-standing entry has dropped off this list: Amazon’s €746 million fine (Luxembourg, 2021) was annulled by Luxembourg’s Administrative Court on March 12, 2026 on procedural grounds and referred back to the regulator — many older articles still cite it as the second-largest GDPR fine, but as of July 2026 it no longer stands.

| Rank | Company | Fine | Authority, year |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Meta Platforms Ireland (Facebook) | €1,200,000,000 | Ireland, 2023 |
| 2 | TikTok Technology Ltd | €530,000,000 | Ireland, 2025 |
| 3 | Meta Platforms (Instagram) | €405,000,000 | Ireland, 2022 |
| 4 | Meta Platforms Ireland | €390,000,000 | Ireland, 2023 |
| 5 | TikTok Ltd | €345,000,000 | Ireland, 2023 |
| 6 | LinkedIn Ireland | €310,000,000 | Ireland, 2024 |
| 7 | Uber B.V. | €290,000,000 | Netherlands, 2024 |

Source: CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker (enforcementtracker.com), retrieved July 4, 2026; Irish Data Protection Commission decision announcements (dataprotection.ie).

## What organizations actually get fined for

Ranked by number of fines across the whole tracker (CMS Enforcement Tracker Report 2026, cut-off March 1, 2026), the most common grounds are: insufficient legal basis for processing (Art. 6) first, non-compliance with the general data-processing principles (Art. 5) second, and insufficient technical and organizational security measures (Art. 32) third.

In 2025 specifically, analyses of the tracker data count 97 fines for insufficient security measures (Art. 32) — about 29% of the year’s fines and up roughly 40% from 2024 — while legal-basis violations, though fewer in number, accounted for roughly 90% of 2025’s fine value because they included the year’s mega-fines.

Enforcement is not only a Big Tech story. By sector, the tracker’s report counts 588 fines against industry and commerce (≈ €394 million, average ≈ €670,000), 327 against the public sector and education, and 257 against finance, insurance and consulting — a long tail of ordinary organizations fined for ordinary failures: no lawful basis, missing records, weak security.

## Maximum penalties under Article 83

The GDPR sets two tiers of maximum administrative fines, and for corporate groups the percentage applies to total worldwide annual turnover — whichever amount is higher.

| Tier | Covers (examples) | Maximum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Higher tier — Art. 83(5)–(6) | Processing principles (Art. 5), legal basis (Art. 6), data-subject rights, unlawful transfers (Arts. 44–49) | €20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher |
| Lower tier — Art. 83(4) | Controller/processor duties incl. security (Art. 32), records of processing (Art. 30), breach notification (Arts. 33–34) | €10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher |

Source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 83 (official consolidated text, e.g. gdpr-info.eu/art-83-gdpr).

## What the numbers mean for the documentation layer

The three most-fined grounds — legal basis, the Art. 5 principles (including the Art. 5(2) accountability duty to be able to demonstrate compliance), and Art. 32 security measures — are all failures a documented, operated privacy program addresses. Records of Processing Activities (Art. 30), a lawful-basis register, security policies and a breach-response procedure are the artifacts regulators ask for first. Documentation alone does not make an organization GDPR compliant — compliance comes from actually operating those controls — but under the accountability principle, being unable to show the documents is itself a violation.

## Frequently asked questions

How much have GDPR fines totaled since 2018?
:   About €6.31 billion across 3,195 published enforcement actions in 32 countries as of July 4, 2026, per the CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker. DLA Piper’s January 2026 survey, which also counts non-public authority totals, puts the cumulative figure at roughly €7.1 billion.

What is the largest GDPR fine ever?
:   The €1.2 billion fine the Irish Data Protection Commission issued against Meta Platforms Ireland in May 2023 for unlawful EU–US data transfers (Art. 46). The second-largest standing fine is TikTok’s €530 million (Ireland, 2025). Amazon’s €746 million fine, long cited as number two, was annulled by Luxembourg’s Administrative Court in March 2026.

How much were GDPR fines in 2025?
:   Roughly €1.2 billion in the twelve months to January 27, 2026, per DLA Piper’s annual survey — broadly matching 2024. The largest single 2025 fine was TikTok’s €530 million from the Irish DPC. Analyses of the Enforcement Tracker data count over 330 individual fines in calendar 2025.

What are the maximum GDPR fines?
:   Up to €20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover (whichever is higher) for violations of the processing principles, legal basis, data-subject rights or transfer rules; up to €10 million or 2% for duties such as security measures, records of processing and breach notification (Art. 83).

Which GDPR violations are fined most often?

This webpage provides comprehensive statistics on GDPR fines and enforcement since May 2018, drawn primarily from the CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker and DLA Piper's annual GDPR fines survey. Key figures include approximately €6.31 billion in cumulative fines across 3,206 enforcement actions (CMS, as of August 19, 2026), with DLA Piper's survey (January 2026) estimating €7.1 billion including non-public totals. About €1.2 billion in fines were issued in 2025, with roughly 330 individual fines in calendar 2025.

The largest fine on record is Meta Platforms Ireland's €1.2 billion (Irish DPC, 2023) for unlawful EU-US data transfers. The second-largest standing fine is TikTok's €530 million (2025). Notably, Amazon's previously second-largest €746 million fine (Luxembourg, 2021) was annulled by Luxembourg's Administrative Court on March 12, 2026, on procedural grounds, though many older articles still cite it. Other major fines include Instagram (€405M, 2022), Meta Ireland (€390M, 2023), TikTok Ltd (€345M, 2023), LinkedIn Ireland (€310M, 2024), and Uber B.V. (€290M, Netherlands, 2024).

The most common grounds for fines, ranked by number, are: insufficient legal basis for processing (Art. 6), violations of general data-processing principles (Art. 5), and insufficient technical/organizational security measures (Art. 32). In 2025, 97 fines were issued for Art. 32 security failures (about 29% of the year's fines, up ~40% from 2024), while legal-basis violations accounted for roughly 90% of 2025's fine value. Enforcement extends beyond Big Tech — 588 fines were issued against industry/commerce (≈€394M), 327 against public sector/education, and 257 against finance/insurance/consulting.

The GDPR maximum penalties under Article 83 are: €20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover (whichever is higher) for violations of processing principles (Art. 5), legal basis (Art. 6), data-subject rights, or transfer rules (Arts. 44-49); and €10 million or 2% for duties such as security measures (Art. 32), records of processing (Art. 30), and breach notification (Arts. 33-34).

The page concludes that the three most-fined grounds are all addressable through a documented, operated privacy program — lawful-basis registers, Records of Processing Activities, security policies, and breach-response procedures are the artifacts regulators ask for first. The page also promotes a GDPR Compliance Pack product and related articles. The average fine (€2,277,122) is heavily skewed by Big Tech mega-fines; the typical published fine is far smaller. Ireland alone accounts for approximately €4.04 billion in cumulative fines. DLA Piper also reports personal-data breach notifications average 443 per day, up 22% year over year.

--- SOURCE 1: Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) GDPR Fines ---
URL: https://gdprfine.com/dpa/ireland-dpc

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a reference profile of the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC), the most-fined GDPR regulator by cumulative amount. Ireland is the EU establishment of choice for US Big Tech, making the DPC the lead supervisory authority (under Article 56 GDPR) for the largest single-issuer fines on the register. ~25 headline decisions are indexed, with the largest single fine being €1.2 billion (Meta 2023) and 5+ EDPB Article 65 cases since 2021. The DPC has been active since 1989 (GDPR: 2018).

**Mandate and constitution:** The DPC is designated under Article 51 GDPR, and as lead authority for controllers with main EU establishment in Ireland. Established under the Data Protection Act 1988, modernised under the Data Protection Act 2018. It reports to the Oireachtas through the Minister for Justice, with headquarters in Dublin (Fitzwilliam Square) and a satellite office in Portarlington. Staff grew from ~110 in 2018 to more than 230 by 2026.

**Fining philosophy:** Characterised by long inquiry timelines (3-5 years), detailed factual analysis, and rigorous Article 83(2) factor-by-factor weighting. Critics accuse the DPC of being insufficiently aggressive; the EDPB Article 65 mechanism has repeatedly recalibrated fines upward (WhatsApp: €30-50M draft to €225M final; Meta Chapter V case).

**Headline decisions:** WhatsApp €225M (Sept 2021, following EDPB BD 1/2021, first ever Article 65 decision); Instagram €405M children's data (Sept 2022, EDPB BD 2/2022); two Meta Ireland decisions totalling €390M (Jan 2023, contractual lawful basis for personalised advertising); Meta €1.2B Chapter V transfer decision (May 2023, largest GDPR fine to date, following EDPB BD 1/2023); TikTok €345M children's data (Sept 2023, EDPB BD 2/2023); TikTok €530M Chapter V China transfers (May 2025, second-largest single GDPR fine).

**Statistical record:** Cumulative DPC fines exceed €3 billion. Distribution is highly skewed; Big Tech share is ~95% of total in years with major decisions, and median annual fine count is in the tens. Complaint volumes rose steadily, exceeding 11,000 in 2024. The 2024 annual report was the most recent available, with 2025 report expected mid-2026.

**How to engage:** Data subjects can lodge complaints under Article 77 GDPR via dataprotection.ie; cross-border complaints use the one-stop-shop mechanism (lodged via local DPA, forwarded to DPC as lead, with original DPA as "concerned" authority under Articles 60/65).

**Recent enforcement trends (2024-2026):** Children's data, AI-system processing (intersecting with EU AI Act), DPIA compliance, and continued one-stop-shop relationships. The DPC moved to a three-Commissioner structure in 2024 (Des Hogan, Dale Sunderland, Niamh Sweeney), replacing the single Commissioner model (Helen Dixon, 2014-2024), to handle the workload.

**FAQ highlights:** The DPC issues many large fines because major US tech firms have EU headquarters in Ireland. The EDPB Article 65 mechanism lets concerned authorities refer draft decisions to the EDPB for binding decisions. The Spanish AEPD issues more decisions by count, but the DPC leads in cumulative amount. Fines are imposed on the EU-established subsidiary, not directly on US parents. Decisions are published on dataprotection.ie and EDPB decisions on edpb.europa.eu.
</summary>

Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) published its 2023 Annual Report, highlighting a record year in which DPC fines accounted for 87% of all GDPR fines issued across the EU. Most incidents originated from the private sector (3,766), followed by the public sector (2,968) and voluntary/charity sector (275).

In 2023, the DPC concluded 11,147 cases, held 89 statutory inquiries on-hand (including 51 cross-border inquiries), and handled over 25,130 electronic contacts, 7,085 phone calls, and 1,253 postal contacts. The most frequent GDPR topics for queries and complaints were access requests, fair-processing, disclosure, direct marketing, and right to erasure. The DPC concluded 19 inquiries in 2023 resulting in fines totaling €1.55 billion.

Notable cross-border inquiries concluded in 2023 included: two social media fines (€5.5 million for relying on contract as a lawful basis for service improvement, and €1.6 billion for transferring EU data to the US without a lawful basis) and a €345 million fine for processing children's personal data. The DPC pursued 7 national judgments or final orders in 2023 (split between the Irish Circuit Court and High Court), with legal costs awarded in favor of the DPC in 5 proceedings. The DPC also had 4 successful prosecutions involving unsolicited marketing messages under the e-Privacy Regulations.

Child protection remained a priority pillar of the DPC's Regulatory Strategy 2022-2027, reflected in the €345 million fine against a major social media company. The DPC was nominated to represent the EDPB on the new Task Force on Age Verification under the Digital Services Act. By the end of 2023, 3,520 DPOs were notified to the DPC. The DPC's participation in the 2023 Coordinated Enforcement Framework identified three DPO issues: insufficient resources, conflicts of interest, and inappropriate tasks. Of 751 supervision engagements in 2023, 391 were from multinational technology companies.

In February 2024, Helen Dixon stepped down as Data Protection Commissioner after 10 years, with Dr. Des Hogan (Chairperson) and Dale Sunderland taking over their new roles. The DPC continues to focus on systemic non-compliance and children's data protection rights in 2024.

On 25 November 2022 (announced 28 November 2022), the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC) imposed a €265 million administrative fine on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (MPIL) over the Facebook "data scraping" incident, concluding an inquiry opened after a dataset of Facebook user data was published online in April 2021.

The inquiry covered Facebook Search, Facebook Messenger Contact Importer, and Instagram Contact Importer tools, and processing between 25 May 2018 and September 2019. During that period, third parties abused these tools to match large lists of phone numbers against user profiles, compiling personal data on more than 500 million users from over 100 countries (including names, Facebook IDs, phone numbers, locations, dates of birth, and email addresses). The incident was not a conventional security breach; the data was assembled by exploiting features working as built because they lacked safeguards against enumeration and bulk matching. The DPC therefore centered the inquiry on Data Protection by Design and Default rather than Article 32 security of processing.

The DPC found infringements of Articles 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR (Data Protection by Design and by Default), concluding that Meta's contact-import and search features did not meet either obligation. Effective measures such as default-private settings, rate limiting, and controls on bulk enumeration were not built in by design or applied by default. Alongside the fine, the DPC imposed a reprimand and an order requiring MPIL to take specified remedial actions within a set timeframe. The EDPB was involved through the Article 60 cooperation process (but not via a binding Article 65 decision, unlike the €1.2 billion transfers fine).

Any feature allowing lookup, matching, or enumeration by identifier must be designed against abuse from the outset, and controllers are responsible for foreseeable misuse of their own tools under Article 25.

--- SOURCE 1: GDPR Enforcement and Fines 2026: Business Categories, ... ---
URL: https://www.uniconsent.com/blog/gdpr-enforcement-fines-2026

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from UniConsent provides a comprehensive overview of GDPR enforcement and fines as of 2026, with a specific focus on the ad tech sector. Key statistics include: over 2,500 fines totaling 7.1 billion euros issued since 2018, with approximately 1.2 billion euros issued in 2025 alone; an average fine of 2.4 million euros; and the largest fine ever being 1.2 billion euros against Meta Platforms Ireland (May 2023) for unlawful EU-US data transfers.

**Top 10 Largest GDPR Fines of All Time:**
1. Meta Platforms Ireland — 1.2B euros (Irish DPC, May 2023) — unlawful EU-US data transfers
2. Amazon Europe Core — 746M euros (Luxembourg CNPD, July 2021) — ad targeting without valid consent (annulled on procedural grounds in March 2026)
3. TikTok — 530M euros (Irish DPC, May 2025) — unlawful EU-China data transfers
4. Meta (Instagram) — 405M euros (Irish DPC, Sept 2022) — mishandling of children's data
5. Meta (Facebook + Instagram) — 390M euros (Irish DPC, Jan 2023) — invalid legal basis for behavioural ads
6. TikTok — 345M euros (Irish DPC, Sept 2023) — children's data processing failures
7. Google — 325M euros (French CNIL, Sept 2025) — Gmail inbox ads + invalid signup consent
8. LinkedIn Ireland — 310M euros (Irish DPC, Oct 2024) — invalid legal basis for behavioural ads
9. Uber — 290M euros (Dutch AP, Aug 2024) — unlawful EU-US data transfers
10. Meta (Facebook) — 265M euros (Irish DPC, Nov 2022) — inadequate protection against data scraping

Eight of the ten largest fines were issued by Ireland's DPC due to Dublin being the European HQ for most major tech companies. Ireland accounts for 4.04 billion euros (~57%) of all GDPR fine value, while Spain has issued the most fines by count (nearly 1,000). Ireland and France together account for ~70% of all GDPR fine value.

**Key structural insights:** The Media, Telecoms and Broadcasting sector accounts for ~70% of all corporate fine value, and "insufficient legal basis for data processing" is the most common violation. Ad tech is uniquely exposed due to: (1) data being the product itself, (2) opaque programmatic supply chains, and (3) consent being the only realistic legal basis for targeted advertising. Ad tech-driven fines approach 5 billion euros — well over half of all GDPR fines ever issued.

**Notable ad tech cases include:** Criteo (40M euros, 2023, for unverified partner consent), Google (50M euros, 2019, first major fine), Google + Amazon (100M + 35M euros, 2020, cookies before consent), Google + Facebook (150M + 60M euros, 2022, dark-pattern banners), Shein (150M euros, Sept 2025, cookie practices), Optimove (1M euros, Dec 2025, processor obligations), and Quantcast (ongoing DPC investigation).

**Critical finding on payment:** Of Ireland's 4.04 billion euros in fines, only ~20 million euros (0.5%) has actually been collected, as most major fines are under appeal. However, companies almost always implement corrective orders despite appealing headline numbers (e.g., Meta localised EU data infrastructure, LinkedIn rewrote consent flows within three months).

**Five common causes of ad tech fines:** (1) Wrong legal basis for targeted advertising, (2) cookies set before user consent, (3) dark pattern consent banners, (4) unverified partner consent in the supply chain, and (5) GDPR transparency/information failures.

**2026 enforcement trends:** Rising average fine sizes in Media/Telecoms/Broadcasting, more regulators becoming active across all member states, the DSA adding a second penalty layer (first DSA fine: 120M euros against X in December 2025), AI Act enforcement beginning August 2026 (penalties up to 35M euros or 7% of turnover), and decentralising cookie-banner challenges via noyb-style coordinated complaints.

The article concludes that consent management has become core infrastructure rather than optional software, with a compliance checklist for publishers and ad tech vendors covering: defaulting to consent for advertising processing, blocking non-essential tags until consent, making reject equal to accept, recording consent with full audit trails, auditing downstream partners, investing in the information layer, and treating international transfers as a separate compliance domain. The FAQ section clarifies the maximum fine (20M euros or 4% of turnover), extraterritorial reach (Article 3(2)), and the distinction between GDPR and ePrivacy fines (e.g., the Shein fine is technically an ePrivacy fine under French law).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"GDPR enforcement is no longer a theoretical risk that lives in a compliance deck. Based on publicly disclosed enforcement data, regulators across the EU and UK have issued more than 2,500 fines totalling over 7 billion euros since 2018, with approximately 1.2 billion euros of that issued in 2025 alone — and the curve is still climbing."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) issued a record 1.2 billion euro fine against Meta Platforms Ireland — the highest penalty to date under the GDPR — for unlawful transfers of EU/EEA users' personal data to the U.S. via Facebook. The decision ordered Meta to suspend future data transfers to the U.S. within five months and to cease unlawful processing and storage of EU user data in the U.S. within six months. The case stemmed from the July 2020 CJEU ruling that invalidated the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield; Meta subsequently relied on standard contractual clauses (SCCs), including those updated by the European Commission in 2021. The European Data Protection Board completed its binding dispute resolution on April 13, 2023, after supervisory authorities disagreed with the DPC's initial draft. EDPB Chair Andrea Jelinek called the infringement "very serious" given the systematic and continuous transfers of massive volumes of data from Facebook's millions of European users. Meta's Global Affairs President Nick Clegg and Chief Legal Officer Jennifer Newstead called the fine "unjustified and unnecessary" and said the company would appeal, noting a "fundamental conflict of law" between U.S. government data access rules and European privacy rights that policymakers are expected to resolve. NOYB Chairman Max Schrems, who had challenged trans-Atlantic data transfer regimes, said unless U.S. surveillance laws are fixed, Meta will need to "fundamentally restructure its systems." The decision has broad implications beyond Meta — the DPC explicitly noted that any internet platform falling under FISA 702 PRISM could face similar GDPR violations, and experts noted the ruling applies to both old and new SCCs and casts doubt on a risk-based approach to data transfers. The decision also raises questions about U.K. adequacy given the UK's proposed "not materially lower" data protection test. Stakeholders await finalization of the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, with a European Commission spokesperson stating it should be "fully functionable by summer" — though experts anticipate legal challenges similar to its predecessors.
</summary>

Facebook has millions of users in Europe, so the volume of personal data transferred is massive. Unless U.S. surveillance laws get fixed, Meta will have to fundamentally restructure its systems." - NOYB Chairman Max Schrems, "The impact of this decision is very broad, going vastly beyond Meta and being of concern for all businesses, universities, clinical trials and whomever is transferring personal data from the EU to the U.S. on the basis of SCCs in the absence of an adequacy decision." - Future of Privacy Forum's Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, "This enforcement action puts international data transfers at the top of the list of regulatory priorities by European data protection authorities.
