messages.content:
# Cleaned Research Findings: GDPR Enforcement Fines > €50M (Final Decisions, 2022–2023)

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

1. **Tavily search (batch of 3 queries):** "GDPR fines more than 50 million euros final decisions 2022 2023 Irish DPC list"; "DPC press release Meta Platforms Ireland Instagram 405 million euro fine September 2022"; "Irish DPC Meta 1.2 billion euro fine May 2023 Facebook data transfers United States"
2. **Tavily search (batch of 6 queries):** "DPC press release Meta Platforms Ireland 265 million euro fine November 2022 Facebook data breach decision"; "DPC press release Meta Platforms Ireland 210 million 180 million January 2023 behavioural advertising contractual basis"; "DPC TikTok 345 million euro fine September 2023 children's personal data decision press release"; "Meta 1.2 billion GDPR fine appeal status 2025 2026 Irish High Court"; "GDPR Enforcement Tracker Meta Instagram 405 million Ireland"; "CNIL Google 150 million Facebook 60 million January 2022 cookie fines GDPR or ePrivacy"
3. **Tavily search (batch of 6 queries):** "Meta 1.2 billion euro fine appeal Irish High Court judgment 2025 2026 status GDPR transfer"; "Meta 405 million Instagram fine appeal Irish High Court 2025 2026 status"; "TikTok 345 million euro DPC fine appeal High Court 2024 2025 status GDPR"; "Meta 265 million euro data scraping fine appeal High Court status"; "Amazon 746 million GDPR fine annulled Luxembourg administrative court March 2026 CNPD"; "GDPR enforcement tracker fines 2023 Ireland DPC list 2022 2023 largest fines"
4. **Tavily search (batch of 3 queries):** "complete list largest GDPR fines issued 2022 all authorities over 50 million"; "Meta Instagram 405 million fine appeal 2026 High Court judgment status Meta 390 million appeal CJEU"; "DLA Piper GDPR fines and penalties database enforcementtracker.com Meta Ireland 1.2 billion 2023"
5. **Think tool:** Reflection recording on final scope verification.

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### A. Executive Summary — Qualifying Fines

Based on all sources gathered, **exactly five final GDPR enforcement fines of more than €50 million were imposed by EU/EEA DPAs during calendar years 2022–2023**, all issued by the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC):

| # | Organization | Amount | Final Decision Date | DPA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Instagram) | €405,000,000 | Adopted 2 Sept 2022; announced 15 Sept 2022 | Ireland – Data Protection Commission (DPC) |
| 2 | Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook) | €265,000,000 | Adopted 25 Nov 2022; announced 28 Nov 2022 | Ireland – DPC |
| 3 | Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook & Instagram) | €390,000,000 (€210M + €180M) | Adopted 31 Dec 2022; announced 4 Jan 2023 | Ireland – DPC |
| 4 | Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook) | €1,200,000,000 | Decision dated 12 May 2023; announced 22 May 2023 | Ireland – DPC |
| 5 | TikTok Technology Limited | €345,000,000 | Adopted 1 Sept 2023; announced 15 Sept 2023 | Ireland – DPC |

Cross-verification from the CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report 2026 and the GDPR Enforcement Tracker statistics page confirms that the only entries in the all-time top 10 falling inside the 2022–2023 window are precisely these five fines ([36], [35]). No other DPA issued a GDPR fine above €50M in this window ([34], [4], [59]).

**Important correction to the user's candidate list:** the candidate described as "Meta WhatsApp-adjacent/Facebook data transfers, January 2023" is a mis-dating. The January 2023 (announced 4 January 2023) decision was the €390M behavioural-advertising fine; the EU–US data-transfer fine (€1.2 billion) was decided on 12 May 2023 and announced 22 May 2023 ([22], [15]).

**Appeal-status caveat (as of August 2026): none of the five fines has been reduced or annulled.** All five were under appeal as of the most recent information; the fines therefore still stand in the amounts above, but payment/collection is stayed or suspended in the major cases. Details per fine below.

---

### B. Fine 1: Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Instagram) — €405 million (September 2022)

**Exact amount:** €405,000,000 total, including €20 million specifically for the Article 6(1) infringement ([6]).

**Dates:** DPC final decision adopted **2 September 2022**; announced by press release **15 September 2022** ([6], [7], [8]). The inquiry was initiated 21 September 2020 following information provided by David Stier (a US data scientist) and the DPC's own examination of the Instagram user registration process ([6]). Some secondary sources date the fine as "September 5, 2022" (announcement per the GDPR Enforcement Tracker: 2022-09-05) and practice guides variously cite 2 September as decision date ([35], [9], [47]).

**Issuing DPA:** Ireland — Data Protection Commission (DPC), acting as lead supervisory authority under Article 56 GDPR ([1], [6]).

**GDPR articles infringed:** Articles **5(1)(a)** (lawfulness/fairness/transparency), **5(1)(c)** (data minimisation), **6(1)** (no lawful basis), **12(1)** (transparency of information), **24** (controller responsibility), **25(1)** (data protection by design), **25(2)** (data protection by default), and **35(1)** (DPIA) ([6], [8]). The Article 6(1) finding was added on the direction of the EDPB; the EDPB found that processing of children's data was not necessary for the performance of a contract or for Meta's legitimate interests, so Meta "infringed Article 6(1) by processing this personal data unlawfully without an appropriate legal basis" ([7]).

**Factual conduct:** The inquiry examined "the public disclosure of email addresses and/or phone numbers of children using the Instagram business account feature and a public-by-default setting for personal Instagram accounts of children" ([6]). Specifically: (1) users aged 13–17 could activate "business accounts," which by default published their phone numbers and/or email addresses; and (2) the registration process set child users' accounts to "public" by default, requiring the child to know to change the setting to "private" ([10], [47], [48]). Children's contact info was published in HTML source code of profiles; default settings allowed anyone to view content; Meta failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures and failed to carry out a DPIA despite high risk to child users ([8]).

**Procedure:** Draft decision submitted to Concerned Supervisory Authorities under Article 60 in December 2021; six regulators (Finland, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, and Norway) objected; referred to the EDPB under Article 65; EDPB adopted binding decision (BD 2/2022) on **28 July 2022**, rejecting many objections but requiring the Article 6(1) finding and fine reassessment ([6], [7], [48]). The original draft had recommended a fine of up to €405M; the final fine remained €405M ([6]).

**Remedies:** In addition to the fine, a reprimand and an order requiring Meta to bring processing into compliance through specified remedial actions within three months ([6], [8]).

**Appeal status:** Meta filed an appeal in the Irish High Court on/about **3 October 2022** ([33], [47], [18], [7]). As of the latest sources (through January–March 2026), the fine remains **under appeal** with no judgment reducing or annulling it; it is reported as "Under appeal" in 2026 trackers ([5], [34]). The EDPB's 2025 annual report notes Meta is challenging EDPB binding decisions including on children's data (Instagram) before the CJEU ([62]).

**Significance:** At issuance, the second-highest GDPR fine ever (after Amazon's €746M); the largest fine ever levied by the DPC at the time; the first EU-wide decision on children's data protection rights ([7], [47], [8]).

**Official DPC URL:** http://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/data-protection-commission-announces-decision-instagram-inquiry ([6])

**Tracker URLs:** GDPR Enforcement Tracker statistics (2022-09-05 entry): https://www.enforcementtracker.com/statistics ([35]); GDPRfine.com DPC profile: https://gdprfine.com/dpa/ireland-dpc ([1]); Tech Fines Directory entry: https://guptadeepak.com/tech-fines/violation/meta-ireland-instagram-children-2022 ([9])

---

### C. Fine 2: Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook) — €265 million (November 2022)

**Exact amount:** €265,000,000 (total administrative fines) ([19], [20]).

**Dates:** Decision adopted **25 November 2022**; announced **28 November 2022** ([19], [17], [35]). Inquiry commenced 14 April 2021 following media reports about a collated dataset of Facebook personal data made available on the internet; the inquiry examined processing between 25 May 2018 and September 2019 ([19], [17]).

**Issuing DPA:** Ireland — Data Protection Commission (DPC) ([19]).

**GDPR articles infringed:** Articles **25(1)** and **25(2)** GDPR (data protection by design and by default) only ([19], [17], [20]). These are lower-tier infringements under Article 83(4) (cap €10M or 2% of worldwide turnover); given Meta's scale the 2% ceiling sat well above €265M ([17]).

**Factual conduct:** The "Facebook data scraping" incident. Third parties abused Facebook Search, Facebook Messenger Contact Importer, and Instagram Contact Importer tools to match large lists of phone numbers against user profiles, compiling personal data on **more than 500 million users** (approx. 533 million) from more than 100 countries — including names, Facebook IDs, mobile phone numbers, real addresses, birth dates, and email addresses, published on an online hacking forum in April 2021 ([16], [20], [17], [53]). The data was assembled by exploiting features working as built because they lacked safeguards against enumeration and bulk matching; the DPC therefore centred the inquiry on Data Protection by Design and Default rather than Article 32 security ([17]). The DPC found Meta's contact-import and search features did not meet either obligation — effective measures such as default-private settings, rate limiting, and controls on bulk enumeration were not built in by design or applied by default ([17]).

**Procedure:** The inquiry involved cooperation with all other EU supervisory authorities under Article 60, all of whom agreed with the DPC's decision — no EDPB Article 65 binding decision was involved (unlike the €1.2B transfers fine) ([19], [17]).

**Remedies:** Reprimand plus an order to bring processing into compliance through specified remedial actions within a timeframe ([19], [16]).

**Appeal status:** Meta appealed; the High Court (Justice Garrett Simons, judgment published 10 May 2024) **adjourned** the appeal until the CJEU resolves Meta's separate appeal against the €225M WhatsApp fine (2021). Simons stated the €265M fine **"will not be legally effective until the EU case is resolved,"** that the issues "cannot sensibly be separated out" because "the question of liability and sanction are inextricably bound up together," and noted Meta had already complied with corrective measures to the DPC's satisfaction ([32]). The DPC and Meta agreed the fine cannot be paid until domestic proceedings conclude ([32]). As of 2026 trackers, the €265M fine remains listed as #8–10 all-time and under appeal ([34], [35], [5]).

**Official DPC URL:** https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/data-protection-commission-announces-decision-in-facebook-data-scraping-inquiry ([19])

**Tracker URLs:** GDPRfine.com case page: https://gdprfine.com/cases/meta-265-million-dpc-2022 ([17]); GDPR Enforcement Tracker statistics (2022-11-25): https://www.enforcementtracker.com/statistics ([35]); CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report: https://cms.law/en/int/publication/GDPR-Enforcement-Tracker-Report/numbers-and-figures ([36])

---

### D. Fine 3: Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook & Instagram) — €390 million (January 2023)

**Exact amount:** €390,000,000 total — **€210 million for Facebook** and **€180 million for Instagram** ([22], [23], [21]).

**Dates:** Two final decisions adopted **31 December 2022**; announced **4 January 2023** ([22], [21], [6]). Inquiries stemmed from two complaints (Austrian data subject re: Facebook; Belgian data subject re: Instagram) lodged **25 May 2018**, the day GDPR came into operation ([22]).

**Issuing DPA:** Ireland — Data Protection Commission (DPC) ([22]).

**GDPR articles infringed:** DPC's final decisions found Meta in contravention of **Article 6 GDPR** (no entitlement to rely on the "contract"/performance-of-contract legal basis for personalised/behavioural advertising); breaches of transparency obligations under Articles **12**, **13(1)(c)**, and **5(1)(a)**; the EDPB additionally directed a finding of breach of the fairness principle ([22], [21], [24], [25]). The DPC originally held that, in principle, GDPR did not preclude reliance on the contract legal basis; the EDPB overruled on this point ([22]).

**Factual conduct:** Prior to 25 May 2018, Meta Ireland changed its Terms of Service for Facebook and Instagram, shifting from a "consent" legal basis to a "contract" legal basis (Article 6(1)(b)) for most processing operations, **including behavioural advertising**. Users were required to click "I accept" to the updated terms to continue accessing the services ([22]). Complainants (notably NOYB, co-founded by Max Schrems) argued this amounted to "forced consent"/forced acceptance of personalised advertising as a condition of service ([24], [25], [23]). The EDPB (binding decision 5 December 2022) reasoned that: (1) Meta is not contractually obligated to offer personalised ads to users (the obligation exists with advertisers instead); (2) transparency requirements are indispensable to the contract basis; and (3) under Article 21(2)–(3) GDPR, users can object to direct-marketing processing at any time without reason, so such processing is not "necessary" for the contract ([21]).

**Procedure:** Draft decision published 6 October 2021 proposed fines of up to €23M (Instagram) and €36M (Facebook); ten European supervisory authorities (including the Dutch DPA) objected that personalised ads are not a core element of Meta's services, triggering the consistency mechanism; EDPB issued binding decision on **5 December 2022** ordering significantly increased fines and a fresh open-ended investigation into all Facebook/Instagram processing including special categories; the DPC adopted the decisions on 31 December 2022 ([21], [22], [24]).

**Remedies:** Directive to bring data processing into compliance within **3 months** ([22], [23]).

**Appeal status:** "Under appeal by both sides" as of 2026 ([5]). Meta announced it would appeal the substance, arguing it "fully compl[ies] with GDPR by relying on Contractual Necessity for behavioural ads" ([23], [25]). Separately, **the DPC itself** stated it would bring an action for annulment before the CJEU contesting the EDPB's jurisdiction to direct a fresh open-ended investigation, arguing the EDPB "does not appear consistent with the structure of the cooperation and consistency arrangements laid down by the GDPR" ([22], [25]). The EDPB's 2025 annual report confirms Meta is challenging EDPB binding decisions on behavioural advertising at the CJEU ([62]). No court has reduced or annulled the fine as of August 2026 ([5], [34], [62]).

**Significance:** IAPP described it as "probably the most significant enforcement decision" since the GDPR's implementation due to the changes Meta will need to make to its services ([25]).

**Official DPC URL:** http://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/data-protection-commission-announces-conclusion-two-inquiries-meta-ireland ([22])

**Tracker URLs:** GDPR Enforcement Tracker statistics (2023-01-04): https://www.enforcementtracker.com/statistics ([35]); CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report: https://cms.law/en/int/publication/GDPR-Enforcement-Tracker-Report/numbers-and-figures ([36])

---

### E. Fine 4: Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook) — €1.2 billion (May 2023)

**Exact amount:** €1,200,000,000 — the largest GDPR fine ever imposed, roughly 60% larger than the next-highest figure ([3], [11], [13]).

**Dates:** Decision dated **12 May 2023** (DPC Reference IN-20-8-1); announced **22 May 2023** ([15], [11], [12], [14]). Inquiry began August 2020; stayed by the Irish High Court until 20 May 2021; draft decision 6 July 2022; EDPB Article 65 binding decision (BD 1/2023) adopted **13 April 2023** ([15], [14]).

**Issuing DPA:** Ireland — Data Protection Commission (DPC) ([15]).

**GDPR articles infringed:** Article **46(1) GDPR** (transfers subject to appropriate safeguards — Chapter V), confirmed by the EDPB; the DPC found Meta could not rely on Article 49 exceptions either ([15], [11]).

**Factual conduct:** Meta Ireland continued transferring EU/EEA Facebook users' personal data to the US after the CJEU's *Schrems II* judgment (Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Limited and Maximillian Schrems, July 2020, which invalidated the EU-US Privacy Shield). Although Meta used the updated 2021 Standard Contractual Clauses plus additional supplementary measures, the DPC concluded these "did not address the risks to the fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects that were identified by the CJEU," given US surveillance powers under FISA 702/PRISM ([15], [11], [12], [13]). The case originated from Max Schrems' June 2013 complaint following the Snowden disclosures ([11], [13]). EDPB Chair Andrea Jelinek called the infringement "very serious since it concerns transfers that are systematic, repetitive and continuous... Facebook has millions of users in Europe, so the volume of personal data transferred is massive" ([14]).

**Procedure:** Draft decision submitted to 47 Concerned Supervisory Authorities under Article 60; the CSAs agreed with the findings and suspension proposal, but four objected that corrective powers should include an administrative fine (the DPC's initial draft included no fine); the matter went to the EDPB under Article 65, which on 13 April 2023 directed the DPC to impose a fine; the DPC set the amount at €1.2B per the EDPB's assessments ([15], [12], [14]).

**Remedies:** (1) Order under Article 58(2)(j) to suspend future transfers of personal data to the US within five months; (2) the €1.2B administrative fine; (3) order under Article 58(2)(d) to bring processing into compliance with Chapter V by ceasing unlawful processing, including storage in the US, within six months ([15]).

**Appeal status:** Meta appealed in the Irish High Court on **26 June 2023** under Section 150 of the Irish Data Protection Act 2018, and was granted an extension of an interim stay on the decision until 31 July 2023 (with the EU-US Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision then expected in mid-July 2023) ([52]). Meta's Nick Clegg and Jennifer Newstead called the fine "unjustified and unnecessary," citing a "fundamental conflict of law between the U.S. government's rules on access to data and European privacy rights," and said the company would appeal ([14], [13]). As of 2026, the fine remains **under appeal with payment suspended**; no reduction or annulment has been issued ([5], [34], [3], [4]). The EDPB's 2025 annual report notes Meta is challenging EDPB binding decisions on data transfers outside the EU ([62]). PrivacyTerms.io's July 2026 ranking still lists it as #1 all-time ([3]).

**Significance:** Largest GDPR fine ever (record held for over three years); decision applies only to Facebook (not WhatsApp or Instagram); the DPC explicitly noted any internet platform falling under FISA 702 PRISM could face similar violations; experts noted the ruling applies to both old and new SCCs ([11], [14]).

**Official DPC URL (decision page):** http://www.dataprotection.ie/en/dpc-guidance/decisions/inquiry-concerning-data-transfers-eueea-us-meta-platforms-ireland-limited-its-facebook-service ([15])

**Tracker URLs:** GDPR Enforcement Tracker statistics (2023-05-12): https://www.enforcementtracker.com/statistics ([35]); CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report: https://cms.law/en/int/publication/GDPR-Enforcement-Tracker-Report/numbers-and-figures ([36]); DLA Piper GDPR Fines and Data Breach Survey January 2025: https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2025/01/dla-piper-gdpr-fines-and-data-breach-survey-january-2025 ([60])

---

### F. Fine 5: TikTok Technology Limited — €345 million (September 2023)

**Exact amount:** €345,000,000 ([29]).

**Dates:** Final decision adopted **1 September 2023**; announced **15 September 2023** ([29], [35]). The inquiry examined the period **31 July 2020 to 31 December 2020** (own-volition inquiry, opened September 2021) ([29], [26], [13]).

**Issuing DPA:** Ireland — Data Protection Commission (DPC) ([29]).

**GDPR articles infringed:** Articles **5(1)(c)** (data minimisation), **5(1)(f)** (security/integrity and confidentiality), **24(1)** (controller responsibility), **25(1)** (data protection by design), **25(2)** (data protection by default), **12(1)** (transparency), **13(1)(e)** (information to data subjects about recipients/categories), and — added by EDPB binding decision of 2 August 2023 (BD 2/2023) — **5(1)(a)** (fairness, regarding "dark patterns") ([29]).

**Factual conduct:** (1) **Public-by-default settings:** child user profiles (users under 16/under 18) were configured as public by default, allowing anyone to access content posted by children, with an option to "skip" making accounts private during setup — violating data minimisation, data protection by design, and data protection by default (TikTok's web browser version can be accessed by non-registered users) ([26], [28], [30]). (2) **Family Pairing:** the feature allowed non-child users who couldn't be verified as parents or guardians to pair with child accounts and send direct messages, posing "severe possible risks to child users" and violating the security principle ([26], [28]). (3) **Transparency failures:** TikTok failed to provide sufficient transparency information to child users; ambiguous wording in privacy notices (terms like "public," "anyone," and "everyone" not clearly distinguishing between registered and non-registered users) ([26], [27]). (4) **Dark patterns:** TikTok implemented "dark patterns" that nudged users toward more privacy-intrusive options during registration and when posting videos, violating the fairness principle ([26]). (5) **Age verification:** TikTok failed to properly take into account risks posed to children under 13 who gained access to the platform — the first EDPB/pan-European examination of age-verification measures under GDPR ([28], [27]).

**Procedure:** Draft decision submitted to CSAs on 13 September 2022 under Article 60(3); objections raised by the SAs of Italy and Berlin (Berlin also acting for Baden-Württemberg); referred to EDPB under Article 65; EDPB binding decision **2 August 2023** directed the DPC to add the fairness finding and extend the remedial order ([29]).

**Remedies:** Order to bring processing of child users' data into compliance within three months; reprimand for some findings ([26], [29]).

**Appeal status:** TikTok stated it "respectfully disagree[s] with the decision, particularly the level of the fine," noting the criticised features dated back three years ([30], [26]). TikTok took legal action in the Irish High Court against both the DPC and Ireland's Attorney General, seeking to overturn the decision ([49]). As of 2026, the fine remains listed as standing (2023-09-01) and **under appeal** per 2026 trackers ([5], [34], [35]).

**Significance:** Among the largest GDPR fines ever imposed; the largest fine TikTok had received from regulators at that date; the first EU-wide decision examining age-verification measures ([27], [30]).

**Official DPC URL:** https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/DPC-announces-345-million-euro-fine-of-TikTok ([29])

**Tracker URLs:** GDPR Enforcement Tracker statistics (2023-09-01): https://www.enforcementtracker.com/statistics ([35]); CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report: https://cms.law/en/int/publication/GDPR-Enforcement-Tracker-Report/numbers-and-figures ([36])

---

### G. Excluded Candidates and Out-of-Window Cases (verified)

**1. Luxembourg CNPD fine on Amazon (July 2021) — excluded from the 2022–2023 window, and since annulled.**
- The CNPD fined **Amazon Europe Core S.à r.l. €746 million** on **15 July 2021** for violations of the GDPR — the largest GDPR fine at the time ([4], [57], [50]).
- Conduct: processing personal data for targeted/behavioural advertising without valid consent/opt-out (reliance on legitimate interest rejected; information procedures non-compliant with GDPR Articles 12–14) ([4], [23]).
- **Annulled 12 March 2026** by Luxembourg's Administrative Court (judgment No 52757C) **on procedural grounds only**: the CNPD failed to establish whether Amazon acted with fault (intent or negligence) before fining it, a step made mandatory by CJEU rulings of 5 December 2023 in *Deutsche Wohnen* (C-807/21) and the Lithuanian "Nacionalinis" case (C-683/21); the CNPD's own counsel conceded at a 8 January 2026 hearing that the required fault inquiry had not been attempted ([41], [42], [43], [44]). The court also found the CNPD "adopted an approach of almost automatically imposing a fine following the identification of GDPR violations" without first considering whether other measures were more appropriate ([44]).
- The court **upheld the substantive findings** (legitimate interest not justified; transparency/information procedures non-compliant) and **remanded to the CNPD** to redo the fault and sanction-selection analysis; the underlying violation was not overturned ([41], [42], [43], [44]). The €746,000-per-day coercive penalty became moot as Amazon had already complied ([43], [44]).
- Therefore, as of August 2026, the Amazon €746M fine is **not in effect** — no adjusted final amount has yet been set ([3], [34], [41]).
- Official CNPD statement: https://cnpd.public.lu/en/actualites/national/2026/03/arret-ca-amazon-cnpd.html ([41])

**2. CNIL fines on Google and Facebook (announced January 2022) — excluded: outside window and not GDPR fines.**
- On **31 December 2021** (announced 6 January 2022), France's CNIL fined **Google a total of €150 million** (€90M for Google LLC for google.fr; €60M for Google Ireland Limited for youtube.com) and **Facebook Ireland €60 million** (for facebook.com) for cookie refusal mechanisms in France ([61], [60], [59]).
- These fines were based on **Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act**, transposing **Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive** — not on GDPR articles; the CNIL held the GDPR one-stop-shop mechanism does not apply to cookie read/write operations ([61], [60]). They are therefore not GDPR fines and fall outside the 2022–2023 window in any event ([59], [50]).
- (Note: Reuters summary incorrectly describes them as France's record GDPR-style fines; both the DLA Piper and activeMind analyses clarify the ePrivacy legal basis ([61], [59], [60]).)

**3. TikTok Technology Limited — €530 million (May 2025) — outside window.** DPC decision of 30 April 2025 (announced 2 May 2025) for EU/EEA-to-China transfers (remote access by ByteDance personnel in China): €485 million for Article 46(1) + €45 million for Article 13(1)(f); appeal history through 2026 — High Court upheld the fine on 3 June and 30 June 2026 and referred fining-methodology questions to the CJEU; a stay on suspension/compliance orders was granted Nov 2025 and upheld by the Supreme Court 30 April 2026 ([31], [50], [51]). Second-largest standing GDPR fine ([35], [34]).

**4. 2024 fines (outside window):** LinkedIn Ireland €310 million (DPC, 24 Oct 2024); Uber B.V. €290 million (Dutch AP, 22 July 2024 per Enforcement Tracker; 26 August 2024 per CookieScript); Meta Platforms Ireland €251 million (DPC, 17/27 Dec 2024) ([35], [4], [34]).

**5. WhatsApp Ireland €225 million (September 2021) — outside window;** case taken to the CJEU ([4], [5]).

---

### H. Ranking Among Largest GDPR Fines Ever

Per multiple 2026-dated sources, the five qualifying fines rank as follows (all-time list):

1. **Meta Platforms Ireland — €1.2 billion (2023)** — #1 largest GDPR fine ever; record held for over three years ([3], [4], [35], [36]).
2. Amazon Europe Core — €746M (2021) — originally #2, but **annulled 12 March 2026** (procedural) and remanded ([3], [34], [41]).
3. TikTok — €530M (2025) — now effectively #2 among standing fines ([35], [34]).
4. **Meta (Instagram) — €405M (2022)** — #3 or #4 (depending on treatment of annulled Amazon/2025 TikTok) ([3], [4], [34], [35]).
5. **Meta (Facebook + Instagram) — €390M (2023)** — #4 or #5 ([3], [4], [34], [35]).
6. **TikTok — €345M (2023)** — #5 or #6 ([3], [4], [34], [35]).
7. LinkedIn — €310M (2024) ([35]).
8. Uber — €290M (2024) ([35]).
9. **Meta (Facebook) — €265M (2022)** — #8–#10 ([34], [35], [4]).
10. Meta — €251M (2024) and WhatsApp — €225M (2021) ([35], [36]).

All five 2022–2023 qualifying fines are from the Irish DPC, which has issued 7–9 of the top 10 fines and holds the highest cumulative GDPR fine value of any regulator (~€4.04 billion, ~57–66% of all GDPR fine value) ([3], [34], [35], [36], [64]).

---

### I. Enforcement Context and Statistics (relevant background)

- Cumulative GDPR fines since 25 May 2018: approximately **€6.11 billion** (CMS Enforcement Tracker Report 2026, 2,685 recorded fines, cut-off 1 March 2026) ([36]); approximately **€6.31 billion** across 3,206 cases (enforcementtracker.com statistics, as of 2026) ([35]); approximately **€7.1 billion** per DLA Piper's January 2026 survey ([65], [42]); approx. €5.88 billion at January 2025 ([4]).
- In 2023, the DPC concluded 19 inquiries resulting in fines totaling **€1.55 billion**, and DPC fines accounted for **87% of all GDPR fines issued across the EU in 2023** ([2]).
- The 2023 total included "two social media fines (€5.5 million for relying on contract as a lawful basis for service improvement, and €1.6 billion [sic — in context, the combined value of the €1.2B transfer fine] for transferring EU data to the US without a lawful basis) and a €345 million fine for processing children's personal data" ([2]).
- Of Ireland's ~€4.04 billion in fines, only ~€20 million (0.5%) has actually been collected as most major fines are under appeal; companies almost always implement corrective orders despite appealing headline numbers (e.g., Meta localised EU data infrastructure) ([34]).
- Meta's cumulative DPC fines (including WhatsApp) approach/total roughly €1.86 billion across the top-10 entries alone ([3]); as of 2022, DPC fines against Meta totalled nearly €1 billion ([16]).
- The EDPB's Article 65 mechanism has repeatedly recalibrated fines upward (WhatsApp: €30–50M draft to €225M final; Instagram; Meta Chapter V case where the DPC's draft had no fine but the EDPB directed €1.2B) ([1], [12]).
- Ongoing litigation: Meta is challenging EDPB binding decisions on children's data (Instagram), behavioural advertising, data transfers outside the EU, and the "consent or pay" model; TikTok and WhatsApp also have ongoing annulment actions against EDPB decisions; in January 2025 the General Court closed three cases where the Irish DPC sued the EDPB over jurisdictional competence ([62]).

**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

### 1. Meta Platforms Ireland Limited – €251 million (Irish DPC, 17 December 2024)

**Final amount:** €251,000,000 total (four administrative fines: €8M + €3M + €130M + €110M) [1][3][5].
**Date:** Final decisions adopted 12 December 2024; announced 17 December 2024 [1][5]. The DPC press release is dated 17 December 2024 [1][17].
**Issuing DPA:** Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC), Commissioners for Data Protection Dr. Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland [1][5].

**Article breakdown:**
- Decision 1 (inquiry IN-18-10-1): €8 million for infringement of Article 33(3) GDPR (failure to include necessary details in breach notification – nature of breach, categories of data subjects, categories of personal data records, likely consequences); €3 million for infringement of Article 33(5) GDPR (failure to create a contemporaneous documentary record of breach facts and remedial steps) [3][5].
- Decision 2 (inquiry IN-18-11-1): €130 million for infringement of Article 25(1) GDPR (failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures ensuring data protection by design); €110 million for infringement of Article 25(2) GDPR (failure to ensure data protection by default – tokens gave unnecessarily broad access to personal data) [3][5].
- Corrective measures included reprimands under Article 58(2)(b) GDPR and fines under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83 GDPR [1][5].

**Factual summary of conduct:** The fines stem from a personal data breach reported by Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (MPIL, formerly Facebook Ireland Ltd) in September 2018, impacting approximately 29 million Facebook accounts globally, including roughly 3 million in the EU/EEA [1][3][4]. The breach originated from a vulnerability created when a video upload function was deployed on Facebook in July 2017: Facebook's 'View As' feature combined with the 'Happy Birthday Composer' facility could be exploited to generate fully permissioned user tokens (coded identifiers) granting full access to other users' profiles [3][5]. Between 14 and 28 September 2018, unauthorized persons used scripts to exploit this vulnerability, gaining the ability to log on as account holders for approximately 29 million accounts globally [1][4][5]. Affected personal data categories included user full names, email addresses, phone numbers, locations, places of work, dates of birth, religion, gender, timeline posts, group memberships, and children's personal data [1][3][4]. Facebook security personnel were alerted by anomalous video upload activity and removed the vulnerable functionality; MPIL notified the DPC on 28 September 2018 [3][5].

**Procedure:** The DPC submitted a draft decision to the GDPR cooperation mechanism under Article 60 in September 2024; no objections were raised by peer EU/EEA supervisory authorities, though three comments per decision were received and considered [1][5]. Euractiv reports the fine was split as €11 million for failure to notify/full document the breach and €240 million for the nature of the breach itself [16]. Reuters reported the fine as 251 million euros ($263.5 million) on 17 December 2024 [17].

**Appeal status (as of August 2026):** Meta said "We took immediate action to fix the problem" and announced it would appeal (per Reuters: "Meta said it will also appeal Tuesday's decision") [16][17]. The Legit.eu summary also states "Meta has announced plans to appeal the decision" [18]. No court judgment confirming the finality of this specific €251M fine was found in the searches. Flag as **under appeal / appeal expected; final amount not yet confirmed by a court**.

**DPC Deputy Commissioner statement (verbatim):** "This enforcement action highlights how the failure to build in data protection requirements throughout the design and development cycle can expose individuals to very serious risks and harms, including a risk to the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals. Facebook profiles can, and often do, contain information about matters such as religious or political beliefs, sexual life or orientation, and similar matters that a user may wish to disclose only in particular circumstances. By allowing unauthorised exposure of profile information, the vulnerabilities behind this breach caused a grave risk of misuse of these types of data." – DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle [1][3][4].

### 2. LinkedIn Ireland Unlimited Company – €310 million (Irish DPC, 24 October 2024)

**Date:** Decision notified to LinkedIn on 22 October 2024; announced 24 October 2024; Pinsent Masons states the decision was published 25 October 2024 [13][14][17].
**Issuing DPA:** Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC); Commissioners Dr. Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland [14].

**Articles infringed:**
- Article 6(1)(a) GDPR – invalid reliance on consent for third-party data (consent was not "freely given, sufficiently informed, specific, and unambiguous") [11][13][14].
- Article 6(1)(f) GDPR – unlawful reliance on legitimate interests (rights and freedoms of members outweighed LinkedIn's commercial interests) [11][13][14].
- Article 6(1)(b) GDPR – unlawful reliance on contractual necessity [11][13][14].
- Article 5(1)(a) GDPR – breach of the principle of fairness [11][13][14].
- Articles 13(1)(c) and 14(1)(c) GDPR – transparency failures (failure to provide clear, transparent information about the lawful bases relied upon) [11][14].

**Factual summary of conduct:** The inquiry examined LinkedIn's processing of personal data of its registered members (data provided directly by members and data obtained via third-party partners) for behavioural analysis and targeted advertising. The complaint-based inquiry commenced 20 August 2018 following a complaint made by the French non-profit organisation La Quadrature Du Net to the French DPA [14][17]; the matter was redirected to the DPC as lead supervisory authority for LinkedIn (EU operations headquartered in Ireland) [13][14].

**Corrective measures:** A reprimand under Article 58(2)(b); three administrative fines totalling €310 million under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83; an order under Article 58(2)(d) to bring processing into compliance within three months [14][17][44].

**Procedure:** The DPC submitted its draft decision to the GDPR cooperation mechanism in July 2024 under Article 60; no objections were raised by peer EU/EEA supervisory authorities [13][14]. ### 3. Uber Technologies Inc. and Uber B.V. – €290 million (Dutch AP, 26 August 2024)

**Final amount:** €290,000,000 [6][9][10]. This was the largest fine ever imposed by the Dutch DPA [7][10].
**Date:** GDPRhub records the decision date as 22 July 2024, published 25 August 2024 [6]. The AP press release and Willkie article state the fine was imposed/announced on 26 August 2024 [8][9].
**Issuing DPA:** Dutch Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP, Dutch Data Protection Authority), acting as lead supervisory authority because Uber's European headquarters are in the Netherlands [6][9][10].

**Article infringed:** Article 44 GDPR – transfer of personal data to a third country without appropriate safeguards under Chapter V (the AP found no valid transfer mechanism from 6 August 2021 to 27 November 2023) [6][10]. The AP rejected Uber's defenses under Article 3 (territorial scope), Article 49(1)(b) and (c) derogations, and arguments that no "transfer" occurred because drivers provided data directly [6][7][10].

**Factual summary of conduct:** Uber Technologies Inc. (UTI, San Francisco) and Uber B.V. (UBV, Netherlands) were found to be joint controllers for Uber drivers' personal data. Uber used a centralized IT infrastructure with servers in the US; EEA drivers' data was processed in the US in two situations: (1) data collected through the driver app and stored on US servers (including account details, taxi licences, location data, photos, payment details, identity documents, and in some cases criminal and medical data of drivers), and (2) when drivers exercised GDPR rights, UTI made data available to UBV [6][9]. Uber had used the European Commission's Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) but removed them from its joint controllership agreement effective 6 August 2021, arguing SCCs could not be used when processing falls directly under GDPR scope [6][8]. The violation lasted approximately 27 months, until Uber certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework in November 2023 [8][10]. The investigation began after more than 170 French drivers complained to the French human rights group Ligue des droits de l'Homme (LDH), which submitted a complaint to the French DPA (CNIL) on 12 June 2020; it was forwarded to the Dutch AP under the one-stop-shop mechanism [6][9][10].

**Key legal holdings:** The AP rejected Uber's argument that Article 3 and Chapter V are mutually exclusive, holding Chapter V is complementary and prevents circumvention; applied the EDPB Guidelines 05/2021's three cumulative criteria to find a "transfer" (including finding UBV was the exporter because drivers have little influence over processing purposes/means); rejected Uber's claim that drivers themselves were exporters; and rejected Article 49 derogations because transfers were systematic, repetitive, and ongoing, not incidental [6][7].

**Fine calculation:** The fine represents up to 4% of worldwide annual turnover; Uber reported approximately €34.5 billion in worldwide turnover in 2023 [9]. The fine was calculated per EDPB guidelines considering gravity and duration, Uber's global scale and financial capacity, the two-year period of non-compliance, the exposure of sensitive driver data, and insufficient mitigation measures; the AP determined Uber "could have known" the transfer would require additional safeguards based on GDPR, CJEU case law, and prior regulator decisions [8][10].

**Appeal status (as of August 2026):** Uber has indicated its intention to object/appeal the fine [9][10]. Taylor Wessing: "Uber has announced its intention to appeal"; Willkie: "Uber is expected to appeal"; European Law Blog: "Uber is appealing; Dutch courts are likely to refer questions to the CJEU on the Article 3/Chapter V relationship"; Measured Collective lists the fine as "Under appeal" [7][8][10][39]. **Under appeal.**

**Quote (verbatim), AP Chairman Aleid Wolfsen:** "In Europe, the GDPR protects the fundamental rights of people, by requiring businesses and governments to handle personal data with due care. But sadly, this is not self-evident outside Europe. Think of governments that can tap data on a large scale. That is why businesses are usually obliged to take additional measures if they store personal data of Europeans outside the European Union. Uber did not meet the requirements of the GDPR to ensure the level of protection to the data with regard to transfers to the US. That is very serious." [9]

### 4. TikTok Technology Limited – €530 million (Irish DPC, 2 May 2025)

**Final amount:** €530,000,000 total – €485 million for infringement of Article 46(1) GDPR (transfers of EEA user data to China without appropriate safeguards) and €45 million for infringement of Article 13(1)(f) GDPR (transparency failure) [19][21][22].
**Date:** Final decision announced 2 May 2025 [19][20]; some sources date the DPC's decision 30 April 2025 [22][25]. Draft decision submitted to the GDPR cooperation mechanism on 21 February 2025 under Article 60; no objections raised [19][20].
**Issuing DPA:** Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC), Commissioners Dr. Des Hogan and Dale Sunderland, as Lead Supervisory Authority for TikTok [19][20].

**Factual summary of conduct:** The inquiry (IN-21-9-2) examined TikTok's transfers of EEA user personal data to China, including remote access by ByteDance personnel in China to data stored in Singapore and the US (and Malaysia per one source) [19][22]. The DPC found TikTok failed to verify, guarantee, and demonstrate that EEA users' data remotely accessed by staff in China was afforded a level of protection essentially equivalent to EU standards; TikTok's own assessment of Chinese law identified material divergences from EU standards under the Anti-Terrorism Law, Counter-Espionage Law, Cybersecurity Law, and National Intelligence Law [19][21]. The DPC rejected TikTok's reliance on SCCs plus supplementary measures, finding its Transfer Risk Assessments were not substantively robust, and found Article 49 derogations inapplicable because transfers were systematic, repetitive and continuous [22].

**Transparency finding:** TikTok's October 2021 EEA Privacy Policy failed to name third countries (including China) to which data was transferred and failed to explain the processing operations (remote access by personnel in China to data stored in Singapore and the US). The infringement period ran from 29 July 2020 to 1 December 2022; the December 2022 privacy policy was deemed compliant [19][21].

**Notable aggravating disclosure:** Throughout the inquiry TikTok claimed it did not store EEA user data on servers in China, but in April 2025 disclosed that limited EEA user data had in fact been stored on servers in China (discovered in February 2025), meaning TikTok had provided inaccurate information to the inquiry. The DPC stated it is considering further regulatory action regarding this [19][21][23].

**Corrective measures:** TikTok was ordered to bring processing into compliance within 6 months; if not compliant, transfers to China would be suspended [19][21].

**Appeal and litigation timeline (crucial for finality):**
- 27 May 2025: TikTok filed an appeal at the Irish High Court against the fine and suspension order [20][83].
- 14 July 2025: High Court granted TikTok leave to proceed with the legal challenge [20][83].
- 13/14 November 2025: High Court granted TikTok's application to stay (suspend) the data transfer suspension order [20][22][83].
- 30 April 2026: Supreme Court dismissed the DPC's appeal against the High Court ruling [20][83].
- 3 June 2026: Irish High Court (judgment [2026] IEHC 347) largely upheld the DPC's decision: rejected most of TikTok's 11 grounds of appeal; upheld the Article 46 and Article 13(1)(f) infringement findings and the €530 million fine [20][24][25][26][83]. Freevacy: "The DPC's €530 million in administrative fines remain valid, although the court has indicated that it will consider TikTok's appeal regarding the amount of the fines imposed" [26].
- 30 June 2026: High Court of Ireland upheld the DPC's decision to impose the fine [20][83].
- **However**: The High Court found the DPC erred in refusing to consider a third expert opinion on Chinese law and in not stating the basis for concluding that TikTok's "Project Clover" measures (a €12 billion data security initiative with advanced pseudonymisation/encryption) did not justify a different corrective approach; the corrective orders (suspension/compliance) were **vacated and remitted to the DPC for reconsideration** [25][26][27]. The fine amount remains subject to TikTok's appeal regarding quantum [26].

**Bottom line on finality:** The €530 million fine was upheld by the Irish High Court on 3 June 2026 (with quantum still open to argument), and the corrective/suspension orders were remitted. So as of August 2026, the fine amount stands but remains under appeal regarding its amount. **Flag as: upheld at first instance but not fully final (quantum under appeal).**

**Quote (verbatim), DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle:** "The GDPR requires that the high level of protection provided within the European Union continues where personal data is transferred to other countries. TikTok's personal data transfers to China infringed the GDPR because TikTok failed to verify, guarantee and demonstrate that the personal data of EEA users, remotely accessed by staff in China, was afforded a level of protection essentially equivalent to that guaranteed within the EU." [19]

### 6. Google LLC / Google Ireland Limited – €325 million (CNIL, 1 September 2025) – FLAGGED AS ePrivacy, NOT GDPR

**Final amount:** €325,000,000 total – €200 million against GOOGLE LLC and €125 million against GOOGLE IRELAND LIMITED [55][56][57].
**Date:** Deliberation NoSAN-2025-004 of 1 September 2025; Reuters reported 3 September 2025 [55][57][59][58].
**Issuing DPA:** Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL), France – restricted committee [57].

**Important classification flag:** The CNIL explicitly stated these proceedings fall under the **ePrivacy Directive** (transposed into French law as Article L.34-5 of the French Postal and Electronic Communications Code and Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act), NOT the GDPR, and therefore the GDPR "one-stop shop" mechanism did not apply [56][57]. Several trackers nonetheless rank it among GDPR fines (e.g., UniConsent lists it at #7 of largest fines) [40]. **This fine must be EXCLUDED from a strict list of final GDPR fines, but is reported here because the user asked about CNIL fines above €50M and it is frequently miscategorized.**

**The two violations:**
1. Displaying advertisements in the form of emails inserted between private emails in Gmail users' "Promotions" and "Social" tabs without prior consent, violating Article L.34-5 CPCE (direct electronic marketing). The CNIL, citing CJEU judgment of 25 November 2021 (Case C-102/20), held these ads required consent [55][56][57].
2. Collecting invalid consent for advertising cookies/trackers during Google account creation until October 2023 – consent was not freely given (harder to refuse than accept – "dark patterns") and not informed (users were not told service access was conditional on tracker placement), violating Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act [55][56][57].

**Scale:** The cookie breach affected more than 74 million accounts; 53 million individuals in France illegally saw the ads in their Gmail tabs [55][56][57]. Aggravating factors: Google's central position in the online advertising market, Gmail's global scale, and Google having been sanctioned twice before by the CNIL (€100 million in 2020 and €150 million in 2021 for cookie-related breaches) [56][57].

**Compliance order:** Google must cease displaying ads between emails without prior consent and obtain valid consent for advertising trackers within six months, with a penalty of €100,000 per day of delay per company [55][56][57].

**Appeal status:** A Google spokesperson said the company was reviewing the decision and noted users have always been able to control ads; Google pointed to updates made over the prior two years [59]. **Under review; no court ruling found.**

## C. Verified Out-of-Window Fines and Status of the Meta €1.2 Billion Fine (2023)

**Meta Platforms Ireland Limited – €1.2 billion (Irish DPC/EDPB, 22 May 2023):**
- The largest GDPR fine ever imposed. Imposed 22 May 2023 following the EDPB's Binding Decision 1/2023 (13 April 2023), which overruled the Irish DPC's initial draft decision not to fine Meta [28][30][33][41]. One source (GDPRLocal) states "imposed on May 12, 2023" [28]; the DPC announcement and majority of sources date it 22 May 2023 [30][33][34].
- Conduct: unlawful transfers of EU users' personal data to the US after the Schrems II ruling (16 July 2020), using SCCs that the EDPB found did not adequately address US surveillance laws (FISA Section 702); the EDPB described the infringement as "systematic, repetitive and continuous" involving "massive" volumes of data, with Meta acting with "at least the highest degree of negligence" [28][30][33].
- Alongside the fine, Meta was ordered to suspend EU-US transfers within five months and to cease unlawful processing/storage in the US within six months [30][33][34].
- **Appeal status as of August 2026:** Under appeal (case T-325/23 before the EU General Court) with payment suspended [28][38][39][40]. GDPR Local (2025): "Meta called the fine 'flawed, unjustified and unnecessary' and is appealing (case T-325/23)"; Measured Collective (Jan 2026): "Under appeal with payment suspended"; Meta's total penalties documented by Tech Fines lists the €1.2B as "under appeal" [38]. **This fine is outside the 2024–2026 window; it remains the largest GDPR fine ever, but is not a "final" in-effect fine as of August 2026 (under appeal, payment suspended).**
- The maximum possible fine was over €4 billion (4% of global turnover) [30].
- NOYB (Max Schrems) stated: "We are happy to see this decision after ten years of litigation. The fine could have been much higher, given that the maximum fine is more than 4 billion and Meta has knowingly broken the law to make a profit for ten years." [30]

**Amazon Europe Core – €746 million (Luxembourg CNPD, 2021):**
- Per PrivacyTerms.io and UniConsent (as of July 2026): the €746 million Amazon fine was **annulled by Luxembourg's Administrative Court on 12 March 2026 on procedural grounds** (the CNPD did not properly assess intentionality/negligence or weigh a more lenient measure); the case was remanded to the CNPD for reassessment; the underlying violation was not overturned [40][41]. An earlier appeal had been dismissed in March 2025 [39][41]. **Excluded from the final list – annulled.**

**WhatsApp CJEU ruling (context):** The EU Court of Justice ruled (decision reported in 2026) that WhatsApp can directly challenge a binding EDPB decision before the EU courts; the top court sent the case back to the General Court on substance. This "unlocks six pending appeals by Meta in similar cases against the board" [82]. The Irish Court of Appeal judgment of 13 March 2025 (DPC v Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd) refused to stay Meta proceedings pending the WhatsApp CJEU case, emphasizing challenges to DPC decisions must be prosecuted with "economy and celerity" [36].

messages.content:
# Cleaned Research Findings: GDPR Enforcement Fines > €50M (Final Decisions, 2022–2023)

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

1. **Tavily search (batch of 3 queries):** "GDPR fines more than 50 million euros final decisions 2022 2023 Irish DPC list"; "DPC press release Meta Platforms Ireland Instagram 405 million euro fine September 2022"; "Irish DPC Meta 1.2 billion euro fine May 2023 Facebook data transfers United States"
2. **Tavily search (batch of 6 queries):** "DPC press release Meta Platforms Ireland 265 million euro fine November 2022 Facebook data breach decision"; "DPC press release Meta Platforms Ireland 210 million 180 million January 2023 behavioural advertising contractual basis"; "DPC TikTok 345 million euro fine September 2023 children's personal data decision press release"; "Meta 1.2 billion GDPR fine appeal status 2025 2026 Irish High Court"; "GDPR Enforcement Tracker Meta Instagram 405 million Ireland"; "CNIL Google 150 million Facebook 60 million January 2022 cookie fines GDPR or ePrivacy"
3. **Tavily search (batch of 6 queries):** "Meta 1.2 billion euro fine appeal Irish High Court judgment 2025 2026 status GDPR transfer"; "Meta 405 million Instagram fine appeal Irish High Court 2025 2026 status"; "TikTok 345 million euro DPC fine appeal High Court 2024 2025 status GDPR"; "Meta 265 million euro data scraping fine appeal High Court status"; "Amazon 746 million GDPR fine annulled Luxembourg administrative court March 2026 CNPD"; "GDPR enforcement tracker fines 2023 Ireland DPC list 2022 2023 largest fines"
4. **Tavily search (batch of 3 queries):** "complete list largest GDPR fines issued 2022 all authorities over 50 million"; "Meta Instagram 405 million fine appeal 2026 High Court judgment status Meta 390 million appeal CJEU"; "DLA Piper GDPR fines and penalties database enforcementtracker.com Meta Ireland 1.2 billion 2023"
5. **Think tool:** Reflection recording on final scope verification.

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### A. Executive Summary — Qualifying Fines

Based on all sources gathered, **exactly five final GDPR enforcement fines of more than €50 million were imposed by EU/EEA DPAs during calendar years 2022–2023**, all issued by the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC):

| # | Organization | Amount | Final Decision Date | DPA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Instagram) | €405,000,000 | Adopted 2 Sept 2022; announced 15 Sept 2022 | Ireland – Data Protection Commission (DPC) |
| 2 | Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook) | €265,000,000 | Adopted 25 Nov 2022; announced 28 Nov 2022 | Ireland – DPC |
| 3 | Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook & Instagram) | €390,000,000 (€210M + €180M) | Adopted 31 Dec 2022; announced 4 Jan 2023 | Ireland – DPC |
| 4 | Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook) | €1,200,000,000 | Decision dated 12 May 2023; announced 22 May 2023 | Ireland – DPC |
| 5 | TikTok Technology Limited | €345,000,000 | Adopted 1 Sept 2023; announced 15 Sept 2023 | Ireland – DPC |

Cross-verification from the CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report 2026 and the GDPR Enforcement Tracker statistics page confirms that the only entries in the all-time top 10 falling inside the 2022–2023 window are precisely these five fines ([36], [35]). No other DPA issued a GDPR fine above €50M in this window ([34], [4], [59]).

**Important correction to the user's candidate list:** the candidate described as "Meta WhatsApp-adjacent/Facebook data transfers, January 2023" is a mis-dating. The January 2023 (announced 4 January 2023) decision was the €390M behavioural-advertising fine; the EU–US data-transfer fine (€1.2 billion) was decided on 12 May 2023 and announced 22 May 2023 ([22], [15]).

**Appeal-status caveat (as of August 2026): none of the five fines has been reduced or annulled.** All five were under appeal as of the most recent information; the fines therefore still stand in the amounts above, but payment/collection is stayed or suspended in the major cases. Details per fine below.

---

### B. Fine 1: Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Instagram) — €405 million (September 2022)

**Exact amount:** €405,000,000 total, including €20 million specifically for the Article 6(1) infringement ([6]).

**Dates:** DPC final decision adopted **2 September 2022**; announced by press release **15 September 2022** ([6], [7], [8]). The inquiry was initiated 21 September 2020 following information provided by David Stier (a US data scientist) and the DPC's own examination of the Instagram user registration process ([6]). Some secondary sources date the fine as "September 5, 2022" (announcement per the GDPR Enforcement Tracker: 2022-09-05) and practice guides variously cite 2 September as decision date ([35], [9], [47]).

**Issuing DPA:** Ireland — Data Protection Commission (DPC), acting as lead supervisory authority under Article 56 GDPR ([1], [6]).

**GDPR articles infringed:** Articles **5(1)(a)** (lawfulness/fairness/transparency), **5(1)(c)** (data minimisation), **6(1)** (no lawful basis), **12(1)** (transparency of information), **24** (controller responsibility), **25(1)** (data protection by design), **25(2)** (data protection by default), and **35(1)** (DPIA) ([6], [8]). The Article 6(1) finding was added on the direction of the EDPB; the EDPB found that processing of children's data was not necessary for the performance of a contract or for Meta's legitimate interests, so Meta "infringed Article 6(1) by processing this personal data unlawfully without an appropriate legal basis" ([7]).

**Factual conduct:** The inquiry examined "the public disclosure of email addresses and/or phone numbers of children using the Instagram business account feature and a public-by-default setting for personal Instagram accounts of children" ([6]). Specifically: (1) users aged 13–17 could activate "business accounts," which by default published their phone numbers and/or email addresses; and (2) the registration process set child users' accounts to "public" by default, requiring the child to know to change the setting to "private" ([10], [47], [48]). Children's contact info was published in HTML source code of profiles; default settings allowed anyone to view content; Meta failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures and failed to carry out a DPIA despite high risk to child users ([8]).

**Procedure:** Draft decision submitted to Concerned Supervisory Authorities under Article 60 in December 2021; six regulators (Finland, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, and Norway) objected; referred to the EDPB under Article 65; EDPB adopted binding decision (BD 2/2022) on **28 July 2022**, rejecting many objections but requiring the Article 6(1) finding and fine reassessment ([6], [7], [48]). The original draft had recommended a fine of up to €405M; the final fine remained €405M ([6]).

**Remedies:** In addition to the fine, a reprimand and an order requiring Meta to bring processing into compliance through specified remedial actions within three months ([6], [8]).

**Appeal status:** Meta filed an appeal in the Irish High Court on/about **3 October 2022** ([33], [47], [18], [7]). As of the latest sources (through January–March 2026), the fine remains **under appeal** with no judgment reducing or annulling it; it is reported as "Under appeal" in 2026 trackers ([5], [34]). The EDPB's 2025 annual report notes Meta is challenging EDPB binding decisions including on children's data (Instagram) before the CJEU ([62]).

**Significance:** At issuance, the second-highest GDPR fine ever (after Amazon's €746M); the largest fine ever levied by the DPC at the time; the first EU-wide decision on children's data protection rights ([7], [47], [8]).

**Official DPC URL:** http://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/data-protection-commission-announces-decision-instagram-inquiry ([6])

**Tracker URLs:** GDPR Enforcement Tracker statistics (2022-09-05 entry): https://www.enforcementtracker.com/statistics ([35]); GDPRfine.com DPC profile: https://gdprfine.com/dpa/ireland-dpc ([1]); Tech Fines Directory entry: https://guptadeepak.com/tech-fines/violation/meta-ireland-instagram-children-2022 ([9])

---

### C. Fine 2: Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook) — €265 million (November 2022)

**Exact amount:** €265,000,000 (total administrative fines) ([19], [20]).

**Dates:** Decision adopted **25 November 2022**; announced **28 November 2022** ([19], [17], [35]). Inquiry commenced 14 April 2021 following media reports about a collated dataset of Facebook personal data made available on the internet; the inquiry examined processing between 25 May 2018 and September 2019 ([19], [17]).

**Issuing DPA:** Ireland — Data Protection Commission (DPC) ([19]).

**GDPR articles infringed:** Articles **25(1)** and **25(2)** GDPR (data protection by design and by default) only ([19], [17], [20]). These are lower-tier infringements under Article 83(4) (cap €10M or 2% of worldwide turnover); given Meta's scale the 2% ceiling sat well above €265M ([17]).

**Factual conduct:** The "Facebook data scraping" incident. Third parties abused Facebook Search, Facebook Messenger Contact Importer, and Instagram Contact Importer tools to match large lists of phone numbers against user profiles, compiling personal data on **more than 500 million users** (approx. 533 million) from more than 100 countries — including names, Facebook IDs, mobile phone numbers, real addresses, birth dates, and email addresses, published on an online hacking forum in April 2021 ([16], [20], [17], [53]). The data was assembled by exploiting features working as built because they lacked safeguards against enumeration and bulk matching; the DPC therefore centred the inquiry on Data Protection by Design and Default rather than Article 32 security ([17]). The DPC found Meta's contact-import and search features did not meet either obligation — effective measures such as default-private settings, rate limiting, and controls on bulk enumeration were not built in by design or applied by default ([17]).

**Procedure:** The inquiry involved cooperation with all other EU supervisory authorities under Article 60, all of whom agreed with the DPC's decision — no EDPB Article 65 binding decision was involved (unlike the €1.2B transfers fine) ([19], [17]).

**Remedies:** Reprimand plus an order to bring processing into compliance through specified remedial actions within a timeframe ([19], [16]).

**Appeal status:** Meta appealed; the High Court (Justice Garrett Simons, judgment published 10 May 2024) **adjourned** the appeal until the CJEU resolves Meta's separate appeal against the €225M WhatsApp fine (2021). Simons stated the €265M fine **"will not be legally effective until the EU case is resolved,"** that the issues "cannot sensibly be separated out" because "the question of liability and sanction are inextricably bound up together," and noted Meta had already complied with corrective measures to the DPC's satisfaction ([32]). The DPC and Meta agreed the fine cannot be paid until domestic proceedings conclude ([32]). As of 2026 trackers, the €265M fine remains listed as #8–10 all-time and under appeal ([34], [35], [5]).

**Official DPC URL:** https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/data-protection-commission-announces-decision-in-facebook-data-scraping-inquiry ([19])

**Tracker URLs:** GDPRfine.com case page: https://gdprfine.com/cases/meta-265-million-dpc-2022 ([17]); GDPR Enforcement Tracker statistics (2022-11-25): https://www.enforcementtracker.com/statistics ([35]); CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report: https://cms.law/en/int/publication/GDPR-Enforcement-Tracker-Report/numbers-and-figures ([36])

---

### D. Fine 3: Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook & Instagram) — €390 million (January 2023)

**Exact amount:** €390,000,000 total — **€210 million for Facebook** and **€180 million for Instagram** ([22], [23], [21]).

**Dates:** Two final decisions adopted **31 December 2022**; announced **4 January 2023** ([22], [21], [6]). Inquiries stemmed from two complaints (Austrian data subject re: Facebook; Belgian data subject re: Instagram) lodged **25 May 2018**, the day GDPR came into operation ([22]).

**Issuing DPA:** Ireland — Data Protection Commission (DPC) ([22]).

**GDPR articles infringed:** DPC's final decisions found Meta in contravention of **Article 6 GDPR** (no entitlement to rely on the "contract"/performance-of-contract legal basis for personalised/behavioural advertising); breaches of transparency obligations under Articles **12**, **13(1)(c)**, and **5(1)(a)**; the EDPB additionally directed a finding of breach of the fairness principle ([22], [21], [24], [25]). The DPC originally held that, in principle, GDPR did not preclude reliance on the contract legal basis; the EDPB overruled on this point ([22]).

**Factual conduct:** Prior to 25 May 2018, Meta Ireland changed its Terms of Service for Facebook and Instagram, shifting from a "consent" legal basis to a "contract" legal basis (Article 6(1)(b)) for most processing operations, **including behavioural advertising**. Users were required to click "I accept" to the updated terms to continue accessing the services ([22]). Complainants (notably NOYB, co-founded by Max Schrems) argued this amounted to "forced consent"/forced acceptance of personalised advertising as a condition of service ([24], [25], [23]). The EDPB (binding decision 5 December 2022) reasoned that: (1) Meta is not contractually obligated to offer personalised ads to users (the obligation exists with advertisers instead); (2) transparency requirements are indispensable to the contract basis; and (3) under Article 21(2)–(3) GDPR, users can object to direct-marketing processing at any time without reason, so such processing is not "necessary" for the contract ([21]).

**Procedure:** Draft decision published 6 October 2021 proposed fines of up to €23M (Instagram) and €36M (Facebook); ten European supervisory authorities (including the Dutch DPA) objected that personalised ads are not a core element of Meta's services, triggering the consistency mechanism; EDPB issued binding decision on **5 December 2022** ordering significantly increased fines and a fresh open-ended investigation into all Facebook/Instagram processing including special categories; the DPC adopted the decisions on 31 December 2022 ([21], [22], [24]).

**Remedies:** Directive to bring data processing into compliance within **3 months** ([22], [23]).

**Appeal status:** "Under appeal by both sides" as of 2026 ([5]). Meta announced it would appeal the substance, arguing it "fully compl[ies] with GDPR by relying on Contractual Necessity for behavioural ads" ([23], [25]). Separately, **the DPC itself** stated it would bring an action for annulment before the CJEU contesting the EDPB's jurisdiction to direct a fresh open-ended investigation, arguing the EDPB "does not appear consistent with the structure of the cooperation and consistency arrangements laid down by the GDPR" ([22], [25]). The EDPB's 2025 annual report confirms Meta is challenging EDPB binding decisions on behavioural advertising at the CJEU ([62]). No court has reduced or annulled the fine as of August 2026 ([5], [34], [62]).

**Significance:** IAPP described it as "probably the most significant enforcement decision" since the GDPR's implementation due to the changes Meta will need to make to its services ([25]).

**Official DPC URL:** http://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/data-protection-commission-announces-conclusion-two-inquiries-meta-ireland ([22])

**Tracker URLs:** GDPR Enforcement Tracker statistics (2023-01-04): https://www.enforcementtracker.com/statistics ([35]); CMS GDPR Enforcement Tracker Report: https://cms.law/en/int/publication/GDPR-Enforcement-Tracker-Report/numbers-and-figures ([36])

---

### E. Fine 4: Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Facebook) — €1.2 billion (May 2023)

**Exact amount:** €1,200,000,000 — the largest GDPR fine ever imposed, roughly 60% larger than the next-highest figure ([3], [11], [13]).

**Dates:** Decision dated **12 May 2023** (DPC Reference IN-20-8-1); announced **22 May 2023** ([15], [11], [12], [14]). Inquiry began August 2020; stayed by the Irish High Court until 20 May 2021; draft decision 6 July 2022; EDPB Article 65 binding decision (BD 1/2023) adopted **13 April 2023** ([15], [14]).

**Issuing DPA:** Ireland — Data Protection Commission (DPC) ([15]).

**GDPR articles infringed:** Article **46(1) GDPR** (transfers subject to appropriate safeguards — Chapter V), confirmed by the EDPB; the DPC found Meta could not rely on Article 49 exceptions either ([15], [11]).

**Factual conduct:** Meta Ireland continued transferring EU/EEA Facebook users' personal data to the US after the CJEU's *Schrems II* judgment (Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Limited and Maximillian Schrems, July 2020, which invalidated the EU-US Privacy Shield). Although Meta used the updated 2021 Standard Contractual Clauses plus additional supplementary measures, the DPC concluded these "did not address the risks to the fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects that were identified by the CJEU," given US surveillance powers under FISA 702/PRISM ([15], [11], [12], [13]). The case originated from Max Schrems' June 2013 complaint following the Snowden disclosures ([11], [13]). EDPB Chair Andrea Jelinek called the infringement "very serious since it concerns transfers that are systematic, repetitive and continuous... Facebook has millions of users in Europe, so the volume of personal data transferred is massive" ([14]).

**Procedure:** Draft decision submitted to 47 Concerned Supervisory Authorities under Article 60; the CSAs agreed with the findings and suspension proposal, but four objected that corrective powers should include an administrative fine (the DPC's initial draft included no fine); the matter went to the EDPB under Article 65, which on 13 April 2023 directed the DPC to impose a fine; the DPC set the amount at €1.2B per the EDPB's assessments ([15], [12], [14]).

**Remedies:** (1) Order under Article 58(2)(j) to suspend future transfers of personal data to the US within five months; (2) the €1.2B administrative fine; (3) order under Article 58(2)(d) to bring processing into compliance with Chapter V by ceasing unlawful processing, including storage in the US, within six months ([15]).

**Appeal status:** Meta appealed in the Irish High Court on **26 June 2023** under Section 150 of the Irish Data Protection Act 2018, and was granted an extension of an interim stay on the decision until 31 July 2023 (with the EU-US Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision then expected in mid-July 2023) ([52]). Meta's Nick Clegg and Jennifer Newstead called the fine "unjustified and unnecessary," citing a "fundamental conflict of law between the U.S. government's rules on access to data and European privacy rights," and said the company would appeal ([14], [13]). As of 2026, the fine remains **under appeal with payment suspended**; no reduction or annulment has been issued ([5], [34], [3], [4]). The EDPB's 2025 annual report notes Meta is challenging EDPB binding decisions on data transfers outside the EU ([62]). PrivacyTerms.io's July 2026 ranking still lists it as #1 all-time ([3]).

**Significance:** Largest GDPR fine ever (record held for over three years); decision applies only to Facebook (not WhatsApp or Instagram); the DPC explicitly noted any internet platform falling under FISA 702 PRISM could face similar violations; experts noted the ruling applies to both old and new SCCs ([11], [14]).

**Official DPC URL (decision page):** http://www.dataprotection.ie/en/dpc-guidance/decisions/inquiry-concerning-data-transfers-eueea-us-meta-platforms-ireland-limited-its-facebook-service ([15])

### F. Fine 5: TikTok Technology Limited — €345 million (September 2023)

**Exact amount:** €345,000,000 ([29]).

**Dates:** Final decision adopted **1 September 2023**; announced **15 September 2023** ([29], [35]). The inquiry examined the period **31 July 2020 to 31 December 2020** (own-volition inquiry, opened September 2021) ([29], [26], [13]).

**Issuing DPA:** Ireland — Data Protection Commission (DPC) ([29]).

**GDPR articles infringed:** Articles **5(1)(c)** (data minimisation), **5(1)(f)** (security/integrity and confidentiality), **24(1)** (controller responsibility), **25(1)** (data protection by design), **25(2)** (data protection by default), **12(1)** (transparency), **13(1)(e)** (information to data subjects about recipients/categories), and — added by EDPB binding decision of 2 August 2023 (BD 2/2023) — **5(1)(a)** (fairness, regarding "dark patterns") ([29]).

**Factual conduct:** (1) **Public-by-default settings:** child user profiles (users under 16/under 18) were configured as public by default, allowing anyone to access content posted by children, with an option to "skip" making accounts private during setup — violating data minimisation, data protection by design, and data protection by default (TikTok's web browser version can be accessed by non-registered users) ([26], [28], [30]). (2) **Family Pairing:** the feature allowed non-child users who couldn't be verified as parents or guardians to pair with child accounts and send direct messages, posing "severe possible risks to child users" and violating the security principle ([26], [28]). (3) **Transparency failures:** TikTok failed to provide sufficient transparency information to child users; ambiguous wording in privacy notices (terms like "public," "anyone," and "everyone" not clearly distinguishing between registered and non-registered users) ([26], [27]). (4) **Dark patterns:** TikTok implemented "dark patterns" that nudged users toward more privacy-intrusive options during registration and when posting videos, violating the fairness principle ([26]). (5) **Age verification:** TikTok failed to properly take into account risks posed to children under 13 who gained access to the platform — the first EDPB/pan-European examination of age-verification measures under GDPR ([28], [27]).

**Procedure:** Draft decision submitted to CSAs on 13 September 2022 under Article 60(3); objections raised by the SAs of Italy and Berlin (Berlin also acting for Baden-Württemberg); referred to EDPB under Article 65; EDPB binding decision **2 August 2023** directed the DPC to add the fairness finding and extend the remedial order ([29]).

**Remedies:** Order to bring processing of child users' data into compliance within three months; reprimand for some findings ([26], [29]).

**Appeal status:** TikTok stated it "respectfully disagree[s] with the decision, particularly the level of the fine," noting the criticised features dated back three years ([30], [26]). TikTok took legal action in the Irish High Court against both the DPC and Ireland's Attorney General, seeking to overturn the decision ([49]). As of 2026, the fine remains listed as standing (2023-09-01) and **under appeal** per 2026 trackers ([5], [34], [35]).

**Significance:** Among the largest GDPR fines ever imposed; the largest fine TikTok had received from regulators at that date; the first EU-wide decision examining age-verification measures ([27], [30]).

**Official DPC URL:** https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/press-releases/DPC-announces-345-million-euro-fine-of-TikTok ([29])
